Drawn early to deep prayer, she dedicated her life to interior surrender and spiritual renewal. Her teachings stirred both devotion and controversy, eventually leading to imprisonment. She died in 1717, but her writings still influence Christian spirituality today. Her autobiography remains a classic of spiritual literature. Guyon's emphasis on pure love and abandonment to God challenged formal religion.
fields.bio_html:
Jeanne-Marie Bouvier de la Motte Guyon was born on the 13th of April, 1648, in the town of Montargis, south of Paris, into a prosperous and devout bourgeois family. From her earliest years she was drawn toward God, yet also, by her own frank account, toward vanity and the flattering attentions of a world that prized her beauty and wit. Educated in turn by the Ursuline and Benedictine nuns, she was a girl of tender conscience and restless longing, alternately reaching for holiness and slipping back into the pride of a comfortable life. She would later look on these years without illusion, naming her own frivolity as plainly as her piety.

At fifteen, in 1664, her mother gave her in marriage to Jacques Guyon, a wealthy man twenty-two years her senior. It was not a happy union. The household was ruled by a domineering mother-in-law, and Jeanne, young and sensitive, found her home a place of daily mortification. Of the children she bore, several died young; grief became an early and familiar companion. Yet it was precisely in this narrow, sorrowful house that God began His deeper work in her, teaching her by disappointment to seek a joy the world could not give.

The Word That Opened Her Heart

For years Jeanne had labored at prayer as at a task, straining after devotion and finding only dryness. The turning point came in 1668, when a Franciscan friar, himself lately returned from a long retreat, gave her a single sentence of counsel that she would carry the rest of her life. Her efforts had failed, he told her, because she sought outside herself what she already possessed within; let her accustom herself to seek God in her own heart, and she would find Him there. From that moment, she wrote, her heart was wholly changed. The prayer she had chased fruitlessly for so long was suddenly given — not as an achievement, but as a discovery of what had been there all along, waiting to be known.

After her husband's death, Guyon gave herself to what she called the prayer of the heart — a simple, silent, continual turning of the soul toward God that she practiced not merely at set hours but through the ordinary business of her day. She taught that prayer was less a labor of the mind than an application of the heart, and that its fruit was a strong and quiet faith. It was this habit of interior recollection, cultivated in obscurity long before she ever wrote a word for the public, that became the wellspring of everything she later left the church.

The death of her husband in 1676 left Jeanne a widow of twenty-eight, wealthy and free. She might have chosen ease. Instead she turned decisively toward God, and toward a life that would cost her nearly everything. Under the direction of the Barnabite priest François La Combe, she left her settled world and traveled through Savoy and Switzerland — to Geneva, Annecy, Grenoble, Turin — teaching her method of inward prayer to convents and to ordinary lay people alike. She poured out her fortune in charity and her strength in ministry, convinced that the simplest soul, unlettered and poor, could pray as truly as any scholar.

The only way to Heaven is prayer; a prayer of the heart, which every one is capable of, and not of reasonings which are the fruits of study. Let the poor come, let the ignorant and carnal come; let the children without reason or knowledge come, and they shall become wise.

— Jeanne Guyon

A Ministry Under Suspicion

In 1685 Guyon published A Short and Easy Method of Prayer, a small book that would outlive every controversy that swirled around her. In it she urged that all believers, without exception, are called and enabled to pray — that God is not the private possession of the cloister but the near and living portion of the plowman and the child. The same year she completed a commentary on the Song of Songs. Her writings spread quickly, and with them her influence at the very heart of France. In 1688 she met François Fénelon, the future archbishop of Cambrai, and their spiritual friendship became one of the most consequential in the history of French religion. For a season she was welcomed at court, befriended by Madame de Maintenon, and honored as a woman of rare devotion.

But her teaching alarmed the guardians of orthodoxy. Her language of self-abandonment, of pure and disinterested love, of passive receptivity to God, sounded to her critics dangerously close to the condemned Quietism of Miguel de Molinos. Chief among her opponents rose Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, the formidable Bishop of Meaux, who saw in her doctrine a recipe for spiritual sloth and moral indifference. What had been admiration curdled into suspicion. The conferences at Issy in 1694 and 1695 examined her teaching, and though they did not name her, they closed the door on her public standing.

The Prisons

The years that followed were years of imprisonment. La Combe had already been shut away in 1687, never to be freed, his mind failing under the long confinement. Guyon herself, after interrogations at Meaux, was arrested in December 1695 and held at Vincennes, then Vaugirard, and at last, in 1698, in the Bastille. Forged letters were produced against her; she was denied the sacraments, subjected to abuse and squalor, and at times feared poisoning. She would not be released until March 1703 — some four years in the great fortress-prison, and near eight in confinement altogether.

What is remarkable is not that she suffered, but how she suffered. She wrote that the very stones of her prison shone in her eyes like rubies, so filled was she with the presence of God. She sang in her cell. In verses later translated into English by the poet William Cowper, she likened herself to a caged bird that sits and sings to the One who placed it there — content, if it were His will, to spend the remainder of her life behind those walls. This was the harvest of that long-cultivated prayer of the heart: a soul so anchored in God that four walls could not narrow it.

In the Bastille, stripped of the sacraments and expecting she might die in prison, Guyon prayed not for release but for the grace to accept whatever God willed. The peace she asked for was granted her so fully that she described her captivity as a place of joy — declaring that the stones of her cell looked to her like precious rubies, and singing hymns of praise where despair would have been natural. The deliverance she received was not first of body but of spirit: a freedom in prison that her jailers could neither give nor take away, and that outlasted her chains.

The theological storm reached its height around Fénelon, whose defense of pure love in his Maxims of the Saints was condemned by Pope Innocent XII in 1699. Fénelon submitted at once and in humility. Guyon's own name became, in France, almost a synonym for suspected error, and much of her work was cast onto the Index of forbidden books. She had become, in the eyes of her church, a danger — this woman whose only weapons had ever been prayer and the pen.

Death and Legacy

Released at last, Guyon lived out her final years under restriction at Blois, near her daughter. She continued to write and to correspond with a wide circle of disciples, many of them now Protestants who found in her the very interior religion their own traditions prized. She bore her constraint as she had borne her cell — quietly, and without bitterness. She died at Blois on the 9th of June, 1717, at the age of sixty-nine, having asked pardon of the church she had never meant to wound and commending her soul to the God she had sought within her heart for half a century.

A little bird I am, shut from the fields of air; and in my cage I sit and sing to Him who placed me there.

— Jeanne Guyon

Condemned in Catholic France, she was received with open arms elsewhere. The Dutch editor Pierre Poiret gathered and published her works; the German Pietist Gerhard Tersteegen carried her poetry into the Protestant heart of Europe. John Wesley abridged her autobiography, commending her devotion while warning against her excesses. Quakers drew on her for their manuals of silent prayer; the Holiness and Higher Life movements of the nineteenth century, and later writers such as A. W. Tozer and the Chinese teacher Watchman Nee, pressed her little books into the hands of new generations hungry for the depths of God.

Her story is not one to romanticize. She held convictions that her own church judged mistaken, and honest readers have long weighed her teaching with care. Yet across three centuries and every dividing wall of tradition, the substance of her witness has endured — that God is nearer than we know, that the humblest soul may seek and find Him in the heart, and that a life given wholly to prayer can sing in a prison and call its stones rubies. That witness, tried in the fire of real suffering, is why her small books outlived the great men who silenced her.

fields.name: Susanna Wesley
fields.bio: Susanna Wesley, born in 1669 in London, England, was the mother of John and Charles Wesley, founders of Methodism. A devout Anglican and mother of nineteen children (ten survived to adulthood), she provided rigorous religious education to her children, establishing daily routines of prayer and Scripture study. Despite financial hardships and her husband's absences, she maintained a strong spiritual household. Susanna's theological letters and writings influenced her sons' ministry and the development of Methodist doctrine.
fields.bio_html:
Susanna Wesley never preached a sermon, never published a book, and never founded a church. She spent her life within the walls of a country rectory in the flat Lincolnshire fenland, bearing children and burying them, teaching them their letters and their prayers, keeping a household together through poverty, fire, and estrangement. Yet from that ordinary kitchen came two of the most consequential lives in Christian history, and a whole movement learned to call her its mother. Hers is a story of grace hidden in the daily round, of a faith that met real sorrow without flinching, and of prayer so woven into the hours that it became the very architecture of a home.

A Dissenter's daughter

She was born Susanna Annesley in London on 20 January 1669, the youngest of some twenty-five children of Dr. Samuel Annesley, a leading Dissenting minister. She grew up in a home of learning and rigorous conviction, and by the age of thirteen she had, remarkably, thought her way through the controversies of her day and chosen for herself the Church of England over her father's Nonconformity. That early habit of examined, independent belief never left her. In 1688, at nineteen, she married Samuel Wesley, an ambitious and difficult clergyman, and in time settled with him at the rectory of Epworth, where she would spend the rest of her days.

Theirs was not an easy marriage, and Susanna never pretended otherwise. Money was always short; Samuel was imprisoned for debt; his temper and hers could clash. In 1701 the two fell into a bitter dispute when Susanna, out of conscience, refused to say “Amen” to her husband's prayer for King William, whom she did not regard as England's rightful king. Samuel vowed not to live with her until she relented, and for some months he left the household altogether. It was a painful, public rupture, and it reveals a woman who would not surrender her conscience even to the husband she was bound to honour. The estrangement ended, and their last child, Charles, was born after their reconciliation; but Susanna carried her convictions unbowed to the end of her life.

A house of many children, and many graves

Of the nineteen children she bore, nine died in infancy, including two sets of twins, and one was accidentally smothered by a weary nursemaid. Only eight lived to adulthood. It is impossible to read her life without reckoning with that weight of buried children, and Susanna did not hide it behind piety. She grieved, and she went on, and she poured herself into the ones who remained. She resolved to educate every child herself, and did so with a discipline that became legendary. School began on a child's fifth birthday; the alphabet was learned in a day; each morning and evening opened and closed with the reading of psalms and Scripture. She held that the first task of a Christian parent was to teach a child obedience, and she wrote of it plainly.

In order to form the minds of children, the first thing to be done is to conquer their will and bring them to an obedient temper. To inform the understanding is a work of time, and must with children proceed by slow degrees; but the subjecting the will is a thing that must be done at once, and the sooner the better.

— Susanna Wesley, letter to John Wesley, 1732

To modern ears this can sound severe, and it was strict; but her aim was never mere control. She wanted each child free from the tyranny of self-will so that reason and religion could take root. And she matched severity with astonishing tenderness of attention. In the great household she set aside a fixed evening every week to be alone with each child in turn, to talk with them about their souls one at a time. Years later, when her grown son John asked her to write down her method, she did, and the letter she sent him in 1732 became one of the most treasured documents of Christian parenting. Behind the method lay a conviction about what a child truly was.

I cannot but look upon every soul you leave under my care as a talent committed to me under trust by the great Lord.

— Susanna Wesley

A brand plucked from the burning

That sense of sacred trust was fired white-hot by the event that came to define her family's story. In February 1709 the Epworth rectory caught fire in the night. The household fled into the darkness, and only when they had gathered outside did they realise that one child, five-year-old John, was still trapped at an upper window. Neighbours formed a human ladder and pulled him out moments before the roof fell in. Susanna received her son back as one raised from the dead, and she never forgot it. John himself would speak of being “a brand plucked from the burning” for the rest of his life. In her private papers his mother wrote a resolution about the boy she had almost lost.

I do intend to be more particularly careful of the soul of this child, that Thou hast so mercifully provided for, than ever I have been, that I may do my endeavour to instil into his mind the principles of Thy true religion and virtue. Lord, give me grace to do it sincerely and prudently, and bless my attempts with good success.

— Susanna Wesley, private meditation

Under the apron

Prayer was not, for Susanna Wesley, an occasional refuge; it was the discipline that ordered everything else. Amid the noise and press of a house full of children, she set apart time every day to be alone with God, and she guarded it fiercely. When she could not leave the room, she would simply draw her long apron up over her head, and every child in the house knew that when Mother was under her apron she was with God and must not be disturbed except in the direst need. Beneath that homespun tent she read her Bible, examined her conscience, and interceded for her household by name.

By her own account Susanna Wesley set apart roughly two hours of every day for private devotion, dividing the time between prayer for her own soul and prayer for each of her children individually. Unable to find a quiet room in so crowded a house, she made one by pulling her apron over her head as a signal that she was at prayer; her children learned to honour it in silence. She counted prayer the chief weapon against temptation, and meditation “incomparably the best means to spiritualise our affections, confirm our judgement, and add strength to our pious resolutions.”

The answer to those prayers came in ways she could see. The child snatched from the flames grew up to be John Wesley, and after him Charles, and between them they carried a gospel of the new birth across Britain and the American colonies, kindling the great evangelical revival and founding the Methodist movement that today numbers in the tens of millions. Susanna's fingerprints are everywhere upon it: in its “method,” born of her ordered rectory; in its love of hymn and psalm; in its insistence that religion is a matter of the heart made new.

The rescue of five-year-old John from the burning rectory in 1709 was, to his mother, a direct providence, and she answered it not with mere relief but with dedication, resolving to be “more particularly careful of the soul of this child” whom God had “so mercifully provided for.” The prayer was answered beyond anything she could have asked: the boy she consecrated at the window became the preacher whose ministry, with his brother Charles, awakened a nation and gave rise to a worldwide movement. The mother who could not preach preached, in the end, through her sons.

A preacher in the kitchen

There is one more scene from Epworth that belongs to this story. During a long absence of her husband, Susanna began holding Sunday evening devotions in the rectory kitchen for her own children, reading a sermon and singing a psalm. Servants asked to come, then neighbours, until the little gathering swelled to two hundred souls, more than filled the parish church. When word reached Samuel and he objected that it was unseemly for a woman, she answered that she could not in conscience abandon so plain a good, and that if he truly wished it stopped he must command her expressly and answer for it before God. He did not. In an age that gave women no pulpit, Susanna Wesley had, without ever intending it, become a preacher of sorts to her village.

Sing a psalm of praise

Her last years were quieter and, at the end, marked by a peace she had long sought. She died on 23 July 1742, aged seventy-three, with several of her grown children gathered at her bedside. Before her speech failed she gave them a final charge that gathered up her whole life into a single sentence.

Children, as soon as I am released, sing a psalm of praise to God.

— Susanna Wesley, her last words

And when she was gone they did. John Wesley, who preached at her burial in Bunhill Fields to what he called one of the most solemn assemblies he had ever seen, recorded the moment in his Journal: “without any struggle, or sign, or groan, the soul was set at liberty.” She was laid to rest among the Dissenters and the saints of that famous burying ground, a fitting home for a Dissenter's daughter who had crossed into the Church and given it two of its brightest lights.

Susanna Wesley left no grand monument of her own making. She left something rarer: a household so ordered by love and prayer that God built a revival out of it. She reminds every ordinary believer, and especially every weary parent, that the kingdom of God most often comes not through platforms and crowds but through faithfulness in small rooms, through a mother under her apron lifting her children by name before the throne of grace. Her sons changed the world; but she taught them to pray, and she taught them to sing, and that was enough.

fields.title: The Baptism with the Holy Spirit: What it is and what it does
fields.body_html:
Baptism with the Holy Spirit is a distinct work of God that empowers believers for service. It clarifies that this experience is separate from salvation, clear and recognisable, and brings spiritual gifts and strength tailored to each person’s calling.

Through Scripture and real-life examples, the chapter shows how this baptism equips believers to serve effectively, bringing both power and moral uplift.

While a great deal is said these days concerning the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, it is to be feared that there are many who talk about it and pray for it, who have no clear and definite idea of what it is. But the Bible, if carefully studied, will give us a view of this wondrous blessing that is clear and remarkably definite.

I. First of all, we find that there are several designations in the Bible for this one experience. In Acts 1:5, Jesus said, ''For John baptised with water, but in a few days you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit." In Acts 2:4, when this promise was fulfilled, we read ''All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit." In Acts 1:4, the same experience is spoken of as ''the promise of the Father,'' and in Luke 24:49 as "I am going to send you what my Father has promised; but stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." By a comparison of Acts 10:44, 45, 47 with Acts 11:15, 16, we find that the expressions " Holy Spirit came on them, and “The gift of the Holy Spirit,” and “receive the Holy Spirit are all equivalent to "baptised with the Holy Spirit."

2. We find in the next place that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is an exact experience of which one may know whether he has received it or not. This is evident from our Saviour's command to the Apostles: "but stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49) If this enduement with power or Baptism with the Holy Ghost were not an experience so definite that one could know whether he had received it or not, how could they tell when those commanded days of tarrying were at an end? The same thing is clear from Paul's very definite question to the disciples at Ephesus.

Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? (Acts 19:2.) Paul expected a definite "yes" or a definite "no" for an answer. Unless the experience were definite and of such a character that one could know whether he had received it or not, how could these disciples answer Paul's question? They knew they had not "received" or been "baptised with" the Holy Ghost, and a short time afterward, they knew they had "received" or been "baptised with" the Holy Ghost.

(Acts 19: 6.) Ask many a man to-day who prays that he may be baptised with the Holy Ghost: ''Well, my brother, did you get what you asked, were you baptised with the Holy Ghost," and he would be suprised. He did not expect anything so clear that he could answer positively to a question like that, "yes" or ''no." However, we find in the Bible nothing of the uncertainty and lack of clarity that we often encounter in much of our modern prayer and speech regarding this subject. The Bible is an obvious book.

It is very clear about salvation that a man who knows his Bible can say positively "yes" or "no” to the question, "Are you saved?" It is equally clear about "the Baptism with the Holy Ghost:" so that a man who knows his Bible can say positively, “yes, “or” no, ' ' to the question, "Have you been baptised with the Holy Ghost." There may be those who are saved but do not know it, because they do not understand their Bibles; however, it is their privilege to know it. There may be those who have been baptised with the Holy Spirit, but do not know the biblical name for what has come to them; however, it is their privilege to know.

3. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is a work of the Holy Spirit, separate and distinct from His regenerating work. To be regenerated by the Holy Spirit is one thing, to be baptised with the Holy Spirit is something different, something further. This is evident from Acts 1:5. There, Jesus said: "But in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”'' They were not then as yet "baptised with the Holy Ghost." But they were already regenerated. Jesus Himself had already pronounced them so. In John 15:3, he had said to the same men, “You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you."

(James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23) and in John 13:10 "And you are clean, though not every one of you," the one unsaved man in the Apostolic company, Judas Iscariot, from the statement "You are clean." (See John 13:11.) The Apostles, excepting Judas Iscariot, were then already changed men, but they were not yet "baptised with the Holy Ghost." From this, it is evident that being born again is one thing, and that the baptism with the Holy Spirit is something different, something further. One can be born again and still not yet be baptised with the Holy Ghost.

The same thing is evident from Acts 8:12-16. Here we find a company of believers who had been baptised. Surely in this company of baptised believers, there were some saved men. But the record informs us that when Peter and John came down, they "prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Ghost: (the Holy Spirit had not yet come on any of them).”It is clear then that one may be a believer, may be a saved man, and yet not have the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. In other words, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is something distinct from and beyond His saving work. Not every saved man has the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, though, as we shall see later, every saved man may have this Baptism.

If a man has experienced the transforming work of the Holy Spirit, he is a saved man, but he is not fitted for service until, in addition to this, he has received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit.

4. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is always connected with testimony and service.

Look carefully at every passage in which the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is mentioned, and you will see it is connected with and is for testimony and service. (For example, Acts 1:5, 8; Acts 2:4; Acts 4:31, 33.) This will come out very clearly when we come to consider what the Baptism with the Holy Spirit does. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is not to cleanse from sin, but to empower for service.

There is a line of teaching, put forward by a very serious but mistaken body of people, that has brought the whole doctrine of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit into disgrace. It runs this way: First proposition: there is a further experience (or second blessing) after transforming, namely, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. This proposition is true and can be easily proven from the Bible. Second proposition: This baptism with the Holy Spirit can be immediately received. This proposition is also true and can be easily proven from the Bible. Third proposition, this baptism with the Holy Spirit is the elimination of the sinful nature. This proposition is untrue. Not a line of Scripture can be mentioned to show that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is the cleansing of the sinful nature.

The conclusion drawn from these three propositions, two true and one false, is necessarily false. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is not to cleanse from sin, but to empower for service. It is indeed the work of the Holy Spirit to cleanse from sin.

Furthermore, there is a work of the Holy Spirit where the believer is strengthened with might in the inner being: that Christ may dwell in their heart by faith, that they might be filled with all the fullness of God.

(Ephesians 3:16-19) There is a work of the Holy Spirit of such a character that the believer is "made free from the law of sin and death," (Romans 8:2) and through the Spirit does ''mortify (put to death) the deeds of the body." (Romans 8:13.) It is our privilege to walk daily and hourly in the power of the Spirit that the carnal nature is kept in the place of death. But this is not the Baptism with the Spirit, nor is it the elimination of the sinful nature. It is not something done once for all; it is something that must be momentarily maintained. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." (Galatians 5:16) While insisting that the Baptism with the Spirit is primarily for the purpose of empowering for service, it should be added that a great moral uplift accompanies the Baptism. (See Acts 2:44-46; Acts 4:31-35.) This is necessarily so, from the steps one must take to obtain this blessing.

5. We will get a still clearer and fuller view of what the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is; we will notice what this Baptism does. This is stated briefly in Acts 1:8. ''But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses," etc.

The Baptism with the Holy Spirit imparts "power," power for service. This power will not manifest itself in precisely the same way in each individual.

This is brought out very clearly in 1 Corinthians 12:4-13 "There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit distributes them, To one there is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge by means of the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues.

All these are the work of the same Spirit, and he distributes them to each one, just as he determines.

"In my early study of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, I noticed that in many instances those who were so baptised "spoke with tongues," and the question came often into my mind, if one is baptised with the Holy Spirit, will he not speak with tongues. But I saw no one speaking, and I often wondered, is there anyone today who actually is baptised with the Holy Spirit? This twelfth chapter of 1st Corinthians cleared me up on that, especially when I found Paul asking those who had been baptised with the Holy Spirit, "Do all speak in tongues?" (1 Corinthians 12:30) But I fell into another error, namely, that anyone who received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit would receive power as an evangelist, or as a preacher of the Word. This is equally contrary to the teaching of the chapter, that "there are diversities of gifts, but the one Spirit." There are three evils arising from the mistake just mentioned: first, disappointment. Many will seek the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, expecting power as an evangelist, but God has not called them to that work, and the power that comes from the Baptism with the Holy Spirit manifests itself in another way in them; many cases of bitter disappointment and almost despair have arisen from this cause.

The second evil is more serious than the first, presumption. A man whom God has not called to the work of an evangelist or minister rushes into it because he has received, or thinks he has received, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. Many a man has said, "All a man needs to succeed as a preacher is the Baptism with the Holy Spirit." This is not true: he needs a call to that specific work, and he needs the study of the Word of God that will prepare him for the work.

The third evil is still greater, indifference. Many know they are not called to the work of preaching. For example, a mother with a large family of children knows this. If then, they think that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit simply imparts power to preach, it is a matter of no personal concern to them; but when we come to see the truth that, while the Baptism with the Spirit imparts power, the way in which that power will be manifested, depends upon the work to which God has called us, and that no efficient work can be done without it, then the mother will see that she equally with the preacher needs this Baptism, for that most important and hallowed of all work, to bring up her children ''in the nurture and admonition of the Lord."

I have recently met a very happy mother. A few months ago, she heard of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, sought it, and received it. "Oh," she joyfully exclaimed as she told me the story, "Since I received it, I have been able to get into the hearts of my children, which I was never able to do before."

It is the Holy Spirit Himself who decides how the power will manifest itself in any given case; "the spirit dividing to each one severally as He will (I Cor. xii: ii R. V.). We have a right to desire eagerly the greater gifts." (1 Corinthians 12:31), but the Holy Spirit is sovereign, and He, not we, must determine in the final issue. It is not for us then to select some gift and look to the Holy Spirit to impart the self-chosen gift; it is not for us to select some field of service and then look to the Holy Spirit to impart to us power in that field which we, and not He, have chosen. It is rather for us to recognize the divinity and sovereignty of the Spirit, and put ourselves openly at His disposal; for Him to select the gift that "He will" and impart to us that gift, and to select for us the field that "He will" and impart to us the power that will qualify us for the field He has chosen.

I once knew a child of God who, hearing of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and the power that resulted from it, gave up at a great sacrifice the secular work in which he was engaged and entered upon the work of an evangelist. But the expected power in that line did not follow. The man fell into great doubt and darkness until he was led to see that the Holy Spirit divided "to each one separately, even as He will." Then, giving up selecting his own field and gifts, he put himself at the Holy Spirit's disposal for Him to choose.

In the final outcome, the Holy Spirit imparted to this man power as an evangelist and a preacher of the Word. We must then surrender ourselves absolutely to the Holy Spirit to work as He will.

But, while the power that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit brings manifests itself in different ways in different individuals, there will always be power. Just as surely as a man is baptised with the Holy Spirit, there will be new power, a power not his own, "the power of the Highest!" Religious biography is exemplary in instances of men who have worked as best they could until one day they were led to see that there was such an experience as the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and to seek it and obtain it; from that hour, there came into their service a new power that utterly transformed their character.

Finney, Brainerd, and Moody are cases in point. But cases of this character are not confined to a few exceptional men; they are becoming common.

The writer has personally met and corresponded with hundreds during the past twelve months, who could testify to the new power that God had granted them through the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. These hundreds of men and women were in all branches of Christian service. Many of them were ministers of the gospel, others mission workers, Y.

M. C. A. secretaries, Sundayschool teachers, personal workers, fathers, and mothers.

Nothing could exceed the clearness, confidence, and joyfulness of many of these testimonies. What we have in promise in the words of Christ, many have, and all may have, in glad experience: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you.”

To sum up the contents of this chapter: The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God coming upon the believer, taking possession of his faculties, imparting to him gifts not naturally his own, but which qualify him for the service to which God has called him.

Through Scripture and real-life examples, the chapter shows how this baptism equips believers to serve effectively, bringing both power and moral uplift. While a great deal is said these days concerning the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, it is to be feared that there are many who talk about it and pray for it, who have no clear and definite idea of what it is. But the Bible, if carefully studied, will give us a view of this wondrous blessing that is clear and remarkably definite. I. First of all, we find that there are several designations in the Bible for this one experience. In Acts 1:5, Jesus said, ''For John baptised with water, but in a few days you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit." In Acts 2:4, when this promise was fulfilled, we read ''All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit." In Acts 1:4, the same experience is spoken of as ''the promise of the Father,'' and in Luke 24:49 as "I am going to send you what my Father has promised; but stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." By a comparison of Acts 10:44, 45, 47 with Acts 11:15, 16, we find that the expressions " Holy Spirit came on them, and “The gift of the Holy Spirit,” and “receive the Holy Spirit are all equivalent to "baptised with the Holy Spirit." 2. We find in the next place that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is an exact experience of which one may know whether he has received it or not. This is evident from our Saviour's command to the Apostles: "but stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49) If this enduement with power or Baptism with the Holy Ghost were not an experience so definite that one could know whether he had received it or not, how could they tell when those commanded days of tarrying were at an end? The same thing is clear from Paul's very definite question to the disciples at Ephesus. Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? (Acts 19:2.) Paul expected a definite "yes" or a definite "no" for an answer. Unless the experience were definite and of such a character that one could know whether he had received it or not, how could these disciples answer Paul's question? They knew they had not "received" or been "baptised with" the Holy Ghost, and a short time afterward, they knew they had "received" or been "baptised with" the Holy Ghost. (Acts 19: 6.) Ask many a man to-day who prays that he may be baptised with the Holy Ghost: ''Well, my brother, did you get what you asked, were you baptised with the Holy Ghost," and he would be suprised. He did not expect anything so clear that he could answer positively to a question like that, "yes" or ''no." However, we find in the Bible nothing of the uncertainty and lack of clarity that we often encounter in much of our modern prayer and speech regarding this subject. The Bible is an obvious book. It is very clear about salvation that a man who knows his Bible can say positively "yes" or "no” to the question, "Are you saved?" It is equally clear about "the Baptism with the Holy Ghost:" so that a man who knows his Bible can say positively, “yes, “or” no, ' ' to the question, "Have you been baptised with the Holy Ghost." There may be those who are saved but do not know it, because they do not understand their Bibles; however, it is their privilege to know it. There may be those who have been baptised with the Holy Spirit, but do not know the biblical name for what has come to them; however, it is their privilege to know. 3. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is a work of the Holy Spirit, separate and distinct from His regenerating work. To be regenerated by the Holy Spirit is one thing, to be baptised with the Holy Spirit is something different, something further. This is evident from Acts 1:5. There, Jesus said: "But in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”'' They were not then as yet "baptised with the Holy Ghost." But they were already regenerated. Jesus Himself had already pronounced them so. In John 15:3, he had said to the same men, “You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you." (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23) and in John 13:10 "And you are clean, though not every one of you," the one unsaved man in the Apostolic company, Judas Iscariot, from the statement "You are clean." (See John 13:11.) The Apostles, excepting Judas Iscariot, were then already changed men, but they were not yet "baptised with the Holy Ghost." From this, it is evident that being born again is one thing, and that the baptism with the Holy Spirit is something different, something further. One can be born again and still not yet be baptised with the Holy Ghost. The same thing is evident from Acts 8:12-16. Here we find a company of believers who had been baptised. Surely in this company of baptised believers, there were some saved men. But the record informs us that when Peter and John came down, they "prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Ghost: (the Holy Spirit had not yet come on any of them).”It is clear then that one may be a believer, may be a saved man, and yet not have the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. In other words, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is something distinct from and beyond His saving work. Not every saved man has the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, though, as we shall see later, every saved man may have this Baptism. If a man has experienced the transforming work of the Holy Spirit, he is a saved man, but he is not fitted for service until, in addition to this, he has received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. 4. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is always connected with testimony and service. Look carefully at every passage in which the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is mentioned, and you will see it is connected with and is for testimony and service. (For example, Acts 1:5, 8; Acts 2:4; Acts 4:31, 33.) This will come out very clearly when we come to consider what the Baptism with the Holy Spirit does. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is not to cleanse from sin, but to empower for service. There is a line of teaching, put forward by a very serious but mistaken body of people, that has brought the whole doctrine of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit into disgrace. It runs this way: First proposition: there is a further experience (or second blessing) after transforming, namely, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. This proposition is true and can be easily proven from the Bible. Second proposition: This baptism with the Holy Spirit can be immediately received. This proposition is also true and can be easily proven from the Bible. Third proposition, this baptism with the Holy Spirit is the elimination of the sinful nature. This proposition is untrue. Not a line of Scripture can be mentioned to show that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is the cleansing of the sinful nature. The conclusion drawn from these three propositions, two true and one false, is necessarily false. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is not to cleanse from sin, but to empower for service. It is indeed the work of the Holy Spirit to cleanse from sin. Furthermore, there is a work of the Holy Spirit where the believer is strengthened with might in the inner being: that Christ may dwell in their heart by faith, that they might be filled with all the fullness of God. (Ephesians 3:16-19) There is a work of the Holy Spirit of such a character that the believer is "made free from the law of sin and death," (Romans 8:2) and through the Spirit does ''mortify (put to death) the deeds of the body." (Romans 8:13.) It is our privilege to walk daily and hourly in the power of the Spirit that the carnal nature is kept in the place of death. But this is not the Baptism with the Spirit, nor is it the elimination of the sinful nature. It is not something done once for all; it is something that must be momentarily maintained. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." (Galatians 5:16) While insisting that the Baptism with the Spirit is primarily for the purpose of empowering for service, it should be added that a great moral uplift accompanies the Baptism. (See Acts 2:44-46; Acts 4:31-35.) This is necessarily so, from the steps one must take to obtain this blessing. 5. We will get a still clearer and fuller view of what the Baptism with the Holy Spirit is; we will notice what this Baptism does. This is stated briefly in Acts 1:8. ''But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses," etc. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit imparts "power," power for service. This power will not manifest itself in precisely the same way in each individual. This is brought out very clearly in 1 Corinthians 12:4-13 "There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit distributes them, To one there is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge by means of the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. All these are the work of the same Spirit, and he distributes them to each one, just as he determines. "In my early study of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, I noticed that in many instances those who were so baptised "spoke with tongues," and the question came often into my mind, if one is baptised with the Holy Spirit, will he not speak with tongues. But I saw no one speaking, and I often wondered, is there anyone today who actually is baptised with the Holy Spirit? This twelfth chapter of 1st Corinthians cleared me up on that, especially when I found Paul asking those who had been baptised with the Holy Spirit, "Do all speak in tongues?" (1 Corinthians 12:30) But I fell into another error, namely, that anyone who received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit would receive power as an evangelist, or as a preacher of the Word. This is equally contrary to the teaching of the chapter, that "there are diversities of gifts, but the one Spirit." There are three evils arising from the mistake just mentioned: first, disappointment. Many will seek the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, expecting power as an evangelist, but God has not called them to that work, and the power that comes from the Baptism with the Holy Spirit manifests itself in another way in them; many cases of bitter disappointment and almost despair have arisen from this cause. The second evil is more serious than the first, presumption. A man whom God has not called to the work of an evangelist or minister rushes into it because he has received, or thinks he has received, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. Many a man has said, "All a man needs to succeed as a preacher is the Baptism with the Holy Spirit." This is not true: he needs a call to that specific work, and he needs the study of the Word of God that will prepare him for the work. The third evil is still greater, indifference. Many know they are not called to the work of preaching. For example, a mother with a large family of children knows this. If then, they think that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit simply imparts power to preach, it is a matter of no personal concern to them; but when we come to see the truth that, while the Baptism with the Spirit imparts power, the way in which that power will be manifested, depends upon the work to which God has called us, and that no efficient work can be done without it, then the mother will see that she equally with the preacher needs this Baptism, for that most important and hallowed of all work, to bring up her children ''in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." I have recently met a very happy mother. A few months ago, she heard of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, sought it, and received it. "Oh," she joyfully exclaimed as she told me the story, "Since I received it, I have been able to get into the hearts of my children, which I was never able to do before." It is the Holy Spirit Himself who decides how the power will manifest itself in any given case; "the spirit dividing to each one severally as He will (I Cor. xii: ii R. V.). We have a right to desire eagerly the greater gifts." (1 Corinthians 12:31), but the Holy Spirit is sovereign, and He, not we, must determine in the final issue. It is not for us then to select some gift and look to the Holy Spirit to impart the self-chosen gift; it is not for us to select some field of service and then look to the Holy Spirit to impart to us power in that field which we, and not He, have chosen. It is rather for us to recognize the divinity and sovereignty of the Spirit, and put ourselves openly at His disposal; for Him to select the gift that "He will" and impart to us that gift, and to select for us the field that "He will" and impart to us the power that will qualify us for the field He has chosen. I once knew a child of God who, hearing of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and the power that resulted from it, gave up at a great sacrifice the secular work in which he was engaged and entered upon the work of an evangelist. But the expected power in that line did not follow. The man fell into great doubt and darkness until he was led to see that the Holy Spirit divided "to each one separately, even as He will." Then, giving up selecting his own field and gifts, he put himself at the Holy Spirit's disposal for Him to choose. In the final outcome, the Holy Spirit imparted to this man power as an evangelist and a preacher of the Word. We must then surrender ourselves absolutely to the Holy Spirit to work as He will. But, while the power that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit brings manifests itself in different ways in different individuals, there will always be power. Just as surely as a man is baptised with the Holy Spirit, there will be new power, a power not his own, "the power of the Highest!" Religious biography is exemplary in instances of men who have worked as best they could until one day they were led to see that there was such an experience as the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and to seek it and obtain it; from that hour, there came into their service a new power that utterly transformed their character. Finney, Brainerd, and Moody are cases in point. But cases of this character are not confined to a few exceptional men; they are becoming common. The writer has personally met and corresponded with hundreds during the past twelve months, who could testify to the new power that God had granted them through the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. These hundreds of men and women were in all branches of Christian service. Many of them were ministers of the gospel, others mission workers, Y. M. C. A. secretaries, Sundayschool teachers, personal workers, fathers, and mothers. Nothing could exceed the clearness, confidence, and joyfulness of many of these testimonies. What we have in promise in the words of Christ, many have, and all may have, in glad experience: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you.” To sum up the contents of this chapter: The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God coming upon the believer, taking possession of his faculties, imparting to him gifts not naturally his own, but which qualify him for the service to which God has called him.

fields.title: Necessity and Possibility of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
The necessity and availability of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit are highlighted in this chapter, which shows, using Christ and His disciples as examples, that even the most prepared believers must receive this empowering gift before beginning God’s work. The Baptism with the Holy Spirit equips every believer to serve effectively, witness boldly, and accomplish God’s purposes, remaining available to all Christians in every generation.

Shortly before Christ was received up into heaven, having committed the preaching of the gospel to his disciples, He laid upon them this very solemn charge concerning the beginning of the great work He had committed to their hands: " I am going to send you what my Father has promised; but stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.” (Luke 24:49) There is no doubt as to what Jesus meant by the "promise of my Father" for which they were to wait before beginning the ministry which He had entrusted to them; in Acts 1:4-5, we read that Jesus ''charged them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father" which, ''For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” "The promise of the Father," through which the enduement of power was to come, was the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. (Acts 1:8). Christ then strictly instructed his disciples not to assume to undertake the work to which He had called them until they had received, as the necessary and all-essential preparation for that work, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit.

The men to whom Jesus said this seemed to have already received thorough preparation for the work in hand. They had been to school to Christ Himself for more than three years. They had heard from His lips the great truths that they were to proclaim to the world. They had been eyewitnesses to His miracles, His death, and resurrection, and were about to be eyewitnesses to His ascension. The work before them was simply to go forth to proclaim what their eyes had seen and what their ears had heard from the lips of Christ Himself. Were they not fully prepared for this work? It would seem so to us. But Christ said, "No. You are so utterly unprepared that you must not stir a step yet.

There is further preparation, so all-essential to effective service, you must abide at Jerusalem until you receive it. This further preparation is the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. When you receive that, and not until then, you will be prepared to begin the work to which I have called you." If Christ did not permit these men who had received so rare a schooling for the work to which He had so definitely and clearly called them to undertake this work without receiving, in addition to that, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, what is it for us to undertake the work to which He has called us until we have received, in addition to any amount of schooling we may have had for the work, the Baptism with the Holy Spirit? Is it not the most daring presumption?

But this is not all. In Acts 10:38, we read "how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and how he went around doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil." When we look into the gospels for an explanation of these words, we find it in Luke 3:21-22, Luke 4:1-14, 15, 18, and 21. We find that at the Baptism of Jesus at Jordan, as He prayed, the Holy Spirit came upon Him. Then, ''Full of the Holy Ghost," He has the temptation experience. Then," in the power of the Spirit, "He begins his ministry, and proclaims Himself ''anointed to preach" because "the Spirit of the Lord is upon Him." In other words, Jesus Christ never entered upon the ministry for which He came into this world until He was baptised with the Holy Spirit.

If Jesus Christ, who had been supernaturally conceived through the Holy Spirit's power, the only begotten Son of God, who was divine, very God of very God, and yet truly man, if Christ, "leaving us an example that we should follow in His steps," did not venture upon the ministry for which the Father had sent Him until thus baptised with the Holy Ghost, what is it for us to dare to do it?

If, in the light of these recorded facts, we dare to do it, it seems like an offence going beyond presumption. Doubtless, it has been done in ignorance by many, but can we plead ignorance any longer? The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is a necessary preparation for elective service for Christ along every line of service.

We may have a clear call to service, as clear as it may be, as the Apostles had, but the charge is laid upon us, as upon them, that before we begin that service, we must "stay in the city until we are clothed with power from on high." This enduement with power is through the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. There are certainly few greater mistakes that we are making today than that of setting men to teach Sunday-school classes, and do personal work, and even to preach the gospel, simply because they have been converted and received a certain amount of education, perhaps including a college and seminary course, but have not as yet been baptised with the Holy Spirit.

Any man who is in Christian work, who has not received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, ought to stop his work right where he is, and not go on with it until he has been "clothed with power from on high." But what will our work do while we are waiting?

What did the world do during those ten days while the early disciples were waiting?

They alone knew the saving truth, yet, in obedience to the Lord's command, they were silent. When the power came, they accomplished more in one day than they would have accomplished in years, if they had gone on in presumptuous disobedience to Christ's charge; so will we, after we have received the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, accomplish more in one day than we ever would in years without His power. Days spent in waiting, if it were necessary, would be well spent, but we shall see further on that there is no need for us to spend days in waiting. It may be said that the Apostles had gone out on missionary tours during Christ's lifetime before they were baptised with the Holy Spirit.

This is true, but that was before the Holy Ghost was given, and before the charge, “stay in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high”.

After that, it would have been disobedience and presumption to have gone forth without this enduement, and we are living today after the Holy Ghost has been given and after the charge to "tarry until clothed" has been given. We come now to the question of the Possibility of Baptism with the Holy Spirit. Is the Baptism with the Holy Spirit for us?

This is a question that has the most plain and direct answer in the Word of God. In Acts 2:39, we read: "The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call." What is "the promise" of this passage? Turning back to the fourth and fifth verses of the preceding chapter, we read: "but wait for the gift my Father promised”. “For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

“Again, in the thirty-third verse of the second chapter, we read: "Having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost. '' It would seem to be clear that "the promise" of the thirty-ninth verse must be the same as "the promise" of the thirty-third verse, and "the promise" of the fourth and fifth verses of the preceding chapter; i.e., the promise of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. This conclusion is made clear by the context: "Repent and be baptised, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit," etc.

The promise then of this verse is the promise of the gift or Baptism with the Holy Ghost.

(Acts 10:45 with Acts 11:15-16.) Who is this gift for? "To you," says Peter to the Jews whom he was immediately addressing. Then looking over their heads to the next generation, ''And to your children." Then looking down all the coming ages of the Church's history to Gentile as well as Jew, "And to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call unto him." The Baptism with the Holy Spirit is for every child of God in every age of the Church's history. If it is not ours in experimental possession, it is because we have not taken (the exact force of the word "receive" in verse 38 is take) what God has provided for us in our exalted Saviour.

(Acts 2:33; John 7:38-39.) A minister of the Gospel once came to me after a lecture on the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and said, "The church to which I belong teaches that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit was for the apostolic age alone." "It does not matter," was replied, "what the church to which you belong or the church to which I belong teaches. What says the Word of God?"

Acts 2:39 was read: “The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call. " I asked. "Yes, he certainly has." "Is the promise for you?" "Yes, it is." And it was. And it is for every child of God who reads these pages. What an exciting thought it is that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, the enduement with power from on high, is for ME individually. But that unspeakably joyous thought has its solemn side. If I may be baptised with the Holy Spirit, I must be.

If I am baptised with the Holy Spirit, then will souls be saved through my instrumentality who are not so saved if I am not so baptised? If then I am not willing to pay the price of this Baptism, and therefore am not so baptised, I am responsible before God for all the souls that might have been saved but were not saved through me because I was not baptised with the Holy Spirit.

I oftentimes tremble for my brethren in Christian work and myself. Not because we are teaching deadly error to men; some are guilty of even that, but I do not refer to that now. Not that we are not teaching the full truth as it is in Jesus. It must be confessed that many do not teach positive error who do not preach a full gospel, but I do not refer to that. I tremble for those who are preaching the truth, the truth as it is in Jesus, the Gospel in its simplicity, in its purity, in its fullness, but preaching it "in persuasive words of wisdom" and not "in demonstration of the spirit and of power" (1 Corinthians 2:4), preaching it in the energy of the flesh and not in the power of the Holy Spirit.

There is nothing more deadly than the gospel without the Spirit's power. “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life ."

It is awfully solemn business preaching the gospel either from the pulpit or in more quiet ways. It means death or life to those who hear, and whether it means death or life depends very largely on whether we preach it without or with the Baptism with the Holy Spirit.

We must be baptised with the Holy Spirit. It is sometimes argued that "the Baptism with the Holy Spirit" was intended solely for the purpose of imparting miracle-working power and applied only to the apostolic age. In favor of this position, it is asserted that the Baptism with the Holy Spirit was followed quite uniformly by miracles. The indefensibility of this position is seen:" (1) By the fact that Christ Himself declared that the purpose of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit was to impart power for witnessing, not especially power to work miracles. (Acts 1:5-8; Luke 24:48-49.)

(2) By the fact that Paul distinctly taught that there were diversities of gifts, and that "workings of miracles" was only one of the multiple manifestations of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. (1 Corinthians 12:4, 8-10.)

(3) By the fact, that Peter distinctly declares that "the gift of the Holy Ghost," "the promise," is for all believers in all generations (Acts 2:38-39), and it is evident from a comparison of Acts 2: 39 with Luke 24: 49; Acts 1: 4- 5; Acts 2, 33, and of Acts 2: 38 with Acts 10: 45 and Acts 11: 15-16, that each of these two expressions, "the promise," and "the gift of the Holy Ghost," refers to the Baptism with the Holy Spirit.

If we take miracles in a broad sense to mean all results worked by supernatural power, then it is true that each one baptized with the Holy Spirit does receive miracle-working power; for each one baptized receives a power not naturally his own, but supernatural power, God's own power. The result of the Baptism with the Holy Spirit that was most noticeable and essential was convincing power.

(Acts 2:4, 37, 41. Acts 4:8:13. Acts 4:31, 33. Acts 9:17, 20-22.) There appears to have been no displays of miracle-working power immediately following Paul's Baptism with the Holy Spirit, even though he became uniquely gifted in this direction at a later time. It was the power to witness for Jesus as the Son of God that he received in immediate connection with the Baptism with the Holy Spirit.
