We do not, and cannot, see the remedy and the supply for these, and naturally, we are defeated. The remedy and the supply are there all the time, but they are not to be found in the place where we are looking, for they are not in self but in Christ. We cannot be looking at ourselves and looking at Christ at the same time. Again, I repeat that it is the unavoidable nature of things that we see what we look at. If we want to see the Lord, we must look at the Lord, and not at self. It is a simple question of choice for us, whether it shall be “I” or Christ; whether we shall turn our backs on Christ and look at ourselves, or whether we shall turn our backs on self and look at Christ. I was very much helped many years ago by the following sentence in a book by Adelaide Proctor: “For every one look at self, take ten looks at Christ.” It was entirely contrary to everything I had previously thought was right, but it convinced my soul and delivered me from a habit of morbid self-examination and introspection that had made my life miserable for years. It was an unspeakable deliverance. And my experience since leads me to believe that an even better motto would be: “Take no looks at self at all, but look only and always at Christ.” The Bible law regarding the self-life is not that the self-life must be watched and made better, but that it must be “put off.” The Apostle, when urging the Ephesian Christians to live in a way worthy of the calling to which they had been called, tells them that they must “put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires.” The “old self” is, of course, the self-life, and this self-life (which we know only too well is indeed corrupt through deceitful desires) is not to be improved, but to be “put off.” It is to be crucified. Paul says our old self was crucified—that is, put to death—with Christ; and he declares to the Colossians that they could no longer lie, seeing that they had “put off the old self with its practices.” Some people's idea of crucifying the “old self” is to set it up on a pedestal and then walk around it and stick nagging pins into it to make it miserable, but keeping it alive all the time. But, if I understand language, crucifixion means death, not making someone miserable; and to crucify the old self means to kill it outright, and to put it off as a snake puts off its dead and useless skin. It is of no use then for us to examine self, and to tinker with it, in the hope of improving it, for what the Lord wants us to do with it is to get rid of it. Fénelon, in his Spiritual Letters, says that the only way to treat self is to refuse to have anything to do with it. He says we must turn our backs on this great big "I" of ours, and say to it, "I do not know you, and am not interested in you, and I refuse to pay any attention to you whatever." But self is always determined to secure attention, and would rather be thought badly of than not to be thought of at all. And self- examination, with all its miseries, often gives a sort of morbid satisfaction to the self-life in us; and even deludes self into thinking it is a very humble and pious sort of self after all. The only safe way and scriptural way is to have nothing to do with self at all, either with good self or with bad self, but simply to ignore self altogether; and to fix our eyes, and our thoughts, and our expectations, on the Lord, and on him alone. We must substitute for the personal pronouns "I," "me," and "my," the pronouns "he," "him," and "his"; and must ask ourselves, not "am I good?" but "is he good?" The Psalmist says, "My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the net" (Psalm 25:15). As long as our eyes are toward our own feet, and toward the net in which they are entangled, we only get into worse tangles. But when we keep our eyes toward the Lord, he plucks our feet out of the net. This is a point in practical experience that I have tested hundreds of times, and I know it is a fact. No matter what sort of a snarl I may have been in, whether inward or outward, I have always found that, while I kept my eyes on the snarl and tried to unravel it, it grew worse and worse; but, when I turned my eyes away from the snarl and kept them fixed on the Lord, he always, sooner or later, unravelled it and delivered me. Have you ever watched a farmer ploughing a field? If you have, you will have noticed that, in order to make straight furrows, he is obliged to fix his eyes on a tree, or a post in the fence, or some object at the farther side of the field, and to guide his plough unwaveringly towards that object. If he begins to look back at the furrow behind him in order to see whether he has made a straight furrow, his plough begins to jerk from side to side, and the furrow he is making becomes a zigzag. If we would make straight paths for our feet, we must do what the Apostle says he did; we must "forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:13-14). To forget the things that are behind is an essential part of pressing forward towards the prize of our high calling; and I am convinced this prize can never be reached unless we will consent to this forgetting. When we do consent to it, we come near to putting an end to all our self- examination; for, if we may not look back over our past misdoings, we shall find but little food for self-reflective acts. We complain of spiritual hunger and torment ourselves to know why our hunger is not satisfied. The Psalmist says, "The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season" (Psalm 145:15). Having our eyes upon ourselves, and on our own hunger, will never bring a supply of spiritual meat. When a man's larder is empty and he is starving, his eyes are not occupied looking at the emptiness of his larder, but are turned toward the source from which he hopes or expects to get a supply of food. To examine self is to be like a man who should spend his time examining his empty larder, instead of going to the market for a supply to fill it. No wonder such Christians seem to be starving to death in the midst of all the fullness there is for them in Christ. They never see that fullness, for they never look at it; and again I repeat that the thing we look at is the thing we see. I feel as if I could not repeat this evident truism too often, for somehow people seem to lay aside their common sense when they come to the subject of religion, and seem to expect to see things upon which they have deliberately kept their backs turned. They cry out, "O Lord, reveal yourself;" but, instead of looking at him, they look at themselves and keep their gaze steadily fixed on their own inward feelings, and then wonder at the "mysterious dealings" of God in hiding his face from their fervent prayers. But how can they see what they do not look at? It is never God who hides his face from us, but it is always we who hide our faces from him, by "turning their back to me and not their face" (Jeremiah 32:33). The prophet reproaches the children of Israel with this, and adds that they "set up their abominations in the house that is called by my name" (Jeremiah 32:34). When Christians spend their time examining into their own condition, raking up all their sins, and bemoaning their shortcomings, what is this but to set up the "abomination" of their own sinful self upon the chief pedestal in their hearts, and to make it the centre of their whole religious life, and of all their care and efforts. They gaze at this great, big, miserable self until it fills their whole horizon, and they "turn their back" on the Lord, until he is lost sight of altogether. I will venture to say that there are many Christians who, for one look at the Lord, will give a thousand looks at self, and who, for one hour spent in rejoicing in him, will spend hundreds of hours bemoaning themselves. We are never anywhere commanded to behold our emotions, nor our experiences, nor even our sins, but we are commanded to turn our backs upon all these, and to "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29). One look at Christ is worth more for salvation than a million looks at self; and yet, so mistaken are our ideas, we seem unable to avoid thinking that the mortification which results from self-examination must have in it some saving power, because it makes us so miserable; for we have to travel a long way on our heavenly journey before we fully learn that there is no saving power in misery, and that a cheerful, confident faith is the only successful attitude for the aspiring soul. In Isaiah we see God's people complaining that they fasted and he did not see, and afflicted their souls and he took no knowledge; and God gave them this significant answer, "Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself? Is it to bow down his head like a reed, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? Will you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?" (Isaiah 58:5). Whoever else is pleased with the miseries of our self-examination, it is very certain that God is not. He does not want us to bow down our heads like a reed, any more than he wanted his people of old to do it; and he calls upon us, as he did upon them, to forget our own miserable selves and to go to work to lessen the miseries of others. "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover him?" (Isaiah 58:6-7). This service for others is of infinitely greater value to the Lord than the longest seasons of self- examination and self-abasement; and I am convinced that he has shown us here what is the surest way of deliverance out of the slough of misery into which our habits of self-examination have plunged us. He declares emphatically that if we will only keep the sort of "fast" he approves of, by giving up our own "fast" of afflicting our souls and bowing down our heads like a reed, and will instead "pour yourself out for the hungry and satisfy the desire of the afflicted, then shall your light rise in the darkness and your gloom be as the noonday. And the Lord will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong; and you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring of water, whose waters do not fail" (Isaiah 58:10-11). All this is exactly what we have been striving after, but our strivings have been in our own way, not in God's. The "fast" we have chosen has been to afflict our souls, and to bow down our heads like reeds, and to sit in sackcloth and ashes; and, as a consequence, instead of our bones being made strong and our souls refreshed like a watered garden, we have found only leanness, and thirst, and misery. Our own "fasts," no matter how fervently they may be carried on, nor how many groans and tears may accompany them, can never bring us anything else. Now let us try God's "fast." Let us lay aside all care for ourselves and care instead for our needy brothers and sisters. Let us stop trying to do something for our own poor miserable self-life and begin to try and do something to help the spiritual lives of others. Let us give up our hopeless efforts to find something in ourselves to delight in, and delight ourselves only in the Lord and in his service. And if we will but do this, all the days of our misery will be ended. But some may ask whether it is not necessary to examine ourselves in order to find out what is wrong and what needs mending. This would of course be necessary if we were our own workmanship, but since we are God's workmanship and not our own, he is the one to examine us, for he is the only one who can tell what is wrong. The man who makes watches is the one to examine a watch when it is out of order and to set it straight. We have too much good sense to meddle with our watches; why is it that we have not enough good sense to give up meddling with ourselves? Surely we must see that the examining of the Lord is the only kind of examination that is of any use. His examination is like that of a physician, who examines in order to cure; while our self-examination is like that of the patient, who only becomes more of a hypochondriac the more he examines the symptoms of his disease. But the question may be asked whether, when there has been actual sin, there ought not to be self-examination and self-reproach, at least for a time. This is a fallacy which deceives a great many. It seems too much to believe that we can be forgiven without first going through a season of self-reproach. But what is the Bible teaching? John tells us that "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). All that God wants is that we should turn to him at once and acknowledge our sin and believe in his forgiveness; and every minute that we delay doing this, in order to spend the time in self- examination and self-reproach, is only adding further sin to that which we have already committed. If ever we need to look away from self and to have our eyes turned to the Lord, it is just when we become conscious of having sinned against him. The greater the multitude of our enemies, the greater and more immediate our need of God. All through the Bible, we are taught this lesson of death to self and life in Christ alone. "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20) was not intended to be a unique experience for St Paul, but was simply a declaration of what ought to be the experience of every Christian. We sometimes sing, "Thou, O Christ, art all I want," but in reality, we actually want a great many other things. We want good frames of mind and feelings; we want fervour and earnestness; we want realisations and satisfying experiences; and we continually examine ourselves to try and find out why we do not have these things. We think if we could only discover our points of failure, we would be able to set them straight. But there is no healing or transforming power in gazing at our failures. The only road to Christlikeness is to behold, not our own hatefulness, but his goodness and beauty. We grow like what we look at, and if we spend our lives looking at our hateful selves, we will become more and more hateful. Do we not find as a fact that self-examination, instead of making us better, always seems to make us worse? By beholding self, we are more and more changed into the image of self. On the contrary, if we spend our time beholding the glory of the Lord—that is, letting our minds dwell upon his goodness and his love, and trying to drink in his spirit—the inevitable result will be that we shall be, perhaps slowly but surely, changed into the image of the Lord upon whom we are gazing. Fénelon says that we should never indulge in any self-reflective acts, whether of mortification at our failures or of congratulation at our successes. Instead, we should continually consign self and all self's doings to oblivion and should keep our interior eyes upon the Lord only. It is very hard during self-examination not to try to find excuses for our faults, and our self-reflective acts are often in danger of being turned into self-glorying ones. The only way is to ignore self altogether and to forget there is any such being in existence. No one who does not understand this can possibly appreciate the comfort and relief it is to be done with self and all self-reflective acts. I have known Christian workers whose lives have been one long torment because of these acts; and I am convinced that the "Black Mondays," of which so many clergymen complain, are nothing but the result of indulging in self-reflective acts concerning their services in the church the day before. The only way to treat all forms of self-reflective acts, of whatever kind, is simply to give them up. They always do harm and never good. They are bound to result in one of two things: either they fill us with self-praise and self-satisfaction, or they plunge us into the depths of discouragement and despair. Whichever it may be, the soul is inevitably shut out from any sight of God and his salvation. One of the most effective ways of conquering the habit is to make a rule that, whenever we are tempted to examine ourselves, we will always at once begin to examine the Lord instead. We should let thoughts of his love and his all-sufficiency sweep out all thoughts of our own unworthiness or our own helplessness. I have been trying in this book to set the Lord before our eyes in all the beauty of his character and his ways, in the hope that the sight will be so ravishing as to take our eyes off everything else. But no revelation of God will be of any use if we will not look at it, but instead persist in turning our backs on what has been revealed and gazing at our own inward experiences. For again I must repeat that we cannot see self and see the Lord at the same time, and while we are examining self, we cannot be looking at him. Fénelon says concerning self-examination: "There is something very hidden and very deceptive in the suffering it causes; for while you seem to yourself to be wholly occupied with the glory of God, in your inmost soul it is self alone that occasions all your trouble. You are indeed desirous that God should be glorified, but you wish it should take place by means of your perfection, and you thus cherish the sentiments of self-love. It is simply a refined pretext for dwelling in self... It is a sort of infidelity to simple faith when we desire to be continually assured that we are doing well. It is, in fact, a desire to know what we are doing, which we shall never know, and of which it is the will of God we should be ignorant. It is trifling by the way, in order to reason about the way. The safest and shortest course is to renounce, forget, and abandon self, and, through faithfulness to God, to think no more of it. This is the whole of religion—to get out of self and self-love, in order to get into God." What we must do, therefore, is to shut the door definitely and resolutely, once and for all, upon self and all of self's experiences, whether they are good or bad. We should say with the Psalmist, "I have set the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure" (Psalm 16:8-9).

fields.title: Things That Cannot Be Shaken
fields.body_html:
"This phrase, 'Yet once more,' indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain" (Hebrews 12:27).

After all we have been considering regarding the unfathomable love and care of God, it might seem to those who do not understand the deepest ways of love that no trials or hardness could ever come into the lives of his children. But if we look deeply into the matter, we shall see that often love itself must bring the hardness. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons" (Hebrews 12:6-8).

If love sees those it loves going wrong, it must, because of its very love, do what it can to save them; and the love that fails to do this is only selfishness. Therefore, just because of his unfathomable love, the God of love—when he sees his children resting their souls on things that can be shaken—must necessarily remove those things from their lives in order that they may be driven to rest only on the things that cannot be shaken. This process of removing is sometimes very hard.

We will all acknowledge, I think, that if our souls are to rest in peace and comfort, it can only be on unshakable foundations. It is no more possible for the soul to be comfortable when it is trying to rest on "things that can be shaken" than it is for the body. No one can rest comfortably in a shaking bed or sit in comfort on a rickety chair.

Foundations, to be reliable, must always be unshakable. "Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it" (Matthew 7:24-27).

It is very possible in the Christian life to build one's spiritual house on such insecure foundations that, when storms beat upon it, the ruin of that house is great. Many a religious experience that has seemed fair enough when all was going well in life has tottered and fallen when trials have come, because its foundations were insecure. It is therefore of vital importance to each one of us to see to it that our religious life is built upon "things that cannot be shaken."

Of course, the immediate thought that will come to every mind is that it must be built upon the Rock, Christ Jesus. This is true; but the great point is what is meant by that expression. It is one of those religious phrases that is often used conventionally, with no definite or real meaning attached to it. Conventionally, we believe that Christ is the only Rock upon which to build, but practically—though perhaps unconsciously—we believe that in order to have a rock upon which it will be really safe to build, many other things must be added to Christ. We think, for instance, that the right frames of mind and feelings must be added, or the right doctrines or dogmas, or whatever else may seem to each one of us to constitute the necessary degree of security. And if we were only perfectly honest with ourselves, I suspect we would often find that our dependence was almost wholly upon these additions of our own, and that Christ himself, as our rock of dependence, was of altogether secondary importance.

What we ought to mean when we talk of building upon the Rock, Christ Jesus, is what I am trying all through this book to make plain: that the Lord is enough for our salvation—just the Lord only, without any additions of our own. It is the Lord himself, as he is in his own intrinsic character, our Creator and Redeemer, and our all-sufficient portion.

"But God's firm foundation stands" (2 Timothy 2:19), and it is the only foundation that does.

Therefore, we need to be "shaken" off every other foundation so that we may be forced to rest on the foundation of God alone. This explains the necessity for those "shakings" through which so many Christians seem called to pass. The Lord sees that they are building their spiritual houses on flimsy foundations which will not be able to withstand the "stream [that] broke against that house" (Luke 6:48) during the storms of life. Not in anger, but in tenderest love, he shakes our earth and our heaven until all that "can be shaken" is removed, and only those "things which cannot be shaken" are left behind.

The Apostle tells us that the things that are shaken are the "things that have been made" (Hebrews 12:27); that is, the things that are manufactured by our own efforts—feelings that we stir up, doctrines that we elaborate, and good works that we perform. It is not that these are bad things in themselves. It is only when the soul begins to rest on them instead of upon the Lord that he is compelled to "shake" us off them. And this shaking applies, we are told, "not only the earth but also the heavens" (Hebrews 12:26). This means, I am sure, that it is possible to have "things that are made" even in religious matters. How much of the so-called religiousness of many Christians consists of these "things that are made," I cannot say; but I sometimes think the great overturnings and tossings in matters of faith, which so distress Christians in these times, may be only the necessary shaking of the "things that are made," in order that only that which "cannot be shaken" may remain.

There are times, perhaps, in our religious lives, when our experience seems as settled and immovable as the roots of the everlasting mountains. But then comes an upheaval; all our foundations are shaken and thrown down, and we are ready to despair and to question whether we can be Christians at all. Sometimes it is an upheaval in our outward circumstances, and sometimes it is in our inward experience. If people have rested on their good works and their faithful service, the Lord is often obliged to take away all power for work or all opportunity, so that the soul may be driven from its false resting place and forced to rest in the Lord alone.

Sometimes the dependence is upon good feelings or pious emotions, and the soul has to be deprived of these before it can learn to depend only upon God. Sometimes dependence is placed upon "sound doctrine," and a person feels they occupy an invulnerable position because their "views" are so correct and their doctrines are so "orthodox." Then the Lord is obliged to "shake" those doctrines and to plunge that person, perhaps, into confusion and darkness regarding their "views." It was at just such a moment as this that my own soul caught its first real sight of God; what had seemed like certain spiritual ruin and defeat was turned into the most triumphant victory.

Or it may be that the upheaval comes in our outward circumstances. Everything has seemed so firmly established in prosperity that no dream of disaster disturbs us. Our reputation is assured, our work has prospered, our efforts have all been successful beyond our hopes, and our soul is at ease; the need for God is in danger of becoming far off and vague. Then the Lord is obliged to put an end to it all. Our prosperity crumbles around us like a house built on the sand, and we are tempted to think he is angry with us. But in truth, it is not anger, but tenderest love. His very love compels him to take away the outward prosperity that is keeping our souls from entering the interior spiritual kingdom for which we long.

"Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

Then, and often not until then, will our souls learn to rejoice in the Lord only.

Paul declared that he "count[ed] everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). When we learn to say the same, the peace and joy that the gospel promises become our permanent possession.

"What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless?" asks the Lord of the children of Israel (Jeremiah 2:5).

"For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13).

Like the Israelites, we too forsake the fountain of living waters and try to dig out cisterns of our own devising. We seek to quench our thirst with our own experiences or activities, and then wonder why we still thirst. It is to save us from perishing for want of water that the Lord finds it necessary to destroy our broken cisterns; only then can we be forced to drink from the fountain of living waters.

We are told that if we "trust in emptiness," then "emptiness will be [our] payment" (Job 15:31), and many times we have found this to be true. Have you ever crossed a dangerous swamp full of quicksands, where every step was a risk? Firm-looking hillocks continually deceived you into a false dependence, causing you to sink into the mire and water hidden beneath them. If you have, you will understand what it means to "trust in vanity," and you will appreciate the blessing of any situation that reveals the rottenness of your false dependencies and drives you to trust in what is safe and permanent. When our feet are walking on "miry bog," we should welcome the Divine Guide who brings us out of the mud and "set[s] my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure" (Psalm 40:2), even though the paths he calls us to walk may seem narrow and hard.

The prophet Jeremiah, when lamenting the sins of his people, says, "we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15). He adds that the Lord declared, "hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter" (Isaiah 28:17). It might look as though it were God's wrath doing this, and many frightened Christians think it is; but his wrath is only against the refuges of lies, not against us. Love could do no less than destroy these refuges so that we may be delivered.

A dear old friend of mine, who was very interested in my spiritual welfare, once gave me a little book called The Seventeen False Rests of the Soul. He evidently felt I was in danger of settling down upon one of these false rests. The book explained, in quaint old language, that the soul is continually tempted to sit down upon something false as if it were a final resting place. God is then continually obliged to "unbottom" all such false resting places, much like someone might remove the seat of a chair and let the sitter fall through. All seventeen false rests were described, showing how the soul—being "unbottomed" from each one in turn—settled down at last upon the only true rest in God.

This "unbottoming" is just another word for the "shakings" and "emptyings" I have been writing about. It is always a painful process and often a discouraging one. Everything seems unstable, and rest seems utterly unattainable. No sooner do we find an experience or a doctrine in which we think we may surely rest, than a great "shaking" comes and we are forced out again. This process must continue until all that can be shaken is removed, and only "those things which cannot be shaken" remain. Often the answer to our most fervent prayers for deliverance comes in such a form that it seems as if "the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked" (Psalm 18:7). We do not always see at first that it is through this very shaking that the deliverance we prayed for is accomplished, bringing us into the "broad place" (Psalm 18:19) for which we long.

The old mystics used to teach what they called "detachment," meaning the cutting loose of the soul from all that could hold it back from God. This need for detachment is the secret of many of our "shakings." We cannot follow the Lord fully as long as we are tied fast to anything else, any more than a boat can sail into the boundless ocean while it is tied to the shore.

If we would reach the "city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God" (Hebrews 11:10), we must go out like Abraham from all other cities and be detached from every earthly tie.

Everything in Abraham’s life that could be shaken was shaken. He was, as it were, emptied from vessel to vessel—here today and gone tomorrow. All his resting places were disturbed, with no settlement or comfort anywhere. We, like Abraham, are looking for a city with foundations, and therefore we too will need to be emptied from vessel to vessel. We do not realise this, and when the shakings come, we are in despair, thinking we shall never reach that city at all. But it is these very shakings that make it possible for us to reach it.

The Psalmist had learned this, and after all the shakings of his eventful life, he cried, "For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God" (Psalm 62:5-7). At last, God was everything to him; and then he found that God was enough.

It is the same with us. When everything in our lives and experience is shaken that can be shaken, and only that which cannot be shaken remains, we are brought to see that God only is our rock and our foundation. We learn to have our expectation from him alone. "Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling... God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns" (Psalm 46:2-3, 5).

"Shall not be moved"—what an inspiring declaration! Can it be possible that we, who are so easily moved by the things of earth, can arrive at a place where nothing can upset our temper or disturb our calm? Yes, it is possible; and the Apostle Paul knew it. When he was on his way to Jerusalem, where he foresaw that "imprisonment and afflictions" awaited him, he could say triumphantly, "But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself" (Acts 20:23- 24). In the older language, he said, "None of these things move me." Everything in Paul’s life that could be shaken had been shaken. If we let God have his way with us, we may come to the same place. Neither the small irritations of life nor its great trials will have the power to move us from the "peace of God, which surpasses all understanding" (Philippians 4:7), which is the portion of those who have learned to rest only on God.

In the Revelation made to John on the island of Patmos, the Spirit tells the churches what awaits those who overcome: "The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.

Never shall he go out of it" (Revelation 3:12). To be as immovable as a pillar in the house of our God is an end for which one would gladly endure all the "shakings" and "unbottomings" necessary to get there!

"Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:28-29). A great many people are afraid of the consuming fire of God, but that is only because they do not understand what it is. It is the fire of God’s love that must, by its very nature, consume everything that can harm his people. If our hearts are set on being what the love of God wants us to be, his fire is something we shall warmly welcome rather than fear.

"Implacable is love.

Foes may be bought or teased From their malign intent; But he goes unappeased, Who is on kindness bent."

Let us thank God then that he is "on kindness bent" towards us, and that the consuming fire of his love will not cease to burn until it has refined us as silver is refined. For the promise is that "he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the Lord" (Malachi 3:3). He gives us this inspiring assurance: if we will but submit to this purifying process, we shall become "pleasing to the Lord" (Malachi 3:4). "Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a land of delight, says the Lord of hosts" (Malachi 3:12).

To be "pleasing" and a "delight" to the Lord may seem impossible to us when we look at our shortcomings and our unworthiness. But when we think of this lovely, consuming fire of God’s love, we can take heart and be courageous. He will not fail or be discouraged until all our dross and inferior silver is burned away, and we ourselves come forth in his likeness, conformed to his image.

Our souls long for the "kingdom that cannot be shaken" (Hebrews 12:28). He who is "on kindness bent" will, if we let him, shake everything in our lives that can be shaken. He will "unbottom" us from every false rest until only that which cannot be shaken remains.

One of the most impressive sermons I ever heard was preached by a sweet-faced old Quaker lady. She rose in the stillness and said, "Yesterday, sister Tabitha broke my best china teapot into pieces. But the Lord, whom I trust, kept my soul in perfect peace and enabled me not to utter a single word of reproach." That was all; the sermon was ended. But into every heart there entered a sense of what it would mean to be kept in the immovable kingdom of the love of God. This kingdom can be our home if we will only submit to the shakings of God and learn to rest only and always on him.

May he hasten that day for each one of us!
fields.body_text: "This phrase, 'Yet once more,' indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain" (Hebrews 12:27). After all we have been considering regarding the unfathomable love and care of God, it might seem to those who do not understand the deepest ways of love that no trials or hardness could ever come into the lives of his children. But if we look deeply into the matter, we shall see that often love itself must bring the hardness. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons" (Hebrews 12:6-8). If love sees those it loves going wrong, it must, because of its very love, do what it can to save them; and the love that fails to do this is only selfishness. Therefore, just because of his unfathomable love, the God of love—when he sees his children resting their souls on things that can be shaken—must necessarily remove those things from their lives in order that they may be driven to rest only on the things that cannot be shaken. This process of removing is sometimes very hard. We will all acknowledge, I think, that if our souls are to rest in peace and comfort, it can only be on unshakable foundations. It is no more possible for the soul to be comfortable when it is trying to rest on "things that can be shaken" than it is for the body. No one can rest comfortably in a shaking bed or sit in comfort on a rickety chair. Foundations, to be reliable, must always be unshakable. "Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it" (Matthew 7:24-27). It is very possible in the Christian life to build one's spiritual house on such insecure foundations that, when storms beat upon it, the ruin of that house is great. Many a religious experience that has seemed fair enough when all was going well in life has tottered and fallen when trials have come, because its foundations were insecure. It is therefore of vital importance to each one of us to see to it that our religious life is built upon "things that cannot be shaken." Of course, the immediate thought that will come to every mind is that it must be built upon the Rock, Christ Jesus. This is true; but the great point is what is meant by that expression. It is one of those religious phrases that is often used conventionally, with no definite or real meaning attached to it. Conventionally, we believe that Christ is the only Rock upon which to build, but practically—though perhaps unconsciously—we believe that in order to have a rock upon which it will be really safe to build, many other things must be added to Christ. We think, for instance, that the right frames of mind and feelings must be added, or the right doctrines or dogmas, or whatever else may seem to each one of us to constitute the necessary degree of security. And if we were only perfectly honest with ourselves, I suspect we would often find that our dependence was almost wholly upon these additions of our own, and that Christ himself, as our rock of dependence, was of altogether secondary importance. What we ought to mean when we talk of building upon the Rock, Christ Jesus, is what I am trying all through this book to make plain: that the Lord is enough for our salvation—just the Lord only, without any additions of our own. It is the Lord himself, as he is in his own intrinsic character, our Creator and Redeemer, and our all-sufficient portion. "But God's firm foundation stands" (2 Timothy 2:19), and it is the only foundation that does. Therefore, we need to be "shaken" off every other foundation so that we may be forced to rest on the foundation of God alone. This explains the necessity for those "shakings" through which so many Christians seem called to pass. The Lord sees that they are building their spiritual houses on flimsy foundations which will not be able to withstand the "stream [that] broke against that house" (Luke 6:48) during the storms of life. Not in anger, but in tenderest love, he shakes our earth and our heaven until all that "can be shaken" is removed, and only those "things which cannot be shaken" are left behind. The Apostle tells us that the things that are shaken are the "things that have been made" (Hebrews 12:27); that is, the things that are manufactured by our own efforts—feelings that we stir up, doctrines that we elaborate, and good works that we perform. It is not that these are bad things in themselves. It is only when the soul begins to rest on them instead of upon the Lord that he is compelled to "shake" us off them. And this shaking applies, we are told, "not only the earth but also the heavens" (Hebrews 12:26). This means, I am sure, that it is possible to have "things that are made" even in religious matters. How much of the so-called religiousness of many Christians consists of these "things that are made," I cannot say; but I sometimes think the great overturnings and tossings in matters of faith, which so distress Christians in these times, may be only the necessary shaking of the "things that are made," in order that only that which "cannot be shaken" may remain. There are times, perhaps, in our religious lives, when our experience seems as settled and immovable as the roots of the everlasting mountains. But then comes an upheaval; all our foundations are shaken and thrown down, and we are ready to despair and to question whether we can be Christians at all. Sometimes it is an upheaval in our outward circumstances, and sometimes it is in our inward experience. If people have rested on their good works and their faithful service, the Lord is often obliged to take away all power for work or all opportunity, so that the soul may be driven from its false resting place and forced to rest in the Lord alone. Sometimes the dependence is upon good feelings or pious emotions, and the soul has to be deprived of these before it can learn to depend only upon God. Sometimes dependence is placed upon "sound doctrine," and a person feels they occupy an invulnerable position because their "views" are so correct and their doctrines are so "orthodox." Then the Lord is obliged to "shake" those doctrines and to plunge that person, perhaps, into confusion and darkness regarding their "views." Then, and often not until then, will our souls learn to rejoice in the Lord only. When we learn to say the same, the peace and joy that the gospel promises become our permanent possession. "What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless?" asks the Lord of the children of Israel (Jeremiah 2:5). "For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Like the Israelites, we too forsake the fountain of living waters and try to dig out cisterns of our own devising. We seek to quench our thirst with our own experiences or activities, and then wonder why we still thirst. It is to save us from perishing for want of water that the Lord finds it necessary to destroy our broken cisterns; only then can we be forced to drink from the fountain of living waters. We are told that if we "trust in emptiness," then "emptiness will be [our] payment" (Job 15:31), and many times we have found this to be true. Have you ever crossed a dangerous swamp full of quicksands, where every step was a risk? Firm-looking hillocks continually deceived you into a false dependence, causing you to sink into the mire and water hidden beneath them. If you have, you will understand what it means to "trust in vanity," and you will appreciate the blessing of any situation that reveals the rottenness of your false dependencies and drives you to trust in what is safe and permanent. When our feet are walking on "miry bog," we should welcome the Divine Guide who brings us out of the mud and "set[s] my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure" (Psalm 40:2), even though the paths he calls us to walk may seem narrow and hard. The prophet Jeremiah, when lamenting the sins of his people, says, "we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15). He adds that the Lord declared, "hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter" (Isaiah 28:17). It might look as though it were God's wrath doing this, and many frightened Christians think it is; but his wrath is only against the refuges of lies, not against us. Love could do no less than destroy these refuges so that we may be delivered. A dear old friend of mine, who was very interested in my spiritual welfare, once gave me a little book called The Seventeen False Rests of the Soul. He evidently felt I was in danger of settling down upon one of these false rests. The book explained, in quaint old language, that the soul is continually tempted to sit down upon something false as if it were a final resting place. God is then continually obliged to "unbottom" all such false resting places, much like someone might remove the seat of a chair and let the sitter fall through. All seventeen false rests were described, showing how the soul—being "unbottomed" from each one in turn—settled down at last upon the only true rest in God. This "unbottoming" is just another word for the "shakings" and "emptyings" I have been writing about. It is always a painful process and often a discouraging one. Everything seems unstable, and rest seems utterly unattainable. No sooner do we find an experience or a doctrine in which we think we may surely rest, than a great "shaking" comes and we are forced out again. This process must continue until all that can be shaken is removed, and only "those things which cannot be shaken" remain. Often the answer to our most fervent prayers for deliverance comes in such a form that it seems as if "the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked" (Psalm 18:7). We do not always see at first that it is through this very shaking that the deliverance we prayed for is accomplished, bringing us into the "broad place" (Psalm 18:19) for which we long. The old mystics used to teach what they called "detachment," meaning the cutting loose of the soul from all that could hold it back from God. This need for detachment is the secret of many of our "shakings." We cannot follow the Lord fully as long as we are tied fast to anything else, any more than a boat can sail into the boundless ocean while it is tied to the shore. If we would reach the "city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God" (Hebrews 11:10), we must go out like Abraham from all other cities and be detached from every earthly tie. Everything in Abraham’s life that could be shaken was shaken. He was, as it were, emptied from vessel to vessel—here today and gone tomorrow. All his resting places were disturbed, with no settlement or comfort anywhere. We, like Abraham, are looking for a city with foundations, and therefore we too will need to be emptied from vessel to vessel. We do not realise this, and when the shakings come, we are in despair, thinking we shall never reach that city at all. But it is these very shakings that make it possible for us to reach it. The Psalmist had learned this, and after all the shakings of his eventful life, he cried, "For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God" (Psalm 62:5-7). At last, God was everything to him; and then he found that God was enough. It is the same with us. When everything in our lives and experience is shaken that can be shaken, and only that which cannot be shaken remains, we are brought to see that God only is our rock and our foundation. We learn to have our expectation from him alone. "Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling... God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns" (Psalm 46:2-3, 5). "Shall not be moved"—what an inspiring declaration! Can it be possible that we, who are so easily moved by the things of earth, can arrive at a place where nothing can upset our temper or disturb our calm? Yes, it is possible; and the Apostle Paul knew it. When he was on his way to Jerusalem, where he foresaw that "imprisonment and afflictions" awaited him, he could say triumphantly, "But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself" (Acts 20:23- 24). In the older language, he said, "None of these things move me." Everything in Paul’s life that could be shaken had been shaken. If we let God have his way with us, we may come to the same place. Never shall he go out of it" (Revelation 3:12). fields.title: A Word to the Wavering Ones
fields.body_html:
"But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord" (James 1:6-7).

It would be difficult to find anything that produces more discomfort in the religious life than a wavering faith. The image given to us by the Apostle James describes it exactly: "a wave of the sea... driven and tossed". Just as it is impossible for a traveller to reach a destination by moving forward one day and retracing their steps the next, it is equally impossible for the wavering soul to reach a place of settled peace while it continues to waver.

In our last chapter, we considered the shakings of God. It might be thought that our wavering is similar to his shaking, but they are very different. God’s shakings are caused by his love for our blessing; they always lead to rest and peace. Our waverings are caused by our lack of faith; they always lead to discomfort and turmoil.

A wavering Christian is someone who trusts in the love of God one day and doubts it the next, and is alternately happy or miserable as a result. They climb to the hilltop of joy at one time, only to descend into the valley of despair the next. They are driven back and forth by every "wind of doctrine," always striving but never attaining. They are a victim of every changing influence—whether it is their physical health, the people around them, or even the weather.

You would suppose that even the most inexperienced child of God would know that this sort of experience is wrong. Wavering in one's faith in such a way is deeply dishonouring to the Lord, as it questions his truth and faithfulness. Yet, many Christians are so blinded that they actually think this tendency to waver is a sign of humility. They treat every new attack of doubt as if it were a pious virtue.

A wavering Christian might say complacently, "Oh, but I know I am so unworthy that I'm sure it's right for me to doubt." They often imply that if their listener were truly humble, they would doubt as well. I once knew a devoted Christian whose religious life was a constant torment of doubt. After I urged him to have more faith, he said in all seriousness, "My dear friend, if I were ever so arrogant as to feel sure that God loved me, I would be certain I was on the direct road to hell."

He clearly thought that such assurance could only come from feeling he was "good enough" to deserve God’s love. He was right that thinking we are worthy of God’s love is arrogant.

However, the ground for our assurance does not come from our own goodness, but from the goodness of God. While we should never be satisfied with our own goodness, there can be no question—for anyone who believes the Bible—regarding the total sufficiency of his.

To see how absurd this position of doubt is, consider how it would work in human relationships.

Imagine a marriage, or the relationship between a child and a parent—both of which the Lord uses as symbols for our relationship with him. If a wife or husband had a "wavering experience" of confidence in their spouse—trusting one day and doubting the next—would that be seen as a sign of humility or a virtue to be cherished? Similarly, if children wavered in their confidence toward their parents the way Christians do with their heavenly Father, what word would be harsh enough for such unfilial conduct? In human relationships, such wavering might be excused if one person were actually untrustworthy. But with God, there is no such excuse. The wavering faith of his children may even lead outsiders to conclude that he isn't worthy of much confidence.

We would shrink in horror from causing people to think poorly of God’s character. But if we are honest, we must acknowledge that a wavering faith conveys exactly that impression. It is, in essence, disloyalty to a trustworthy God and should be viewed as a serious sin.

The truth is that our wavering comes from a subtle, often unconscious form of pride rather than humility. True humility accepts the love and gifts bestowed upon it with a meek and happy thankfulness. Pride, on the other hand, shrinks from accepting kindness and is afraid to believe in the selfless goodness of the giver. If we were truly humble, we would accept God’s love with thankful meekness. While acknowledging our own unworthiness, we would see it only as something that highlights his grace and goodness in choosing us.

A wavering faith is not only disloyal to God, but it is a source of great misery for us. It cannot advance our spiritual interests; it can only hinder them. The Apostle tells us that "we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end" (Hebrews 3:14). To be steadfast is the exact opposite of wavering. Expecting the results of steadfastness while wavering is as foolish as trying to reach a mountain peak by alternating short climbs with long, disastrous slides back down.

Yet many people expect exactly that. They make a "beginning of confidence" and, while the freshness lasts, they are full of joy. Then trials and temptations come, and doubts begin to intrude. Instead of treating these doubts as enemies to be resisted, they welcome them as friends.

Before long, they begin to waver in their faith and allegiance, and their peace is gone. When life is bright, their faith revives; when things go wrong, doubts win and they waver again.

I once spoke with an eminent clergyman about the possibility of a religious life of abiding peace.

He frankly told me he didn't think it was possible and that most Christian experiences were like his own. "When I want to write my sermons," he said, "I get to the mountain-top through prayer and effort. I put my foot on one promise and then another until I reach the summit and can begin.

It goes well for a while, but then an interruption comes—a problem with my children or a quarrel with a neighbour—and I tumble down. I can only get back by another wearisome climb. I might stay on the summit for a few days, or once in a great while, a few weeks. But as for 'abiding' there continually, I cannot believe it."

This describes the experience of many of God’s children who hunger for the peace Christ promised but only find it for moments at a time. They get a glimmer of faith, but then the old doubts return. "Look at your heart," they say; "see how cold and indifferent it is. How can you believe God loves a poor, unworthy creature like you?" It sounds so reasonable that they are plunged back into darkness.

The whole trouble comes from a lack of faith. In the spiritual life, it is always according to our faith. This is a spiritual law that cannot be ignored or avoided. It is inherent in the nature of things and is therefore unalterable. Equally, if it is to be according to our faith, it will also be to us according to our doubts.

The cause of our wavering is not our sins, but our doubts. Doubts create an impassable gap between our souls and the Lord, just as they do between us and our friends. No amount of earnestness can bridge that gap. "For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord" (James 1:7). This isn't because God is angry; it is because the nature of things makes it impossible for doubt and confidence to exist together. "And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief" (Hebrews 3:18-19). It wasn't that God wouldn't let them in as a punishment; they simply could not enter. It was an impossibility. Faith is the only door into the Kingdom of Heaven, and there is no other. If we will not go in by that door, we cannot get in at all, for there is no other way.

God's salvation is not a purchase to be made, nor wages to be earned, nor a summit to be climbed, nor a task to be accomplished; but it is simply and only a gift to be accepted, and it can only be accepted by faith. Faith is a necessary element in the acceptance of any gift, whether earthly or heavenly. My friends may put their gifts upon my table, or even place them in my lap, but unless I believe in their friendliness and honesty of purpose enough to accept these gifts, they can never truly become mine.

It is therefore plain that the Bible is simply announcing the nature of things, as it always does, when it declares, "Be it done to you according to your faith" (Matthew 9:29). The sooner we settle down to this, the better. All our wavering comes from the fact that we do not believe in this law. We acknowledge, of course, that it is in the Bible, but we think it cannot really mean what it says. We think there must be some additions made to it, such as "according to our fervency it shall be unto us," or "according to our persistence," or "according to our worthiness."

If the whole truth were told, we are inclined to think that these additions of ours are, if anything, by far the most important part of the matter. As a consequence, our attention is mostly directed to getting these matters settled. We watch our own states of mind and feelings, and search into our own worthiness or unworthiness with so much diligence that we almost entirely overlook the one fundamental principle of faith, without which nothing can be done. Moreover, as our moods and feelings are the most variable things in the universe, and our sense of worthiness changes with those feelings, our experience cannot help but waver. The possibility of a steadfast faith recedes further into the background. In short, we make the faithfulness of God and the truth of his word depend upon the state of our feelings.

I am certain that if any of our friends treated us in this doubting fashion, we would be wounded and indignant beyond measure. No feeling of unworthiness on their part could excuse them in our eyes for such a wavering of their confidence in us. In fact, we would far rather our friends even sinned against us than doubted us. No form of sinfulness ever hindered the Lord Jesus while on earth from doing his mighty works. The only thing that hindered him was unbelief. In his own town, among his own neighbours and friends where he would have liked to perform miracles, we are told that "he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief" (Matthew 13:58). It was not that he would not, but simply that he could not. And he cannot in our case, any more than in theirs.

But I am afraid some of you may think I am making a mistake. You might think that, in spite of what God has said, the person whose faith wavers can still receive something from the Lord if they are only fervent and earnest enough. That would mean you do not believe God understands the laws of his kingdom as well as you do, and that it is safer to follow your own ideas rather than his word. Yet you must know that, up until now, your doubts have brought you nothing but darkness and misery. Recall the days, weeks, or even years of a halting, stumbling, uncomfortable religious life, and ask yourself honestly whether the cause of it all has not been your wavering faith.

If you believe one day that God loves you and is favourable to you, and the next day doubt his love and fear he is angry with you, does it not stand to reason that your experience must waver from joy to misery? Only a steadfast faith in his love and care could give you an unwavering experience.

The one question, therefore, for all whose faith wavers, is how to put an end to that wavering once and for all. Here, I am thankful to say, I know of a perfect remedy. The only thing you have to do is to GIVE IT UP. Your wavering is caused by your doubting, and by nothing else. Give up your doubting, and your wavering will stop. Keep on with your doubting, and your wavering will continue. The whole matter is as clear as daylight, and the choice is in your own hands.

Perhaps you think this is an extreme statement, for it has probably never entered your head that you could give up doubting altogether. But I assert that you can. You can simply refuse to doubt.

You can shut the door against every suggestion of doubt that comes and, by faith, declare exactly the opposite. Your doubt says, "God does not forgive my sins." Your faith must say, "He does forgive me; he says he does, and I choose to believe him. I am his forgiven child." You must assert this steadfastly until all your doubts vanish. You have no more right to say that you are of such a "doubting nature" that you cannot help doubting than to say you are of such a "thieving nature" that you cannot help stealing. One is as easily controlled as the other. You must give up your doubting just as you would give up thieving. You must treat the temptation to doubt exactly as a person struggling with alcohol must treat the temptation to drink; you must take a pledge against it.

The process I believe to be most effective is to lay our doubts—just as we lay our other sins— upon God's altar and make a total surrender of them. We must give up all liberty to doubt and must consecrate our power of believing to him, trusting him to keep us trusting. We must make our faith in his word as inevitable and necessary a thing as is our obedience to his will. We must be as loyal to our heavenly Friend as we are to our earthly friends. We must refuse to recognise the possibility of any questioning or doubting of his love or his faithfulness.

Our steadfast faith will unfailingly bring us a glorious victory.

It will often seem as if it would be a "righteous" thing—given our many shortcomings—to waver in our faith and question whether salvation is meant for us. While we know it would be wrong to join in with swearing, we often have a lingering feeling that doubts might be "pious" and should be encouraged. I believe one is as displeasing to God as the other.

He says he does, and his word is worth a million times more trust than any of your feelings. If you cannot find anyone to whom to say this, then write it in a letter or say it aloud to yourself and to God. Be very definite about it.

"Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours" (Mark 11:24).

Let nothing shake your faith. Should even sin unhappily overtake you, you must not let it make you doubt. At once, upon discovering any sin, act on the truth that "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

Believe it, not because you feel it or see it, but because he says it. The earth may give way and the mountains may be moved into the heart of the sea; our whole universe may seem to be in ruins; but while we trust in the Lord, we "shall not be moved" (Psalm 46:5).

The person who wavers in their faith is upset by the smallest trifles; the person who is steadfast in their faith can look on calmly even at the ruin of their universe. To be thus immovable is a blessing most ardently to be desired, and it may be ours if we will only hold the beginning of our confidence steadfast to the end.

"Faith is sweetest of worships to him who so loves His unbearable splendours in darkness to hide; And to trust in Thy word, dearest Lord, is true love, For those prayers are most granted which seem most denied.

And faith throws her arms around all Thou hast told her, And able to hold as much more, can but grieve; She could hold Thy grand self, Lord! if Thou wouldst reveal it, And love makes her long to have more to believe."
fields.body_text: "But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord" (James 1:6-7). It would be difficult to find anything that produces more discomfort in the religious life than a wavering faith. The image given to us by the Apostle James describes it exactly: "a wave of the sea... driven and tossed". Just as it is impossible for a traveller to reach a destination by moving forward one day and retracing their steps the next, it is equally impossible for the wavering soul to reach a place of settled peace while it continues to waver. In our last chapter, we considered the shakings of God. It might be thought that our wavering is similar to his shaking, but they are very different. God’s shakings are caused by his love for our blessing; they always lead to rest and peace. Our waverings are caused by our lack of faith; they always lead to discomfort and turmoil. A wavering Christian is someone who trusts in the love of God one day and doubts it the next, and is alternately happy or miserable as a result. They climb to the hilltop of joy at one time, only to descend into the valley of despair the next. They are driven back and forth by every "wind of doctrine," always striving but never attaining. They are a victim of every changing influence—whether it is their physical health, the people around them, or even the weather. You would suppose that even the most inexperienced child of God would know that this sort of experience is wrong. Wavering in one's faith in such a way is deeply dishonouring to the Lord, as it questions his truth and faithfulness. Yet, many Christians are so blinded that they actually think this tendency to waver is a sign of humility. They treat every new attack of doubt as if it were a pious virtue. A wavering Christian might say complacently, "Oh, but I know I am so unworthy that I'm sure it's right for me to doubt." They often imply that if their listener were truly humble, they would doubt as well. I once knew a devoted Christian whose religious life was a constant torment of doubt. After I urged him to have more faith, he said in all seriousness, "My dear friend, if I were ever so arrogant as to feel sure that God loved me, I would be certain I was on the direct road to hell." He clearly thought that such assurance could only come from feeling he was "good enough" to deserve God’s love. He was right that thinking we are worthy of God’s love is arrogant. However, the ground for our assurance does not come from our own goodness, but from the goodness of God. While we should never be satisfied with our own goodness, there can be no question—for anyone who believes the Bible—regarding the total sufficiency of his. To see how absurd this position of doubt is, consider how it would work in human relationships. Imagine a marriage, or the relationship between a child and a parent—both of which the Lord uses as symbols for our relationship with him. If a wife or husband had a "wavering experience" of confidence in their spouse—trusting one day and doubting the next—would that be seen as a sign of humility or a virtue to be cherished? Similarly, if children wavered in their confidence toward their parents the way Christians do with their heavenly Father, what word would be harsh enough for such unfilial conduct? In human relationships, such wavering might be excused if one person were actually untrustworthy. But with God, there is no such excuse. The wavering faith of his children may even lead outsiders to conclude that he isn't worthy of much confidence. We would shrink in horror from causing people to think poorly of God’s character. The truth is that our wavering comes from a subtle, often unconscious form of pride rather than humility. True humility accepts the love and gifts bestowed upon it with a meek and happy thankfulness. While acknowledging our own unworthiness, we would see it only as something that highlights his grace and goodness in choosing us. Instead of treating these doubts as enemies to be resisted, they welcome them as friends. Before long, they begin to waver in their faith and allegiance, and their peace is gone. When life is bright, their faith revives; when things go wrong, doubts win and they waver again. I once spoke with an eminent clergyman about the possibility of a religious life of abiding peace. This describes the experience of many of God’s children who hunger for the peace Christ promised but only find it for moments at a time. They get a glimmer of faith, but then the old doubts return. Equally, if it is to be according to our faith, it will also be to us according to our doubts. The cause of our wavering is not our sins, but our doubts. As a consequence, our attention is mostly directed to getting these matters settled. If you believe one day that God loves you and is favourable to you, and the next day doubt his love and fear he is angry with you, does it not stand to reason that your experience must waver from joy to misery?
