And yet Joseph, in speaking of it, said, “ As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. ” Genesis 50:20.Now, do not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me. “ God sent me here to preserve life." To the eye of sense, it was surely Joseph's wicked brethren who had sent him into Egypt. Yet, with faith, Joseph could say, "God sent me." His brothers had sinned. But by the time it reached Joseph, it was God's will. It was, though it didn't seem so at first, the greatest blessing of his life. So we see how the Lord can turn even man's anger to praise Him. And, how all things, even others' sins, shall work for good to those who love Him. I learned this lesson, practically and experimentally, long before I knew the scripture. I was at a prayer meeting for scriptural holiness. A strange lady rose to speak. I wondered who she was, not knowing she would teach me a grand lesson. She said she had great difficulty in living a life of faith. The second cause that seemed to control everything about her caused it. Her confusion grew. She began to ask God to teach her the truth. Was he really in everything, or not? After praying this for a few days, she had what she described as a vision. She thought she was in a dark place. Then, a body of light advanced towards her from a distance. It gradually surrounded and enveloped her and everything around her. As it approached, a voice seemed to say, “This is the presence of God; this is the presence of God.” This presence showed her all the great and awful things in life. She saw fighting armies, wicked men, raging beasts, storms, and plagues. She saw every kind of sin and suffering. At first, she shrank back in terror. But, she soon saw that God's presence surrounded and enveloped each one of these. Not a lion could reach out its paw, nor a bullet fly through the air, except as His presence moved to permit it. She knew that, if there were the thinnest of sheets of this glorious presence between her and the terrible violence, nothing could touch her. Not a hair on her head could be ruffled. But, the presence must divide to let the evil through. Then, all the small annoyances of life flashed before her. She saw they were so wrapped in God's presence that nothing could touch her. Not a cross look, harsh word, or petty trial could reach her unless He let them through. Her difficulty vanished. Her question was answered forever. God was in everything, and to her henceforth there were no second causes. She saw that her life came to her, day by day, and hour by hour, from His hand. It did not matter what seemed to control it. And, she never again found it hard to trust in His care. But if we focus on the seen things, we won't understand this secret. The children of God must "not look at the things which are seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal." If we could see His unseen forces around us, we'd feel safe. We would walk through this world in an unbreakable fortress. For "the angel of the Lord encamped round about them that fear Him, and delivered them." We have a striking illustration of this in the history of Elisha. The king of Syria was at war with Israel. His evil plans were foiled by a prophet. So, he sent his army to the prophet's city to capture him. We read, “He sent their horses and chariots and a great host; and they came by night and compassed the city about.” This was the seen thing. A nd the servant of the prophet, whose eyes had not yet been opened to see the unseen things, was alarmed. We read, "And when the man, God's servant, rose early and went forth, a host encompassed the city, with horses and chariots." His servant said, "Alas, my master, how shall we do?” But his master could see the unseen things, and he replied, “Fear not; for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And then he prayed, saying, “Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes that he may see. The Lord opened the young man's eyes, and he saw. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. The presence of God is the fortress of His people. Nothing can withstand it. At His presence, the wicked perish. The earth trembles. The hills melt like wax. The cities crumble. "The heavens also dropped, and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God." In this secret, He has promised to hide His people from man's pride and from the strife of tongues. "My presence shall go with thee," He says, "and I will give you rest." I wish every Christian could see this truth as plainly as I do. It is the only clue to a completely restful life. Nothing else will let a soul live only in the present, as we are commanded to do. We must not think of tomorrow. Nothing else will remove all the risks from a Christian's heart. It won't let him say, "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life." Abiding in God’s presence, we run no risks. A soul like that can say: "I know not what it is to doubt. My heart is always gay. "I run no risks, for, come what will, God always has His way." I once heard of a colored woman. She earned a precarious living by daily labor. But, she was a joyous, triumphant Christian. “Ah!”Nancy," said a gloomy Christian lady one day. She almost disapproved of her constant cheerfulness, yet envied it. "Ah!" Nancy, it is all well enough to be happy now, but I should think the thoughts of your future would sober you. Only suppose, for instance, that you fell sick and couldn't work. Or, suppose your employers moved away, and no one else hired you. Or suppose -- "Stop!” cried Nancy, “I never supposes. The Lord is my shepherd, and I know I shall not want. And, honey,” she added to her gloomy friend, “I know it’s all those things they’re suggesting that are making you so miserable . You should give them all up and just trust in the Lord. ” One text can end a believer's "suppose." If only it is received and acted on with childlike faith. It is in Heb. 3:5- 6 “ Now Moses was f aithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope . ” Be content with what you have. For He said, “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ' I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, the Lord is my Helper, I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Hebrews 13:5-6 What if dangers threaten you from every side? What if men's malice, foolishness, or ignorance combine to harm you? You may face every contingency with these words: "The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.” If the Lord is your helper, how can you fear what man may do unto you? No man, nor any company of men, can touch you. Unless, of course, your God, in whom you trust, allows it. “He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. The Lord is your keeper; the Lord is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. The Lord will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The Lord will keep you going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.” (Psalm 121:3 - 8) Only seeing God in everything will make us loving and patient with those who annoy us. They will be only instruments for His wise, tender purposes. We'll end up thanking them for the blessings they bring. Nothing else will completely put an end to all murmuring or rebellious thoughts. Christians often feel a liberty to murmur against man when they would not dare to murmur against God. But this way of receiving things would make it impossible ever to murmur. If our Father allows a trial, it must be the best thing for us. We must accept it with thanks from His dear hand. The trial itself may be hard to flesh out and blood, and I do not mean that we can like or enjoy the suffering of it. But we can and must love the will of God in the trial, for His will is always sweet, whether it be in joy or in sorrow. Our trials may be our chariots. We long for some victory over sin and self, and we ask God to grant it to us. His answer comes in the form of a trial, which He means shall be the chariot to bear us to the longed for triumph. We may either let it roll over us and crush us like an unstoppable force. Or we may mount into it and ride triumphantly onward. Joseph's chariots, which raised him to glory, were his trials. They were being sold into slavery and unjustly imprisoned. Our chariots may be less than these. They may be just annoying people or tough situations. But whatever they are, God means them to be our forces of triumph. They shall bear us to the victories we have prayed for. If we are impatient and long to be patient, our chariot will probably be a trying person. Their ways or words will test our very souls. If we accept the trial as from God and submit, it will be the best discipline. It will give us the patience we seek. God does not order the wrong thing. But, He uses it for our blessing. He did this with the cruelty of Joseph's wicked brethren. And, with Pharaoh's wife's false accusations. It makes life a long thanksgiving. It gives us a deep peace and a joy beyond words. Someone says, “God’s will on earth is always joy, always tranquility.” He must have His own way with His children. The soul that learns this secret finds green pastures and still waters. They offer rest and refreshment. If the will of God is our will, and if He always has His way, then we always have our way also, and we reign in a perpetual kingdom. He who sides with God will win every time. Whatever the outcome, we can join the ap ostle's victory shout: “ But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains uplifted , because only through Christ is it taken away.” (2Corinthians 2:14)

fields.title: Growth
fields.body_html:
Believers' spiritual journey begins with surrender and trust, but true growth in grace continues beyond that. Scripture calls for ongoing development, as seen in 2 Peter 3:18, which encourages growth in grace and knowledge. Growth happens when believers are rooted in God's grace, allowing the Divine Husbandman to nurture them.

By abiding in God's presence and trusting His guidance, without relying on self-effort, believers will mature spiritually, becoming fruitful and strong, just like a tree planted by waters.

After a believer fully surrenders and trusts, they find a life of happy communion and peace. This raises the question, "Is this the end? “I answer emphatically “No, it is only the beginning.” But, this is so little understood that many oppose the faith advocates. They claim the advocates do not believe in growth in grace. They are to teach that the soul can reach a perfect state. There is no further advance beyond it. This teaching voids all the Scriptural calls for growth and development.

Since the opposite is true, I must, next, consider this subject. I want to, if possible, fully answer such objections. I also want to show the scriptural place and way for the soul to grow. The most quoted text is 2 Pet 3:18. It says, " But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. " This text expresses our belief in God's will for us. It also reflects our belief that He has made it possible for us to experience it. We accept, in their fullest meaning, all commands and promises. They concern our growth into Christ in all things, until we are perfect, and measure up to His fullness.

We are glad that we don't always have to be like babies, needing milk. We may, by use and growth, become skilled in the word of righteousness. We should then be able to discern good from evil and need strong meat. And none would grieve more than we at the thought of an end to the Christian life.

There could be no advance beyond it. But, we believe in a growth that produces maturity. We believe in a development that, in fact, bears ripe fruit. We expect to reach the aim set before us, and if we do not, we feel sure there must be some fault in our growing. No parent would be satisfied if, year after year, their child remained a helpless babe. And no farmer would be pleased if his grain grew only to the blade, but never produced the ear or the full corn in the ear.

Growth, to be real, must be progressive. The days, weeks, and months must bring a maturity in the thing growing. But is this the case with a large part of that which is called growth in grace?

Doesn't the very Christian who longs for it, too often find that, at year's end, he is not as far in his Christian experience as at the beginning? His zeal, devotion, and separation from the world are not as complete as when his Christian life began.

I was urging a group of Christians to take an immediate, definite step into the Promised Land. A very intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She exclaimed, "Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was the answer. "I fear I am not nearly so much so." Her eyes opened to see that, at least, her growth had failed. It had done the opposite.

The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace, instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders.

A few steps would have taken them into it.

Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth.

A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. "Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some thirty-fold." But, what does "growing in grace" mean? Few people understand what the grace of God is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of "love" with God. We understand it well in its human use.

But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves.

Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt.

Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts.

Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it, and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well.

To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He who planted us made us to grow.

Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" Or, when He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" There is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain.

They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them.

And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.

Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care.

If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives.

Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, "No man can add to his stature by thinking." His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end.

Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort.

It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way.

Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one.

He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our Divine Husbandman may bring.

Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him.

Look, and your soul shall live. You need to make no efforts to grow, but let your efforts instead be all concentrated on this, that you abide in the Vine. The gardener who tends the vine will care for its branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last.

Like the lily, their glory will surpass even Solomon's.

What if you seem to yourselves to be planted at this moment in a desert soil where nothing can grow!

Trust fully in the great gardener. He will make that desert blossom and create springs in its sands. The promise is sure. The man who trusts in the Lord, “He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.”(Jeremiah 17:8)It i s the great prerogative of our Divine gardener. He can turn any soil into the soil of grace, the moment we put our growing into His hands. He does not need to move us to a different field. Right where we are, with just the circumstances around us, He makes His sun to shine and His dew to fall on us. He turns our greatest obstacles into the best means of our growth. I care not what the circumstances may be, His wonder- working power can accomplish this. And we must trust Him with it all.

Surely He is a man we can trust.

If He sends storms, winds, rains, or sunshine, we must accept it. We must trust, with unwavering faith, that He will cultivate us and bring us to maturity. He knows the best way to do this. He controls the elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him.

Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.

I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon.

His shoots shall sp read out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”(Hosea 14:4- 6) “They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon." (Hosea 14:7) And again He says, " Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield."(Joel 2:22-26) And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.” (Joel 2:25 -26) Oh! You could. But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin"(Mathew 6:28 ).

These words show a life and a growth far different from the ordinary life and growth of Christians.

They show a life of rest and growth without effort. Yet, this life and growth have glorious results. To every soul that becomes a lily in the Lord's garden, and grows as the lilies do, the same glorious array will be given. They will know a mystical passage about their Beloved: "He feeds among the lilies."

We who fully trust believe in a growth in grace. It is a growth that brings desired results. It blossoms into a flower and fruit, becoming a tree planted by rivers of water. It bears fruit in season. Its leaves do not wither. It prospers in all it does. We rejoice to know that, in the Lord's heritage, many such plants are growing up now. As the lilies grow by seeing the sun, they are changed into the same image by beholding the Lord's glory, from glory to glory, by the Lord's spirit.

If you ask them how they grow so fast and well, they would say they don't worry about it. They hardly notice their growth. Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good Husbandman, who alone can manage it. You will find that such souls are not engaged in watching self, but in looking unto Jesus.

They do not toil nor spin for their spiritual clothes. They leave it to the Lord to dress them as He pleases.

Self-effort and self-dependence are at an end with them. Their interest in self is gone, transferred over into the hands of another. Self has become really nothing, and Christ alone is all in all to such as these.

And the blessed result is, that not Even Solomon, in all his glory, was arrayed like these will be. Let us examine this subject practically.

We all know that growing is not a thing of effort, but is the result of an inward life, a principle of growth. All the stretching and pulling in the world could not make a dead oak grow. But a live oak grows without stretching. It is plain, then, that the key is to get within you the growing life. Then you cannot help but grow. And this life is the life hid with Christ in God, the wonderful divine life of an indwelling Holy Ghost. Be filled with this, dear believer. You must grow, whether you know it or not.

Do not worry about your growth. Just ensure you have the growing life.

Abide in the Vine. Let the life from Him flow through all your spiritual veins. Interpose no barrier to His mighty life-giving power, working in you all the good pleasure of His will. Surrender completely to His gentle guidance. Put your growing into His hands, as completely as you have put all your other affairs. Suffer Him to manage it as He will. Do not concern yourself about it, nor even think of it.

Trust Him without reservation, and at all times.

Accept each moment's gift, from His dear hands. It is the needed sunshine or dew for your growth. Say a continual "Yes" to your Father's will. Until now, you may have tried, as many do, to be both the lily and the gardener, both the vineyard and the gardener. You have taken on the burdens and duties that belong only to the Divine gardener. Only He can bear them. Henceforth consent to take your rightful place and to be only what you really are. Say to yourself, "If I am only the garden, not the gardener; if I am only the vine, not the gardener, then I must keep the garden and act its part."" I must not usurp the gardener's place or try to act his part."

Do not choose your own soil or set your borders. Do not plant your own seeds, prune, or tend your vines. Be content with what the Divine Husbandman arranges for you, and with the care He gives. Let Him choose which plants and fruits to cultivate. If He wills it, let Him grow a potato as gladly as a rose. And, let Him value everyday virtues as much as exalted passions. Be content with the seasons He sends, and the sun and rain. Accept your growth, whether fast or slow. In short, be satisfied with all His ways, even if we don't understand them.

There is infinite repose in this. As the violet rests in its nook, it contentedly accepts its daily portion. It lets the rains fall, the suns rise, and the earth whirl, without one anxious pang. So, we must repose in the present as God gives it to us. We should accept, without worry, our daily portion in His grand plan.

It is creative and redemptive.

The wind that blows can never kill the tree God plants. It blows east, it blows west. The tender leaves have little rest. But any wind that blows is best. The tree God plants Strikes deeper root, grows higher still, spreads wider boughs. For God's goodwill meets all its wants. No frost can blight the tree God shields. The roots are warm beneath the soft snows. When spring comes, it knows, and every bud will blossom. The tree God shields Grows on apace by day and night, Till, sweet to taste and fair to sight, its fruit it yields.

No storm can blast the tree, God knows. No thunder, rain, lightning, or hurricane can. When they spend, it remains. The tree God knows. Through every tempest, it stands fast. From its first day to its last, it grows ever fairer.

If in the soul's still garden, a seed God sows a little seed, it will soon grow. And, all men will know it.

For heavenly land, He bids it blow. A seed God sows, and up it springs by day and night; through life, through death, it grows right, forever grows.

A very intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She exclaimed, "Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was the answer. "I fear I am not nearly so much so." Her eyes opened to see that, at least, her growth had failed. It had done the opposite. The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace, instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders. A few steps would have taken them into it. Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth. A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. "Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some thirty-fold." But, what does "growing in grace" mean? Few people understand what the grace of God is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of "love" with God. We understand it well in its human use. But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves. Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt. Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts. Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it, and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well. To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He who planted us made us to grow. Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" Or, when He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" There is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain. They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them. And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care. If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives. Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, "No man can add to his stature by thinking." His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end. Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort. It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way. Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one. He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our Divine Husbandman may bring. Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him. Look, and your soul shall live. You need to make no efforts to grow, but let your efforts instead be all concentrated on this, that you abide in the Vine. The gardener who tends the vine will care for its branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last. Like the lily, their glory will surpass even Solomon's. What if you seem to yourselves to be planted at this moment in a desert soil where nothing can grow! Trust fully in the great gardener. He will make that desert blossom and create springs in its sands. The promise is sure. The man who trusts in the Lord, “He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.”(Jeremiah 17:8)It i s the great prerogative of our Divine gardener. He can turn any soil into the soil of grace, the moment we put our growing into His hands. He does not need to move us to a different field. Right where we are, with just the circumstances around us, He makes His sun to shine and His dew to fall on us. He turns our greatest obstacles into the best means of our growth. I care not what the circumstances may be, His wonder- working power can accomplish this. And we must trust Him with it all. Surely He is a man we can trust. If He sends storms, winds, rains, or sunshine, we must accept it. We must trust, with unwavering faith, that He will cultivate us and bring us to maturity. He knows the best way to do this. He controls the elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him. Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them. I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon. His shoots shall sp read out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”(Hosea 14:4- 6) “They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon." (Hosea 14:7) And again He says, " Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield."(Joel 2:22-26) And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.” (Joel 2:25 -26) Oh! You could. But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin"(Mathew 6:28 ). These words show a life and a growth far different from the ordinary life and growth of Christians. They show a life of rest and growth without effort. Yet, this life and growth have glorious results. To every soul that becomes a lily in the Lord's garden, and grows as the lilies do, the same glorious array will be given. They will know a mystical passage about their Beloved: "He feeds among the lilies." We who fully trust believe in a growth in grace. It is a growth that brings desired results. It blossoms into a flower and fruit, becoming a tree planted by rivers of water. It bears fruit in season. Its leaves do not wither. It prospers in all it does. We rejoice to know that, in the Lord's heritage, many such plants are growing up now. As the lilies grow by seeing the sun, they are changed into the same image by beholding the Lord's glory, from glory to glory, by the Lord's spirit. If you ask them how they grow so fast and well, they would say they don't worry about it. They hardly notice their growth. Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good Husbandman, who alone can manage it. You will find that such souls are not engaged in watching self, but in looking unto Jesus. They do not toil nor spin for their spiritual clothes. They leave it to the Lord to dress them as He pleases. Self-effort and self-dependence are at an end with them. Their interest in self is gone, transferred over into the hands of another. Self has become really nothing, and Christ alone is all in all to such as these. And the blessed result is, that not Even Solomon, in all his glory, was arrayed like these will be. Let us examine this subject practically. We all know that growing is not a thing of effort, but is the result of an inward life, a principle of growth. All the stretching and pulling in the world could not make a dead oak grow. But a live oak grows without stretching. It is plain, then, that the key is to get within you the growing life. Then you cannot help but grow. And this life is the life hid with Christ in God, the wonderful divine life of an indwelling Holy Ghost. Be filled with this, dear believer. You must grow, whether you know it or not. Do not worry about your growth. Just ensure you have the growing life. Abide in the Vine. Let the life from Him flow through all your spiritual veins. Interpose no barrier to His mighty life-giving power, working in you all the good pleasure of His will. Surrender completely to His gentle guidance. Put your growing into His hands, as completely as you have put all your other affairs. Suffer Him to manage it as He will. Do not concern yourself about it, nor even think of it. Trust Him without reservation, and at all times. Accept each moment's gift, from His dear hands. It is the needed sunshine or dew for your growth. Say a continual "Yes" to your Father's will. Until now, you may have tried, as many do, to be both the lily and the gardener, both the vineyard and the gardener. You have taken on the burdens and duties that belong only to the Divine gardener. Only He can bear them. Henceforth consent to take your rightful place and to be only what you really are. Say to yourself, "If I am only the garden, not the gardener; if I am only the vine, not the gardener, then I must keep the garden and act its part."" I must not usurp the gardener's place or try to act his part." Do not choose your own soil or set your borders. Do not plant your own seeds, prune, or tend your vines. Be content with what the Divine Husbandman arranges for you, and with the care He gives. Let Him choose which plants and fruits to cultivate. If He wills it, let Him grow a potato as gladly as a rose. And, let Him value everyday virtues as much as exalted passions. Be content with the seasons He sends, and the sun and rain. Accept your growth, whether fast or slow. In short, be satisfied with all His ways, even if we don't understand them. There is infinite repose in this. As the violet rests in its nook, it contentedly accepts its daily portion. It lets the rains fall, the suns rise, and the earth whirl, without one anxious pang. So, we must repose in the present as God gives it to us. We should accept, without worry, our daily portion in His grand plan. It is creative and redemptive. The wind that blows can never kill the tree God plants. It blows east, it blows west. The tender leaves have little rest. But any wind that blows is best. The tree God plants Strikes deeper root, grows higher still, spreads wider boughs. For God's goodwill meets all its wants. No frost can blight the tree God shields. The roots are warm beneath the soft snows. When spring comes, it knows, and every bud will blossom. The tree God shields Grows on apace by day and night, Till, sweet to taste and fair to sight, its fruit it yields. No storm can blast the tree, God knows. No thunder, rain, lightning, or hurricane can. When they spend, it remains. The tree God knows. Through every tempest, it stands fast. From its first day to its last, it grows ever fairer. If in the soul's still garden, a seed God sows a little seed, it will soon grow. And, all men will know it. For heavenly land, He bids it blow. A seed God sows, and up it springs by day and night; through life, through death, it grows right, forever grows.

fields.title: Service
fields.body_html:
Christian service often starts as a burden, but through trust ing God’s will, it becomes a joy. As believers surrender their will to God, they find freedom and strength in serving Him. True service comes from yielding to God’s guidance, trusting Him for the results, and letting go of self-reflection. This life of faith brings rest, freedom, and power, as believers rely on God’s strength rather than their own.

Perhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light.

One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. "After my conversion," she said, "I was full of joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open door." But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit the sick, and pray beside their beds.

I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last, it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash- tubs.”

This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian?

Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work was done.

You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden.

You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun.

You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This, too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord.

He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him.

How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions?

They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home, friends, and ease.

It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for money.

What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6- 13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”

“And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord, for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

“He says it shall no more be the old covenant made on Sin ai. That is, a law given from the outside, controlling a man by force. But it shall be a law written within, constraining a man by love. “I will put my laws,” He says, “in their mind, and write them in their hearts.” This can mean nothing but that we shall love His law, for anything written on our hearts we must love.

Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could possibly be conceived more effectual than this. How often have we thought, "If I could get inside my kids and make them want to do what I want, managing them would be so easy!" We have found, in practice, that to deal with cross-grained people, we must avoid suggesting our wishes to them. We must instead induce them to suggest their own. Then, we will face no opposition. We, a stiff-necked people by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us.

God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must exclaim, "This happy service!" Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes, Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into harmony with His lovely will. I have seen this done over and over, in cases where it looked beforehand an utterly impossible thing.

In one case, a lady had long feared and hated a thing she knew was right. I saw her, in despair and without feeling, give her will to her Lord. She began to say to Him, "Your will be done; your will be done!” And in one short hour that very thing began to look sweet and precious to h er. It is wonderful what miracles God works in wills that are utterly surrendered to Him. He turns hard things into easy and bitter things into sweet. It is not that He puts easy things in the place of the hard, but He actually changes the hard thing into an easy one. And this is salvation. It is grand. Do try it. You, who find daily Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious liberty!

Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service.

Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not!

The Master has the right to use any tool for His work. It is not the tool's place to decide if it is the right one. He knows; and if He chooses to use us, of course we must be fit. And in truth, if we only knew it, our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I can give you a convincing illustration of this.

I once visited an asylum for people with intellectual disabilities. I watched the children doing dumbbell ex ercises. We know that it’s hard for people with intellectual disabilities to control their movements.

They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements.

Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the time, it was all out of sync .

One little girl, however, I noticed, who made perfect movements. Not a jar nor a break disturbed the harmony of her exercises. And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his hands, and he did it all.

The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Paul could say, "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Who would not glory in being so weak and helpless, that the Lord Jesus Christ should find no hindrance to the perfect working of His mighty power through us and in us?

Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it.

Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. The most effective workers I know have no anxiety about their work. They commit it to their dear Master. They ask Him to guide them and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment.

One might think they were too carefree, with such at stake. But, when you learn God's secret of trusting, you will see the beauty and power of a life yielded to His work. You will cease to condemn. You will wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear.

There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become personal and individual.

The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special guidance needed for that hour.

His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. Many Christians make the mistake of expecting to receive God’s commands all in a lump, as it were. They think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command.

Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived in constant shame.

At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others' work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them.

She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance.

She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes easy and natural. It develops the divine work within.

Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives.

Another form of bondage is to service. The life of faith delivers the soul from it. It refers to the after reflections that always follow any Christian work. These self-reflections are of two sorts. The soul both congratulates itself on its success and is uplifted. Or, it is distressed over its failure and is cast down.

One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all.

Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: "Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self- reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair." Forget the things that are behind, the moment they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses.

In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not pray, "Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me." Then, rise from your knees and take back the burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself. Leave it with the Lord, and remember that what you trust to Him, you must not worry over nor feel anxious about. Trust and worry cannot go together.

If your work is a burden, it is because you are not trusting it to Him. If you trust it to Him, you will find the yoke He puts on you is easy. The burden He gives you is light. Even amid a life of ceaseless activity, you will find rest for your soul.

But some may say that this teaching would make us into mere puppets. I answer, No, it would simply make us into servants. A servant must not plan, arrange, decide, or supply materials. He must only obey. It is for the Master to do all the rest. The servant is not responsible, either, for results. The Master alone knows what results he wished to have produced, and so he alone can judge of them. Intelligent service must, of course, sympathize with the Master's plans. But, there cannot be a full understanding.

The Master cannot shift his responsibility to the servant. With our limited view and great ignorance, we can do little but accept God's will. We shouldn't expect to fully understand it. We must leave all results to Him.

What seems like failure on the surface is often, on the unseen side, a great success. If we allow ourselves to lament and worry, we will be foolish. We should be singing and rejoicing, not weeping. It is far better to avoid all self-reflection. We should not think about ourselves at all, whether for good or ill.

We are not our own property, nor our own business. We belong to God. We are His instruments and His business. He always attends to His own business. So, He will, of course, attend to us.

I once heard of a slave on a ship during a violent storm. While everyone else was scared, he whistled happily. Finally, someone asked if he was afraid of drowning. He smiled and said, "Well, maybe I am.

But I don’t belong to myself, and it will only be my master’s loss." This attitude could help us avoid many worries in our work. With a group of people fully dedicated to serving and trusting in our Master, imagine what He could do. One person like this could defeat a thousand, and two could put ten thousand to flight. Nothing would be impossible for them because, with the Lord, it doesn’t matter whether we have many or few.

May God quickly raise such an army! And may you, my dear reader, enroll in this army today. Yield yourself to God as one alive from the dead. May every part of you be His instrument of righteousness, to be used by Him as He wishes.
fields.body_text: Christian service often starts as a burden, but through trust ing God’s will, it becomes a joy. As believers surrender their will to God, they find freedom and strength in serving Him. True service comes from yielding to God’s guidance, trusting Him for the results, and letting go of self-reflection. This life of faith brings rest, freedom, and power, as believers rely on God’s strength rather than their own. Perhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light. One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. "After my conversion," she said, "I was full of joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open door." But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit the sick, and pray beside their beds. I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last, it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash- tubs.” This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian? Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work was done. You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden. You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun. You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This, too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord. He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him. How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions? They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home, friends, and ease. It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for money. What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6- 13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” “And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord, for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away. “He says it shall no more be the old covenant made on Sin ai. That is, a law given from the outside, controlling a man by force. But it shall be a law written within, constraining a man by love. “I will put my laws,” He says, “in their mind, and write them in their hearts.” This can mean nothing but that we shall love His law, for anything written on our hearts we must love. Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could possibly be conceived more effectual than this. How often have we thought, "If I could get inside my kids and make them want to do what I want, managing them would be so easy!" We have found, in practice, that to deal with cross-grained people, we must avoid suggesting our wishes to them. We must instead induce them to suggest their own. Then, we will face no opposition. We, a stiff-necked people by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us. God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must exclaim, "This happy service!" Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes, Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into harmony with His lovely will. I have seen this done over and over, in cases where it looked beforehand an utterly impossible thing. In one case, a lady had long feared and hated a thing she knew was right. I saw her, in despair and without feeling, give her will to her Lord. She began to say to Him, "Your will be done; your will be done!” And in one short hour that very thing began to look sweet and precious to h er. It is wonderful what miracles God works in wills that are utterly surrendered to Him. He turns hard things into easy and bitter things into sweet. It is not that He puts easy things in the place of the hard, but He actually changes the hard thing into an easy one. And this is salvation. It is grand. Do try it. You, who find daily Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious liberty! Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service. Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not! The Master has the right to use any tool for His work. It is not the tool's place to decide if it is the right one. He knows; and if He chooses to use us, of course we must be fit. And in truth, if we only knew it, our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I can give you a convincing illustration of this. I once visited an asylum for people with intellectual disabilities. I watched the children doing dumbbell ex ercises. We know that it’s hard for people with intellectual disabilities to control their movements. They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements. Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the time, it was all out of sync . One little girl, however, I noticed, who made perfect movements. Not a jar nor a break disturbed the harmony of her exercises. And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his hands, and he did it all. The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Paul could say, "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me." Who would not glory in being so weak and helpless, that the Lord Jesus Christ should find no hindrance to the perfect working of His mighty power through us and in us? Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it. Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. The most effective workers I know have no anxiety about their work. They commit it to their dear Master. They ask Him to guide them and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment. One might think they were too carefree, with such at stake. But, when you learn God's secret of trusting, you will see the beauty and power of a life yielded to His work. You will cease to condemn. You will wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear. There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become personal and individual. The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special guidance needed for that hour. His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. Many Christians make the mistake of expecting to receive God’s commands all in a lump, as it were. They think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command. Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived in constant shame. At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others' work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them. She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance. She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes easy and natural. It develops the divine work within. Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives. Another form of bondage is to service. The life of faith delivers the soul from it. It refers to the after reflections that always follow any Christian work. These self-reflections are of two sorts. The soul both congratulates itself on its success and is uplifted. Or, it is distressed over its failure and is cast down. One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all. Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: "Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self- reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair." Forget the things that are behind, the moment they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses. In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not pray, "Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me." Then, rise from your knees and take back the burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself.
