fields.title: Starting or Reviving a Library A Call to Build and Restore
fields.body_html:
As you arrive at this final chapter, you stand at the doorway of action. Everything you have learned so far—about organisation, service, discipline, and community—now becomes the foundation for something real. Whether you are beginning a library from an empty room or breathing life back into one that has been forgotten, your work is sacred. You are building a place of learning, shaping a space for growth, and restoring hope where it may have faded.

A neglected library is not a defeat. It is an invitation—an opportunity to rebuild with clarity, wisdom, and renewed purpose. And a brand-new library is a chance to plant something that generations will benefit from. This chapter gives you a clear, steady path forward for both beginnings and restorations.

Starting a New Library Laying a Strong Foundation Creating a library from scratch is one of the most rewarding tasks you can undertake. At the beginning, everything is open. You can choose the right systems, set clear values, and establish a culture of service from day one.

Understanding Your Mission Every library begins with a mission. Ask yourself: Who am I building this library for, and what needs will it meet?

Maybe you want to support children’s literacy, help students succeed in exams, or give adults a place to learn new skills. When your purpose is clear, your decisions become easier—what books to buy, what programs to run, and how the space should feel.

Preparing the Space Choose a location that people can reach easily—somewhere safe, clean, and welcoming. Even a small room can become a powerful resource if it is well-lit, organised, and inviting.

Shelves, tables, a few chairs, and a small registration area are enough to begin. Start small, but start intentionally.

Finding Resources Every new library needs an initial collection. You may buy some books, receive donations, or partner with schools and organisations. Aim for materials that truly fit your users—not just whatever happens to come your way.

And if your budget is limited, that’s perfectly fine. One computer for registration, one printer, and a few essential supplies are enough to begin operating responsibly.

Setting Simple Policies Your first policies should be short, clear, and easy to explain.

For example: • Who can borrow books • How long can they keep them • How to treat library materials • How to behave in the library Think of policies as gentle boundaries that help the library run peacefully.

Organising and Launching Process each new book carefully. Stamp it, label it, add it to your catalogue, and shelve it correctly. When your collection is ready, practise your circulation steps. Make sure staff or volunteers know how to issue and return books, search the catalogue, and assist users politely.

Starting a library is less about perfection and more about consistent, thoughtful action.

Reviving a Failing Library Restoring Order, Purpose, and Life Sometimes, a library loses its way. Books become outdated or damaged. Records fall behind.

Users stop visiting because the space no longer meets their needs. If this is the situation you face, do not be discouraged. Revival is possible—and it begins with honest assessment.

Step 1: Understanding What Went Wrong Walk slowly through the library with open eyes.

Ask simple but important questions: • Are the books still useful?

• Are they organised properly?

• Do people still visit? Why or why not?

• Are staff motivated and trained?

• Are digital systems being used or ignored?

You cannot fix what you have not seen clearly.

Step 2: Clearing, Cleaning, and Rebuilding Begin with the collection. Remove the books that no longer serve. Outdated science, torn materials, irrelevant topics—these weigh the library down. Freeing shelf space makes room for better things.

Next, refresh the physical space. Clean the shelves, repair broken furniture, replace blown bulbs, and repaint if possible. A freshly cleaned library sends a strong message: something new is beginning.

Then, restart your systems. Re-catalogue where necessary. Reset passwords. Update records.

Simplify your procedures so that staff do not feel overwhelmed.

Finally, retrain your team. Encourage kindness, attentiveness, and responsibility. The attitude of the staff can revive a library faster than any new book can.

Step 3: Reintroducing the Library to the Community Once the basics are restored, it is time to reopen the doors with confidence. Remind the community that the library is here for them. Share new policies, new opening hours, or special programs. Even a single well-planned activity—story time, a digital skills class, or a reading challenge—can bring excitement back.

Revival is not about making everything perfect. It is about restoring trust, order, and hope.

Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them Even the most passionate library managers fall into avoidable traps. Here are some lessons that protect you from unnecessary struggle.

Buying Books Nobody Needs A library serves the community, not the personal tastes of the manager. Always choose materials based on real users and real needs.

Weak or Inconsistent Organisation If cataloguing and shelving are done carelessly, books become invisible. A misplaced book is a lost book. Keep your systems simple, consistent, and disciplined.

Too Many Rules Policies should help people, not chase them away. Keep rules light, clear, and easy to understand.

Waiting Instead of Reaching Out A library should not hide. Visit schools, talk to leaders, and remind the community of the services you offer. An active library has an active voice.

Ignoring Backup and Safety Always protect your catalogue and digital records. One computer crash should never destroy years of work.

Mistakes are normal. The wise manager learns from them early and adjusts quickly.

Growing the Library Over Time Steady, Sustainable Development.

Growth does not happen overnight. It is built one wise decision at a time.

Begin by expanding the collection slowly—based on what people actually borrow. If students love storybooks, buy more storybooks. If adults borrow business guides, strengthen that section.

Let usage guide growth.

Next, expand your services. Can you run a mobile reading day at a nearby school? Can you start a small reading corner in a church or community centre? Growth does not always mean a bigger building; sometimes it means a wider reach.

And do not underestimate volunteers. Retired teachers, youth leaders, university students, or parents can bring energy and skills that elevate your library without adding cost.

Finally, seek partnerships and grants only when they fit your direction. A library grows best when it grows with purpose.

Conclusion Your Work is a Gift to the Future You have reached the end of this guide, but the real work is ahead. Building or reviving a library is not just an administrative duty—it is an act of service. Every catalogued book, every organised shelf, every child helped, and every adult guided is a seed planted for the future.

Your library will shape minds, support families, empower communities, and open doors that may stay open for a lifetime.

Stand firm in wisdom.

Serve with patience.

Lead with clarity.

And build something that lasts.

Your library may begin as a room of books, but with dedication and heart, it will become a place of transformation for generations to come.

END

fields.title: Life and Consciousness
fields.body_html:
Understanding the Life God Gives Us When God saves you, He doesn’t just wipe your record and hand you a clean page. He hits the reset button on your entire inner world. He pours His own life into you — and that life isn’t silent. It comes with spiritual senses you didn’t have before.

It’s like suddenly going from black-and-white to full HD. Like you finally woke up from a long sleep, you never realised you were in.

Your physical body already knows how to live. Touch fire, and your hand snatches back instantly. Stay up too late, and your body begs you to rest. Hug someone you love, and your whole body calms down.

Your spiritual life, the life God gives, acts the exact same way — but for the invisible world.

It feels God's nearness.

It reacts when sin comes close.

It senses right and wrong like a pressure in your chest.

It pulls you toward spiritual things even when your friends don't get it.

It knits you into a community of believers before you even know their names.

This is what the Bible means when it says, “In Him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4). His life is light — and the moment it enters you, the lamp inside turns on and you finally start seeing things for what they really are.

And just like that, sin loses its “normal.”

You don’t need ten sermons to explain what displeases God; the Holy Spirit inside you reacts faster than any human voice could. It’s like your spiritual nervous system suddenly wakes up.

You lie — and something stings inside.

You gossip — and something feels “off.”

You click on something dirty — and your heart closes up.

You disrespect someone, and your spirit won’t settle.

You drift from prayer — and a quiet ache starts forming.

This is not guilt from your parents, your pastor, or your youth leader. This is the Holy Spirit firing off inner alarms. The Bible calls this “not grieving the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 4:30).

When you touch fire, your nerves scream. When you touch sin, the Holy Spirit grieves, and because He lives in you, you feel that grief.

It’s proof that the life inside you is real.

That Natural Craving: God Becomes Your Dad Before you were saved, prayer felt like talking to the ceiling. But once God gives you life, something inside you recognises Him instantly. It's like your spirit suddenly whispers, “I know this voice… this is my Father.”

Romans 8:16 describes this beautifully: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.”

You start experiencing things you can’t always explain: Prayer feels more like home than a homework assignment.

You feel convicted when you wander, like a child missing their parent.

You feel safe and understood in God’s presence.

Sometimes you just want to talk to Him without being told to.

You begin craving God the way a newborn craves milk — naturally, instinctively.

This is what life does. Life cries out for its Source.

And then comes something even deeper — something many Christians overlook: You don’t just become conscious of God .

You become conscious of God’s people .

Body Consciousness: Feeling What They Feel Your physical body is a genius. If just one part suffers, everything reacts.

Stub your toe? Your whole face reacts, your hands reach down, your body pauses.

Get dust in your eye? Everything stops until it’s dealt with.

Burn your hand? Your entire system jumps to rescue mode.

Sprain your ankle? Your arms, legs, and brain instantly coordinate to balance you.

Your body doesn’t behave like separate parts.

It behaves like one single living unit.

Paul wasn’t being poetic when he said, “If one member suffers, all suffer together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). That’s how the Body of Christ was designed to function.

God doesn’t create isolated Christians. He creates connected members .

So when your friend at school is hurting — spiritually crushed, overwhelmed, or falling into sin — you feel something inside. It may be compassion, heaviness, or concern, but it hits you. You don’t shrug and say, “That’s their problem.” Your spiritual senses react the way your physical body reacts to a cut finger. Life responds to life.

When someone in your youth group is spiritually weak — losing motivation, slipping away, or fading in their walk — the stronger ones naturally feel the pull to slow down, help, pray, reach out, or cover for them. Like a sprained ankle makes the other leg step in, believers with strength instinctively support believers who are struggling.

This inner sensitivity makes unity feel precious and drama feel dangerous.

It makes gossip feel painful instead of entertaining.

It makes you hate division because division feels like a wound.

It makes you protective of your spiritual family because the same life runs through all of you.

But here’s the truth most people miss: You can know all the verses.

You can follow all the rules.

You can sing all the songs.

You can go to every service.

And still be spiritually numb.

Knowledge is Not Life; Sensitivity Is Life is not measured by how much you know, but by how deeply you sense.

You know God’s life is truly becoming your life when: You feel God before you think about obligations.

You sense danger before anyone corrects you.

You hunger for Scripture without being forced.

Prayer becomes a need, like breathing.

Sin unsettles your peace instead of just hurting your reputation.

Repentance feels like fresh air instead of punishment.

You feel connected to believers even when they’re nothing like you.

This is why Jesus said, “My sheep hear My voice” (John 10:27).

He wasn’t talking about information — He was talking about sensitivity.

A soft heart is a living heart.

A hard heart is a sick heart.

So pray: “Lord, keep my heart soft.

Keep my spirit awake.

Let me feel sin before it grows.

Let me feel Your presence even on ordinary days.

Give me love for Your people, because they are part of me.”

The more sensitive you become to the life inside you, The stronger, healthier, and more connected your place in the Body becomes.
fields.body_text: Understanding the Life God Gives Us When God saves you, He doesn’t just wipe your record and hand you a clean page. He hits the reset button on your entire inner world. He pours His own life into you — and that life isn’t silent. It comes with spiritual senses you didn’t have before. It’s like suddenly going from black-and-white to full HD. Like you finally woke up from a long sleep, you never realised you were in. Your physical body already knows how to live. Touch fire, and your hand snatches back instantly. Stay up too late, and your body begs you to rest. Hug someone you love, and your whole body calms down. Your spiritual life, the life God gives, acts the exact same way — but for the invisible world. It feels God's nearness. It reacts when sin comes close. It senses right and wrong like a pressure in your chest. It pulls you toward spiritual things even when your friends don't get it. It knits you into a community of believers before you even know their names. This is what the Bible means when it says, “In Him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4). His life is light — and the moment it enters you, the lamp inside turns on and you finally start seeing things for what they really are. And just like that, sin loses its “normal.” You don’t need ten sermons to explain what displeases God; the Holy Spirit inside you reacts faster than any human voice could. It’s like your spiritual nervous system suddenly wakes up. You lie — and something stings inside. You gossip — and something feels “off.” You click on something dirty — and your heart closes up. You disrespect someone, and your spirit won’t settle. You drift from prayer — and a quiet ache starts forming. This is not guilt from your parents, your pastor, or your youth leader. This is the Holy Spirit firing off inner alarms. The Bible calls this “not grieving the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 4:30). When you touch fire, your nerves scream. When you touch sin, the Holy Spirit grieves, and because He lives in you, you feel that grief. It’s proof that the life inside you is real. That Natural Craving: God Becomes Your Dad Before you were saved, prayer felt like talking to the ceiling. But once God gives you life, something inside you recognises Him instantly. It's like your spirit suddenly whispers, “I know this voice… this is my Father.” Romans 8:16 describes this beautifully: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.” You start experiencing things you can’t always explain: Prayer feels more like home than a homework assignment. You feel convicted when you wander, like a child missing their parent. You feel safe and understood in God’s presence. Sometimes you just want to talk to Him without being told to. You begin craving God the way a newborn craves milk — naturally, instinctively. This is what life does. Life cries out for its Source. And then comes something even deeper — something many Christians overlook: You don’t just become conscious of God . You become conscious of God’s people . Get dust in your eye? Everything stops until it’s dealt with. Burn your hand? Your entire system jumps to rescue mode. Sprain your ankle? Your arms, legs, and brain instantly coordinate to balance you. Your body doesn’t behave like separate parts. It behaves like one single living unit. fields.title: The Consciousness of the Body of Christ
fields.body_html:
When God gives you His life, He doesn’t give it to you in isolation.

That life never arrives alone.

The same life that connects you to God also connects you to everyone else who carries that life .

This is where many people get confused. They think salvation is personal — and it is —, but they forget it is never private.

From the moment God’s life enters you, you are no longer just an individual Christian. You become part of something living, breathing, and connected. You become part of a Body .

And just like your physical body, this Body has its own awareness.

You don’t have to be taught this awareness first.

You don’t have to understand theology to feel it.

You don’t need a title, a position, or years in church.

If the life of Christ is in you, the consciousness of the Body comes with it .

It’s automatic.

Think about your physical body again.

Your hand doesn’t wake up in the morning and decide whether it belongs to your arm. It doesn’t vote on unity. It doesn’t debate the connection.

It’s already part of the body — and it knows it.

Your hand moves when your brain sends signals.

Your eyes blink without permission.

Your heart beats without asking for instructions.

Life inside the body creates awareness, coordination, and submission naturally.

The Body of Christ works the same way.

Scripture says, “For by one Spirit we were all baptised into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13).

Not many bodies.

Not independent units.

One body.

The moment God’s life enters you, you are spiritually wired into everyone else who carries that same life.

That’s why something inside you reacts when believers are divided.

That’s why isolation feels wrong, even when it feels easier.

That’s why gossip doesn’t sit well.

That’s why pride and independence feel dangerous, even when they feel strong.

The life inside you knows: you are not alone — and you are not meant to live alone .

This body-consciousness shows up in everyday life in quiet but powerful ways.

You walk into a room full of believers, and something feels familiar, even if you’ve never met them before.

You worship together, and your heart syncs with theirs.

You pray for someone, and their burden feels personal.

Someone falls into sin, and your spirit feels heavy.

Someone grows spiritually, and you feel encouraged — even inspired.

No one had to explain this to you.

Life recognised life.

Paul explains it simply: “Now you are the body of Christ, and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27).

Not visitors.

Not fans.

Members.

And members don’t live disconnected.

Your physical body also teaches you something important: no part exists for itself .

Your eyes don’t see for themselves.

Your feet don’t walk for their own benefit.

Your lungs don’t breathe just to feel important.

Every part exists to serve the whole body.

In the same way, God didn’t save you just so you could feel spiritual, go to heaven, or build a personal faith bubble. He placed you in the Body so that His life could flow through you to others.

This is why Christianity breaks down when it becomes “me and Jesus” only.

A hand that refuses to connect to the arm doesn’t become more spiritual — it dies.

A Christian who cuts themselves off from the Body doesn’t become stronger — they slowly lose sensitivity.

Life flows through connection , not independence.

There’s another thing your body teaches you: Two parts are not the same, but all are necessary .

Your heart doesn’t compete with your brain.

Your lungs don’t feel inferior to your eyes.

Your hands don’t feel useless because they aren’t feet.

Each part has its own function — and the body needs all of them.

The Body of Christ works the same way.

Some believers speak.

Some serve quietly.

Some encourage.

Some pray deeply.

Some lead.

Some support behind the scenes.

Not everyone is visible, but everyone is vital.

Scripture says, “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

When comparison enters the Body, sensitivity dies.

When pride rises, connection weakens.

When jealousy grows, the body limps.

But when each member accepts their place, life flows freely.

This body-consciousness also explains why independence feels spiritual but isn’t.

Your culture might tell you: “Stand alone.”

“Be self-made.”

“Don’t depend on anyone.”

But your body says something different.

A body part that tries to live independently doesn’t become strong — it becomes dangerous to itself and to the whole body.

God never designed Christians to function alone.

That’s why Scripture warns against separation: “Do not forsake the assembling of ourselves together” (Hebrews 10:25).

This isn’t about attendance.

It’s about connection .

Life weakens in isolation.

Sensitivity dulls.

Spiritual hearing fades.

Just like nerves lose feeling when blood flow is cut off, believers lose spiritual awareness when they disconnect from the Body.

One of the clearest signs that the consciousness of the Body is healthy in you is this: You naturally come under the direction of the Head .

Your physical body doesn’t argue with your head.

Your hand doesn’t say, “I’ll move when I feel like it.”

Your foot doesn’t choose its own path.

The head directs.

The body responds.

Scripture says Christ is “the Head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18).

When the Body is healthy, members don’t push their own agendas.

They listen.

They respond.

They move together.

When someone insists on always being right, always being seen, always doing their own thing — that’s not strength. That’s a body part refusing the Head.

And when the Head is ignored, the Body loses coordination.

Here’s the simple truth: If God’s life is strong in you, the consciousness of the Body will grow naturally.

You won’t need to force unity.

You won’t need to fake love.

You won’t need to perform spirituality.

You’ll feel when something threatens the Body.

You’ll feel when someone needs support.

You’ll feel when pride needs to die.

You’ll feel when obedience is required.

This awareness doesn’t make you weak — it makes you alive .

And just like in your physical body, the more sensitive the parts are, the healthier the whole body becomes.

So pray — not just for personal growth, but for body awareness: “Lord, keep me connected.

Keep me sensitive to Your people.

Protect me from isolation and pride.

Help me take my place without comparison.

Teach me to move when You move and stop when You stop.”

Because the life God gives always leads to this truth: You were saved into a Body.

You live by the Body.

And you grow through the Body.

fields.title: Hold Fast to the Head
fields.body_html:
This chapter teaches us a very important lesson: Jesus Christ is the Head of the church, and we must remain closely connected to Him. The church is called Christ’s body, and just like a real body cannot live without its head, believers cannot live or grow without Christ. Holding fast to the Head means trusting Jesus completely, obeying Him, and allowing Him to lead every part of our lives.

The Bible tells us that God placed everything under Jesus’ authority and made Him the Head of the church (Ephesians 1:22). It also says that when we grow into Christ, the whole body grows together in love because each part is connected to Him (Ephesians 4:15–16). When people stop holding on to Christ, the body becomes weak and unhealthy (Colossians 2:19).

1. Jesus is the Source of Our Life Before Christ can be the Head over everything in the universe, God first made Him the Head of the church. This shows how important the church is to God and how central Jesus must be in our lives today.

Think about your own body. Every movement you make starts in your head. If the head is disconnected, the body cannot survive. In the same way, our spiritual life comes from Jesus .

The Bible says that anyone who has the Son has life, and that life is found in Him (1 John 5:11– 12). We do not receive a “piece” of Jesus and then go live on our own. Instead, God joins us completely to Christ.

This means we cannot live independently from Him. When we ignore Jesus or stop listening to Him, we become spiritually weak. Even though we have received life from Christ, that life remains in Him. So every day, we must depend on Him, stay connected to Him, and live in Him.

2. Jesus is Also Our Authority Because Jesus gives us life, He also has authority over us. Where life is, authority follows. Just as your body obeys signals from your head, believers must obey Christ.

To follow Jesus means letting Him decide the direction of our lives. We don’t get to say, “I know what God says, but I think…” When Jesus is truly our Head, we submit our opinions, choices, and plans to Him.

Many people say they follow Christ, but still want to stay in control. Yet Jesus is not only our Saviour— He is our Lord . When Paul met Jesus, the first thing he said was, “Who are You, Lord?” (Acts 9:5). True Christian life begins when we surrender and say, “Lord, You lead. I will follow.”

3. Holding Fast to the Head Brings Unity Holding fast to the Head means recognising that Jesus alone is in charge . When each believer stays connected to Christ, the whole church grows in love and unity.

Good relationships with other Christians come from a strong relationship with Jesus. If you are right with the Head, you will be right with the body. Problems among believers often start when people stop listening to Christ and start following their own ideas.

Christian fellowship is not built on personalities, talents, or friendships. It is built on Christ living in each of us . Even though we are different, the same Christ lives in every believer. That is why we can walk together.

4. Avoiding Cliques and Divisions God does not want divisions, cliques, or groups in the church. When believers form tight groups based only on personal friendships and leave Christ out, they stop holding fast to the Head. This creates separation and spiritual damage.

True love among Christians must include everyone in the body, not just a few. When we let Jesus lead our relationships, our hearts become as wide as His heart. Holding fast to the Head helps us love others without creating sides or divisions.

5. Walking by the Spirit To truly hold fast to Christ, two things must happen: • Our selfish nature must be dealt with through the cross • We must learn to walk by the Spirit.

The cross helps us say “no” to selfish desires and “yes” to God’s will. The Bible describes believers who follow the Lamb wherever He goes (Revelation 14:4). That kind of following is only possible when we let Jesus lead every step.

When our relationship with Christ is right, our relationships with others will also be right. Every believer has a direct connection to Jesus, the Head. When we help others, we do it because Christ leads us—not just because of human friendship.

Final Thought Holding fast to the Head is the key to growing as a Christian. Jesus is our life, our leader, and our source of unity. When we stay connected to Him, the church becomes strong, loving, and healthy. Without Him, nothing works. With Him, everything grows.

fields.title: The Service of the Member
fields.body_html:
This chapter helps us understand that being a Christian means more than simply believing in Christ. It means becoming an active member of His body . The Bible teaches that all believers form one body in Christ, and that each person belongs to one another (Romans 12:4–5).

Christianity, therefore, is not an individual journey but a shared life.

Many believers struggle not because they lack sincerity, but because they remain individualistic .

Individualism is not simply being an individual; it is an attitude that insists on living independently, acting alone, and focusing mainly on “my life”, “my calling”, and “my success”.

This spirit belongs to the old Adamic life and must be dealt with if we are to live in the reality of the body of Christ.

The opposite of the body is not sin alone — it is individualism . To truly experience the body of Christ, we must be delivered from the desire to live as though we are complete in ourselves.

I. From Believer to Member A person may be saved and yet still not live as a member of the body of Christ. Salvation brings us into Christ, but entering into the reality of the body requires further spiritual sight. Just as someone who is saved can recognise another saved person, so those who truly live in the body of Christ can discern when others are still living independently.

It is possible to understand biblical teaching without experiencing spiritual reality. Someone may understand the book of Romans and still not truly know salvation. In the same way, someone may appreciate the letter to the Ephesians and yet not know the body of Christ. Entering the body is not a matter of agreeing with teaching, but of being inwardly changed.

God allows us to be individuals, but He does not permit us to remain individualistic. Before seeing the body, much of our spiritual pursuit is centred on ourselves: • We want holiness so we can be holy.

• We desire power so we can be strong.

• We want fruit so we can be successful.

All of this revolves around “I”. This is not the body — it is self-centred spirituality.

When Peter preached at Pentecost and three thousand were saved, the other apostles did not compete with him, nor did Peter boast. Why? Because they saw the body. God is not seeking impressive individuals, but a corporate vessel . When the body is truly seen, jealousy and pride disappear.

To realise, “I am only a member”, is a great deliverance. A member is not the whole body, nor even half of it, but a part. Once a person truly sees the body, individualism loses its power.

Living as a Member To live as a member means allowing the body to be the boundary of our living and service. In the human body, when the hand works, it is the body that works; when the feet walk, it is the body that moves. No member acts for itself.

The same is true spiritually. A member of the body of Christ does not act for personal glory or ambition. Whether God places a person in a visible or hidden role makes no difference to one who truly knows the body. Pride and jealousy only exist where the body has not been fully seen.

Yet every member matters. One person’s spiritual failure affects the whole body, even if no one else sees it. Hidden sin, neglected prayer, or private disobedience weaken the church. In the body of Christ, when one member suffers, all suffer.

This is why we must pursue holiness, love, and spiritual growth — not merely for ourselves, but for the sake of the body .

II. Each Member’s Service Every member of the body has a function. Each believer has Christ within, and the way Christ is known and experienced becomes that believer’s portion of service .

Service in the church is not based on natural ability or talent, but on specific knowledge of Christ gained through life experience. This knowledge is not general or theoretical. It is personal, tested, and real.

In the human body, each part has a distinct function. Eyes see, ears hear, and the nose smells.

Each uniquely serves the body. In the same way, every believer has a particular ministry formed through what they have learned from the Lord.

Your ministry is not something you choose for yourself. It is what God forms in you through experience — often through trials, discipline, and suffering. What you gain from Christ in life becomes what you can supply to the church.

Life Before Doctrine True service flows from life, not from teaching alone. Doctrine without life cannot build the church. God always works in this order: life first, then teaching .

This pattern runs throughout Scripture. Abraham’s life revealed faith long before it became doctrine. Abel’s offering revealed the need for blood long before it was explained in writing. In the New Testament, the Gospels come before the Epistles — experience before explanation.

The same is true today. A person who has not learned Christ through experience cannot truly minister Him to others. Even a simple word spoken by someone with life can strengthen the church, while many words spoken without life can bring death.

God is seeking people in whom He can deposit life so that it may flow through them to others.

Life must have a channel, and God chooses believers to be those channels.

If life stops flowing in a member, the body suffers. There is no purely private defeat. Everything in the body is shared. Therefore, we must not live to ourselves, but hold fast to the Head and walk in fellowship.

fields.body_text: This chapter helps us understand that being a Christian means more than simply believing in Christ. It means becoming an active member of His body . The Bible teaches that all believers form one body in Christ, and that each person belongs to one another (Romans 12:4–5). Christianity, therefore, is not an individual journey but a shared life. Many believers struggle not because they lack sincerity, but because they remain individualistic . Individualism is not simply being an individual; it is an attitude that insists on living independently, acting alone, and focusing mainly on “my life”, “my calling”, and “my success”. This spirit belongs to the old Adamic life and must be dealt with if we are to live in the reality of the body of Christ. The opposite of the body is not sin alone — it is individualism . To truly experience the body of Christ, we must be delivered from the desire to live as though we are complete in ourselves. I. From Believer to Member A person may be saved and yet still not live as a member of the body of Christ. Salvation brings us into Christ, but entering into the reality of the body requires further spiritual sight. Just as someone who is saved can recognise another saved person, so those who truly live in the body of Christ can discern when others are still living independently. It is possible to understand biblical teaching without experiencing spiritual reality. Someone may understand the book of Romans and still not truly know salvation. In the same way, someone may appreciate the letter to the Ephesians and yet not know the body of Christ. Entering the body is not a matter of agreeing with teaching, but of being inwardly changed. God allows us to be individuals, but He does not permit us to remain individualistic. Before seeing the body, much of our spiritual pursuit is centred on ourselves: • We want holiness so we can be holy. • We desire power so we can be strong. • We want fruit so we can be successful. All of this revolves around “I”. This is not the body — it is self-centred spirituality. When Peter preached at Pentecost and three thousand were saved, the other apostles did not compete with him, nor did Peter boast. Why? Because they saw the body. God is not seeking impressive individuals, but a corporate vessel . When the body is truly seen, jealousy and pride disappear. To realise, “I am only a member”, is a great deliverance. A member is not the whole body, nor even half of it, but a part. Once a person truly sees the body, individualism loses its power. Living as a Member To live as a member means allowing the body to be the boundary of our living and service. In the human body, when the hand works, it is the body that works; when the feet walk, it is the body that moves. No member acts for itself. The same is true spiritually. A member of the body of Christ does not act for personal glory or ambition. Whether God places a person in a visible or hidden role makes no difference to one who truly knows the body. Pride and jealousy only exist where the body has not been fully seen. Yet every member matters. One person’s spiritual failure affects the whole body, even if no one else sees it. Hidden sin, neglected prayer, or private disobedience weaken the church. In the body of Christ, when one member suffers, all suffer. This is why we must pursue holiness, love, and spiritual growth — not merely for ourselves, but for the sake of the body . II. Each Member’s Service Every member of the body has a function. Each believer has Christ within, and the way Christ is known and experienced becomes that believer’s portion of service . Service in the church is not based on natural ability or talent, but on specific knowledge of Christ gained through life experience. This knowledge is not general or theoretical. It is personal, tested, and real. In the human body, each part has a distinct function. Eyes see, ears hear, and the nose smells. Each uniquely serves the body. In the same way, every believer has a particular ministry formed through what they have learned from the Lord. Your ministry is not something you choose for yourself. It is what God forms in you through experience — often through trials, discipline, and suffering. What you gain from Christ in life becomes what you can supply to the church. Life Before Doctrine True service flows from life, not from teaching alone. Doctrine without life cannot build the church. God always works in this order: life first, then teaching . This pattern runs throughout Scripture. Abraham’s life revealed faith long before it became doctrine. Abel’s offering revealed the need for blood long before it was explained in writing. In the New Testament, the Gospels come before the Epistles — experience before explanation. The same is true today. A person who has not learned Christ through experience cannot truly minister Him to others. Even a simple word spoken by someone with life can strengthen the church, while many words spoken without life can bring death. God is seeking people in whom He can deposit life so that it may flow through them to others. Life must have a channel, and God chooses believers to be those channels. If life stops flowing in a member, the body suffers. There is no purely private defeat. Everything in the body is shared. Therefore, we must not live to ourselves, but hold fast to the Head and walk in fellowship. Concluding Appeal Before making decisions, we must learn to seek fellowship. Nothing in the Christian life is merely individual. Everything is in the body, through the body, and for the body . May God give us light to see the body of Christ clearly. And having seen it, may we live as members and serve the church according to the real measure of Christ we have received.

fields.title: The Function and Harmony of the Members
fields.body_html:
This chapter shows us that although the body of Christ is one, it is made up of many members, and each member has a different function. Unity in the church does not mean sameness. Rather, it means that one life — the life of Christ — is expressed through many different people in many different ways . Scripture teaches that we are “one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Romans 12:4–5).

God’s purpose is that every believer should grow, serve, and function so that the body of Christ may be built up. The church matures as each part works properly (Ephesians 4:15–16). However, this oneness and growth are constantly attacked by Satan, whose aim is to weaken the body through division, impurity, and distraction. True unity is preserved only when Christ’s life has the central place in every member.

The Function of the Members For a believer who truly lives for the Lord and has been delivered from self-centred living, the most important outward expression of their life is that they function as a member of the church . Every member has a place, and every place matters.

If a believer does not express their function in the church, it reveals something inward. It may indicate that, although they appear spiritual, they have not yet been fully delivered from self.

When the self-life is truly dealt with, a believer will naturally begin to express their God-given function in the body.

No member should ever think that their portion is too small to matter. As long as a person has the life of God, that person is a member of the body and therefore has a function. Even the smallest function is irreplaceable. No member can take the place of another, and no function — however great — can substitute for the smallest one. If we truly saw this, it would bring us joy and freedom.

The New Testament itself illustrates this truth. Four Gospels present four distinct views of Christ. Matthew shows Him as King, Mark as Servant, Luke as the Holy and Perfect Man, and John as the Son of God, full of glory. Each Gospel reveals something essential, and none can replace the others.

In the same way, Peter, Paul, and John each express Christ differently in their writings. Christ is so rich that it takes believers from different backgrounds, ages, and experiences to express Him fully. The church is the place where the one life of Christ is displayed in many forms.

One Life, Many Functions The life of Christ is one, yet it expresses itself through many functions. When this life flows to the eyes, there is seeing; to the ears, hearing; to the feet, walking; and to the mouth, speaking.

Life is the same, but the functions differ.

What one believer can do in the body may not be done in the same way by anyone else. Some matters require a particular brother; others require a particular sister. Change the person, and the work may not be done at all. This is because each member has a specific function formed by the life of Christ within them.

A simple test of whether someone is living as a member is this: if their presence or absence in the church seems optional — not because of the smallness of their function, but because their function is not felt — then something is wrong inwardly. Where Christ’s life is active, function will be evident.

Satan’s Work of Disintegration God does His work on earth through the church, not through isolated individuals. For this reason, Satan’s primary strategy is to break the body apart . He works to create suspicion, misunderstanding, and quiet division among believers.

Often, these divisions are not caused by serious issues. Small offences, misinterpretations, or unspoken frustrations are enough. Satan uses our flesh, our stubbornness, and our love for the world as tools to weaken the body. When these things are allowed to remain, they create space for Satan to work.

True oneness is not based on agreement of opinions or outward organisation. Oneness is God Himself . When believers allow God to fully occupy them, they become one naturally. Satan does not need loud arguments to destroy oneness; he only needs to introduce something impure that replaces God in the heart.

An illustration helps us understand this. When concrete is mixed, even a small amount of clay prevents it from setting properly. In the same way, a small impurity — an unchecked desire, a personal ambition, a hidden sin — can weaken the unity of the body. Everything may appear normal outwardly, yet inwardly, the body is disintegrating.

The Need for Purification and the Cross The church is not primarily a doctrine or a system; it is the expression of Christ’s life . Oneness comes from life, not from effort. Therefore, the real need is not outward revival, but inward cleansing.

Each believer must ask searching questions: What place do my own desires have in me?

What place do my goals and plans have?

Is Christ truly central, or has something else taken His place?

God uses the cross and the Holy Spirit to purify us. The cross deals with our self-life, and the Spirit exposes and removes impurities. Even our confidence in being “right” can be used by Satan to cause division if it replaces humility before God.

Believers must be willing to receive light from God and correction from one another. This requires humility and a readiness to accept the dealings of the cross. Only in this way can the life of Christ flow freely and the body be built up in harmony.

Concluding Appeal If we truly love the Lord and have consecrated ourselves to Him, we must be willing to pay the cost of purification. We must allow Him to remove anything incompatible with His life so that Christ may be fully expressed through us.

When each member functions, when impurities are removed, and when Christ holds the central place, the body grows in unity and strength. This is the testimony God desires — a church where many members live and serve in harmony, expressing one life: the life of Christ .

fields.title: Obeying the Law of the Body of Christ
fields.body_html:
To live the Christian life properly, we must understand that God does not save believers to live alone . From the moment we are saved, we are brought into something much larger than ourselves — the Body of Christ . This body has its own life, its own order, and its own spiritual laws. To live well as Christians, we must learn to obey these laws.

This chapter focuses on one central truth: believers are members of one body and must live accordingly . Christianity is not meant to be individualistic. Every believer is joined to others, and no one can live, grow, or serve rightly apart from the Body.

The Scriptures show us that God places great importance on unity, fellowship, mutual submission, and shared responsibility among believers. The laying on of hands, the role of elders and apostles, and the principles of covering, restraint, and supply all reveal how seriously God takes the life of the Body.

The Revelation of the Body Comes Before the Life of the Body If we wish to live the life of the Body of Christ, we must first see the Body of Christ. Without this revelation, we will naturally continue to live independently, even while calling ourselves Christians.

Some people speak about the Body of Christ as though it were a small or obvious matter. But the truth is this: no one who has truly seen the Body can continue living as an individual . Once a believer receives this revelation, his entire way of living must change.

In the same way that a person who has truly seen Christ no longer trusts in his own good works for salvation, a person who has truly seen the Body will no longer act independently. If someone claims to understand the Body of Christ but continues to ignore fellowship, refuses submission, and insists on doing things his own way, that person has not truly seen the Body.

A genuine revelation always brings transformation.

Authority in the Body is the Authority of Life In the Body of Christ, authority belongs only to the Head — Jesus Christ . No member possesses authority in himself. Whatever authority a member has is received from the Head and expressed through life , not position.

This means that authority in the church is not about titles, background, education, age, or social standing. Authority is not given because someone is appointed; it is recognised because life is present .

A person does not become an eye because he is appointed as one. He is an eye because he can see. He does not become a hand because of a title, but because he can serve. As life functions, authority becomes evident.

It is a serious mistake when churches treat authority as a matter of position rather than life. God’s Word shows us clearly that authority is established through spiritual experience, obedience, and growth , not through human appointment alone.

When life and God’s appointment agree, submission becomes necessary. To refuse such submission is to lose the flow of life and become disconnected from the Body. When there is something wrong between you and another believer, you cannot say you have a normal relationship with Christ, the Head.

Learning Mutual Submission Many believers may grow in knowledge, manners, or religious activity, yet experience little growth in the life of the Body. This is deeply tragic.

In the church, we must learn mutual submission . Without it, the life described in Romans 8 cannot be expressed. When believers resist submission, they often feel dry, empty, and spiritually exhausted. But to those who truly discern the Body, submission is not a burden — it is a joy .

Submission keeps the Body healthy and allows life to flow freely.

Philip, the Apostles, and the Law of the Body (Acts 8) Acts 8 gives us a clear example of how the law of the Body works.

Philip, though not an apostle, preached Christ in Samaria with great power. Many believed miracles occurred, and the city was filled with joy. Yet something was missing — the Holy Spirit had not fallen upon the new believers .

Why? Because God was preserving the principle of the Body.

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard about the work in Samaria, they sent Peter and John. Only when the apostles laid hands on the believers did they receive the Holy Spirit. This showed that God does not recognise independent works . There was one Body, one work, and one anointing.

Had the Spirit fallen before the apostles arrived, Samaria might have become separate from Jerusalem. God prevented this to preserve the unity of the Body.

The Meaning of the Laying on of Hands Throughout Scripture, the laying on of hands represents union, fellowship, and identification .

In the Old Testament, when a person laid hands on a sacrifice, he was identifying himself with it.

In the New Testament, the laying on of hands signifies being joined to the Body .

This is why Scripture warns believers not to be careless in the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 5:22). To lay hands on someone is to share fellowship, and fellowship carries responsibility.

Baptism brings a believer into Christ.

The laying on of hands brings a believer into the Body.

It declares, “I am no longer independent. I belong to the Body, and I submit to its life and authority.”

The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Body The Holy Spirit is not given for personal independence. He is the Spirit of the one Body .

Seeking spiritual power for personal glory or private ambition opens the door to deception.

God desires a corporate vessel , not isolated individuals. Personal fruit alone does not satisfy God’s ultimate purpose.

Where the Body is recognised, the Spirit flows freely.

Gifts Imparted Through the Body Paul reminded Timothy that the gift he had received came through the laying on of hands. God used the apostles and elders as representatives of the Body to impart spiritual gifts.

These gifts were not for personal advancement, but for the building up of the Body . A believer who has received such a gift should no longer compete, envy, or seek recognition. Whether God uses him or another should not matter.

Healing, Anointing, and Discerning the Body James 5 teaches that some sickness comes from violating the law of the Body . Such sickness requires restoration to fellowship.

The elders anoint with oil to bring the believer back under the Head and into the Body. This is not about ordinary sin — that is dealt with by the Blood of Christ. This is about disharmony with the Body .

When one member is sick, all share responsibility. Confession and prayer must be mutual.

Healing flows where humility and fellowship are restored.

Paul’s Conversion and the Revelation of the Body When Saul persecuted believers, Jesus said, “Why are you persecuting Me ?” This revealed the deep union between Christ and His Body.

Later, the Lord refused to instruct Paul directly and instead sent Ananias, an unknown brother.

This taught Paul from the very beginning that no believer lives independently , no matter how greatly God uses him.

The Judgment and Help of the Brethren (Matthew 18) God places great authority in the gathered Body. When two or three believers deny themselves and gather in Christ’s name, the Lord stands in their midst .

When such believers agree that something is wrong, their judgment must be taken seriously — even above personal feelings. This is not blind obedience, but obedience grounded in humility and fellowship.

God uses apostles, elders, sent believers, and gathered brethren to represent the Body.

The Covering, Restraint, and Supply of the Body The Body of Christ provides: • Covering in spiritual warfare • Restraint against independence • Supply through fellowship Spiritual warfare is not fought alone. The armour of God belongs to the whole Body. Satan targets isolated believers, but trembles before united prayer.

No member can survive without the Body’s protection.

The Three Cardinal Principles of Life in the Body 1. Subjection to the Head (Christ) Life and authority go together. Obedience is the proof of life.

2. Fellowship with the Body Through fellowship, we receive what others have and supply what we possess.

3. Service as a Member We are not only receivers, but suppliers of life.

Final Word The Body of Christ is not merely a teaching — it is a life to be lived . Once a believer truly sees the Body, independence becomes impossible. Fellowship becomes natural. Supply flows freely.

God is not recovering a doctrine.

He is recovering a living Body .

Reflection Questions for Teens 1. In what ways do you tend to act independently instead of seeking fellowship?

2. Why do you think God places so much importance on unity in the church?

3. How does understanding the Body of Christ change the way you see authority?

4. What gifts or strengths has God given you to supply others?

5. Are you under the covering of the Body, or trying to fight spiritual battles alone?

END

fields.title: The Love Of Jesus—what It Is
fields.body_html:
There are times when something comes into our lives so charged with love that it seems, for a moment, to open the Eternal to us—or at least to open something of the Eternal. Of all eternal realities, the greatest is love.

It may come as a small and deeply personal touch upon us or our affairs, as gentle as the morning breeze moving through the leaves of a tree—something that cannot be captured or fully explained to another. Yet we know it is our Lord. And then perhaps the room we are in, with its furniture, books, and flowers, feels less real than His presence, and the heart is drawn into that sweetness of which the old hymn speaks: The love of Jesus—what it is; none but His loved ones know. Or it may be the human love around us, enfolding us like warm summer seas and bringing rest to the whole being. Can we ever stop wondering at the love of those who walk with us? And then, suddenly, we recognise our Lord in them. It is His love that they pour out upon us. O Love of God, made visible in those who love You, we worship You.

Or—perhaps not often, for a certain dimness seems more fitting for us in this life, yet sometimes, because our Lord is rich in mercy—we are allowed to lift our eyes and glimpse the love of God itself. And even then, how little we truly see. “That you may be able to comprehend the breadth and length and depth and height, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” —the words themselves reach beyond us.

What do we truly understand? What do we really know? Humbled and brought low, we take refuge in the Rock and bow in the dust before the glory of love in all its majesty—the love whose sign and symbol is the Cross.

And then the question breaks through, sharp and searching: What do I know of Calvary love?
fields.body_text: There are times when something comes into our lives so charged with love that it seems, for a moment, to open the Eternal to us—or at least to open something of the Eternal. Of all eternal realities, the greatest is love. It may come as a small and deeply personal touch upon us or our affairs, as gentle as the morning breeze moving through the leaves of a tree—something that cannot be captured or fully explained to another. Yet we know it is our Lord. fields.title: What Do I Know Of Calvary Love?
fields.body_html:
If I do not have compassion on my fellow servant, just as my Lord had compassion on me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I belittle those whom I am called to serve, speaking of their weaknesses, perhaps in contrast to what I think of as my strengths; if I adopt a superior attitude, forgetting, “Who made you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can easily discuss the shortcomings and sins of others; if I can speak casually even of a child’s wrongdoing, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I find myself almost carelessly taking failures for granted—“Oh, that’s what they always do,” or “Of course she talks like that; he always acts like that”—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I enjoy a joke at another’s expense; if I slight another in conversation, or even in thought, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can write an unkind letter, speak an unkind word, or think an unkind thought without grief and shame, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, when troubling things happen, I feel far more for my own anxiety than for the wounded heart of my Saviour, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I know little of His tenderness ( “The Lord turned and looked at Peter” ); if I know little of His courageous hopefulness for the truly humble and repentant ( “He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs’” ), then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I deal with wrongdoing for any reason other than that implied in the words, “From His right hand went a fiery law for them. Yes, He loved the people” ; if I can rebuke without inner pain, then I know nothing of Calvary love. If, when dealing with one who does not respond, I grow weary of the strain and step out from under the burden, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot be like the father who did not soften the hardships of the far country; if, in this sense, I refuse to allow the law of God— “the way of transgressors is hard” —to take effect because it pains me to watch that law at work, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am troubled by the reproach and misunderstanding that may follow action taken for the good of souls for whom I must give account, if I cannot commit the matter to God and go on in peace and silence, remembering Gethsemane and the Cross, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot hear “the sound of the rain” long before it falls, and, going up to some spiritual high place as near to God as I can, lack the faith to wait there with my face between my knees— though six times or sixty times I am told, “There is nothing” —until at last “a little cloud arises out of the sea,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

1 Kings 18:41 If my attitude towards one who has disappointed me is fear rather than faith; if I say, “Just what I expected,” when a fall occurs, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not look with eyes of hope upon all in whom there is even the faintest beginning, as our Lord did when, just after His disciples had argued about who should be greatest, He softened His rebuke with those melting words, “You are those who have continued with Me in My trials,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I hold against another a sin that has been confessed, repented of, and forsaken, allowing the memory of it to colour my thoughts and feed my suspicions, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not have the patience of my Saviour with souls who grow slowly; if I know little of that painful travail until Christ is fully formed in them, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I sympathise weakly with weakness, saying to one who is turning back from the Cross, “Spare yourself” ; if I withhold the bracing sympathy and the brave, strengthening word of true comradeship, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot keep silence about a disappointing soul—unless speaking is necessary for that soul’s good or for the good of others—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can wound another by speaking truthfully without careful preparation of spirit, and without being wounded far more deeply myself, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am afraid to speak the truth for fear of losing affection, or of hearing, “You do not understand,” or of losing my reputation for kindness; if I place my own good name above another’s highest good, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am content to heal a wound lightly, saying “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace; if I forget the piercing command, “Let love be without hypocrisy,” and blunt the edge of truth by speaking smooth things instead of right things, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I fear holding another to the highest calling because it is easier not to do so, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cling to choices simply because they are my choices; if I give any room to personal likes and dislikes, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I put my own happiness before the wellbeing of the work entrusted to me; if, though I have received this ministry and so much mercy, I grow weary and faint, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am gentle with myself and slide easily into the habit of self-pity and self-sympathy; if I do not, by God’s grace, practise endurance, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I myself dominate my thoughts; if my mind revolves around me; if I am so occupied with myself that I rarely have “a heart at leisure from itself,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, the moment I sense self crossing my threshold, I do not shut the door—and by the power of Him who works in us both to will and to act, keep that door firmly shut—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot happily take the second place—or the twentieth; if I cannot take the first without drawing attention to my unworthiness, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, when I discover something that has puzzled others, I forget Him who reveals deep and hidden things, who knows what lies in darkness and brings it to light; if I forget that He granted that insight to His most unworthy servant, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I cannot rest under what I do not understand, forgetting the words, “Blessed is anyone who is not offended because of Me,” or if I allow even a shadow of resentment to enter, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not give a friend the benefit of the doubt, but choose the worst interpretation rather than the best of what is said or done, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I take offence easily, if I am content to continue in a cold unfriendliness when friendship could be restored, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If a sudden jolt can make me speak an impatient, unloving word, then I know nothing of Calvary love.* A cup filled to the brim with sweet water cannot spill even one drop of bitter water, however suddenly it is shaken.

If I feel wronged when others accuse me of things I do not recognise in myself, forgetting that my sinless Saviour walked this road to the very end, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I feel bitterness towards those who condemn me, as I think, unjustly—forgetting that if they knew me as I know myself they would condemn me far more—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I say, “Yes, I forgive, but I cannot forget,” as though the God who washes all the sands of every shore each day could not cleanse such memories from my mind, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If someone whose help I greatly need seems content to build with wood, hay, and straw instead of gold, silver, and precious stones, and I hesitate to obey the light given to me and go on without that help because so few will understand, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the care of a soul—or a community—is entrusted to me, and I allow it to be weakened because the voice of the world, even my immediate Christian world, is loud in my ears, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I can best help others by doing work that undiscerning people call “not spiritual,” and inwardly I resist because what I truly crave is not the spiritual but the interesting and exciting, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If monotony tests me and I cannot endure drudgery; if slow minds irritate me and small disturbances unsettle me; if I magnify the trifles of life, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I am careless about the comfort or feelings of others, or about their small weaknesses; if I overlook their minor hurts and miss chances to smooth their path; if I make the gentle running of daily life more difficult, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If interruptions irritate me and private worries make me impatient; if I cast a shadow over others because I myself feel shadowed, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If souls suffer beside me and I scarcely notice, because the spirit of discernment is lacking in me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If there is any reserve in my giving to Him who loved me enough to give His dearest for me; if there is a hidden “but” in my prayer— “anything but that, Lord” —then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I become entangled in any inordinate affection; if things, places, or people hold me back from obedience to my Lord, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If something I am asked to do for another feels heavy, and yielding to inner reluctance I avoid doing it, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If praise lifts me up and blame casts me down; if I cannot rest under misunderstanding without defending myself; if I love being loved more than loving, being served more than serving, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I long to be the one who leads a captive soul into freedom, rather than caring only that it is set free; if I nurse disappointment when I fail instead of praying that another may be given the word of release, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I want to be known as the one who did what proved right, or as the one who first suggested it, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I do not forget such a trifle as personal success, so that it scarcely enters my mind—or, if it does, is never allowed to linger; if the taste of spiritual flattery is sweet to me, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If it is not simple and natural for me to say, “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If, in the fellowship of service, I seek to bind a friend to myself in a way that leaves others feeling excluded; if my friendships do not draw others in but remain self-centred, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I refuse to allow one dear to me to suffer for Christ’s sake; if I do not see such suffering as the highest honour offered to any follower of the Crucified; if I step into a place that belongs to Christ alone, making myself essential to a soul instead of leading it to cling to Him, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If my interest in the work of others is lukewarm; if I think mainly in terms of my own work; if the burdens of others are not my burdens, nor their joys my joys, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If an answer comes to prayer that I did not expect, though I believed I truly meant it, and I shrink back from it; if the burden my Lord asks me to carry is not the one I would choose, and I fret inwardly instead of welcoming His will, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I avoid being “ploughed under,” with all that such ploughing involves—rough handling, loneliness, uncongenial situations, unfamiliar tests—then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I question why something difficult is allowed and urge prayer that it be removed; if I cannot be trusted with disappointment or go on in peace amid mystery, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I exaggerate anything appointed to me, magnifying it in my own mind or subtly in the minds of others; if I allow it to appear “hard” ; if I look back with longing on what once was and linger in memory’s side paths until my usefulness is weakened, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the love that “alone makes light of every heavy thing and bears evenly every uneven thing” is not my heart’s desire, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I refuse to be a grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies— separated from all that once sustained it —then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I ask to be spared trial rather than delivered through it to the praise of His glory; if I forget that the way of the Cross leads to the Cross and not to a bed of flowers; if I shape my life—or even my thinking—so that I am surprised when the path is rough, despite the command, “Do not think it strange,” “Count it all joy,” then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If the ultimate demand, the hardest demand, cannot be made of me; if my fellow workers hesitate to ask it and turn to someone else, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

If I desire any place on earth other than the dust at the foot of the Cross, then I know nothing of Calvary love.

What I do not know, teach me, O Lord my God.

fields.title: What I Do Not Know, Teach Me, O Lord My God
fields.body_html:
Ihave felt these words to be scorching as I have written them. Yet it has been pressed upon me that, despite all our hymns and prayers—so many of them prayers for love—it is possible to be content with the shallows of love, if indeed such shallows deserve to be called love at all.

(Perhaps prayer often needs to be followed by a pause, so that we may have time to open our hearts to what we have asked for. We rush too quickly from one prayer to another, without waiting for the inward word that says, “I have heard you, My child.” ) The more we ponder our Lord’s words about love, and the burning words the Spirit inspired His followers to write, the more keenly we become aware of our deadly lack. The searchlight of the Spirit exposes us to ourselves, and such a revelation leaves us appalled. How can even He, who is the God of all patience, have patience with us? Like Job, we loathe ourselves and repent in dust and ashes.

But the light is not turned upon us to strip us of hope. There is a lifting up. If only we truly desire to be cleansed from self, with its entangling nets, its subtleties and disguises—its falsehoods, its easy substitution of brass for gold, as the Tamil saying puts it—if, hating unlove from the depths of our hearts, we cry out to be delivered, then our God will indeed be to us a God of deliverances.

No vision of the night, no spoken word, can reveal the depth of longing with which divine love waits until the heart, weary and sick of itself, turns to its Lord and says, “Take full possession.”

There is no need to plead with God to fill us with His love, as though He were reluctant. He is as willing as light is willing to flood a room opened to its brightness, as willing as water is to flow into an emptied channel. Love presses around us on every side, like the air we breathe. Cease to resist, and at once love takes possession.

As the fifteenth-century poem Quia Amore Langues says: Long and love thou never so high, my love is more than thine may be. More—far more. For just as His abundance of pardon surpasses our ability to tell it, so does His abundance of love. It is as far as the east is from the west, as high as the heavens are above the earth. Words fail us. Love rises beyond them all.

To look at ourselves leads only to despair. Thank God, the Blood cleanses.

If you are defiled, I will make you clean; if you are sick, I will heal you—have you ever found love so real?

Never, Lord—never.

Sometimes, when we are distressed by past failure and tormented by fear of failing again should we set our faces once more toward Jerusalem, nothing helps so much as allowing a familiar Scripture to sink into us and become part of our being. The words “grace upon grace” have helped me ever since I read, in a small old book by Bishop Moule, an explanation that opened their meaning to me—for until then, I had not understood them.

He explains that “for” means simply instead . The image is one of continual supply, an unceasing exchange—a constant replacement as needs arise.

He writes of a river: stand by its bank and watch the waters flow. A minute passes, then another.

Is it still the same river? Yes. But is it the same water? No. The water that passed a moment ago has moved on; fresh water has taken its place— water instead of water . So it is hour by hour, year by year, century by century: one river, ever-changing waters, living and not stagnant, because within the unchanging identity there is constant renewal. Grace takes the place of grace—and love the place of love—ever new, ever old, ever the same, ever fresh and young, through Christ.

There is no power strong enough to hold us together as a company and give life to all we do except this one power: love. That is why love is constantly attacked, for without it we become sounding brass and clanging cymbals.

This explains why, from time to time, those who desire to live the life of love are compelled to seek the searching and cleansing of the Spirit of God—first in the secret places of our own hearts, and then together. And we know how graciously God has met us, so that although we must always say, “Not that I have already attained,” yet by His enabling we press on.

There is another reason why the enemy attacks love. Something may occur on the outermost edge of our work that is, in a sense, the reflection of something hidden in the heart of one at the very centre. I have seen this again and again. It may never have been expressed in word or action; eye did not see it, ear did not hear it. Yet spiritual influences move where sight and sound do not reach. Unlove in any one of us—or even the absence of that quality of love we have been considering—can allow a slow stain to spread, until it reaches a soul at a moment of weakness, with harm that cannot be undone.

O Lord, forgive—Your very nature is mercy. Restore to me the comfort of Your help. Be pleased to deliver me, O Lord my God.

The way of love is never the easy way. If our hearts are set on walking in it, we must be prepared to suffer. “It was the way the Master went; should not the servant tread it still?” There may be times when we are shut in by circumstances that drain natural love until we feel as dry as grass on an Indian hillside under a blazing sun.

We have laboured for someone dear to us without ever thinking of it as labour. We have spent reserves of health that can never be recovered, yet we never counted the cost, nor would we have done so, because we loved so deeply. Our one hope was that the one so cherished would become a blessing to others—but it did not happen.

Slowly and unwillingly we become aware of a strange lack of response in the one for whom nothing had seemed too much; of a coldness that chills, a hardness that pushes away the heart that nearly broke to save that life from destruction.

Then—only those who have passed through such an hour will understand—a fear more terrible than pain grips us: Is the love of the years slipping away? *“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”—*is that fading from us? *“Love never fails”—*is love failing now?

Shall we meet lovelessness with lovelessness?

In such an hour, words written long ago gave voice to a desperate prayer: Deep calls to deep, O Lord, within me; Gathering strength, I come, Lord, to You. Jesus of Calvary, wounded for me, Ask what You will—but give me love.

Yes—ask what You will. Take hopes, joys, even the rewards of human affection, but do not let love depart. Nothing ordinary can meet this call; nothing in me is enough. O Lord of Love and Lord of Pain, abound in me in love. Love through me, Love of God.

Our dear Lord listens to prayers that rise from honest lips. For our comfort it is written that He causes those who love Him to inherit substance—the marvellous substance of “grace instead of grace,” the unending gift of His fullness. This grace is not an impersonal thing, but God Himself at work within us—the Lord active in the deepest springs of thought and will. God is love; therefore love itself is this blessed substance which the children of the Father inherit.

Once again, the river speaks. The empty riverbed inherits the water that pours into it from the heights. It does not create the water; it only receives it. Its channels are filled, its pools overflow, and the land is refreshed. So it is with us. Our treasuries of time—our years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes—are filled with the flowing wealth of love, so that we may bless others.

Who could have imagined such joy for us but He whose name is Love?

Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to the power at work within us—to Him be glory.

Let us end on a simple note. Let us listen to simple words. Our Lord speaks gently: “Trust Me, My child. Trust Me with a humbler heart and a fuller surrender to My will than ever before. Trust Me to pour My love through you, minute by minute. And if you become aware of anything that hinders that flow, do not wound My love by withdrawing in discouragement—for nothing hurts more than that. Draw closer. Come and hide in Me, even from yourself. Tell Me what troubles you. Trust Me to put My hand upon you and remove completely the boulder that has blocked the riverbed, and clear away the silt that has choked the channel. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised. I will perfect what concerns you. Do not fear, child of My love—do not fear.”

And now, to gather all into one page: Beloved, let us love.

Lord, what is love?

Love is that which shaped My life, led Me to My Cross, and held Me upon it.

Love is that which will make it your joy to lay down your life for your brothers.

Lord, always give me this love.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for love, for they shall be filled.

END
fields.body_text: Ihave felt these words to be scorching as I have written them. Yet it has been pressed upon me that, despite all our hymns and prayers—so many of them prayers for love—it is possible to be content with the shallows of love, if indeed such shallows deserve to be called love at all. (Perhaps prayer often needs to be followed by a pause, so that we may have time to open our hearts to what we have asked for. We rush too quickly from one prayer to another, without waiting for the inward word that says, “I have heard you, My child.” ) The more we ponder our Lord’s words about love, and the burning words the Spirit inspired His followers to write, the more keenly we become aware of our deadly lack.
