fields.title: How to Bear Sorrow
fields.body_html:
As believers our comfort must be in God, who refines us through trials rather than punishing us, as Christ bore all punishment on the cross. Sorrow reveals and strengthens virtues like patience, sympathy, and hope. Though friends may not fully understand, Jesus is a constant source of compassion and comfort. Instead of isolating ourselves, we find healing in helping others. This suffering, while painful, sows seeds of future joy, wisdom, and strength that will one day be realized.

You are passing through a time of deep sorrow. The love in which you placed your trust has failed you without warning. It has dried up like a brook in the desert that is now a dwindling stream, then shallow pools, and at last drought. You are always listening for footsteps that do not come. Waiting for a word that is not spoken, pining for a reply that tarries overdue. The savings of your life have vanished without warning. Instead of helping others, someone must help you. You must leave the warm nest that sheltered you from life’s storms. You must venture alone into a hostile world. Or, you receive an unexpected call to take on another's life. You must take no rest until you have guided it through dark, difficult seas to safety.

Your health, sight, and energy are failing. You carry a death sentence. The anguish of awaiting the future is almost unbearable. In other cases, there is a sense of recent loss.

The gap in the forest shows where the woodsman has been felling trees. At such times life seems almost insupportable. Will every day be as long as this? Will the slow-moving hours ever again quicken their pace?

Will life ever array itself in another garb than the torn autumn remnants of past summer glory? “Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?” (Psalm 77:9).

This road has been trodden by myriads. Think of the wars that have devastated every land. Of the Nimrods, the Nebuchadnezzars, the Timurs, and the Napoleons. Of the merciless slave trade. And of all the tyranny, oppression, and wrongs the weak have suffered at the hands of their fellows. Of the unutterable sorrows of women and children. You must see that most of our race shares your grief.

Jesus Christ Himself trod this difficult path, leaving traces of His blood on its flints. Apostles, prophets, confessors, and martyrs have passed by the same way. It is comforting to know that others have crossed the same dark valley. The vast crowd before the Lamb, wearing victory palms, came out of great tribulation. Where they were, we are; and, by God’s grace, where they are, we will be.

Do Not Talk About Punishment. You may talk of chastisement or correction. Our Father deals with us as with sons. You may speak of reaping the results of mistakes and sins, once planted in life's furrows. Or, you may bear the consequences of others' sins and mistakes. But, do not speak of punishment.

Jesus took on all the guilt and penalty of sins, and He removed them forever. His were the stripes and the chastisement of our peace. If God punishes us for our sins, Christ's sufferings were incomplete.

If He began to punish us, life would be too short for the infliction of all that we deserve. Also, how could we explain life's anomalies? The saints endure suffering, while the ungodly live peacefully. Surely, if our sufferings were penal, there would be a reversal of lots of these.

Sorrow is a refiner’s crucible. Another's neglect or cruelty may cause it. It might be due to uncontrollable circumstances or a dark past. But, since God allowed it, we must accept it. It is His test, a furnace to search and purify the soul. Suffering searches us as fire does metal. We think we completely devote ourselves to God until the cleansing fire of pain exposes us. Then we discover, as Job did, how much dross there is in us, and how little real patience, submission, and faith. Nothing detaches us from this world, its pleasures, and earthly loves more than this. Nothing but the life of Jesus in our mortal flesh can likely stop the self-life's power.

But God always keeps the discipline of sorrow in His own hands. Our Lord said, “My Father is the husbandman.” His hand holds the pruning knife. His eye watches the crucible. His gentle touch is on the pulse while the operation is in progress. He will not allow even the devil to have his own way with us. As in the case of Job, so always. The team allocates the moments with care. The test's severity is exact. It lies in unrecognized reserves of grace and strength. They will be sought and used under the pain of great pressure.

He holds the winds in His fist and the waters in the hollow of His hand. He doesn’t dare risk the loss of that which has cost Him the blood of His Son. “ No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it . (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In sorrow, the Comforter is near. “Very present in times of trouble.” He sits by the crucible, a Refiner of silver. He regulates the heat, marking every change. He waits for the scum to float away and for the clear, molten metal to mirror his face. No earthly friend may tread the winepress with you. But, the Savior is there, His garments stained with the blood of the grapes of your sorrow. Dare to repeat it often, though you do not feel it, and though Satan insists that God has left you, “You are with me.” Mention His name again and again, “Jesus, Jesus, You are with me.” So you will become conscious that He is there.

When friends come to console you, they speak of time's healing touch. They think forgetting is the best cure for sorrow. In their kindness, they suggest travel or fun. But they fail to see the dark night that hangs over your soul. So you turn from them sick at heart and prepared to say, as Job, “Miserable comforters are you all.” But, Jesus is nearer than they are. He knows their pain. He feels for them. His love is too deep for words. He waits to comfort them, like a mother with a suffering baby.

Study the art of this divine comfort. Then, you can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort you received from God (2 Corinthians 1:4). Some trials may come to us, as they do to our Lord. They exist to help us give "sympathy to others." We should observe each symptom of the pain with attention. We should also note each prescription of the Great Physician. We may have to help those with similar experiences in the future. So, we learn from our suffering. When we are perfect, we can help tormented souls. Our help will be priceless and eternal.

Do Not Shut Yourself Up with Your Sorrow. A friend, in deep grief, wrote that he must give up the Christian ministries he had loved. I replied, urging him not to. There is no solace for heart pain like ministry. Great suffering tempts us to isolate and withdraw. We want to sit alone and be silent. Do not yield to it. Break through the icy chains of the reserve, if they have already gathered. Arise, anoint your head and wash your face; go forth to your duty, with willing though chastened steps. All selfishness, in action or thought, is hurtful. It shuts out God's help and love.

Sorrow is apt to be selfish. The soul, full of grief and refusing comfort, becomes a Dead Sea. It is a place where no birds fly and nothing grows. And thus we miss the very lesson that God would teach us. His constant war is against the self-life, and every pain He inflicts is to lessen its hold upon us. But we may thwart His purpose. We may extract poison from His gifts, as men do with opium and alcohol from innocent plants.

A Hindu woman, a beautiful Eastern legend tells us, lost her only child. Wild with grief, she implored a prophet to give back her little one to her love. He looked at her tenderly for a long while and said: “Go, my daughter, bring me a handful of rice from a house into which Death has never entered, and I will do as you desire.” The woman at once began her search. She went from dwelling to dwelling and easily got rice. But, when they granted it, she asked, "Is everyone at the hearth—father, mother, children—none missing?"

The people invariably shook their heads, with sighs and looks of sadness. As far and wide as she wandered, there was always some vacant seat by the hearth. The legend says, as she passed on, her grief faded. The sorrow everywhere had overwhelmed her. Her heart, once consumed by its own pain, now yearned to share in the world's suffering. Her anguish turned to pity; her passion to compassion. She lost herself in the interest of all. She found redemption in redeeming.

Refrain from criticizing yourself for your intense feelings. Tears are natural. Jesus wept. A rainless thunderstorm is perilous. The pattering raindrops cool the air and relieve the charged atmosphere. The swollen brooks state that the snow is melting on the hills and spring is near. “Daughters of Jerusalem,” said our Lord, “Weep for yourselves and for your children.” (Luke 23:28). To bear sorrow with dry eyes and a stolid heart may befit a Stoic, but not a Christian. We should not scold nature, longing for its mate, its lost joy, the touch of a vanished hand, the sound of a still voice. We ask only that you surrender the will. This is the one consideration for those who suffer, is the will right? If it isn’t, God Himself cannot comfort. If it is, then the path will lead from the valley of the shadow of death to the banqueting table and the overflowing cup.

Many say, “I cannot feel surrendered. It is bad enough to have my grief to bear, but I have this added trouble, that I cannot feel surrendered.” My constant reply is: “You probably never can feel surrender, but you can.

The Lord Jesus, in the Garden of Gethsemane, has shown us how to suffer. He chose His Father’s will. Satan prompted Judas to mix the cup and give it to the Savior. But the Savior looked past Judas to the Father, who allowed his cruel act. He then said, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?" He then added, "If I cannot pass this unless I drink it, may your will be done." He gave up His own way, saying, "If you are willing, remove this cup from me." Still, not my will, but yours, be done.”

Let all sufferers who read these lines go apart and dare to say the same words: “Your will, and not mine. Your will be done in the earth of my life, as in the heaven of Your purpose. I choose Your will.” Say this thoughtfully and deliberately. Not because you feel it, but because you will. Not because the way of the cross is pleasant, but because it must be right. Say it, whenever the pain returns, whenever the wound bleeds. “Not my will, but Yours be done.” Dare to say yes to God.

“Even so, Father, for so it seems good in Your sight.”

And so you will be led to feel that all is right and well. A great calm will settle on your heart. It will be a peace beyond understanding. You will find a rest that coexists with suffering.

It will walk amid it, like the three young men in the fiery furnace. The burning coals must have felt like the dewy grass of a forest glade. The doctor told us my little child was dying. I felt like a stone. But in a moment, I seemed to give up my hold on her. She appeared no longer mine, but God’s.”

Be Sure to Learn God’s Lessons. Each sorrow carries at its heart a germ of holy truth. If you get and sow in your heart, you will bear fruit, as seed-corns from mummy cases do in modern soil. God has a meaning in each blow of His chisel, each incision of His knife. He knows the way that He takes. But his object is not always clear to us. In suffering, God touches the minor chords. He develops the passive virtues.

He reveals the treasures of darkness, the constellations of promise, the rainbow of hope, and the silver light of the covenant. What is character without sympathy, submission, patience, and trust? What is it without hope that grips the unseen as an anchor? But these Graces are only possible through sorrow.

Sorrow is a garden. Its trees bear the fruits of righteousness. They are peaceful. Do not leave without bringing them with you. Sorrow is a mine, its walls glistening with precious stones. Do not return to daylight without some specimens. Sorrow is a school.

You are sent to sit on its hard benches and learn from its black-lettered pages lessons that will make you wise forever; do not trifle away your chance of graduating there. Miss Havergal used to talk of “turned lessons."

Count on the afterward. God will not always be causing grief. He ploughs the dull brown acres. He wants to sow precious seed.

Believe that in days of sorrow, He is sowing light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. Look forward to the reaping. Expect the joy ahead. It will fill your heart with song when patience has done her perfect work.

You will live to recognize the wisdom of God’s choice for you. One day, you will see that the thing you wanted was only second best. You will be surprised to remember. You nearly broke your heart and wasted your life on something that would not have satisfied you. It was like a child chasing a butterfly or a soap bubble. You will meet your beloved again. You will have your love again. You will gain a deep character, great sympathy, and patience. You will understand and help others. If you give these to Christ, you will be glad you were afflicted. You will see God’s plan and purpose; you will reap His harvest; you will behold His face and be satisfied. Each wound will have its pearl. Each carcass will have a swarm of bees. Each foe will yield its goodly spoil, like Midian did to Gideon.

The way of the cross, rightly borne, is the only way to the everlasting light. Only the path through Gethsemane and over Calvary's hill leads to the Easter visions and the Ascension's glories. If we do not drink His cup, or are not baptized with His baptism, we cannot expect to share in the joys of His espousals and the ecstasy of His triumph. We must also fill up what is lacking in His sufferings. If we meet these conditions, we will not miss a note in the everlasting song or an element in the bliss possible to men.

Not possible to remove the adverb. The death of Hallam was the birthday of Tennyson’s beautiful poem “In Memoriam.” The cloud of insanity that brooded over Cowper gave us the hymn “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.” Milton’s blunders taught him to sing of “Holy light, offspring of heaven’s first-born.” Rist used to say, “The cross has pressed many songs out of me.” No one likely suffers without helping to ease grief, to triumph good over evil, love over hate, and light over darkness.

If you believe this, could you not bear to suffer? Isn't the worst part of suffering its loneliness? And, its aimlessness? Then dare to believe that no man dies to himself. Fall into the ground, bravely and cheerfully, to die. If you refuse, you will be alone. But if you yield, you will bear fruit. It will sweeten and strengthen the lives of others.

They may never know your name or thank you for your help.

fields.title: In the Secret of His Presence
fields.body_html:
Though God is omnipresent to all creation, many often fail to feel His presence due to our unawareness. Figures like Brother Lawrence found God's nearness even in humble tasks, while others felt divine connection through stillness and purity. This chapter encourages us to cultivate a sense of God’s presence through prayer, purity, and meditation on Scripture. God’s presence brings peace, purity, and strength, transforming life.

In one sense, God is always near us. He is not an absentee; he does not need anyone to bring him down from the heavens or up from the deep. He is near at hand. His Being pervades all being. Every world that floats like an island in space shows signs of His presence. It's like how your friend's home is full of clues of his house. They prove he lives there, though you have not seen his face. Every crocus pushing through the dark mould. Every firefly in the forest. Every bird that springs up from its nest before your feet. All that exists is as full of God's presence as the burning bush. Before it, Moses bared his feet in acknowledgment of God. But we do not always realise it. We often pass hours, and days, and weeks.

We sometimes pray. We go back and forth to His house, where the ladder of communication rests. Still, He is a shadow, a name, a tradition, a dream of days gone by. “Oh that I knew where find him!

That even come to his seat! I seek him, but he's not there.

Behold, I go forward, but he is not there,and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.” (Job 23:3, 8–9).

How different is this failure to see God's presence from the bliss of those who felt His nearness! Brother Lawrence, a simple cook, felt God's presence for over sixty years. He felt it while doing his humble duties.

Office as when partaking of the Holy Supper. John Howe, on the blank page of his Bible, wrote in Latin: "This morning I awoke from a most delightful dream. A bright stream of celestial rays from the Divine Majesty's throne seemed to dart into my open and expanded breast. I have often reflected on that great pledge of Divine favor. It has brought me much joy.”

Are not these, so blessed and inspiring, experiences like those of the author of the longest, and in some ways, the sublimest Psalm in the Psalter? He had been pounding out the golden ore of thought through the paragraphs of great power and beauty. Then, he seemed to sense that He of whom he had been speaking was near and bending over him.

The sense of the presence of God was born upon this inner consciousness. And, lifting up a face on which reverence and ecstasy met and mingled, he cried, “But you are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are true.” (Psalm 119:151).

The patriarch would find God in the bleak, joyless moors of our lives. We had trodden them without reverence.

Some have stood beside him, unaware of that Presence. If alive now, Elijah would sense it in the wind, the babbling of babies, and the rhythm of heartbeats.

" And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news ” (see 1 Kings 17:1; Luke 1:19).

To have Him as Friend, and Referee, and Counselor, and Guide. To know that, without the Captain of the Lord's host, there can be no Jericho in our lives. His invisible but mighty legions will make all walls fall. What wonder that saints of old waxed valiant in fight as they heard Him say, “ No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you. ”(Joshua 1:5). Be gone fear and sorrow and dread of the dark valley! “In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues.”(Psalm 31:20).

fields.title: The Fullness of the Spirit
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit plays a vital role in empowering believers to live holy lives, serve with boldness, and bear fruit. It urges Christians to seek the fullness of the Spirit for spiritual strength and victory over sin, emphasizing the need to have the right motives in doing so. The chapter calls for faith, obedience, and openness to the Holy Spirit's work in their lives “ And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit .” (Ephesians 5:18) Nothing can compensate the church, or the Christian, for the lack of the Holy Spirit! What the full stream is to the mill wheel that the Holy Spirit is to the church. What the principle of life is to the body that the Holy Spirit is to the individual. We will be helpless and ashamed before our troubles and enemies. Until we learn what He can be, as a mighty tide of love and power in the hearts of His Saints.

Some readers may suffer from spiritual weakness. It is due to a lack of the Holy Spirit. They are not completely without Him. If they were, they wouldn't be Christians. But, within them, He is only a faint presence, like a silver streak or a shallow brook. Why should we be content with this? The fullness of the Day of Pentecost, the endowment of power, the baptism of fire, are all within our reach.

Let us inspire ourselves with a holy ambition to get all that our God is willing to give. It is not difficult to show this contrast by analogies drawn from the Word of God. Can we not say, with reverence, that our Lord's ministry owed much of its power to His baptism? The Holy Spirit filled Him from His birth, but they anointed Him anew at His baptism. People said, with marked emphasis, that He filled with the Spirit. “ And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness .”(Luke 4:1).

And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. (v. 14). 14), and stood in the synagogue of His native town. He claimed the ancient prophecy and declared that the Spirit of God was upon Him. T he Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, (v. 18). His wondrous words and works come from the Holy Spirit's marvellous work on His human life. How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. (Acts 10:38).

Do you lack assurance? Sometimes you have felt happy and content.

But, those happy hours have fled. Someone breaks your rest. The mountain lake is overcast and ruffled by a gathering storm. You need a settled peace. You can find it in two things. First, you must understand what Jesus has done for you. Second, you must have the sealing of the Holy Spirit.

It is His sacred office to witness with our spirit that we are the children of God. He is the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, “Abba, Father!” Do you lack victory over sin? You should not wonder at this if you neglect the Holy Spirit. He is the blessed antidote to the risings and dominion of the flesh. He wars against the flesh, so that we may not fulfill its lusts. His glory fills the heart. Temptation's suggestions quench like sparks in the ocean. Sin cannot stand against the Holy Spirit. Darkness cannot resist the morning light.

If He feels grief, faces resistance, or gets quenched, His power and presence will hold back. There is no escape for the spirit. No remedy for its bitter remorse. Fasting, self-torture, and regrets will not help. The law of the spirit of life, which is in Christ Jesus, can alone make us free from the law of sin and death. But it can, and it will, only if we yield ourselves to its operation. Do you lack the fruits of holiness? Some we know are so righteous, they praise God.

We are instinctively drawn to them. Their faces are bright with the presence of the Lord, although they drink from the cup of His sorrows. They have a tender spirit. Their sweet, unselfish nature shines with a childlike humility. This creates an indescribable beauty in all they do. We lack these graces. There is little in us to attract men to Christ, much to repel. Locusts have stripped our boughs, leaving them naked and bare. And the reason is evident.

We have not let the Holy Spirit have His way with our inner life. If His presence had been within us, we would have borne much fruit. It would have been impossible not to. Do you lack power for service?

You have no burning thirst for the salvation of others.

You are not on fire for souls. You have never been in agony over the alienation of men from God. And when you speak, there is no power in what you say. The demons laugh at your attempts to exercise them. The sleeper turns for a moment, feeling restless, but soon falls into a deeper slumber than ever.

The home, the class, and the congregation yield no results. No handpicked fruit fills your basket. No shoal of fish breaks your nets. No recruits accept your call to arms. You cannot expect otherwise until you gain the power our Lord promised. He said, "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” (Acts 1:8). When the Holy Spirit filled the early Christians, they spoke the Word of God with boldness.

They bore strong witness to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. We would meet these and many other deficiencies if only the Holy Spirit filled us. If we sought only the full indwelling of the Holy Spirit, we would find joy, power, and a consciousness of Jesus. We would also find a habitual rest in the will of God. This would be a joyful discovery. Mr. Spurgeon once said he felt the Lord's presence every moment he was awake.

When the Spirit fills the heart, Jesus feels real and close. What is He to you? Do you awake in the morning beneath His light touch and spend the hours with Him? Can you often look up from your work and perceive His face? Do you seek power, grace, and direction from Him on a consistent basis? If He is but a fitful vision, you have not realised the first mark of the gift of Pentecost.

Total dedication to the Lord Jesus is a big step for most Christians. But, even that is not enough. It is often negative. But, we need something positive to meet our hearts and our times. We must seek this in our entire possession. It is for that mighty Spirit whose advent at Pentecost began a new era for the church and the world. Of course, He was always in the world. It was the Holy Spirit of Pentecost. He brooded over chaos. He spoke through the prophets and holy men. He gave nerve to the heroes and saints of the Old Testament.

The Day of Pentecost did not introduce a new Spirit into the world. It began an era in which even the weakest saints might have Him as much as those who lived before it. Before that day, only a few elite people had His fullness. They were the Elijahs, Isaiahs, and Daniels. Since then, He has poured out His plenitude on the many. This includes women, children, obscure thinkers, hidden workers, handmaids, and servants. It is for all who are ready to meet the conditions and accept the results. Why not on us? We are willing to admit that the special gifts of the Holy Spirit belong to the apostolic age. Given for a specific purpose, they are now withdrawn. It is a serious question. Would they have continued if the church had been more faithful to her sacred trust? But the special gifts of the Holy Spirit are altogether apart from His blessed fullness. That is not the exclusive right of any age.

Confined to no limited era or epoch in the history of the church, His fullness pours its tide of light, and it is as powerful as the Nile in flood. It will reach every remote plot and garden. If we keep the channel clear, it will fertilize and enrich them.

Alas, many believe the Almighty, like a bankrupt builder, built His church's portico with marble and finished it with common brick!

“ And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, ” (Ephesians 5:18) is an injunction as wide-reaching in its demands as “ Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her , ” (v. You can find 25) on the same page. It is a positive command, which we must obey for our good, and all God’s commands are enabling.

In other words, He prepares us to become what He tells us to be. On the Day of Pentecost, the apostle Peter spoke to the crowds. His words are our charter to the fullness of the Holy Spirit. He told them that the ascended Lord's sudden fullness fulfilled an ancient prophecy. It was not for them only or for their children, but for as many as were afar off. It was for those whom the Lord God will call. Are you one of His called ones? Then rejoice because that fullness is for you! Be not faithless but believing! Claim the covenant part at once. Thank God for your lot in an age of such marvellous possibilities.

Excite the Holy Desire by Considering What the Fullness of the Spirit Means.

We cannot expect to have it if we are quite content to live without it. Our Father is unlikely to trust this priceless gift to those indifferent to it. If desire is weak, do not expect the Holy Spirit's fullness. A fleeting desire is not enough. It may burn bright today, but it will lie dormant for months and years. There must be a strong purpose. It must withstand ten days of waiting and the silence or denial that may come.

And yet the flame of desire needs fuel.

We must muse before that fire can burn. So, we must, by quiet thought, stir up the gift within us. This is what it means to be Spirit- filled.” There is no book that will so move us in this direction as the Acts of the Apostles. It is a marvel to see the impact this fullness had on those who first received it. Cowards became brave. Dull minds, once stumped by simple truths, now grasped the Master's plan. Rivalry, suspicion, and a desire for power had once stirred their bosoms. Each thought herself superior and sought to excel in her service to the saints. Their words held such power that crowds became congregations. Christ's murderers became His worshipers and friends.

No council of clever men could withstand the simple power of facts. Shook towns and countries. Thousands converted to the unlearned but eager preachers of the Cross. This was due to the power that the whole church now owned. And there is not a fragment of reason that it should not do so much for us. As we compare that success to our slow progress, won't we long for Him to work similar results through us?

Studying the biographies of recent, saintly men may yield the same results. Happy the person within reach of a library, the shelves of which are well lined with books of holy biography! He will never lack for more stimulus. He will read the stories of McCheyne and W. C. Burns, of Brainerd and Martyn, of Jonathan Edwards and others. He will not envy or complain. He will, instead, pray to heaven. He will ask that he may do much. Moreover, the promises of the Scriptures are enough to incite us to the uttermost.

Rivers of living water should flow from us. We should never be anxious about our words. They would give them to us.

We should teach ourselves all things and lead ourselves to the truth. We should know Christ and change into His image. We should have power. It is all so fascinating. One can't help but want the Holy Spirit to charge them, like a jar with electricity. And, if need be, we will prepare to bear the test of long waiting, as the faithful few did in the Upper Room.

Seek This Blessed Fullness from the Right Motive.

If you seek this fullness to attract people or transform a difficulty, you may miss it. You must be set on the one purpose of magnifying the Lord Jesus in your body, whether by life or death. Ask that you destroy all inferior motives and that this burns strong and clear within you. God will not find water for us to use to turn our own waterwheels. He will do nothing to minister to our pride. He will not give us the Holy Spirit to gain celebrity, a name, or an easy, self-satisfied life. If we seek the Holy Spirit only for our happiness, it is unlikely He will be given. His one passion is the glory of the Lord Jesus, and He can only make His abode with those who are willing to be at one with Him in this. “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?” (Amos 3:3).

But, if you desire to magnify the Lord Jesus in you, rejoice. If you long, above all, for men to turn to Him, as they did from John the Baptist, then rejoice. You are near a blessing beyond words to describe. If your motives fall below this standard, trust Him to purify them. Offer Him a free entrance within.

It will not then be long before there shall be a gracious response; and the Lord, whom you seek, shall suddenly come to His temple, and He shall sit as a refiner of silver, that ministers may offer an offering in righteousness.

“ Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming, says the LORD of hosts. But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the LORD.” (Malachi 3:1–3).

Consider That Holy Scripture Is His Special Organ. A subtle danger besets the teaching of this most helpful doctrine, and it is one that we need to guard against. Some earnest people have overemphasized the Holy Spirit's inner light and guidance. They have neglected the Word He gave, which still works on human hearts. This is a great mistake and the prolific parent of all kinds of evil.

If we ignore the Word of God, we open ourselves to many voices in our hearts. We then lack a test, a standard of truth, or an appeal. How can we know the Spirit of God in complex cases brought to the court of conscience, without a judgement based on the Word of God?

We must not be content with the Spirit without the Word, or with the Word without the Spirit. Our life must travel along these two, as the locomotive along the parallel rails The Word is the Spirit's chosen organ. Only through devout contact with it can we detect His voice. The Spirit will enter our hearts by the Word. It is like the heart of the sun passing into our rooms with its beams of light that enter through the open window. We need a widespread revival of Bible study. These mines of Scripture, lying beneath the surface, call for investigation. Those who heed this call and study the Word's inner meaning will soon find the fulfillment they seek.

"To commune with God, there is no better way than to walk in your room or in the open air, with your Bible in hand. Meditate on it, and turn its precepts and promises into prayer." God walks in the glades of Scripture, as of old He walked in those of Paradise.

Be Prepared to Let the Holy Spirit Do As He Will with You. The Holy Spirit is in us, so Christ is too. He dwells in us by the Spirit, as the sun dwells in the world by the atmosphere vibrating with waves of light. But we must yield to Him at all times, just as water conforms to the shape of the containing vessel. This is not easy. It requires constant self-judgment and a deep shame of our own lives. What is our position before God in this respect? We have chosen Jesus as our substitute, but have we also chosen Him by the Holy Spirit as our Life?

Can we say, like the apostle: “ I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. ” (Galatians 2:20). If so, we must be prepared for all that it involves. We must be willing for the principle of the new life to grow at the expense of the self-life. We must consent to one increasing while the other decreases, through painful processes. Nay, we must be ever on the alert. We must hasten the processes of judgment, condemnation, and crucifixion. We must keep true in our allegiance to the least behest of the Holy Spirit, though it costs tears of blood.

The perpetual filling of the Holy Spirit is only possible to those who obey Him and who obey Him in all things. There is nothing trivial in this life. Neglecting small commands may soon let a soul escape the sunlit circle. It would then lose the Spirit's full, gracious power. A look, a word, a refusal may suffice to grieve Him in ourselves and to quench Him in others. Count the cost, yet do not shrink back, afraid of what He may demand. He is the Spirit of love. He loves us too much to cause grief, unless there is a reason. We would approve of it if we knew as much as He.

Receive Him by Faith. “ Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or concerning a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath .” (Colossians 2:16). Faith is the one law of the divine household. You once obtained forgiveness and salvation by faith. So, now claim and receive the Holy Spirit's fullness.

Fulfill the conditions already named. Wait in silence before God in prayer. He gives His Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. Next, accept this gift with reverence. Then, rise and go on your way.

Trust that God has kept His word and that you are now filled with the Spirit. Trust Him day by day to fill you and keep you filled. According to your faith, they will do it to you.

There may not be at first the sound of rushing wind, or the coronet of fire, or the sensible feeling of His presence. Do not look for these, any more than the young convert would look to feeling as an evidence of acceptance. But believe, despite your feelings, that you fill yourself.

Say over and over, “I thank You, O my God, that You have kept Your word with me. I opened my mouth, and You filled it, though yet I am not aware of any special change.” Over time, the feeling will penetrate your mind. You will rejoice with great joy. Then, the fruits of the Spirit will show themselves.

But remember, you must not fill yourself once for all. Like the apostles of old, we must seek perpetual refillings. The second chapter of Acts filled those who filled again in the fourth. Happy is that man. He never leaves his chamber in the morning without the Spirit's fullness! He must be a skilled scholar in God's school. The anointing he has received, like fresh oil, will stay in him and teach him all things. Above all, he will be taught the secret of abiding fellowship with Christ, for it is written, “ But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you.

But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.” (1 John 2:27). When you sense a leak, or when your energy is low, seek a refill. Also, when a new talent or ministry emerges, seek a recharge. Go to the same source for spiritual power and a fresh anointing by the Holy Spirit. The Acts of the Apostles uses three tenses about the filling of the Spirit. They have modern counterparts: Filled: a sudden experience for a specific work. “ Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, 'Rulers of the people and elders,” (Acts 4:8). And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. (Acts 13:52). And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. (Acts 6:8). Of course, this writer does not realise all that is in the doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

The fiery baptism of the Holy Spirit may be something far beyond. Let us not be content to miss anything possible to be redeemed men. But, leaving the past behind, let us press on to the future. Let us strive to grasp all for which Christ Jesus has apprehended us.

THE END

And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. ” (Galatians 2:20). If so, we must be prepared for all that it involves. We must be willing for the principle of the new life to grow at the expense of the self-life. We must consent to one increasing while the other decreases, through painful processes. Nay, we must be ever on the alert. We must hasten the processes of judgment, condemnation, and crucifixion. We must keep true in our allegiance to the least behest of the Holy Spirit, though it costs tears of blood. The perpetual filling of the Holy Spirit is only possible to those who obey Him and who obey Him in all things. There is nothing trivial in this life. Neglecting small commands may soon let a soul escape the sunlit circle. It would then lose the Spirit's full, gracious power. A look, a word, a refusal may suffice to grieve Him in ourselves and to quench Him in others. Count the cost, yet do not shrink back, afraid of what He may demand. He is the Spirit of love. He loves us too much to cause grief, unless there is a reason. We would approve of it if we knew as much as He. Receive Him by Faith. “ Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or concerning a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath .” (Colossians 2:16). Faith is the one law of the divine household. You once obtained forgiveness and salvation by faith. So, now claim and receive the Holy Spirit's fullness. Fulfill the conditions already named. Wait in silence before God in prayer. He gives His Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. Next, accept this gift with reverence. Then, rise and go on your way. Trust that God has kept His word and that you are now filled with the Spirit. Trust Him day by day to fill you and keep you filled. According to your faith, they will do it to you. There may not be at first the sound of rushing wind, or the coronet of fire, or the sensible feeling of His presence. Do not look for these, any more than the young convert would look to feeling as an evidence of acceptance. But believe, despite your feelings, that you fill yourself. Say over and over, “I thank You, O my God, that You have kept Your word with me. I opened my mouth, and You filled it, though yet I am not aware of any special change.” Over time, the feeling will penetrate your mind. You will rejoice with great joy. Then, the fruits of the Spirit will show themselves. But remember, you must not fill yourself once for all. Like the apostles of old, we must seek perpetual refillings. The second chapter of Acts filled those who filled again in the fourth. Happy is that man. He never leaves his chamber in the morning without the Spirit's fullness! He must be a skilled scholar in God's school. The anointing he has received, like fresh oil, will stay in him and teach him all things. Above all, he will be taught the secret of abiding fellowship with Christ, for it is written, “ But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.” (1 John 2:27). When you sense a leak, or when your energy is low, seek a refill. Also, when a new talent or ministry emerges, seek a recharge. Go to the same source for spiritual power and a fresh anointing by the Holy Spirit. The Acts of the Apostles uses three tenses about the filling of the Spirit. They have modern counterparts: Filled: a sudden experience for a specific work. “ Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, 'Rulers of the people and elders,” (Acts 4:8). And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. (Acts 13:52). And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. (Acts 6:8). Of course, this writer does not realise all that is in the doctrine of the Holy Spirit. The fiery baptism of the Holy Spirit may be something far beyond. Let us not be content to miss anything possible to be redeemed men. But, leaving the past behind, let us press on to the future. Let us strive to grasp all for which Christ Jesus has apprehended us. THE END

fields.title: The Personality Of The Holy Spirit
fields.body_html:
This chapter emphasises that before understanding the work of the Holy Spirit, we must know Him as a real Person, not just a force or influence. The Holy Spirit is a Divine Person who deserves our love, trust, worship, and surrender. When believers recognize Him as their ever-present Friend and Helper, their Christian life is transformed. True Christian living comes from daily fellowship with the Holy Spirit, allowing Him to guide and use us.

Before one can correctly understand the work of the Holy Spirit, one must first know the Spirit Himself. A frequent source of error and obsession about the work of the Holy Spirit is the attempt to study and understand His work without first of all coming to know Him as a Person. It is of the highest importance from the standpoint of worship that we decide whether the Holy Spirit is a Divine Person, worthy to receive our adoration, our faith, our love, and our entire surrender to Himself, or whether it is simply an influence emanating from God or a power or an illumination that God imparts to us. If the Holy Spirit is a person, and a Divine Person, and we do not know Him as such, then we are robbing a Divine Being of the worship, faith, and love, and the surrender to Him which are His due.

It is also of the highest importance from the practical standpoint that we decide whether the Holy Spirit is merely some mysterious and wonderful power that we in our weakness and ignorance are somehow to get hold of and use, or whether the Holy Spirit is a real Person, infinitely holy, infinitely wise, infinitely mighty and infinitely tender who is to get hold of and use us. The former conception is utterly heathenish, not essentially different from the thought of the African fetish worshipper who has his god whom he uses. The latter conception is sublime and Christian. Let's think of the Holy Spirit as so many do, as merely a power or influence. Our constant thought will be, “How can I get more of the Holy Spirit?” But if we think of Him in the Biblical way as a Divine Person, our thought will rather be, “How can the Holy Spirit have more of me?” The conception of the Holy Spirit as a Divine influence or power that we are somehow to get hold of and use leads to self-exaltation and self-sufficiency.

Someone who thinks a lot about the Holy Spirit b ut wrongly believes they’ve received Him will almost always become proud, acting like they’re better than other Christians. One frequently hears such persons say, “I am a Holy Ghost man,” or “I am a Holy Ghost woman.” But if we once grasp the thought that the Holy Spirit is a Divine Person of infinite majesty, glory, and holiness, and power, who in marvelous condescension has come into our hearts to make His abode there and take possession of our lives and make use of them, it will make us more reverent. I can think of no thought more humbling or more overwhelming than the thought that a person of Divine majesty and glory dwells in my heart and is ready to use me.

It is of the highest importance from the standpoint of experience that we know the Holy Spirit as a person. Thousands and tens of thousands of men and women can testify to the blessing that has come into their own lives as they have come to know the Holy Spirit, not merely as a gracious influence (emanating, it is true, from God) but as a real Person, just as real as Jesus Christ Himself, an ever- present, loving Friend and mighty Helper, who is not only always by their side but dwells in their heart every day and every hour and who is ready to undertake for them in every emergency of life. Thousands of ministers, Christian workers and Christians in the humblest spheres of life have spoken to me, or written to me, of the complete transformation of their Christian experience that came to them when they grasped the thought (not merely in a theological, but in an experimental way) that the Holy Spirit was a Person and consequently came to know Him. There are at least four distinct lines of proof in the Bible that the Holy Spirit is a person.

1. All the distinctive characteristics of personality are ascribed to the Holy Spirit in the Bible. What are the distinctive characteristics, or marks, of personality? Knowledge, feeling, or emotion, and will. Any entity that thinks and feels and wills is a person. When we say that the Holy Spirit is a person, some understand us to mean that the Holy Spirit has hands and feet and eyes and ears and mouth, and so on, but these are not the characteristics of personality but of corporeity. All of these characteristics or marks of personality are repeatedly ascribed to the Holy Spirit in the Old and New Testaments.

We read in 1 Corinthians 2:10- 11, “God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. Who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.” Here, knowledge is ascribed to the Holy Spirit. We are taught that the Holy Spirit is not merely an influence that illuminates our minds to comprehend the truth, but a Being who Himself knows the truth.

In 1 Corinthians 12:11, we read, “But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only about the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you.” Here, will is ascribed to the Spirit, and we are taught that the Holy Spirit is not a power that we get hold of and use according to our will, but a Person of sovereign majesty, who uses us according to His will. This distinction is of fundamental importance in our getting into right relations with the Holy Spirit. It is at this very point that many honest seekers, who are seeking power and efficiency in service, go astray.

They are reaching out after and struggling to get possession of some mysterious and mighty power that they can make use of in their work according to their own will. They will never get possession of the power they seek until they come to recognize that there is no Divine power for them to get hold of and use in their blindness and ignorance, but that there is a Person, infinitely wise, as well as infinitely mighty, who is willing to take possession of them and use them according to His own perfect will. When we stop to think of it, we must rejoice that there is no Divine power that beings ignorant as we are, so liable to err, to get hold of and use. How appalling might the results be if there were? But what a holy joy must come into our hearts when we grasp the thought that there is a Divine Person, One who never errs, who is willing to take possession of us and impart to us such gifts as He sees best and to use us according to His wise and loving will.

We read in Romans 8:27, “And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.” In this passage mind is ascribed to the Holy Spirit. The Greek word translated as “mind” is a comprehensive word, including the ideas of thought, feeling, and purpose. It is the same that is used in Romans 8:7, where we read that “For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, f or it does not submit to God's law, indeed it cannot.” So then, in this passage, we have all the distinctive marks of personality ascribed to the Holy Spirit.

We find the personality of the Holy Spirit brought out most touchingly and suggestively in Romans 15:30, “I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf”, here we have “love” ascribed to the Holy Spirit. The reader would do well to stop and ponder those five words, “the love of the Spirit.” We dwell often upon the love of God the Father. It is the subject of our daily and constant thought. We dwell often upon the love of Jesus Christ, the Son. Who would think of calling himself a Christian who passed a day without meditating on the love of his Saviour, but how often have we meditated upon “the love of the Spirit”?

Each day of our lives, if we are living as Christians ought, we kneel in the presence of God the Father and look up into His face and say, “I t hank you, Father, for "Your great love led You to give Your one and only Son to die on the cross at Calvary for me."

Each day of our lives, we also look up into the face of our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, and say, “Oh, "Glorious Lord and Saviour, Jesus, Son of God, I thank You for loving me so much that You didn’t cling to Your place as equal with God. Instead, you gave it up, leaving behind all the glory of heaven to come to this broken world, take my sins on yourself, and die in my place on the cross at Calvary.” But how often do we kneel and say to the Holy Spirit? "Oh, eternal and limitless Spirit of God, thank You for loving me so much that You came into this dark and sinful world to find me. You patiently pursued me until I finally saw how lost I was and how much I needed a Savior. You opened my eyes to see that Jesus Christ is exactly the Savior I needed." Yet we owe our salvation just as truly to the love of the Spirit as we do to the love of the Father and the love of the Son. If it had not been for the love of God the Father looking down upon me in my utter ruin and providing a perfect atonement for me in the death of His own Son on the cross of Calvary, I would have been in hell today.

If it had not been for the love of Jesus Christ, the eternal Word of God, looking upon me in my utter ruin and obedience to the Father, putting aside all the glory of heaven for all the shame of earth and taking my place, the place of the curse, upon the cross of Calvary and pouring out His life utterly for me, I would have been in hell to-day. But if it had not been for the love of the Holy Spirit, sent by the Father in answer to the prayer of the Son John 14:16 leading Him to seek me out in my utter blindness and ruin and to follow me day after day, week after week, and year after year, when I persistently turned a deaf ear to His pleadings, following me through paths of sin where it must have been agony for that holy One to go, until at last I listened and He opened my eyes to see my utter ruin and then revealed Jesus to me as just the Saviour that would meet my every need and then enabled me to receive this Jesus as my own Saviour; if it had not been for this patient, long-suffering, never-tiring, infinitely-tender love of the Holy Spirit, I would have been in hell to-day. Oh, the Holy Spirit is not merely an influence or a power or an illumination but is a Person just as real as God the Father or Jesus Christ, His Son.

The personality of the Holy Spirit comes out in the Old Testament as truly as in the New, for we read in Nehemiah 9:20, “You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst.” Here, both intelligence and goodness are ascribed to the Holy Spirit. Some tell us that while it is true the personality of the Holy Spirit is found in the New Testament, it is not found in the Old. But it is certainly found in this passage. As a matter of course, the doctrine of the personality of the Holy Spirit is not as fully developed in the Old Testament as in the New. But the doctrine is there.

There is perhaps no passage in the entire Bible in which the personality of the Holy Spirit comes out more tenderly and touchingly than in Ephesians 4:30: “30 And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” Here, grief is ascribed to the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is not a blind, impersonal influence or power that comes into our lives to illuminate, sanctify, and empower them. No, He is immeasurably more than that, He is a holy Person who comes to dwell in our hearts, One who sees every act we perform, every word we speak, every thought we entertain, even the most fleeting fancy that is allowed to pass through our minds; and if there is anything in act, or word or deed that is impure, unholy, unkind, selfish, mean, petty or untrue, this infinitely holy One is deeply grieved by it. I know of no thought that will help one more than this to lead a holy life and to walk softly in the presence of the Holy One. How often a young man is kept back from yielding to the temptations that surround young manhood by the thought that if he should yield to the temptation that now assails him, his holy mother might hear of it and would be grieved by it beyond expression.

How often some young man has had his hand upon the door of some place of sin that he is about to enter and the thought has come to him, “If I should enter there, my mother might hear of it and it would nearly kill her,” and he has turned his back upon that do or and gone away to lead a pure life, that he might not grieve his mother.

But there is One who is holier than any mother, One who is more sensitive against sin than the purest woman who ever walked this earth, and who loves us as even no mother ever loved, and this One dwells in our hearts, if we are Christians, and He sees every act we do by day or under cover of the night; He hears every word we utter in public or in private; He sees every thought we entertain, He beholds every fancy and imagination that is permitted even a momentary lodgment in our mind, and if there is anything unholy, impure, selfish, mean, petty, unkind, harsh, unjust, or in anywise evil in act or word or thought or fancy, He is grieved by it. If we allow those words, “Grieve not t he Holy Spirit of God,” to sink into our hearts and become the motto of our lives, they will keep us from many a sin.

How often some thought or fancy has knocked for an entrance into my mind and was about to find entertainment when the thought has come, “T he Holy Spirit sees that thought and will be grieved by it,” and that thought has gone.

II. Many acts that only a Person can perform are ascribed to the Holy Spirit. If we deny the personality of the Holy Spirit, many passages of Scripture become meaningless and absurd. For example, we read in 1 Corinthians 2:10, “But these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.” This passage sets before us the Holy Spirit, not merely as an illumination whereby we are enabled to grasp the deep things of God, but a Person who Himself searches the deep things of God and then reveals to us the precious discoveries which He has made.

We read in Revelation 2:7, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spiri t says to the churches.

To the one who conquers, I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God.”

Here, the Holy Spirit is set before us, not merely as an impersonal enlightenment that comes to our mind but as a Person who speaks and, out of the depths of His wisdom, whispers into the ear of His listening servant the precious truth of God.

In Galatians 4:6, we read, “And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father! ” Here, the Hol y Spirit is represented as crying out in the heart of the individual believer. Not merely a Divine influence producing in our hearts the assurance of our sonship, but one who cries out in our hearts, who bears witness together with our spirit that we are sons of God. (See also Romans 8:16) The Holy Spirit is also represented in the Scripture as one who prays. We read in Romans 8:26, “Likewise, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself interc edes for us with groanings too deep for words.” It is plain from this passage that the Holy Spirit is not merely an influence that moves us to pray, not merely an illumination that teaches us how to pray, but a Person who Himself prays in and through us.

There is wondrous comfort in the thought that every true believer has two Divine Persons praying for him, Jesus Christ, the Son who was once upon this earth, who knows all about our temptations, who can be touched with the feeling of our infirmities and who is now ascended to the right hand of the Father and in that place of authority and power ever lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2); and another Person, just as Divine as He, who walks by our side each day, yes, who dwells in the innermost depths of our being and knows our needs, even as we do not know them ourselves, and from these depths makes intercession to the Father for us. The position of the believer is indeed one of perfect security with these two Divine Persons praying for him.

We read again in John 15:26, “But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.” Here the Holy Spirit is set before us as a Person who gives His testimony to Jesus Christ, not merely as an illumination that enables the believer to testify of Christ, but a Person who Himself testifies; and a clear distinction is drawn in this and the following verse between the testimony of the Holy Spirit and the testimony of the believer to whom He has borne His witness, for we read in the next verse, “And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” So there are two witnesses, the Holy Spirit bearing witness to the believer and the believer bearing witness to the world.

The Holy Spirit is also spoken of as a teacher. We read in John 14:26, “But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.” And similarly, we read in John 16:12 - 14, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” And in the Old Testament, Nehemiah 9:20, “You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your m anna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst.”

In all these passages, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is not a mere illumination that enables us to apprehend the truth, but a Person who comes to us to teach us day by day the truth of God. It is the privilege of the humblest believer in Jesus Christ not merely to have his mind illumined to comprehend the truth of God, but to have a Divine Teacher to daily teach him the truth he needs to know (1 John 2:20-27).

The Holy Spirit is also represented as the Leader and Guide of the children of God. We read in Romans 8:14, “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.” He is not merely an influence that enables us to see the way that God would have us go, nor merely a power that gives us strength to go that way, but a Person who takes us by the hand and gently leads us on in the paths in which God would have us walk.

The Holy Spirit is also represented as a Person who has the authority to command men in their service of Jesus Christ. We read of the Apostle Paul and his companions in Acts 16:6- 7: “And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. 7 And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.” Here it is a Person who takes the direction of the conduct of Paul and his companions, and a Person whose authority they recognized and to whom they instantly submit.

Further still than this, the Holy Spirit is represented as the One who is the supreme authority in the church, who calls men to work and appoints them to office. We read in Acts 13:2, “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” And in Acts 20:28, “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God,[a] which he obtained with his blood.” There can be no doubt to a candid seeker after truth that it is a Person, and a person of Divine majesty and sovereignty, who is here set before us.

From all the passages here quoted, it is evident that many acts that only a person can perform are ascribed to the Holy Spirit.

III. An office is predicated of the Holy Spirit that can only be predicated of a person.

Our Saviour says in John 14:16- 17, “ And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper,[a] to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.” Our Lord had announced to the disciples that He was about to leave them. An awful sense of desolation took possession of them. Sorrow filled their hearts (John 16:6) at the contemplation of their loneliness and absolute helplessness when Jesus should thus leave them alone.

To comfort them, the Lord tells them that they shall not be left alone, that in leaving them He was going to the Father, and that He would pray the Father and He would give them another Comforter to take the place of Himself during His absence. Is it possible that Jesus Christ could have used such language if the other Comforter who was coming to take His place was only an impersonal influence? Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you,” if this Comforter whom He was to send was simply an impersonal influence or power?

No, one Divine Person was going, another Person just as Divine was coming to take His place, and it was expedient for the disciples that the One go to represent them before the Father, for another just as Divine and sufficient was coming to take His place. This promise of our Lord and Saviour of the coming of the other Comforter and His abiding with us is the greatest and best of all for the present dispensation. This is the promise of the Father (Acts 4), the promise of promises. We shall take it up again when we come to study the names of the Holy Spirit.

IV. Treatment is predicated on the Holy Spirit, which could only be predicated of a Person. We read in Isaiah 63, “Yet they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit. So he turned an d became their enemy, and he fought against them.” Here we are told that the Holy Spirit is rebelled against and grieved (Ephesians 4:30). Only a person can rebel against, and only a person of authority. Only a person can be grieved.

You cannot grieve a me re influence or power. In Hebrews 10:29, we read, “Of how much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?” Here we are told that the Holy Spirit is “done despite unto” (“treated with contumely”— Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament).

There is but one kind of entity in the universe that can be treated with contumely (or insulted), and that is a person. It is absurd to think of treating an influence or a power or any kind of being except a person with contumely. We read again in Acts 5:3, “But Peter said, 'Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to k eep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land?” Here we have the Holy Spirit represented as one who can be lied to. One cannot lie to anything but a person.

In Matthew 12:31- 32, we read, “Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgi ven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.”

Here we are told that the Holy Spirit is blasphemed against. It is impossible to blaspheme anything but a person. If the Holy Spirit is not a person, it certainly cannot be a more serious and decisive sin to blaspheme Him than it is to blaspheme the Son of man, our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ Himself.

Here, then, we have four distinctive and decisive lines of proof that the Holy Spirit is a Person .

Theoretically, most of us believe this, but do we, in our real thought of Him and our practical attitude towards Him, treat Him as if He were indeed a Person? At the close of an address on the Personality of the Holy Spirit at a Bible conference some years ago, one who had been a church member many years, a member of one of the most orthodox of our modern denominations , said to me, “I never thought of it before as a Person.” Doubtless, this Christian woman had often sung:  Praise God from whom all blessings flow,  Praise Him, all creatures here below,  Praise Him above, ye heavenly host,  Praise Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. ” Doubtless, she had often sung: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and the Holy Ghost, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, World without end, Amen.”

But it is one thing to sing words; it is quite another thing to realize the meaning of what we sing. If this Christian woman had been questioned regarding her doctrine, she would doubtless have said that she believed that there were three Persons in the Godhead, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but a theological confession is one thing, a practical realization of the truth we confess is quite another.

So the question is altogether necessary, no matter how orthodox you may be in your creedal statements, do you regard the Holy Spirit as indeed a real Person, as Jesus Christ, as loving and wise and strong, as worthy of your confidence and love and surrender as Jesus Christ Himself? The Holy Spirit came into this world to be with the disciples of our Lord after His departure, and to us, what Jesus Christ had been to them during the days of His companionship with them (John 14:16-17).

Is He that to you? Do you know Him? Every week in your life, you hear the apostolic benediction, “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the communion of the Holy Ghost be with you all ” (2 Corinthians 13:14), but while you hear it, do you take in the significance of it? Do you know the communion of the Holy Ghost? The fellowship of the Holy Ghost? The partnership of the Holy Ghost?

The comradeship of the Holy Ghost? The intimate personal friendship of the Holy Ghost?

Herein lies the whole secret of a real Christian life, a life of liberty and joy and power and fullness. To have as one's ever-present Friend, and to be conscious that one has as his ever-present Friend, the Holy Spirit, and to surrender one's life in all its departments entirely to His control, this is true Christian living.

The doctrine of the Personality of the Holy Spirit is as distinctive of the religion that Jesus taught as the doctrines of the Deity and the atonement of Jesus Christ Himself. But it is not enough to believe the doctrine one must know the Holy Spirit Himself. The whole purpose of this chapter (God help me to say it reverently) is to introduce you to my Friend, the Holy Spirit.
