But Jesus Christ says, “No.” There is another preparation so all essential that a man must not undertake this work until he has received it. “But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” A distinguished theological professor has said that the question ought to be put to every candidate for the ministry, “Hav e you met God?” Yes, but we ought to go farther than this and be even more clear; to every candidate for the ministry we should put the question, “Have you been baptized with the Holy Spirit?” and if not, we should say to him as Jesus said to the first pre achers of the Gospel, “Sit down until you are endued with power from on high.” But not only is this true of ordained ministers, it is true of every Christian, for all Christians are called to ministry of some kind. Any man who is in Christian work, who has not received the baptism with the Holy Spirit, ought to stop his work right where he is and not go on with it until he has been “clothed with power from on high.” But what will our work do while we are waiting? “What did the world do during these ten da ys while the early disciples were waiting?” They knew the saving truth, they alone knew it; yet in obedience to the Lord's command they were silent. The world was no loser. Beyond a doubt, when the power came, they accomplished more in one day than they would have accomplished in years if they had gone on in disobedience to Christ's command. We, too, after that we have received the baptism with the Spirit, will accomplish more real work for our Lord in one day than we ever would in years without this power. Even if it were necessary to spend days in waiting, they would be well spent, but we shall see later that there is no need that spend days in waiting, that the baptism with the Holy Spirit may be received today. Someone may say that the Apostles had gone on missionary tours during Christ's lifetime, even before they were baptised with the Holy Spirit. This is true, but that was before the Holy Spirit was given, and before the command was given, “But stay in the city until you are clothed with power fr om on high.” After that , it would have been disobedience and foolishness and assumption to have gone forth without this anointing, and we are living today after the Holy Spirit has been given and after the charge has been given to stay until clothed. We come now to the question of first importance, namely, who can be baptised with the Holy Spirit? At a convention some years ago, a very intelligent Christian woman, a well-known worker in educational as well as Sunday school work, sent me this question: “You have told us of the necessity of the baptism with the Holy Spirit, but who can have this baptism? The church to which I belong teaches that the baptism with the Holy Spirit was restricted to the apostolic age. Will you not tell us who can have the baptism with the Holy Spirit?” This question is answered in the most explicit terms in the Bible. We read in Acts 2:38- 39, “And Peter said to them, 'Repent and be baptised every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” What is the promise to which Peter refers in the thirty -ninth verse? There are two interpretations of the passage; one is that the promise of this verse is the promise of salvation; the other is that the promise of this verse is the promise of the gift of the Holy Spirit (or the baptism with the Holy Spirit; a comparison of Scripture passages will show that the two expressions are synonymous). Which is the correct interpretation? There are two laws of interpretation universally recognised among Bible scholars. These two laws are the law of usage (or “usus loquendi” as it is called) and the law o f context. Many a verse in the Bible standing alone might admit of two or three or even more interpretations, but when these two laws of interpretation are applied, it is settled to a certainty that only one of the various possible interpretations is the true interpretation. The law of usage is this, that when you find a word or phrase in any passage of Scripture and you wish to know what it means, do not go to a dictionary but go to the Bible itself, look up the various passages in which the word is used and especially how the particular writer being studied uses it, and especially how it is used in that particular book in which the passage is found. Thus, you can determine what the precise meaning of the word or phrase is in the passage in question. The law of context is this: that when you study a passage, you should not take it out of its connection but should look at what goes before it and what comes after it; for while it might mean various things if it stood alone, it can only mean one thing in the connection in which it is found. Let us apply these two laws to the passage in question. First of all, let us apply the law of usage. We are trying to discover what the expression “the promise” means in Acts 2:39. Turning back to Acts 1:4 - 5, we read, “And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” It is evident, then, that here the promise of the Father means the baptism with the Holy Spirit. Turn now to the second chapter and the thirty- third verse, “Being therefore by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, He hath poured forth this, which ye see and hear.” In this passage, we are told in so many words that the promise is the promise of the Holy Spirit. If this unique expression means the baptism with the Holy Spirit in Acts 1:4-5, and the same thing in Acts 2:33, by what same law of interpretation can it possibly mean something entirely different six verses farther down in Acts 2:39? So the law of usage establishes it that the promise of Acts 2:39 is the promise of baptism with the Holy Spirit. Now, let us apply the law of context, and we shall find that, if possible, this is even more crucial. Turn back to the thirty- eighth verse, “And Peter said to them, 'Repent and be baptised every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” So it is evident that the promise is the promise of the gift or baptism with the Holy Spirit. It is settled then by both laws that the promise of Acts 2:39 is that of the gift of the Holy Spirit, or baptism with the Holy Spirit. Let us then read the verse in that way, replacing this equivalent expression for the expression “the promise,” “For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” “It is to you,” says Peter, that is, to the crowd assembled before him. There is nothing in that for us. We were not there, and that crowd were all Jews, and we are not Jews; but Peter did not stop there, he went further and said , “And to your children,” that is to the next generation of Jews, or all future generations of Jews. Still, there is nothing in it for us, for we are not Jews; but Peter went further and said, “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off.” That does take us in. We are the Gentiles who were once “afar off,” but now “made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13, 17). But lest there be any mistake about it whatever, Peter adds, “ Even as many as the Lord our God shall call unto Him.” So on the very day of P entecost, Peter declares that the baptism with the Holy Spirit is for every child of God in every coming age of the church's history. Some years ago, at a ministerial conference in Chicago, a minister of the Gospel from the Southwest came to me after a l ecture on the Baptism with the Holy Spirit and said, “The church to which I belong teaches that the baptism with the Holy Spirit was for the apostolic age alone.” “I do not care,” I replied, “what the church to which you belong teaches, or what the church to which I belong teaches. My only question is, what does the Word of God teach?” “For the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself. “Has he called you?” I asked. “Yes, He certainly h as.” “Is the promise for you then?” “Yes, it is.” He took it, and the result was a transformed ministry. Some years ago, at a students' conference, the gatherings were led by a prominent Episcopalian minister, a man greatly honoured and loved. I spoke at this conference on the Baptism with the Holy Spirit, and dwelt upon the significance of Acts 2:39. That night, as we sat together after the meetings, this servant of God said to me, “Brother Torrey, I was greatly interested in what you had to say today on the Baptism with the Holy Spirit. If your interpretation of Acts 2:39 is correct, you have your case, but I doubt it. Let us talk it over,” which we did. Several years later, in July 1894, I was at the students' conference at Northfield. As I entered the back door of Stone Hall that day, this Episcopalian minister entered the front door. Seeing me, he hurried across the hall and held out his hand and said, “You were right about Acts 2:39 at Knoxville, and I believe I have a right to tell you something better, that I have been baptised with the Holy Spirit.” I am glad that I was right, not that it is of any importance that I should be right, but the truth thus established is of immeasurable importance. Is it not glorious to be able to go around the world and face audiences of believers and to be able to tell them, and to know that you have God's Word under your feet when you tell them, “You may all be baptised with the Holy Spirit”? But that unspeakably joyous and glorious thought has its solemn side. If we may be baptised with the Holy Spirit, then we must be. If we are baptised with the Holy Spirit, then souls will be saved through our agency, who will not be saved if we are not baptised. If we are not willing to pay the price of this baptism and therefore are not baptised we shall be responsible before God for every soul that might have been saved who was not saved because we did not pay the price and therefore did not obtain the blessing. I often tremble for myself and my brethren in the ministry, and not only for my brethren in the ministry but for my brethren in all forms of Christian work, even the most humble and obscure. Why? Because we are preaching error? No, many in these dark days are doing that, and I tremble for them; but that is not what I mean now. Do I mean that I tremble because we are not preaching the truth? For it is quite possible not to preach error and yet not preach the truth; many a man has never preached a word of error in his life, but still is not preaching the truth, and I do tremble for them; but that is not what I mean now. I mean that I tremble for those of us who are preaching the truth, the very truth as it is in Jesus, the truth as it is recorded in the written Word of God, the truth in its simplicity, its purity and its fullness, but who are preaching it in “persuasive words of man's wisdom” and not “in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4.). Preaching it in the energy of the flesh and not in the power of the Holy Spirit. There is nothing more death- dealing than the Gospel without the Spirit's power. “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” It is solemn business preaching the Gospel either from the pulpit or in quiet ways. It means death or life to those that hear, and whether it means death or life depends largely on whether we preach it with or without the baptism with the Holy Spirit. We must be baptised with the Holy Spirit. Even after one has been baptized with the Holy Spirit, no matter how clear that baptism may be, one needs to be filled with the Spirit. This is the clear teaching of the New Testament. We read in Acts 2:4, “ They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance .” One of those who was present on this occasion a nd who was filled with the Holy Spirit was Peter. Indeed, he stands forth most prominently in the chapter as a man baptised with the Holy Spirit. But we read in Acts 4:8, “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, etc.” Here we read again that Peter was filled with the Holy Ghost. Further down in the chapter, we read, in the thirty-first verse, that being gathered together and praying, they were “ they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness .” We are expressly told in the context that two of those present were John and Peter. Here then was a third instance in which Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit . It is not enough that one be filled with the Holy Spirit once. We, need a new filling for each new emergency of Christian service. The failure to realize this need of constant refilling with the Holy Spirit has led to many a man who at one time was greatly used to God, being utterly laid aside. There are many today who once knew what it was to work in the power of the Holy Spirit who have lost their function and their power. I do not say that the Holy Spirit has left them I do not believe He has but the manifestation of His presence and power has gone. One of the saddest sights among us today is that of the men and women who once toiled for the Master in the mighty power of the Holy Spirit who are now practically of no use, or even a hindrance to the work, because they are trying to go in the power of the blessing received a year, five years or twenty years ago. For each new service that is to be conducted, for each new soul that is to be dealt with, for each new work for Christ that is to be performed, for each new day and each new emergency of Christian life and service, we should seek and obtain a new filling with the Holy Spirit. We must not “neglect” the gift that is in us (1 Timothy 4:14), “For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God” (2 Timothy 1 -6). Repeated fillings with the Holy Spirit are necessary for to continuance and increase of power. The question may arise, “Shall we call these new fillings with the Holy Spirit ‘fresh baptisms’ with the Holy Spirit?” To this we would answer, the expression “baptism” is never used in the Scriptures of a second experience and there is something of an beginning character in the very thought of baptism, so if one wishes to be Biblical, it would seem to be better not to use the term “baptism” of a second experience but to limit it to the first experience. On the other hand “ filled with the Holy Spirit” is used in Acts 2:4 to describe the experience promised in Acts 1:5, where the words used are “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” It is evident from this and from other passages that the two expressions are to a large extent equivalent. However, if we confine the expression “baptism with the Holy Spirit” to our first experience, we shall be more Biblical, and it would be good to speak of one baptism but many fillings. But I would a great deal rather that one should speak about new or fresh baptisms with the Holy Spirit, standing for the all- important truth that we need repeated fillings with the Holy Spirit, than that he should so insist on exact wording that he would lose sight of the truth that repeated fillings are needed, i. e. , I would rather have the right experience by a wrong name, than the wrong experience by the right name. We need to be filled with the Holy Spirit. I am sometimes asked, “Have you received the second blessing ?” Yes, and the third and the fourth and th e fifth and hundreds beside, and I am looking for a new blessing today. We come now to the question of first practical importance, namely, what must one do to obtain baptism with the Holy Spirit? This question is answered most plainly and positively in the Bible. A plain path is laid down in the Bible consisting of a few simple steps that anyone can take, and anyone who takes these steps will certainly enter into the blessing. This is a very positive statement, and we would not dare be so positive if the Bible were not equally positive. But what right have we to be uncertain when the Word of God is positive? There are seven steps in this path: 1. The first step is to we accept Jesus Christ as our Saviour and Lord . We read in Acts 2:38, “Repent and be baptiz ed every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” Is not this statement as positive as the one we made above? Peter says that if we do certain things, the result will be, “Y ou will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” All seven steps are in this passage, but we shall refer later to other passages as throwing light upon this. The first two steps are in the word “repent.” “ You must repent ,” said Peter. What does it mean to rep ent? The Greek word for repentance means “an afterthought” or “change of mind.” To repent then means to change your mind. But change your mind about what? About three things; about God, about Jesus Christ, about sin. What the change of mind is about in any given instance must be determined by the context. As determined by the context in the present case, the change of mind is primarily about Jesus Christ. Peter had just said in the thirty-sixth verse, “Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified. Now, when they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Then it was that Peter said, “You must repent,” “Change your mind about Jesus, change your mind from that attitude of mind that rejected Him and crucified Him to that attitude of mind that accepts Him as Lord and King and Saviour.” This then is the first step towards receiving the baptism with the Holy Spirit; receive Jesus as Saviour and Lord; first of all receive Him as your Saviour. Have you done that? What does it mean to receive Jesus as Saviour? It means to accept Him as the One who carried our sins in our place on the cross (Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21) and to trust God to forgive us because Jesus Christ died in our place. It means to rest all our hope of acceptance before God upon the finished work of Christ upon the cross of Calvary. Many proclaim to be Christians who have not done this. When you go to many who call themselves Christians and ask them if they are saved, they reply, “Yes.” Then if you ask them the question “Upon what are you resting as the ground of your salvation?” they will reply something like this, “I go to church; I say my prayers, I read my Bible, I have been baptised, I have united with the church, I partake of the Lord's supper, I attend prayer-meeting, and I am trying to live as near right as I know how.” If these things are what you are resting upon as the gr ound of your acceptance before God, then you are not saved, for all these things are your works (all proper in their places but still your works). W e are distinctly told in Romans 3:20 that “For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight.” But if you go to others and ask them if they are saved, they will reply “Yes.” And then if you ask them upon what they are resting as the ground of their acceptance before God, they will reply something to this effect, “I am not resting upon anyth ing I ever did, or upon anything I am ever going to do; I am resting upon what Jesus Christ did for me when He carried my sins in His body on the cross. I am resting in His finished work of atonement.” If this is what you are resting upon, then you are saved, you have accepted Jesus Christ as your Saviour and you have taken the first step towards baptism with the Holy Spirit. The same thought is taught elsewhere in the Bible, for example in Galatians 3:2 Here Paul asks of the believers in Galatia, “Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?” Just what did he mean? On one occasion, when Paul was passing through Galatia, he was held there by some illness. We are not told what it was, but at all events, he was not so ill but that he could preach to the Galatians the Gospel, or glad tidings, that Jesus Christ had redeemed them from the curse of the law by becoming a curse in their place, by dying on the cross of Calvary. These Galatians believed this testimony; this was the hearing of faith, and God set the stamp of His approval upon their faith by giving them, as a personal experience, the Holy Spirit. But after Paul had left Galatia, certain Judaizers came down from Jerusalem, men who were substituting the law of Moses for the Gospel and taught them that it was not enough that they simply believe on Jesus Christ but in addition to this they must keep the law of Moses, especially the law of Moses regarding circumcision, and that without circumcision they could not be saved i.e., they could not be saved by simple faith in Jesus (Acts 15:1). These young converts in Galatia became all upset. They did not know whether they were saved or not; they did not know what they must do, and all was confusion. It was just as when modern Judaizers come around and get after young converts and tell them that, in addition to believing in Jesus Christ, they must keep the Mosaic Seventh Day Sabbath, or they cannot be saved. This is simply the old conflict breaking out at a new point. When Paul heard what had happened in Galatia, he was very indignant and wrote the Epistle to the Galatians simply to expose the utter error of these Judaizers. He showed them how Abraham himself was justified before he was circumcised by simply believing God (Galatians 3:6), and how he was circumcised after he was justified as a seal of the faith which he already had while he was in circumcision. In addition to this proof of the error of the Judaizers, Paul appeals to their own personal experience. He says to them, “You received the Holy Spirit, didn’t you? ” “Yes.” “How did you receive the Holy Spirit, by keeping the Law of Moses, or by the hearing of faith, the simple acceptance of God's testimony about Jesus Christ that your sins were laid upon Him, and that you are thus justified and saved?” The Galatians had had an experience of receiving the Holy Spirit and Paul appeals to it, and recalls to their mind how it was by the simple hearing of faith that they had received the Holy Spirit. The gift of the Holy Spirit is God's seal upon the simple acceptance of God's testimony about Jesus Christ, that our sins were laid upon Him, and thus trusting God to forgive us and justify us. This then is the first step towards receiving the Holy Spirit. But we must not only receive Jesus as Saviour, we must also receive Him as Lord. Of this we shall speak further in connection with another passage in the fourth step. 2. The second step in the path that leads into the blessing of being baptised with the Holy Spirit is surrendering to sin . Repentance as we have seen is a change of mind about sin as well as a change of mind about Christ; a change of mind from that attitude of mind that loves sin and indulges sin to that attitude of mind that hates sin and renounces sin. The Holy Spirit is a Holy Spirit, and we cannot have both Him and sin. We must make our choice between the Holy Spirit and unholy sin. We cannot have both. He that will not give up sin cannot have the Holy Spirit. It is not enough that we renounce one sin, two or three, or many sins; we must renounce all sin . If we cling to one single known sin, it will shut us out of the blessing. Here we find the cause of failure in many people who are praying for the baptism with the Holy Spirit, going to conventions and hearing about the baptism with the Holy Spirit, reading books about the baptism with the Holy Spirit, perhaps spending whole nights in prayer for the baptism with the Holy Spirit, and yet obtaining nothing. Why? Because there is some sin to which they are clinging. People often say to me, or write to me, “I have been praying for the baptism with the Holy Spirit for a year (five years, ten years, one man said twenty years). Why do I not receive?” In many such cases, I feel led to reply, “It is sin, and if I could look down into you r heart this moment as God looks into your heart, I could put my finger on the specific sin.” It may be what you are pleased to call a small sin, but there are no small sins. Some sins concern small things, but every sin is an act of rebellion against God, and therefore no sin is a small sin. A conflict with God about the smallest thing is sufficient to shut one out of the blessing. Mr. Finney tells of a woman who was greatly exercised about the baptism with the Holy Spirit. Every night after the meetings, she would go to her rooms and pray way into the night and her friends were afraid she would go insane, but no blessing came. One night as she prayed, some little matter of head adornment, a matter that would probably not trouble many Christians to-day, but a matter of conflict between her and God, came up (as it had often come up before) as she knelt in prayer. She put her hand to her head and took the pins out of her hair and threw them across the room and said, “There they go!” and instantly the Holy Ghost fell upon her. It was not so much the matter of head adornment as the matter of controversy with God that had kept her out of the blessing. If there is anything that always comes up when you get nearest to God that is the thing to deal with. Some years ago at a convention in a Southern state, the presiding officer, a minister in the Baptist Church, called my attention to a man and said, “That man is the pope of our denomination in everything he says goes, but he is not at all with us in this matter, but I am glad to see him here.” This minister kept attending the meetings. At the close of the last meeting where I had spoken upon the conditions of receiving the baptism with the Holy Spirit, I found this man awaiting for me in the vestibule. He said, “I did not stand up to your invitation today.” I replied, “I saw you did not.” “I thought you said,” He continued, “that you only wanted those to stand who could say they had surrendered to God?” “That is what I said,” I replied. “Well, I could not say that.” “Th en you did perfectly right not to stand. I did not want you to lie to God.” “Say,” he continued, “you hit me hard today. You said if there was anything that always comes up when you get nearest to God that is the thing to deal with. Now there is something that always comes up when I get near to God. I am not going to tell you what it is. I think you know.” “Yes,” I replied. (I could smell it.) “Well, I simply wanted to say this to you.” This was on Friday afternoon. I had to go to another city, and returning through that city the following Tuesday morning, the minister who had conducted the meeting was at the station. “I wish you could have been in our Baptist ministers' meeting yesterday morning,” he said; “that man I pointed out to you from the north par t of the state was present. He got up in our meeting and said, ‘Brethren, we have been all wrong about this matter,’ and then he told what he had done. He had settled his controversy with God, had given up the thing which had always come up when he got nearest to God, then he continued and said, ‘Brethren, I have received a more definite experience than I had when I was converted.’ ” Just such an experience is waiting for many others, both minister and layman, just as soon as he will judge his sin, just as soon as he will put away the thing that is a matter of conflict between him and God, no matter how small the thing may seem. If anyone sincerely desires the baptism with the Holy Spirit, he should go alone with God and ask God to search him and bring to light anything in his heart or life that is displeasing to Him, and when He brings it to light, he should put it away. If, after sincerely waiting on God, nothing is brought to light, then we may proceed to take the other steps. But there is no use praying, no use going to conventions, no use in reading books about the baptism with the Holy Spirit, no use in doing anything else, until we judge our sins. 3. The third step is an open confession of our surrender of sin and our acceptance of Jesus Christ . After t elling his hearers to repent in Acts 2:38,”And Peter said to them, Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins”. Heart repentance alone was not enough. There must be an open confession of that repentance, and God's appointed way of confession of repentance is baptism. None of those to whom Peter spoke had ever been baptised, and what Peter meant was water baptism. But suppose one has already been baptised, what then? Even in that case, there must be that for which baptism stands, namely, an open confession of our resurrection of sin and our acceptance of Jesus Christ. The baptism with the Spirit is not for the secret disciple, but for the open confessed disciple. There are many doubtless today who are trying to be Christians in their hearts, many who really believe that they have accepted Jesus as their Savior and their Lord and have renounced sin, but they are not willing to make an open confession of their renunciation of sin and their acceptance of Christ. Such a one cannot have baptism with the Holy Spirit. Someone may ask, “Don’t Friends who do not believe in water baptism give evidence of being baptised with the Holy Spirit?” Doubtless , many of them do, but this does not alter the teaching of God's Word. God doubtless lowers Himself in many instances where people are deceived as to the teaching of His Word to their ignorance, if they are sincere, but that fact does not alter His Word, and even with a member of the congregation of Friends, who sincerely does not believe in water baptism, there must be before the blessing is received that for which baptism stands, namely, the open confession of our acceptance of Christ and our surrender of sin.

fields.title: The Work Of The Holy Spirit In Prophets And Apostles
fields.body_html:
The work of the Holy Spirit in apostles and prophets is entirely distinctive. He imparts to apostles and prophets a special gift for a special purpose.

We read in 1 Corinthians 12:4-11, 28, 29 , “Now there are varieties of gifts, b ut the same Spirit....

For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit; and to another workings of miracles; and to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues: All these are empowered by the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.... And God hath set some in the church, first apostles , secondly prophets , thirdly teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helps, governments, diver’s kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing ? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?” It is evident from these verses that the work of the Holy Spirit in apostles and prophets is distinctive.

The doctrine is becoming very common these days that the work of the Holy Spirit in preachers, teachers, and ordinary believers, guiding them into the truth and opening their minds to understand the Word of God, is the same and differs only in degree from the work of the Holy Spirit in prophets and apostles. It is evident from the passage just cited that this doctrine is thoroughly unscriptural and untrue. It overlooks the fact clearly stated that while there is “the same Spirit” there are “diversities of gifts” “diversities of administrations” “diversities of workings” (1 Corinthians 12:4- 6) and that “not all are prophets” and “not all are apostles” (1 Corinthians 12:29).

A brilliant preacher seeking to minimize the difference between the work of the Holy Spirit in apostles and prophets and His work in other men calls attention to the fact that the Bible says that Bezaleel was to be “filled with the Spirit of God” to devise the work of the temple (Exodus 31:1- 11).

He gives this as a proof that the inspiration of the prophet does not differ from the inspiration of the artist or architect, but in doing this, he loses sight of the fact that the temple was to be built after the “pattern shown to Moses in the Mount” (Exodus 25:9, 40) and that therefore it was itself a prophecy and an exposition of the truth of God. It was not mere architecture. It was the Word of God done into wood, gold, silver, brass, cloth, skin, etc. And Bezaleel needed as much special inspiration to reveal the truth in wood, gold, silver, brass, etc., as the apostle or prophet needs it to reveal the Word of God with pen and ink on parchment. There is much reasoning these days about inspiration that appears at first sight very learned, but that will not bear much rigid analysis with the exact statements of the Word of God. There is nothing in the Bible more inspired than the tabernacle, and if the Destructive Critics would study it more, they would give up their ingenious but weak theories as to the composite structure of the Pentateuch.

2. Truth hidden from man for ages and which they had not discovered and could not discover by the unaided processes of human reasoning, has been revealed to apostles and prophets in the Spirit. We read in Ephesians 3:3- 5, “ By revelation, as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. ” The Bible contains truth that men had neve r discovered before the Bible stated it. It contains truth that men never could have discovered if left to themselves.

Our heavenly Father, in great grace, has revealed this truth to us, His children, through His servants, the apostles and the prophets . The Holy Spirit is the agent of this revelation. Many tell us today that we should test the statements of Scripture by the conclusions of human reasoning or by the “Christian consciousness.” The foolishness of all this is evident when we bear in mind that t he revelation of God exceeds human reasoning, and that any consciousness that is not the product of the study and absorption of Bible truth is not a Christian consciousness. The fact that the Bible contains truth that man has never discovered is stated in the Scriptures, but we know it also as a matter of fact.

There is no one of the most distinctive and precious doctrines taught in the Bible that men have ever discovered apart from the Bible. If our consciousness differs from the statements of this Book, which is so plainly God's Book, it is not yet fully Christian and the thing to do is not to try to pull God's revelation down to the level of our consciousness but to tone our consciousness up to the level of God's Word.

3. The revelation made to the prophets was independent of their thinking. It was made to them by the Spirit of Christ, which was in them. And it was a subject of inquiry to their mind as to its meaning. It was not their thought, but His. We read in 1 Peter 1:10- 12, “Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long to look. ” These words make it clear that a Person in the prophets, and independent of the prophets, and that Person is the Holy Spirit, revealed truth which was independent of their thinking, which they did not altogether understand themselves, and regarding which they needed to make diligent search and study. Another Person than themselves was thinking and speaking, and they were seeking to understand what He said.

4. No prophet's utterance was of the prophet's own will, but he spoke from God, and the prophet was carried along in his utterance by the Holy Spirit. We read in 2 Peter 1:21, “For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.”

Then, the prophet was simply an instrument in the hands of another, as the Spirit of God carried him along, so he spoke.

5. It was the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophetic utterances. It was His word that was upon the prophet's tongue. We read in Hebrews 3:7, “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, 'Today, if you hear his voice.” Again, we read in Hebrews 10:15- 16, “And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, 'this is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds.”

We read again in Acts 28:25, “And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made one statement: ' The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, etc.’ ” Still, we read in 2 Samuel 23:2, “The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me; his word is on my tongue.” In these passages, we are told that it was the Holy Spirit who was the speaker in the prophetic utterances and that it was His word, not theirs, that was upon the prophet's tongue. The prophet was simply the mouth by which the Holy Spirit spoke. As a man, that is except as the Spirit taught him and used him, the prophet might be as weak as other men are but when the Spirit was upon him and he was taken up and carried along by the Holy Spirit, he was perfect in his teachings; for his teachings in that case were not his own, but the teachings of the Holy Spirit.

When thus carried along by the Holy Spirit, it was God who was speaking and not the prophet. For example, there can be little doubt that Paul had many mistaken beliefs about many things, but when he taught as an Apostle in the Spirit's power, he was perfect, or rather the Spirit, who taught through him, was faultless and the consequent teaching was perfect as God Himself. We do well, therefore, to carefully distinguish what Paul may have thought as a man and what he did teach as an Apostle.

In the Bible, we have the record of what he taught as an Apostle. Some think that in 1 Corinthians 7:6, 25, “Now as a concession, not a command, I say this ... but I gi ve my judgment as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy,” Paul admits that he was not sure in this case that he had the word of the Lord. If this is the true interpretation of the passage (which is more than doubtful), we see how careful Paul was when he was unsure to note the fact, and this gives us additional certainty in all other passages.

It is sometimes said that Paul taught in his early ministry that the Lord would return during his lifetime, and that in this he was mistaken. But Paul never taught anywhere that the Lord would return in his lifetime.

He indeed says in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, “ Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord .” A s he was still living when he wrote the words, he did not include himself with those who had already fallen asleep in speaking of the Lord's return. But this is not to assert that he would remain alive until the Lord came.

At this period of his ministry, he entertained the hope that he might remain alive and consequently lived in an attitude of expectancy, but the attitude of expectancy is the true attitude in all ages for each believer. It is possible that Paul expected that he would be alive to the coming of the Lord, but if he expected that, he did not teach it. The Holy Spirit kept him from this as from all other errors in his teachings.

6. The Holy Spirit in the Apostle taught not only the thought (or “concept”) but the words in which the thought was to be expressed. We read in 1 Corinthians 2:13, “And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.” This passage teaches that the words, as well as the thought, were chosen and taught by the Holy Spirit. This is also a necessary conclusion from the fact that thought is conveyed from mind to mind by words, and it is the words which express the thought, and if the words were imperfect, the thought expressed in these words would necessarily be imperfect and, to that extent, be untrue.

Nothing could be clearer than Paul's statement, “ in words taught by the spirit .” The Holy Spirit has Himself expected all the modern ingenious and wholly unbiblical and false theories regarding His work in the Apostles. The more carefully and precisely we study the wording of the statements of this wonderful Book, the more we will become convinced of the marvelous accuracy of the words used to express the thought. Often, the solution to an apparent difficulty is found in studying the exact words used. The accuracy, precision, and perfection of the exact words used are amazing.

To the superficial student, the doctrine of verbal inspiration may appear questionable or even absurd; any regenerated and Spirit-taught man, who considers the words of the Scripture regularly, will become convinced that the wisdom of God is in the very words, as well as in the thought which the words endeavor to convey. A change of a word, letter, a tense, a case, or number, in many instances, would land us into contradiction or untruth, but taking the words exactly as written, difficulties disappear and truth shines forth. The Divine origin of nature shines forth more clearly in the use of a microscope as we see the perfection of form and adaptation of means to the end of the minutest particles of matter.

Similarly, the Divine origin of the Bible shines forth more clearly under the microscope as we notice the perfection with which the turn of a word reveals the absolute thought of God.

But someone may ask, “If the Holy Spirit is the author of the words of Scripture, how do we account for variations in style and wording? How do we explain, for instance, that Paul always used Pauline language and John Johannean language, et c.?” The answer to this is very simple. If we could not account for this fact, it would have little weight against the explicit statement of God's Word with anyone humble and wise enough to recognize that there are a great many things which he cannot account for, which could be easily accounted for if he knew more. But these variations are easily accounted for.

The Holy Spirit is quite wise enough and has quite facility enough in the use of language in revealing truth to and through any given individual, to use words, phrases, and forms of expression and idioms in that person's vocabulary and forms of thought, and to make use of that person's uniqueness. Indeed, it is a mark of the Divine wisdom of this Book that the same truth is expressed with absolute accuracy in such widely variant forms of expression.

7. The utterances of the Apostles and the prophets were the word of God. When we read these words, we are not listening to the voice of man, but to the voice of God. We read in Mark 7:13, “thus making voi d the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” Jesus had been setting the law given through Moses over against the legalistic traditions, and in doing this, He says in this passage that the law given through Mo ses was “ the word of God .” In 2 Samuel 23:2, we read, “The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me; these words are on my tongue.” Here again , we are told that the utterance of God's prophet was the word of God. Similarly God says in1 Thessalonians 2:13 “And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.” Here , Paul declares that the word which he spoke, taught by the Spirit of God, was the very word of God .

fields.title: The Work Of The Holy Spirit In Jesus Christ
fields.body_html:
Jesus Christ is the perfect example of the Holy Spirit’s complete work in a person’s life. He was conceived, empowered, led, taught, and even raised from the dead by the Holy Spirit, accomplishing His ministry through the Spirit's power. This same Spirit is available to believers today for living victoriously, serving God, and overcoming sin.

Jesus Christ Himself is the one perfect manifestation in history of the complete work of the Holy Spirit in man.

1. Jesus Christ was begotten of the Holy Spirit. We read in Luke 1:35. “And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy the Son of God.” As we have already seen, in regeneration the believer is begotten of God, but Jesus Christ was begotten of God in His original generation. He is the only begotten Son of God (John 3:16). It was entirely by the Spirit's power working in Mary that the Son of God was formed within her. The regenerated man has a physical nature received from his earthly father and a new nature conveyed by God. Jesus Christ had only the one holy nature, that which in man is called the new nature. Nevertheless, He was a real man as He had a human mother.

2. Jesus Christ led a holy and spotless life and offered Himself without spot to God through the working of the Holy Spirit. We read in Hebrews 9:14, “How much more wi ll the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.” Jesus Christ met and overcame temptations as other men may meet and overcome them, in the power of the Holy Spirit. He was tempted and suffered through temptation (Hebrews 3:18), He was tempted in all points like we are (Hebrews 4:15), but never once in any way did He yield to temptation. He was tempted entirely apart from sin, but He won His victories in a way that is open for all of us to win victory, in the power of the Holy Spirit.

3. Jesus Christ was anointed and fitted for service by the Holy Spirit. We read in Acts 10:38, “How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.” In a prophetic vision of the coming Messiah in the Old Testament we read in Isaiah 61:1 “ The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound ” In Luke's record of the earthly life of our Lord in Luke 4:14, we read “And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country.”

Similarly, Jesus said of Himself when speaking in the synagogue in Nazareth, “ The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor. ” (Luke 4:18 -19.). All these passages contain the one lesson that it was by the special anointing with the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ was qualified for the service to which God had called Him. As He stood in the Jordan after His baptism, “The Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon H im,” and it was then and there that He was anointed with the Holy Spirit, baptized with the Holy Spirit, and equipped for the service that lay before Him. Jesus Christ received His equipment for service in the same way that we receive ours, by a definite baptism with the Holy Spirit.

4. Jesus Christ was led by the Holy Spirit in His movements here upon earth. We read in Luke 4:1, “And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness.” Living as a man here upon earth and setting an example for us, each step of His life was under the Holy Spirit's guidance.

5. Jesus Christ was taught by the Spirit who rested upon Him. The Spirit of God was the source of His wisdom in the days of His flesh. In the Old Testament prophecy of the coming Messiah we read in Isaiah 11:2- 3, “ And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear .” Further on in Isaiah 42:1, we read, “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations. Etc .” Matthew tells us in Matthew 12:17 -18 that this prophecy was fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth.

6. The Holy Spirit abode upon Jesus in all His fullness, and the words He spoke as a result were the very words of God. We read in John 3:34, “For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure .”

7. After His resurrection, Jesus Christ gave commandments unto His Apostles whom He had chosen through the Holy Spirit. We read in Acts 1:2, “ Until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen .” This relates to the time after His resurrection, and so we see Jesus still working in the power of the Holy Spirit even after His resurrection from the dead.

8. Jesus Christ performed His miracles on earth in the power of the Holy Spirit. In Matthew 12:28, we read, “But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons” It is through the Spirit that miracle working power was given to some in the church after our Lord departed from this earth (1 Corinthians 12:9-10), and in the power of the same Spirit, Jesus Christ performed His miracles.

9. It was by the power of the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead. We read in Romans 8:11, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” The same Spirit who is to quicken our mortal bodi es and is to raise us in some future day raised Jesus. Several things are evident from this study of the work of the Holy Spirit in Jesus Christ: First of all, we see the completeness of His humanity. He lived and He thought, He worked, He taught, He conquered sin and won victories for God in the power of that very same Spirit whom it is our privilege also to have.

In the second place, we see our utter dependence upon the Holy Spirit. If it was in the power of the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, lived and worked, achieved and triumphed, how much more dependent are we upon Him at every turn of life and in every phase of service and every experience of conflict with Satan and sin?

The third thing that is evident is the amazing world of privilege, blessing, and victory that is open to us.

The same Spirit by which Jesus was originally begotten is at our disposal for us to be begotten again of Him. The same Spirit by which Jesus offered Himself without spot to God is at our disposal that we may also offer ourselves without spot to Him. The same Spirit by which Jesus was anointed for service is at our disposal that we may be anointed for service. The same Spirit who led Jesus Christ in His movements on earth is ready to lead us today. The same Spirit who taught Jesus and imparted to Him wisdom and understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the Lord is here to teach us.

Jesus Christ is our pattern (1 John 2:6), “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). Whatever He realized through the Holy Spirit is for us to realize today.

THE END

fields.title: Created to Lead
fields.body_html:
The Biblical Foundation of Male Spiritual Leadership "The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it. And the Lord God commanded the man, 'You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will certainly die.'"

— Genesis 2:15–17 To understand what God asks of a man, we must go back to the beginning. Before polygamy was introduced by Lamech in Genesis 4, before the Fall, before sin entered the human story, God designed a world, and He designed a man to lead it.

Notice how the Bible tells the story. In Genesis 1, male and female are created together on the same day, both in the image of God, both given dominion over the earth. This is our foundation: a man and a woman are equal in dignity, equal in value, equal in their bearing of God's image. No husband should ever treat his wife as less than himself. No father should ever treat his daughters as less than his sons. In the image of God, we are the same.

But in Genesis 2, God gives us a closer look at how He arranged the first family, and here we see something important. God formed Adam first. He placed Adam in the garden. He gave the command about the tree to Adam, before Eve was even created. He gave Adam the work of naming the animals. Then He said, "It is not good for the man to be alone," and He made Eve from Adam's side — not from his head to rule over him, not from his feet to be trampled, but from his side to walk beside him.

From this order, the apostle Paul draws a conclusion in the New Testament. Writing to Timothy, he says, "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). Paul is teaching that God's design for male leadership in the home and church is rooted not in culture, not in sin, not in who is bigger or stronger, but in creation itself. Before the Fall, God had already given the man a particular responsibility.

And what was that responsibility? The text is clear. Adam was placed in the garden "to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The Hebrew word for "take care of" (shamar) means to guard, to keep, to protect. Adam was to be a worker and a watchman. He was to cultivate and to protect.

This is still the calling of every man — to build up, and to guard.

Now watch carefully what happened in Genesis 3. The serpent came to Eve. She listened. She took the fruit. She ate. And then the Bible says something that many men have never noticed: "She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it" (Genesis 3:6).

Who was with her? Adam. Where was he when his wife was being deceived by the serpent?

Standing right there. Doing what? Nothing. Saying nothing. Leading nothing. Protecting nothing.

He was silent when he should have spoken. He was passive when he should have acted. He was a coward when he should have been a man.

Brothers, this is the first sin of masculine leadership, and it is still our most common failure. Not that we are too aggressive, but that we are too passive. Not that we lead too much, but that we lead too little. Our wives are being deceived by the lies of this age, and we are standing next to them saying nothing. Our children are being discipled by social media, bad friends, and worse teachers, and we are sitting on the sofa scrolling our phones. Our churches are being weakened by compromise, and we are silent in the pew.

And then notice what Adam did when God confronted him. He blamed his wife. "The woman you put here with me — she gave me some fruit from the tree" (Genesis 3:12). He even blamed God.

A passive man becomes a blaming man. He will not take responsibility for his home, for his church, for his sin. He points his finger at his wife, at his boss, at the government, at the missionaries, at anyone but himself.

But observe this closely. When God came looking in the garden, whom did He call? "The Lord God called to the man, 'Where are you?'" (Genesis 3:9). God did not call Eve first, even though Eve sinned first. God called Adam. Why? Because Adam was the head. Adam was the one who had been given the command. Adam was responsible. In the same way, when judgment came on the human race, Paul tells us it came "through one man" — through Adam, not through Eve (Romans 5:12). The woman sinned first, but the man was held accountable.

This is sobering for us, brothers. God holds men accountable for what happens in their homes, their churches, their communities. We cannot escape it by blaming our wives. We cannot escape it by blaming our culture. We cannot escape it by blaming our fathers who did not teach us. The Lord is asking you, today, "Where are you?"

But thanks be to God, the story of Adam is not the last word. The Bible tells us of a second Adam — the Lord Jesus Christ. Where the first Adam failed, the last Adam succeeded (1 Corinthians 15:45). Where the first Adam was silent, Christ spoke truth. Where the first Adam hid, Christ stepped forward. Where the first Adam took from his bride and ruined her, Christ gave Himself for His Bride to save her. Where the first Adam brought death, Christ brought life.

Every man who trusts in Jesus is united to the second Adam. Your failure in leadership is not the end of your story. The grace of Christ covers your cowardice, and the Spirit of Christ gives you power to lead. You do not lead in your own strength. You lead in His.

So hear the call, brother. God created you to lead — not to dominate, not to oppress, not to boss your wife around, not to beat your children — but to cultivate and to guard. To build up your family spiritually. To watch over your home. To go to God first before the enemy comes to your wife. To take responsibility when things go wrong. To model Christ.

You were created for this. Will you rise up?

A Prayer Father, I confess that I have been more like the first Adam than the second. I have been silent when I should have spoken. I have been passive when I should have led.

I have blamed others for what You have given me to carry. Forgive me, Lord. Wash me in the blood of Jesus, the second Adam, who succeeded where I failed. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit, that I may lead my home, my church, and my community as You have called me. Teach me to cultivate what You have entrusted to me. Teach me to guard it. And when You come looking for me, may I no longer be found hiding.

Here I am, Lord — send me. In the name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

fields.title: The Inner Man
fields.body_html:
Character Before Charisma "The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

— 1 Samuel 16:7 When the prophet Samuel went to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king over Israel, he saw Eliab, the oldest son — tall, strong, handsome, the kind of man we would quickly call a leader. Samuel said to himself, "Surely the Lord's anointed stands here before the Lord." But God corrected him.

"Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:6–7).

Brother, this is where true spiritual leadership begins: not in your arms, not in your wallet, not in your title, not in your degree, not in your clan, but in your heart. God will not use a man whose heart is rotten, no matter how impressive he looks on the outside. And God will use a man whose heart is right, no matter how unimpressive he looks on the outside.

We live in an age that worships charisma. The loud preacher draws the crowd. The flashy businessman is envied. The man with the biggest car is respected. But God is not impressed with any of this. God is looking for character.

What is character? Character is who you are when no one is watching. Character is what you do when the lights are off, when you are alone in a hotel room in a different city, when your phone is in your hand and no one will ever know, when the money is on the table and the accountant has left the room. Character is the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grown slowly in the soil of your heart over years of walking with Jesus.

The apostle Paul, when he listed the qualifications for an elder in the church, said almost nothing about gifting and almost everything about character. Read 1 Timothy 3 slowly. An elder must be "above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2–3). Notice: able to teach appears only once in this long list. The rest is character. If you cannot keep your temper at home, you are not qualified to lead anywhere else.

The same pattern appears in Titus 1, where Paul says an elder must be "blameless, faithful to his wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient" (Titus 1:6). God looks at how a man is doing as a husband and father before He considers him for leadership in the church. Your home is your first ministry. If your character is not being formed there, it is not being formed at all.

Consider the life of Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda. He was born in 1922 in Acholi, in the north of our country. He was converted as a young schoolteacher and was deeply shaped by the East African Revival. What made him great was not that he had a famous name or a powerful position — both of those came later. What made him great was that for decades before he ever stood before Idi Amin, he was walking with Jesus, confessing his sin, loving his wife Mary Florence, and raising his children in the fear of the Lord. By the time Amin tried to intimidate him in 1977, Luwum had the inner man of a lion. He said, "I can see the hand of God in this. Even if I die, I will not be afraid." When his moment came, he did not flinch, because his heart had been prepared long before in secret.

Charisma can carry you to the top. Only character can keep you there.

The apostle Peter understood this. In 2 Peter 1, he gives us a beautiful chain of virtues: "make every effort to add to your faith goodness; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self- control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, mutual affection; and to mutual affection, love" (2 Peter 1:5–7). Notice the verb: "make every effort."

Character does not happen by accident. It is cultivated, like a garden, by daily labor in prayer, in the Word, in confession, in obedience.

Augustine of Hippo, the great North African father of the Church, spent the first years of his adult life chasing sinful pleasures, ambition, and worldly wisdom. He had brilliance, but he lacked character. It was only when he met Christ in a garden in Milan, weeping and crying, "Take and read, take and read," and opening his Bible to Romans 13, that the Lord began to form in him the inner man that would later write the Confessions and The City of God and shape the Church for centuries. Augustine is a reminder to every African man: your past does not disqualify you, but your character must be rebuilt from the inside out.

Let me ask you some hard questions, brother. When you are alone on your phone, what do you look at? When your wife disagrees with you, how do you respond? When a woman who is not your wife smiles at you, what do you do with your eyes? When the bribe is offered, what do you say? When your child disobeys, do you correct with patience or explode with rage? When the offering plate comes around, do you give, or do you grip? When someone insults you, do you return evil or bless?

These small moments, multiplied over years, are who you really are. These are the inner man. No title from men can replace it. No amount of noisy religion can disguise it. God sees it. Your wife sees it. Your children see it. And one day, the whole of heaven and earth will see it.

But here is the good news. You are not left alone to build your character. "God's divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness" (2 Peter 1:3). In Christ, you have everything you need. The Holy Spirit lives in you. The Word of God is given to you. The Church of God surrounds you. The means of grace are available to you. If your character is weak, it is not because God has withheld anything.

It is because you have not pressed into what He has already provided.

So do not be discouraged. Begin today. Begin with confession. Begin with the Word. Begin with prayer. Begin in the secret place. And let God slowly, patiently, build in you a man whose outside and inside match — a man whose wife trusts him, whose children honor him, whose church can rely on him, and whose Savior can say, "Well done, good and faithful servant."

A Prayer Father, You see what no one else sees. You know what no one else knows. You have looked into my heart, and You have seen the truth about me. Where I am a hypocrite, expose me. Where I am proud, humble me. Where I am lazy in my soul, stir me up. Lord Jesus, You were tempted in every way as I am, yet You were without sin. Form Your character in me by the power of Your Holy Spirit. Make my outside and my inside the same. Make me a man of integrity — whole, undivided, true. Help me to build my inner man in the secret place, so that when my moment comes, I will not fall. In Your holy name I pray, amen.
fields.body_text: Character Before Charisma "The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart." — 1 Samuel 16:7 When the prophet Samuel went to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king over Israel, he saw Eliab, the oldest son — tall, strong, handsome, the kind of man we would quickly call a leader. Samuel said to himself, "Surely the Lord's anointed stands here before the Lord." But God corrected him. "Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:6–7). Brother, this is where true spiritual leadership begins: not in your arms, not in your wallet, not in your title, not in your degree, not in your clan, but in your heart. God will not use a man whose heart is rotten, no matter how impressive he looks on the outside. And God will use a man whose heart is right, no matter how unimpressive he looks on the outside. We live in an age that worships charisma. The loud preacher draws the crowd. The flashy businessman is envied. The man with the biggest car is respected. But God is not impressed with any of this. God is looking for character. What is character? Character is who you are when no one is watching. Character is what you do when the lights are off, when you are alone in a hotel room in a different city, when your phone is in your hand and no one will ever know, when the money is on the table and the accountant has left the room. Character is the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grown slowly in the soil of your heart over years of walking with Jesus. The apostle Paul, when he listed the qualifications for an elder in the church, said almost nothing about gifting and almost everything about character. Read 1 Timothy 3 slowly. An elder must be "above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2–3). Notice: able to teach appears only once in this long list. The rest is character. If you cannot keep your temper at home, you are not qualified to lead anywhere else. The same pattern appears in Titus 1, where Paul says an elder must be "blameless, faithful to his wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient" (Titus 1:6). God looks at how a man is doing as a husband and father before He considers him for leadership in the church. Your home is your first ministry. He was converted as a young schoolteacher and was deeply shaped by the East African Revival. What made him great was not that he had a famous name or a powerful position — both of those came later. What made him great was that for decades before he ever stood before Idi Amin, he was walking with Jesus, confessing his sin, loving his wife Mary Florence, and raising his children in the fear of the Lord. By the time Amin tried to intimidate him in 1977, Luwum had the inner man of a lion. He said, "I can see the hand of God in this. Even if I die, I will not be afraid." When his moment came, he did not flinch, because his heart had been prepared long before in secret. Charisma can carry you to the top. Only character can keep you there. The apostle Peter understood this. In 2 Peter 1, he gives us a beautiful chain of virtues: "make every effort to add to your faith goodness; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self- control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, mutual affection; and to mutual affection, love" (2 Peter 1:5–7). Notice the verb: "make every effort." Character does not happen by accident. It is cultivated, like a garden, by daily labor in prayer, in the Word, in confession, in obedience. Augustine of Hippo, the great North African father of the Church, spent the first years of his adult life chasing sinful pleasures, ambition, and worldly wisdom. He had brilliance, but he lacked character. When someone insults you, do you return evil or bless? These small moments, multiplied over years, are who you really are. These are the inner man. No title from men can replace it. No amount of noisy religion can disguise it. God sees it. Your wife sees it. Your children see it. And one day, the whole of heaven and earth will see it. But here is the good news. You are not left alone to build your character. "God's divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness" (2 Peter 1:3). In Christ, you have everything you need. The Holy Spirit lives in you. The Word of God is given to you. The Church of God surrounds you. The means of grace are available to you. fields.title: The Man Who Prays
fields.body_html:
Power on His Knees "Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing."

— 1 Timothy 2:8 There is one practice that has defined every great man of God in the Bible and every great man of God in church history: he prayed. Not occasionally. Not desperately only in emergencies. Not merely in public to be heard. He prayed — deeply, daily, privately, persistently.

Abraham prayed. When God told him He was about to destroy Sodom, Abraham stood before the Lord and interceded for a city full of strangers (Genesis 18:22–33). Moses prayed. When Israel made the golden calf and God threatened to destroy them, Moses lay on his face for forty days and nights (Deuteronomy 9:18). David prayed. Read the Psalms — they are a man's prayer journal soaked in tears, praise, confession, and faith. Daniel prayed. Three times a day, with his window open toward Jerusalem, even when it cost him the lions' den (Daniel 6:10). Nehemiah prayed.

Before he spoke to the king, before he laid a single stone, he lifted his heart to God (Nehemiah 2:4).

And above them all, our Lord Jesus Christ prayed. The Son of God, perfect in every way, needing nothing, rose before dawn to pray (Mark 1:35), went up into the mountains alone to pray (Luke 6:12), prayed all night before choosing the twelve apostles, prayed for Peter, prayed for His disciples, prayed for you and me in John 17, and prayed in Gethsemane until His sweat became like drops of blood. If the Son of God needed to pray, how can we — weak, sinful, foolish — imagine we can lead without prayer?

A man who does not pray is not a spiritual leader, no matter what he calls himself. He may be a good provider, a strong disciplinarian, a respected businessman. But if he is not on his knees before God, he is leading his family into darkness while stumbling himself.

Paul's instruction to Timothy is striking. He says, "I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing" (1 Timothy 2:8). Paul singles out men. Not because women do not pray — they pray powerfully, and we know it — but because Paul is telling us that visible, leading, holy-handed prayer in the worship of the church is the duty of men. And if we will not pray publicly in the gathering of God's people, it is usually because we are not praying privately in our own closets.

Let me speak directly to husbands and fathers now. Your wife is praying for you. Your mother has been praying for you since before you were born. The women of your church are on their knees for the men. They are carrying the spiritual weight of the home while we discuss politics and football. This must change.

When was the last time you prayed with your wife? Not a quick prayer before food, but a real prayer — holding her hand, confessing your sins, praising God, interceding for your children, asking for His will to be done in your home? Peter warns husbands to treat their wives with understanding, "so that nothing will hinder your prayers" (1 Peter 3:7). Think about that. How you treat your wife can block your prayers from being heard. Many of our prayers have hit the ceiling because there was unrepented sin against the woman in our own bed.

When was the last time you laid hands on your children and prayed a blessing over them? Jacob blessed his sons before he died (Genesis 49). Jesus took children in His arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). A father's blessing is a powerful thing in Scripture. Do not withhold it. Lay hands on your children at night, pray over them by name, speak God's favor over their lives. Many of our sons and daughters have gone astray because a father's blessing was missing.

The East African Revival, which touched Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Burundi, and Tanzania in the 1930s and 40s, was fundamentally a prayer movement. Simeon Nsibambi of Uganda and Dr. Joe Church, a missionary in Rwanda, would meet in a room in Kampala and pray for hours. Men gathered in small huts at dawn to cry out to God, to confess their sins, to walk in the light with one another. William Nagenda, who later became one of the greatest preachers of the revival, was a man marked by prayer. Festo Kivengere — who would later preach the gospel from Uganda to America and Europe — was a man of prayer. These were not professional clergymen at first. They were ordinary Ugandan men who decided that they would not lead their families or their nation without first falling on their knees. And from their prayers, a continent was shaken.

George Müller of Bristol, England, ran orphanages for thousands of children in the 1800s without ever asking anyone for money. When the cupboards were empty and breakfast was about to be served, he would gather the children and pray. Over and over, the food arrived — sometimes a baker knocking at the door saying, "God woke me in the night and told me the orphans needed bread," sometimes a milkman whose cart had broken down outside and who asked if they could use the milk before it spoiled. Müller kept records of over fifty thousand specific answers to prayer in his lifetime. He said, "The business of my life is to trust the Lord." Brother, if a man in England could trust God like that, can you not trust Him for your small shop in Kampala, your farm in the village, your job in Nairobi, your family in Dar es Salaam?

Let me give you a simple pattern for prayer as a husband and father. First, pray alone each morning.

Even fifteen minutes, before your phone comes on, before the radio goes on. Open your Bible, read a Psalm, turn it into prayer, confess your sins, praise God, lay out your day. Second, pray with your wife each night, or at least several times a week. Short is fine at the start. The point is to take her hand and say, "Let us pray." Third, pray over each child by name, ideally at bedtime. Ask God to save them, to keep them pure, to give them wisdom, to call them to serve Him. Fourth, pray with your family at meals — more than just "bless this food," but true thanksgiving. Fifth, join a praying community — in your church, with a few brothers, in a men's group. Do not try to be a praying man alone.

Do not wait until you feel like it. Do not wait until you are holy enough. Do not wait until life slows down. Begin now. Poorly is better than not at all. A stumbling, sincere prayer from a sinful man is more precious to God than the smoothest speech from a hypocrite.

There is great power in a praying man. His wife walks through the day with a covering over her.

His children grow up with a spiritual inheritance. His business is touched by the hand of God. His church is strengthened. His nation is moved. And on the day of judgment, he will not be ashamed, because he will have walked with his God.

A Prayer Father, teach me to pray. I confess I have prayed too little, too shallowly, too selfishly. I have been quicker to scroll my phone than to seek Your face. Quicker to complain to others than to cry out to You. Quicker to plan my day than to consecrate it. Lord Jesus, You who prayed all night on the mountain, teach me. Holy Spirit, who intercedes for us with groans, pray through me. Make me a man whose wife can say, "My husband prays for me." Make me a father whose children know, "Papa prays for us." Make me a brother in the church who can stand and lift holy hands.

And where revival is needed in my home, my village, my nation, let it begin on my knees. In the mighty name of Jesus, amen.
