fields.title: The Battle Within
fields.body_html:
Fighting Sin and Walking in Purity "Flee from sexual immorality. All other sins a person commits are outside the body, but whoever sins sexually, sins against their own body."

— 1 Corinthians 6:18 We have spoken much about leadership outside of ourselves — in the home, in the church, in the community. Now we must speak about the hardest leadership of all: the leadership of ourselves.

The war within. The fight for personal holiness.

Brother, you cannot lead others into places where you refuse to go yourself. You cannot call your wife to purity if you are feeding on pornography in secret. You cannot teach your sons self-control if you are mastered by alcohol. You cannot instruct your daughters about modesty if your eyes wander when you walk down the street. The battle within comes before the battle without. Jesus said, "You hypocrite, first take the plank out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5).

Let us speak honestly about some specific sins that devastate men, especially in our East African context.

First, sexual sin. Sexual immorality has been a stumbling block for men since the Garden of Eden, and our generation has no shortage of it. Adultery is everywhere. Pornography is in every pocket that carries a smartphone. Polygamy, though sometimes dressed in cultural clothing, often feeds the same selfish desires. Young men sleep with girlfriends and call it "just how things are."

Older men keep girls on the side and think their wives do not know. Pastors fall. Deacons fall.

Elders fall. The newspapers are full of scandals.

The Bible's command is simple: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18). Not debate it. Not flirt with it. Not enjoy the edges of it. Flee. Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife so fast he left his cloak behind (Genesis 39:12). That is the pattern. When the temptation comes, your legs are your best friend.

Why flee? Paul gives the answer: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

You are not your own. You were bought at a price. Christ paid for every cell of your body with His blood. To defile what He has bought is to sin not only against your wife, not only against the woman involved, not only against your children, but against Christ Himself.

Practically, how do we flee? Set guardrails. Do not meet alone with a woman who is not your wife, especially not in private settings. Do not text late at night with a woman who is not your wife. Do not keep pornographic material anywhere — on your phone, on your computer, in your mind.

Install accountability software. Confess to a brother when you have stumbled. Do not romanticize your past sins by telling the old stories. Keep your mind and your eyes under the rule of the Spirit.

"I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman," said Job (Job 31:1).

Make that same covenant today.

Second, alcohol. This is a particular plague in East Africa. Home-brewed spirits, local beers, waragi, imported whiskeys — they have destroyed more African homes than almost any other single sin. A man goes out after work "just for one drink." He comes home drunk at midnight. His wife smells it. His children see it. His Sunday sermon dies on his lips.

Scripture does not forbid the moderate use of wine (Psalm 104:15, 1 Timothy 5:23). But it repeatedly condemns drunkenness. "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to debauchery. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). "Wine is a mocker and beer a brawler; whoever is led astray by them is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1). "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to run after their drinks, who stay up late at night till they are inflamed with wine" (Isaiah 5:11).

Let me speak clearly. If alcohol has any grip on you at all — if you need it to relax, if you cannot stop at one, if you spend money on it your family needed for food, if you have ever been drunk in front of your children, if your wife has begged you to stop — then you must put it down completely.

Not reduce. Not manage. Stop. The Bible calls it "not given to drunkenness" as a qualification for leadership (1 Timothy 3:3). Many men in our region cannot lead because they cannot rule their cups.

Third, anger. We have spoken of this in the chapter on gentleness, but it returns here as a deep sin to fight. "In your anger do not sin. Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not give the devil a foothold" (Ephesians 4:26–27). Uncontrolled anger in a man gives the devil a direct doorway into his home. Many of our fathers passed rage down to us like an inheritance. We can break that chain. We can refuse to pass it to our sons.

Fourth, the love of money and corruption. In our culture, bribery is so common it has almost become invisible. Small gifts to get a job done. Larger payments to avoid traffic tickets. Business deals built on kickbacks. Government contracts that line private pockets. Some of this is simply theft from the poor, dressed up in polite language. The Bible is uncompromising: "Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income" (Ecclesiastes 5:10). "A greedy man brings ruin to his household" (Proverbs 15:27). "The Lord detests dishonest scales" (Proverbs 11:1).

If you are in a position where you can give or take bribes, there will be a cost to doing it God's way. You may earn less. You may be passed over. You may be laughed at. But "better a little with righteousness than much gain with injustice" (Proverbs 16:8). You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24). Choose today whom you will serve.

Fifth, pride. This is the root of all the others. Pride is the sin that turned an angel into the devil.

Pride says, "I know better than God." Pride says, "The rules do not apply to me." Pride says, "I do not need accountability." Pride says, "I am the head — obey me." Pride is sneaky, and it hides in everything, even our humility. "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble" (James 4:6). Brother, take note: God opposes the proud. Not just dislikes. Opposes. Actively works against. Do not let pride sit unchallenged in your heart.

How do we fight these sins? Not by trying harder alone. Willpower fails. Resolutions break. The pattern is always the same: repent, confess, run to Christ, be filled with the Spirit, find a brother to walk with you, stay close to the means of grace.

The Gospel is the engine of your holiness. It is not that Jesus saved you by grace and now you must become holy by sweat. No — "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6). The same grace that saved you sanctifies you. You fight sin from a place of acceptance, not for acceptance. Your Father already loves you. Your failures do not drive Him away. They drive you to Him.

Consider Augustine of Hippo once more. He struggled with sexual sin for years. He famously prayed, "Lord, grant me chastity — but not yet!" He knew what was right, but he could not walk in it. When he finally broke through, it was not by his own strength. He was weeping in a garden, heard a child's voice saying "take and read," opened the Bible, and read Romans 13:13–14: "Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ." The light flooded in. The chains snapped. The power of the gospel broke through.

Your breakthrough will come the same way. Not by grit, but by grace. Not by hiding, but by bringing your sin into the light. Not by self-righteousness, but by the righteousness of Christ laid hold of by faith. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1).

So fight, brother. Fight every day. Fight with your Bible open. Fight with your knees bent. Fight with brothers beside you. Fight with your wife aware. Fight with the Holy Spirit as your strength.

And know this: in Jesus Christ, you are on the winning side.

A Prayer Holy God, You are light, and in You there is no darkness at all. I confess I have walked in dark places. I have loved sins that You hate. I have fed desires that will destroy me. Have mercy on me, a sinner. Wash me whiter than snow. Break the power of every sin that has bound me — every lust, every bottle, every outburst, every bribe, every secret pride. Crucify my flesh with its passions and desires. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit. Give me brothers to fight beside me. Make me a man who walks in the light, who confesses quickly, who runs to Christ when he falls. And in the end, present me faultless before the presence of Your glory with great joy. In the name of Jesus, who is mighty to save, amen.

The Bible is uncompromising: "Whoever loves money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income" (Ecclesiastes 5:10). "A greedy man brings ruin to his household" (Proverbs 15:27). "The Lord detests dishonest scales" (Proverbs 11:1). If you are in a position where you can give or take bribes, there will be a cost to doing it God's way. You may earn less. You may be passed over. You may be laughed at. But "better a little with righteousness than much gain with injustice" (Proverbs 16:8). You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24). Choose today whom you will serve. Fifth, pride. This is the root of all the others. Pride is the sin that turned an angel into the devil. Pride says, "I know better than God." Pride says, "The rules do not apply to me." Pride says, "I do not need accountability." Pride says, "I am the head — obey me." Pride is sneaky, and it hides in everything, even our humility. "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble" (James 4:6). Brother, take note: God opposes the proud. Not just dislikes. Opposes. Actively works against. Do not let pride sit unchallenged in your heart. How do we fight these sins? Not by trying harder alone. Willpower fails. Resolutions break. The pattern is always the same: repent, confess, run to Christ, be filled with the Spirit, find a brother to walk with you, stay close to the means of grace. The Gospel is the engine of your holiness. It is not that Jesus saved you by grace and now you must become holy by sweat. No — "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6). The same grace that saved you sanctifies you. You fight sin from a place of acceptance, not for acceptance. Your Father already loves you. Your failures do not drive Him away. They drive you to Him. Consider Augustine of Hippo once more. He struggled with sexual sin for years. He famously prayed, "Lord, grant me chastity — but not yet!" He knew what was right, but he could not walk in it. When he finally broke through, it was not by his own strength. He was weeping in a garden, heard a child's voice saying "take and read," opened the Bible, and read Romans 13:13–14: "Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ." The light flooded in. The chains snapped. The power of the gospel broke through. Your breakthrough will come the same way. Not by grit, but by grace. Not by hiding, but by bringing your sin into the light. Not by self-righteousness, but by the righteousness of Christ laid hold of by faith. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). So fight, brother. Fight every day. Fight with your Bible open. Fight with your knees bent. Fight with brothers beside you. Fight with your wife aware. Fight with the Holy Spirit as your strength. And know this: in Jesus Christ, you are on the winning side. A Prayer Holy God, You are light, and in You there is no darkness at all. I confess I have walked in dark places. I have loved sins that You hate. I have fed desires that will destroy me. Have mercy on me, a sinner. Wash me whiter than snow. Break the power of every sin that has bound me — every lust, every bottle, every outburst, every bribe, every secret pride. Crucify my flesh with its passions and desires. Fill me with Your Holy Spirit. Give me brothers to fight beside me. Make me a man who walks in the light, who confesses quickly, who runs to Christ when he falls. And in the end, present me faultless before the presence of Your glory with great joy. In the name of Jesus, who is mighty to save, amen.

fields.title: Vision and Stewardship
fields.body_html:
Setting Godly Goals "Then the Lord replied: 'Write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets so that a herald may run with it.'"

— Habakkuk 2:2 A man without vision is a drifter. He may work hard, but he does not know where he is going. He may make money, but he does not know what for. He may raise children, but he does not know what he wants to pass to them. Life happens to him, rather than him living life on purpose.

Solomon wrote, "Where there is no vision, the people perish" (Proverbs 29:18, in the older translation). The newer translations put it, "Where there is no revelation, people cast off restraint."

Both ideas are true. A man who has not heard from God about his life, and who has not put his vision on paper, lives without direction and often without restraint.

God is a God of plans. "For I know the plans I have for you," declares the Lord, "plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future" (Jeremiah 29:11). If God plans for your life, should you not also plan with Him? Many Christian men mistake "waiting on the Lord" for passivity. They do nothing and call it faith. But biblical waiting is active. Nehemiah prayed for four months before he acted (Nehemiah 1–2), but when he acted, he had a plan. He counted the days, surveyed the walls, organized the workers, assigned the gates.

Brother, have you set godly goals for your life? Not the world's kind of goals — a bigger car, a bigger house, a bigger title — but goals shaped by Scripture and aimed at the glory of God?

Goals for your walk with Christ? Goals for your marriage? Goals for your children? Goals for your work? Goals for your giving? Goals for your local church? Goals for your nation?

Let me help you think in categories.

Spiritual goals. Where do you want to be with Christ in one year, five years, twenty years? Do you have a plan to read through the Bible? Do you have a plan to memorize Scripture? Do you have a plan for prayer? Do you have books you intend to read to grow in theology and pastoral wisdom?

Ask God to show you the man He wants you to become spiritually, and then ask Him how to get there.

Marriage goals. What kind of husband do you want to be in ten years? What does your wife most need from you this year — healing from some past wound? More time? More prayer? Better communication? Sit down with her and ask. Then write it down. Without a goal for your marriage, you will drift into mediocrity.

Family goals. What do you want to pass to your children? Not just money — character, faith, skills, a love of learning, a love of the Church, a heart for the lost. Name what you want them to know, what you want them to believe, what you want them to be. Then design your fatherhood toward those goals.

Work goals. What is God calling you to do with your hands and your mind? If you are an employee, how will you become excellent? If you are a business owner, what ethical and profitable path lies ahead? If you are a farmer, what is the plan for this season's planting and for five years from now?

Do not drift in your work. Plan it.

Financial goals. What is your plan for saving, giving, investing, and providing? Proverbs says, "The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have a household budget. Set aside for your children's school fees. Give to your local church regularly.

Save for emergencies. Plan for old age. Avoid ruinous debt. These are not optional for a godly man.

Service goals. How do you want to serve God's people? What gifts has He given you, and how will you use them? Maybe you want to disciple three young men next year. Maybe you want to help plant a church. Maybe you want to start a ministry for widows in your community. Dream with God. Write it down.

Habakkuk was told to "write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets, so that a herald may run with it" (Habakkuk 2:2). Write your vision. Get it on paper, or on your phone, or in a notebook.

There is something holy about writing. It forces you to think clearly. It makes the vision survive when your memory fails. It lets you review and adjust. Begin today. Just a page. A few lines under each category. You can refine it over time.

Then pray over your vision regularly. Lay it before the Lord. Say, "Father, if this is not from You, kill it. If this is from You, bring it to pass. I submit every goal to Your will." "Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3). Remember also, "Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that prevails" (Proverbs 19:21). Your goals are not God's orders to Him. They are your honest desires submitted to His sovereign hand.

Stewardship is the twin of vision. If God has given you a life, you are to steward it. If He has given you money, time, talents, children, a wife, influence — all these are on loan. "Now it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2). The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30) is clear: the Master will return and ask what you did with what He gave you. The man who buried his talent in fear was called wicked and lazy. The men who invested and multiplied were welcomed into the joy of their Master.

Do not bury your talents, brother. Do not sit on your hands because you feel small. Do not say, "I am only a farmer, a driver, a clerk, a young man." God gave you your talents. Use them. Start where you are. Trade faithfully. Grow what He has given.

A simple tool: every Sunday evening, look at the week ahead. What are your priorities? Your Bible reading plan? One concrete way you will serve your wife this week? One thing you will teach your children? One person you will disciple or encourage? One hour you will give to the local church?

One person you will pray for by name? Plan it. Then do it. A year of such weeks changes a life.

Consider William Wilberforce, the English Christian statesman of the late 1700s. He set himself "two great objects": the abolition of the slave trade and the reformation of manners (moral renewal of society). He wrote these goals down. He pursued them for decades. He did not live to see all the fruit, but he changed the British Empire. One man with a clear, God-given vision can move mountains.

Consider also our African brothers who have done the same. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Nigerian who was rescued from a slave ship as a boy, set himself to translate the Bible into his mother tongue and to plant the Church among his people. He did it. Today the Yoruba church is one of the strongest in Africa partly because a man set a godly goal and worked toward it for the rest of his life.

Dream big dreams for God, but be faithful in small daily steps. "Do not despise these small beginnings, for the Lord rejoices to see the work begin" (Zechariah 4:10). The oak tree is in the acorn. The revival is in the prayer meeting of three men. The great marriage is in the daily kindness of a husband. The godly son is in the bedtime prayer of a father. Plant well and the harvest will come.

A Prayer Father, You are the God who plans from eternity past to eternity future, the God who numbered my days before one of them came to be. Give me Your vision for my life. Break me free from drifting. Break me free from mediocrity. Break me free from burying my talents in fear. Show me what You are calling me to do, to become, and to leave behind. Give me the discipline to write down what You reveal. Give me the wisdom to plan carefully. Give me the faith to trust You with the outcome.

Let my life not be wasted. Use every year, every week, every hour for Your glory.

And at the end of my days, may I hear from You, "Well done." In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: A Legacy That Outlives You
fields.body_html:
Leaving a Godly Heritage "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children, but a sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous."

— Proverbs 13:22 You will die, brother. I do not say this to be dark. I say it because the Bible says it. "It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27). Your days are numbered (Psalm 90:12). The length of your life is a secret kept by the One who gave it to you. Some men get eighty years. Some men do not see their fortieth birthday. Some men are cut down at twenty- five, leaving a young wife and small children. None of us know.

But this much we do know: you will leave something behind. Every man does. The question is not whether you will leave a legacy. The question is what kind.

Solomon tells us, "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children." Notice the horizon. Not just for your children, but for your children's children — the grandchildren you may or may not live to see. A godly man thinks generationally. He is not building only for his lifetime.

He is building for generations he will not meet on this side of eternity.

What kind of legacy should a godly man aim for? Let us consider three levels: material, moral, and spiritual.

First, a material inheritance. Scripture does honor the passing of material goods. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents," says Proverbs 19:14.

A father who leaves his family with nothing when he could have planned better has not served them well. This does not mean you must become rich. It means you must be faithful. If you have a small plot of land, can you leave it free of debt? If you have a small business, can you leave it in good health? If you have little to leave, can you leave a legacy of honest dealing with those you owed? Some men leave debts and lawsuits behind them — that is a curse to their children. Some leave paid-up accounts and quiet consciences — that is a blessing.

Plan for what happens when you die. Write a will. In many African contexts, when the husband dies without a will, the extended family may come and take what was meant for the widow and the children. Protect your household. A will is not lack of faith; it is an act of love. "The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty" (Proverbs 27:12).

Second, a moral inheritance. This is more valuable than money, and many poor men have left enormous moral wealth to their descendants.

A moral inheritance is the memory of integrity. It is your children saying, "Papa never lied to us."

It is your neighbors saying, "Your father never cheated me." It is your wife saying, "Your father never once raised his hand against me." A reputation for honesty is a shelter that covers your children's children.

A moral inheritance is also the memory of love. It is your grown son remembering, "Papa took me fishing. Papa prayed for me at my bedside. Papa told me he was proud of me." It is your grown daughter remembering, "Papa treated Mama with respect. Papa hugged me. Papa told me I was beautiful in the Lord." Children who are loved well by their fathers are anchored for life.

A moral inheritance is the shape of how you lived. Your working hard. Your faithfulness to one wife. Your kindness to the poor. Your refusal to take bribes. Your laughter in your home. Your songs on the road. Your tears at the funeral of a friend. Your courage at the funeral of a child.

These memories are currency your children will spend for the rest of their lives.

Third, and most important, a spiritual legacy. This is the treasure that outlives every other. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord" (Proverbs 19:14) — how much more is a prudent faith? Money is eaten by inflation and sometimes by corrupt officials.

Land can be stolen. Buildings can burn. Reputations can fade. But a grandchild who knows Jesus because his grandfather prayed for him — that is a legacy no fire can touch, no thief can steal, no government can confiscate.

Think again of Timothy, who had the faith that "first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations of faith. A grandmother who loved Jesus, a mother who loved Jesus, a grandson who became a pastor and apostolic helper because of them.

This is a family we do not hear much about by name, but their legacy shaped the Church forever through Timothy's ministry.

Think of the Wesley family. Susanna Wesley, mother of John and Charles, raised nineteen children in a small English parsonage. She taught them the Scriptures. She prayed for them daily. Two of them — John and Charles — shook the world through the Methodist revival, which reached across England, America, and yes, eventually the continent of Africa. Susanna could not have known that her patient mothering would one day result in churches planted in Uganda. But that is how legacy works. A mother's prayers in 1710 became a missionary's boat sailing in 1870 became an African pastor's sermon in 2026.

Think of the East African Revival fathers — Nsibambi, Nagenda, Kivengere, and many more whose names are not as famous but whose prayers and lives touched generations. Kivengere lived to see his preaching impact churches on three continents. His legacy is not a monument of stone; it is souls in glory, churches still preaching the gospel, children of converts still walking with Jesus.

And think of the Ugandan martyrs. Young men, most of them teenagers and young adults, burned alive at Namugongo in 1886. They did not leave behind material wealth. Many had no children.

But look what they left behind: a Church. A century and a half later, more than 80% of Uganda professes the name of Christ because of the witness of those young men. Their blood became seed, just as Tertullian said centuries earlier, "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church." Every June 3rd, Catholics and Protestants alike still remember them. The smallest spiritual legacy is larger than the grandest earthly one.

So what will your legacy be?

Brother, begin now to live with your end in mind. Every day, ask, "If I died tonight, what would my wife remember? What would my children inherit? What would my church say at my funeral?

What would the Lord Jesus say when He meets me?" This is not morbid. This is wisdom. "Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12).

Live in such a way that when you are old, you can sit and look at your grandchildren and know that you planted well. Live in such a way that when you die, your children say, "Our father loved Jesus, and he loved us." Live in such a way that long after the last person who remembers your face has also died, your great-great-grandchildren are still walking with the Lord because of the family you planted for Him.

The trees you plant today will give shade to generations who will never know your name. Plant well.

A Prayer Eternal Father, the generations come and go, but You remain forever. My days are a breath; Your years have no end. Teach me to live with eternity in view. Let me not waste my one short life on trivial things. Let me lay down a spiritual heritage that will echo through my family long after my bones rest in the earth. Give me grace to love my wife so well that my granddaughters will expect to be loved well.

Give me grace to teach my children so faithfully that my great-grandchildren will sing Your praises. Let the trees I plant give shade to many. And may my name be found written in the Book of Life when the final day comes. In the name of Jesus Christ, the Resurrection and the Life, Amen.

CONCLUSION Rise Up, Men of God A Call to Action and Closing Prayer We have come to the end of this journey, brother, but your journey is only beginning.

We began by looking at the hungry land around us — hungry for godly men. We looked at God's creation design, at the inner man, at the power of prayer, at the husband's calling to love, at the father's duty to disciple, at the gentleness of true strength, at the dignity of work, at the watchman's duty of protection, at the iron of accountability, at service in the local church, at the pulpit of the home, at the war within against sin, at the vision of a well-planned life, and at the legacy that reaches far beyond our own grave.

Fourteen chapters. Fourteen calls. Fourteen areas where God has spoken. And now the book closes, and the question presses: what will you do?

Reading is easy. Applying is hard. Books can be set on a shelf and forgotten, or they can be the match that lights a fire. Which will this book be for you?

Let me lay before you a simple call to action. Not complicated. Not overwhelming. Just a beginning. Take what follows and make it your own, with your pastor, with your wife, with your brothers in the faith.

First, make sure you are a Christian. I ask this of every reader, because no one can lead spiritually who has not first been made alive by the Spirit of God. Have you come to the end of yourself and found only Jesus is enough? Have you repented of your sins and trusted in Christ alone for salvation? If you have never done this, do it today. Right where you are. "If you declare with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). Do not read another chapter of your life without settling this.

Second, commit to a few specific changes. Not all fourteen at once — you cannot carry all of it at the same moment. But pick two or three areas where the Lord has most convicted you, and begin there. Perhaps it is morning prayer. Perhaps it is speaking gently to your wife. Perhaps it is putting away alcohol. Perhaps it is starting family worship. Perhaps it is joining a men's accountability group. Pick two or three and commit before God, in writing if possible, with a witness if possible, to begin.

Third, go to your wife and tell her. Do not promise what you cannot deliver. Simply say, "I have been reading about what God expects of me as a husband and father. I see that I have failed in some areas. I am asking God to change me, and I am asking you to pray for me." Most wives, on hearing such words from their husbands, will weep tears of joy and will pray down heaven upon you. A humble husband is a powerful husband.

Fourth, go to your children, one at a time, and speak to them. If you have harmed them, confess it.

If you have been absent, tell them you are coming home. If you have never blessed them, lay your hand on their head tonight and bless them by name. "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace" (Numbers 6:24–26). That old blessing, spoken over your children tonight, may echo in them for eighty years.

Fifth, find a brother. Do not walk alone. Today, tomorrow at the latest, reach out to one godly man in your church and ask him to meet with you regularly. Tell him, "I am trying to become the man God is calling me to be. Will you walk with me? Will you pray with me? Will you ask me hard questions?" You may be surprised how many men have been waiting for someone to ask them.

Sixth, plant yourself deeply in a local church. Not just attendance — membership, service, submission to elders, participation in the body. Be there in the joys and the struggles. If your current church is not preaching the gospel faithfully and teaching the Word carefully, pray about this with your wife and seek a church that does. But do not be a drifter. The Church is the bride of Christ. Love what He loves.

Seventh, write your vision. Following Habakkuk's instruction, sit down this week — even for thirty minutes — and write what God is calling you to in each area of life. Spiritual. Marriage. Children.

Work. Finance. Service. Let it be imperfect. Refine it over time. But get something on paper. Pray over it. Act on it.

Eighth, pick up this book again in one year. Read it again. See where God has changed you. See where you still need to grow. Let it be a marker on your journey. Share it with another man who needs to read it.

And now, my brother, hear the final word.

East Africa — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, and beyond — is waiting for men like you, men who will rise from their knees with the name of Jesus on their lips and the courage of the Spirit in their hearts.

Our grandfathers in the faith — Charles Lwanga at Namugongo, Simeon Nsibambi on Namirembe Hill, Festo Kivengere in exile, Janani Luwum before the dictator — they fought the good fight.

They finished the race. They kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). They have passed the torch.

Now it is your hand that holds it.

Will you take up the torch, or will you let it fall?

The devil hates a rising man. He will oppose you. He will tempt you. He will try to use your own past failures to convince you it is hopeless. Do not listen. "Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world" (1 John 4:4). The same Christ who conquered death conquers your fear. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will raise you from your spiritual sleep.

Rise up, husband. Your wife has been praying for this day.

Rise up, father. Your children have been waiting for you to lead.

Rise up, brother. The church of God needs your shoulder beside theirs.

Rise up, man of Africa. The nations are watching. Heaven is watching. The Lord Jesus Christ is watching. And one day you will stand before Him and give an account.

May you stand on that day, not trembling in shame, but joyful, weary but not ashamed, your hands rough from faithful labor, your family standing behind you, your brothers beside you, your Savior's words ringing in your ears: "Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter into the joy of your Lord."

Amen, and Amen.

Closing Prayer Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Lord Jesus Christ, You who walked the earth as the perfect Man, the true Husband of the Church, the great Son of the Father, we lift our eyes to You now. Holy Spirit, without whom nothing true can be done, we ask You to fall fresh upon us. We come before You, Father, as men. Some of us are young, some old. Some married, some still waiting. Some have fathered children well, some have failed them deeply. Some have walked with You for years, some are only just beginning. But all of us, in this moment, bow before You and say: we are Yours. Forgive us for the years we have lived for ourselves. Forgive us for the wives we have not loved as Christ loved the Church. Forgive us for the children we have not discipled, the homes we have not led, the churches we have not served, the sins we have not confessed, the brothers we have not supported. Wash us in the blood of Jesus. Clothe us in His righteousness. Fill us with His Spirit. And send us out as men. Make us men who pray before they speak. Men who confess before they accuse. Men who love before they demand. Men who serve before they command.

Men who work hard and trust You for the harvest. Men who stand as watchmen at the gates of our homes. Men who plant ourselves in Your Church and do not drift away. Men who fight the battle within and walk in the purity Your Son bought with His blood. Men of vision. Men of faithfulness. Men who leave behind a legacy that will sing Your praises for generations. For our wives, O Lord, have mercy. For our children, make us the fathers You have called us to be. For our churches, raise us up as servants and elders. For our nations — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Sudan, the Congo, and all of Africa — send us a revival like the fire that fell in the 1930s, a fire that humbles men, purifies families, strengthens churches, and shakes whole nations. We long to see it. We pray for it.

We will be ready for it. Bless the wives who are reading this prayer beside their husbands, those who have prayed for years and are about to see the answer. Bless the single men who are preparing for a holy marriage one day. Bless the widowers who feel alone. Bless the young men who have no father in the home, and be their Father Yourself. Bless the elders of the Church who are weary in shepherding.

Bless the pastors who plead in empty sanctuaries. Bless the evangelists who still walk the village paths with Bibles in hand. And when our days are done, Lord, let us stand before You with joy. Let none of our family be missing at the Wedding Supper of the Lamb. Let our labor not be in vain. Let our lives sing of Your goodness long after our graves have grown quiet. We ask all this in the mighty, glorious, saving, sanctifying name of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, our Lord, our Brother, our King. Amen.

THE END
fields.body_text: Leaving a Godly Heritage "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children, but a sinner's wealth is stored up for the righteous." — Proverbs 13:22 You will die, brother. I do not say this to be dark. I say it because the Bible says it. "It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27). Your days are numbered (Psalm 90:12). The length of your life is a secret kept by the One who gave it to you. Some men get eighty years. Some men do not see their fortieth birthday. Some men are cut down at twenty- five, leaving a young wife and small children. None of us know. But this much we do know: you will leave something behind. Every man does. The question is not whether you will leave a legacy. The question is what kind. Solomon tells us, "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children." Notice the horizon. Not just for your children, but for your children's children — the grandchildren you may or may not live to see. A godly man thinks generationally. He is not building only for his lifetime. He is building for generations he will not meet on this side of eternity. What kind of legacy should a godly man aim for? Let us consider three levels: material, moral, and spiritual. First, a material inheritance. Scripture does honor the passing of material goods. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents," says Proverbs 19:14. A father who leaves his family with nothing when he could have planned better has not served them well. This does not mean you must become rich. It means you must be faithful. If you have a small plot of land, can you leave it free of debt? If you have a small business, can you leave it in good health? If you have little to leave, can you leave a legacy of honest dealing with those you owed? Some men leave debts and lawsuits behind them — that is a curse to their children. Some leave paid-up accounts and quiet consciences — that is a blessing. Plan for what happens when you die. Write a will. In many African contexts, when the husband dies without a will, the extended family may come and take what was meant for the widow and the children. Protect your household. A will is not lack of faith; it is an act of love. "The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty" (Proverbs 27:12). Second, a moral inheritance. This is more valuable than money, and many poor men have left enormous moral wealth to their descendants. A moral inheritance is the memory of integrity. It is your children saying, "Papa never lied to us." It is your neighbors saying, "Your father never cheated me." It is your wife saying, "Your father never once raised his hand against me." A reputation for honesty is a shelter that covers your children's children. A moral inheritance is also the memory of love. It is your grown son remembering, "Papa took me fishing. Papa prayed for me at my bedside. Papa told me he was proud of me." It is your grown daughter remembering, "Papa treated Mama with respect. Papa hugged me. Papa told me I was beautiful in the Lord." Children who are loved well by their fathers are anchored for life. A moral inheritance is the shape of how you lived. Your working hard. Your faithfulness to one wife. Your kindness to the poor. Your refusal to take bribes. Your laughter in your home. Your songs on the road. Your tears at the funeral of a friend. Your courage at the funeral of a child. These memories are currency your children will spend for the rest of their lives. Third, and most important, a spiritual legacy. This is the treasure that outlives every other. "Houses and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord" (Proverbs 19:14) — how much more is a prudent faith? Money is eaten by inflation and sometimes by corrupt officials. Land can be stolen. Buildings can burn. Reputations can fade. But a grandchild who knows Jesus because his grandfather prayed for him — that is a legacy no fire can touch, no thief can steal, no government can confiscate. Think again of Timothy, who had the faith that "first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations of faith. A grandmother who loved Jesus, a mother who loved Jesus, a grandson who became a pastor and apostolic helper because of them. This is a family we do not hear much about by name, but their legacy shaped the Church forever through Timothy's ministry. Think of the Wesley family. Susanna Wesley, mother of John and Charles, raised nineteen children in a small English parsonage. She taught them the Scriptures. She prayed for them daily. Two of them — John and Charles — shook the world through the Methodist revival, which reached across England, America, and yes, eventually the continent of Africa. Susanna could not have known that her patient mothering would one day result in churches planted in Uganda. But that is how legacy works. A mother's prayers in 1710 became a missionary's boat sailing in 1870 became an African pastor's sermon in 2026. Think of the East African Revival fathers — Nsibambi, Nagenda, Kivengere, and many more whose names are not as famous but whose prayers and lives touched generations. Kivengere lived to see his preaching impact churches on three continents. His legacy is not a monument of stone; it is souls in glory, churches still preaching the gospel, children of converts still walking with Jesus. And think of the Ugandan martyrs. Young men, most of them teenagers and young adults, burned alive at Namugongo in 1886. They did not leave behind material wealth. Many had no children. But look what they left behind: a Church. A century and a half later, more than 80% of Uganda professes the name of Christ because of the witness of those young men. Their blood became seed, just as Tertullian said centuries earlier, "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church." Every June 3rd, Catholics and Protestants alike still remember them. The smallest spiritual legacy is larger than the grandest earthly one. So what will your legacy be? Brother, begin now to live with your end in mind. Every day, ask, "If I died tonight, what would my wife remember? What would my children inherit? What would my church say at my funeral? What would the Lord Jesus say when He meets me?" This is not morbid. This is wisdom. "Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12). Live in such a way that when you are old, you can sit and look at your grandchildren and know that you planted well. Live in such a way that when you die, your children say, "Our father loved Jesus, and he loved us." Live in such a way that long after the last person who remembers your face has also died, your great-great-grandchildren are still walking with the Lord because of the family you planted for Him. The trees you plant today will give shade to generations who will never know your name. Plant well. A Prayer Eternal Father, the generations come and go, but You remain forever. My days are a breath; Your years have no end. Teach me to live with eternity in view. Let me not waste my one short life on trivial things. Let me lay down a spiritual heritage that will echo through my family long after my bones rest in the earth. Give me grace to love my wife so well that my granddaughters will expect to be loved well. Give me grace to teach my children so faithfully that my great-grandchildren will sing Your praises. Let the trees I plant give shade to many. And may my name be found written in the Book of Life when the final day comes. In the name of Jesus Christ, the Resurrection and the Life, Amen. We began by looking at the hungry land around us — hungry for godly men. Fourteen chapters. Fourteen calls. Fourteen areas where God has spoken. And now the book closes, and the question presses: what will you do? Reading is easy. Applying is hard. Books can be set on a shelf and forgotten, or they can be the match that lights a fire. Which will this book be for you? Let me lay before you a simple call to action. Not complicated. Not overwhelming. Just a beginning. Take what follows and make it your own, with your pastor, with your wife, with your brothers in the faith. First, make sure you are a Christian. I ask this of every reader, because no one can lead spiritually who has not first been made alive by the Spirit of God. Have you come to the end of yourself and found only Jesus is enough? Have you repented of your sins and trusted in Christ alone for salvation? If you have never done this, do it today. Right where you are. "If you declare with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). Do not read another chapter of your life without settling this. Second, commit to a few specific changes. Not all fourteen at once — you cannot carry all of it at the same moment. But pick two or three areas where the Lord has most convicted you, and begin there. Perhaps it is morning prayer. Perhaps it is speaking gently to your wife. Perhaps it is putting away alcohol. Perhaps it is starting family worship. Perhaps it is joining a men's accountability group. Pick two or three and commit before God, in writing if possible, with a witness if possible, to begin. Third, go to your wife and tell her. Do not promise what you cannot deliver. Simply say, "I have been reading about what God expects of me as a husband and father. I see that I have failed in some areas. I am asking God to change me, and I am asking you to pray for me." Most wives, on hearing such words from their husbands, will weep tears of joy and will pray down heaven upon you. A humble husband is a powerful husband. Fourth, go to your children, one at a time, and speak to them. If you have harmed them, confess it. If you have been absent, tell them you are coming home. If you have never blessed them, lay your hand on their head tonight and bless them by name. "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace" (Numbers 6:24–26). That old blessing, spoken over your children tonight, may echo in them for eighty years. Fifth, find a brother. Do not walk alone. Today, tomorrow at the latest, reach out to one godly man in your church and ask him to meet with you regularly. Tell him, "I am trying to become the man God is calling me to be. Will you walk with me? Will you pray with me? Will you ask me hard questions?" You may be surprised how many men have been waiting for someone to ask them. Sixth, plant yourself deeply in a local church. Not just attendance — membership, service, submission to elders, participation in the body. Be there in the joys and the struggles. If your current church is not preaching the gospel faithfully and teaching the Word carefully, pray about this with your wife and seek a church that does. But do not be a drifter. The Church is the bride of Christ. Love what He loves. Seventh, write your vision. Following Habakkuk's instruction, sit down this week — even for thirty minutes — and write what God is calling you to in each area of life. Spiritual. Marriage. Children. Work. Finance. Service. Let it be imperfect. Refine it over time. But get something on paper. Pray over it. Act on it. Eighth, pick up this book again in one year. Read it again. See where God has changed you. See where you still need to grow. Let it be a marker on your journey. Share it with another man who needs to read it. And now, my brother, hear the final word. East Africa — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, and beyond — is waiting for men like you, men who will rise from their knees with the name of Jesus on their lips and the courage of the Spirit in their hearts. Our grandfathers in the faith — Charles Lwanga at Namugongo, Simeon Nsibambi on Namirembe Hill, Festo Kivengere in exile, Janani Luwum before the dictator — they fought the good fight. They finished the race. They kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). They have passed the torch. Now it is your hand that holds it. Will you take up the torch, or will you let it fall? The devil hates a rising man. He will oppose you. He will tempt you. He will try to use your own past failures to convince you it is hopeless. Do not listen. "Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world" (1 John 4:4). The same Christ who conquered death conquers your fear. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will raise you from your spiritual sleep. Rise up, husband. Your wife has been praying for this day. Rise up, father. fields.title: To You
fields.body_html:
TO YOU

HE WHO SPOKE and wrote this message will be greatly disappointed if it does not lead many to the Lord Jesus. It is sent forth in childlike dependence upon the power of God the Holy Ghost, to use it in the conversion of millions, if so He pleases. No doubt many poor men and women will take up this little volume, and the Lord will visit them with grace. To answer this end, the very plainest language has been chosen, and many homely expressions have been used. But if those of wealth and rank should glance at this book, the Holy Ghost can impress them also; since that which can be understood by the unlettered is none the less attractive to the instructed. Oh that some might read it who will become great winners of souls!

Who knows how many will find their way to peace by what they read here? A more important question to you, dear reader, is this- -Will you be one of them?

A certain man placed a fountain by the wayside, and he hung up a cup near to it by a little chain. He was told some time after that a great art-critic had found much fault with its design. "But," said he, "do many thirsty persons drink at it?" Then they told him that thousands of poor people, men, women, and children, slaked their thirst at this fountain; and he smiled and said, that he was little troubled by the critic's observation, only he hoped that on some sultry summer's day the critic himself might fill the cup, and he refreshed, and praise the name of the Lord.

Here is my fountain, and here is my cup: find fault if you please; but do drink of the water of life. I only care for this. I had rather bless the soul of the poorest crossing-sweeper, or rag-gatherer, than please a prince of the blood, and fail to convert him to God.

Reader, do you mean business in reading these pages? If so, we are agreed at the outset; but nothing short of your finding Christ and Heaven is the business aimed at here. Oh that we may seek this together! I do so by dedicating this little book with prayer. Will not you join me by looking up to God, and asking Him to bless you while you read? Providence has put these pages in your way, you have a little spare time in which to read them, and you feel willing to give your attention to them. These are good signs. Who knows but the set time of blessing is come for you? At any rate, "The Holy Ghost saith, Today, if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts."

fields.title: What Are We At?
fields.body_html:
WHAT ARE WE AT?

I HEARD A STORY; I think it came from the North Country: A minister called upon a poor woman, intending to give her help; for he knew that she was very poor. With his money in his hand, he knocked at the door; but she did not answer. He concluded she was not at home, and went his way. A little after he met her at the church, and told her that he had remembered her need: "I called at your house, and knocked several times, and I suppose you were not at home, for I had no answer." "At what hour did you call, sir?" "It was about noon." "Oh, dear," she said, "I heard you, sir, and I am so sorry I did not answer; but I thought it was the man calling for the rent." Many a poor woman knows what this meant. Now, it is my desire to be heard, and therefore I want to say that I am not calling for the rent; indeed, it is not the object of this book to ask anything of you, but to tell you that salvation is all of grace, which means, free, gratis, for nothing.

Oftentimes, when we are anxious to win attention, our hearer thinks, "Ah! now I am going to be told my duty. It is the man calling for that which is due to God, and I am sure I have nothing wherewith to pay. I will not be at home." No, this book does not come to make a demand upon you, but to bring you something. We are not going to talk about law, and duty, and punishment, but about love, and goodness, and forgiveness, and mercy, and eternal life. Do not, therefore, act as if you were not at home: do not turn a deaf ear, or a careless heart. I am asking nothing of you in the name of God or man. It is not my intent to make any requirement at your hands; but I come in God's name, to bring you a free gift, which it shall be to your present and eternal joy to receive. Open the door, and let my pleadings enter. "Come now, and let us reason together." The Lord himself invites you to a conference concerning your immediate and endless happiness, and He would not have done this if He did not mean well toward you. Do not refuse the Lord Jesus who knocks at your door; for He knocks with a hand which was nailed to the tree for such as you are. Since His only and sole object is your good, incline your ear and come to Him. Hearken diligently, and let the good word sink into your soul. It may be that the hour is come in which you shall enter upon that new life which is the beginning of heaven. Faith cometh by hearing, and reading is a sort of hearing: faith may come to you while you are reading this book. Why not? O blessed Spirit of all grace, make it so!

fields.title: God Justifieth the Ungodly
fields.body_html:
GOD JUSTIFIETH THE UNGODLY

THIS MESSAGE is for you. You will find the text in the Epistle to the Romans, in the fourth chapter and the fifth verse:

To him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.

I call your attention to those words, "Him that justifieth the ungodly." They seem to me to be very wonderful words.

Are you not surprised that there should be such an expression as that in the Bible, "That justifieth the ungodly?" I have heard that men that hate the doctrines of the cross bring it as a charge against God, that He saves wicked men and receives to Himself the vilest of the vile. See how this Scripture accepts the charge, and plainly states it! By the mouth of His servant Paul, by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost, He takes to Himself the title of "Him that justifieth the ungodly." He makes those just who are unjust, forgives those who deserve to be punished, and favors those who deserve no favor. You thought, did you not, that salvation was for the good? that God's grace was for the pure and holy, who are free from sin? It has fallen into your mind that, if you were excellent, then God would reward you; and you have thought that because you are not worthy, therefore there could be no way of your enjoying His favor. You must be somewhat surprised to read a text like this: "Him that justifieth the ungodly." I do not wonder that you are surprised; for with all my familiarity with the great grace of God, I never cease to wonder at it. It does sound surprising, does it not, that it should be possible for a holy God to justify an unholy man? We, according to the natural legality of our hearts, are always talking about our own goodness and our own worthiness, and we stubbornly hold to it that there must be somewhat in us in order to win the notice of God. Now, God, who sees through all deceptions, knows that there is no goodness whatever in us. He says that "there is none righteous, no not one." He knows that "all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags," and, therefore the Lord Jesus did not come into the world to look after goodness and righteousness with him, and to bestow them upon persons who have none of them. He comes, not because we are just, but to make us so: he justifieth the ungodly.

When a counsellor comes into court, if he is an honest man, he desires to plead the case of an innocent person and justify him before the court from the things which are falsely laid to his charge. It should be the lawyer's object to justify the innocent person, and he should not attempt to screen the guilty party. It lies not in man's right nor in man's power truly to justify the guilty. This is a miracle reserved for the Lord alone. God, the infinitely just Sovereign, knows that there is not a just man upon earth that doeth good and sinneth not, and therefore, in the infinite sovereignty of His divine nature and in the splendor of His ineffable love, He undertakes the task, not so much of justifying the just as of justifying the ungodly. God has devised ways and means of making the ungodly man to stand justly accepted before Him: He has set up a system by which with perfect justice He can treat the guilty as if he had been all his life free from offence, yea, can treat him as if he were wholly free from sin. He justifieth the ungodly.

Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. It is a very surprising thing--a thing to be marveled at most of all by those who enjoy it. I know that it is to me even to this day the greatest wonder that I ever heard of, that God should ever justify me. I feel myself to be a lump of unworthiness, a mass of corruption, and a heap of sin, apart from His almighty love. I know by a full assurance that I am justified by faith which is in Christ Jesus, and treated as if I had been perfectly just, and made an heir of God and a joint heir with Christ; and yet by nature I must take my place among the most sinful. I, who am altogether undeserving, am treated as if I had been deserving. I am loved with as much love as if I had always been godly, whereas aforetime I was ungodly. Who can help being astonished at this? Gratitude for such favor stands dressed in robes of wonder.

Is not that the very kind of person that you are? If you are unconverted at this moment, it is a very proper description of you; you have lived without God, you have been the reverse of godly; in one word, you have been and are ungodly. Perhaps you have not even attended a place of worship on Sunday, but have lived in disregard of God's day, and house, and Word--this proves you to have been ungodly. Sadder still, it may be you have even tried to doubt God's existence, and have gone the length of saying that you did so. You have lived on this fair earth, which is full of the tokens of God's presence, and all the while you have shut your eyes to the clear evidences of His power and Godhead. You have lived as if there were no God. Indeed, you would have been very pleased if you could have demonstrated to yourself to a certainty that there was no God whatever. Possibly you have lived a great many years in this way, so that you are now pretty well settled in your ways, and yet God is not in any of them. If you were labeled

UNGODLY

it would as well describe you as if the sea were to be labeled salt water. Would it not?

You have lived without any love to God in your heart, or regard to his commands in your life. The Holy Ghost hath made him so.

Come in your deshabille. I mean, come to your heavenly Father in all your sin and sinfulness. Come to Jesus just as you are, leprous, filthy, naked, neither fit to live nor fit to die. Come, you that are the very sweepings of creation; come, though you hardly dare to hope for anything but death. Come, though despair is brooding over you, pressing upon your bosom like a horrible nightmare. Come and ask the Lord to justify another ungodly one. Why should He not? Come for this great mercy of God is meant for such as you are. I put it in the language of the text, and I cannot put it more strongly: the Lord God Himself takes to Himself this gracious title, "Him that justifieth the ungodly." He makes just, and causes to be treated as just, those who by nature are ungodly. Is not that a wonderful word for you? Reader, do not delay till you have well considered this matter.

fields.title: It Is God That Justifieth
fields.body_html:
"IT IS GOD THAT JUSTIFIETH"

Romans 8:33

A WONDERFUL THING it is, this being justified, or made just. If we had never broken the laws of God we should not have needed it, for we should have been just in ourselves. He who has all his life done the things which he ought to have done, and has never done anything which he ought not to have done, is justified by the law. But you, dear reader, are not of that sort, I am quite sure. You have too much honesty to pretend to be without sin, and therefore you need to be justified.

Now, if you justify yourself, you will simply be a self- deceiver. Therefore do not attempt it. It is never worth while.

If you ask your fellow mortals to justify you, what can they do? You can make some of them speak well of you for small favors, and others will backbite you for less. Their judgment is not worth much.

Our text says, "It is God that justifieth," and this is a deal more to the point. It is an astonishing fact, and one that we ought to consider with care. Come and see.

In the first place, nobody else but God would ever have thought of justifying those who are guilty. They have lived in open rebellion; they have done evil with both hands; they have gone from bad to worse; they have turned back to sin even after they have smarted for it, and have therefore for a while been forced to leave it. They have broken the law, and trampled on the gospel. They have refused proclamations of mercy, and have persisted in ungodliness. How can they be forgiven and justified? Their fellowmen, despairing of them, say, "They are hopeless cases." Even Christians look upon them with sorrow rather than with hope. But not so their God. He, in the splendor of his electing grace having chosen some of them before the foundation of the world, will not rest till He has justified them, and made them to be accepted in the Beloved. Is it not written, "Whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified"? Thus you see there are some whom the Lord resolves to justify: why should not you and I be of the number?

None but God would ever have thought of justifying me. I am a wonder to myself. I doubt not that grace is equally seen in others. Look at Saul of Tarsus, who foamed at the mouth, against God's servants. Like a hungry wolf, he worried the lambs and the sheep right and left; and yet God struck him down on the road to Damascus, and changed his heart, and so fully justified him that ere long, this man became the greatest preacher of justification by faith that ever lived. He must often have marveled that he was justified by faith in Christ Jesus; for he was once a determined stickler for salvation by the works of the law. None but God would have ever thought of justifying such a man as Saul the persecutor; but the Lord God is glorious in grace.

But, even if anybody had thought of justifying the ungodly, none but God could have done it. It is quite impossible for any person to forgive offences which have not been committed against himself. A person has greatly injured you; you can forgive him, and I hope you will; but no third person can forgive him apart from you. If the wrong is done to you, the pardon must come from you. If we have sinned against God, it is in God's power to forgive; for the sin is against Himself. That is why David says, in the fifty-first Psalm: "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight"; for then God, against whom the offence is committed, can put the offence away. That which we owe to God, our great Creator can remit, if so it pleases Him; and if He remits it, it is remitted. None but the great God, against whom we have committed the sin, can blot out that sin; let us, therefore, see that we go to Him and seek mercy at His hands. Do not let us be led aside by those who would have us confess to them; they have no warrant in the Word of God for their pretensions. But even if they were ordained to pronounce absolution in God's name, it must still be better to go ourselves to the great Lord through Jesus Christ, the Mediator, and seek and find pardon at His hand; since we are sure that this is the right way. Proxy religion involves too great a risk: you had better see to your soul's matters yourself, and leave them in no man's hands.

Only God can justify the ungodly; but He can do it to perfection. He casts our sins behind His back, He blots them out; He says that though they be sought for, they shall not be found. With no other reason for it but His own infinite goodness, He has prepared a glorious way by which He can make scarlet sins as white as snow, and remove our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west. He says, "I will not remember your sins." He goes the length of making an end of sin. One of old called out in amazement, "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy" (Micah 7:18 ).

We are not now speaking of justice, nor of God's dealing with men according to their deserts. If you profess to deal with the righteous Lord on law terms, everlasting wrath threatens you, for that is what you deserve. Blessed be His name, He has not dealt with us after our sins; but now He treats with us on terms of free grace and infinite compassion, and He says, "I will receive you graciously, and love you freely." Believe it, for it is certainly true that the great God is able to treat the guilty with abundant mercy; yea, He is able to treat the ungodly as if they had been always godly. Read carefully the parable of the prodigal son, and see how the forgiving father received the returning wanderer with as much love as if he had never gone away, and had never defiled himself with harlots. So far did he carry this that the elder brother began to grumble at it; but the father never withdrew his love. Oh my brother, however guilty you may be, if you will only come back to your God and Father, He will treat you as if you had never done wrong! He will regard you as just, and deal with you accordingly. What say you to this?

Do you not see--for I want to bring this out clearly, what a splendid thing it is--that as none but God would think of justifying the ungodly, and none but God could do it, yet the Lord can do it? See how the apostle puts the challenge, "Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth." If God has justified a man it is well done, it is rightly done, it is justly done, it is everlastingly done. I read a statement in a magazine which is full of venom against the gospel and those who preach it, that we hold some kind of theory by which we imagine that sin can be removed from men. We hold no theory, we publish a fact. The grandest fact under heaven is this- -that Christ by His precious blood does actually put away sin, and that God, for Christ's sake, dealing with men on terms of divine mercy, forgives the guilty and justifies them, not according to anything that He sees in them, or foresees will be in them, but according to the riches of His mercy which lie in His own heart. This we have preached, do preach, and will preach as long as we live. "It is God that justifieth"--that justifieth the ungodly; He is not ashamed of doing it, nor are we of preaching it.

The justification which comes from God himself must be beyond question. If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me? If the highest court in the universe has pronounced me just, who shall lay anything to my charge? Justification from God is a sufficient answer to an awakened conscience. The Holy Spirit by its means breathes peace over our entire nature, and we are no longer afraid. With this justification we can answer all the roarings and railings of Satan and ungodly men. With this we shall be able to die: with this we shall boldly rise again, and face the last great assize.

Bold shall I stand in that great day,
For who aught to my charge shall lay?
While by my Lord absolved I am
From sin's tremendous curse and blame.

Friend, the Lord can blot out all your sins. I make no shot in the dark when I say this. "All manner of sin and of blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men." Though you are steeped up to your throat in crime, He can with a word remove the defilement, and say, "I will, be thou clean." The Lord is a great forgiver.

"I believe in the Forgiveness of Sins." Do You?

He can even at this hour pronounce the sentence, "Thy sins be forgiven thee; go in peace;" and if He do this, no power in Heaven, or earth, or under the earth, can put you under suspicion, much less under wrath. Do not doubt the power of Almighty love. You could not forgive your fellow man had he offended you as you have offended God; but you must not measure God's corn with your bushel; His thoughts and ways are as much above yours as the heavens are high above the earth.

"Well," say you, "it would be a great miracle if the Lord were to pardon me." Just so. It would be a supreme miracle, and therefore He is likely to do it; for He does "great things and unsearchable" which we looked not for.

I was myself stricken down with a horrible sense of guilt, which made my life a misery to me; but when I heard the command, "Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is none else"--I looked, and in a moment the Lord justified me. Jesus Christ, made sin for me, was what I saw, and that sight gave me rest. When those who were bitten by the fiery serpents in the wilderness looked to the serpent of brass they were healed at once; and so was I when I looked to the crucified Saviour. The Holy Spirit, who enabled me to believe, gave me peace through believing. I felt as sure that I was forgiven, as before I felt sure of condemnation. I had been certain of my condemnation because the Word of God declared it, and my conscience bore witness to it; but when the Lord justified me I was made equally certain by the same witnesses. The word of the Lord in the Scripture saith, "He that believeth on him is not condemned," and my conscience bears witness that I believed, and that God in pardoning me is just. Thus I have the witness of the Holy Spirit and my own conscience, and these two agree in one. Oh, how I wish that my reader would receive the testimony of God upon this matter, and then full soon he would also have the witness in himself!

I venture to say that a sinner justified by God stands on even a surer footing than a righteous man justified by his works, if such there be. We could never be surer that we had done enough works; conscience would always be uneasy lest, after all, we should come short, and we could only have the trembling verdict of a fallible judgment to rely upon; but when God himself justifies, and the Holy Spirit bears witness thereto by giving us peace with God, why then we feel that the matter is sure and settled, and we enter into rest. No tongue can tell the depth of that calm which comes over the soul which has received the peace of God which passeth all understanding.
