fields.title: Quaker queries
fields.body_html:
Next in importance to the impression made upon my young mind by the teaching regarding the perceptible guidance of the Holy Spirit was the one made by “Friends’ testimonies,” as they were called, and by the “Queries” founded upon them.

These “Queries” were a series of questions concerning the practice of Quakerism. They were solemnly asked and answered once a month in the Monthly Meetings, which had been appointed for the purpose of transacting the business of the Society. There were eight of these Queries, and they formed a noble code of morals, calculated to produce a people of unflinching uprightness and honesty in all their dealings, and of remarkable self-restraint and self-denial in their private lives. Much as I chafed under them as a child, I have never been able to forget the lessons they taught; even now, I often find myself guided by their precepts.

With such monthly probing of conduct as these Queries demanded, it was almost inevitable that a high standard of righteousness became an integral part of a Quaker’s life, and I feel it to have been an invaluable element in my own religious training.

Behind these Queries lay a body of “Friends’ testimonies” from which the Queries had arisen.

Although unwritten — except insofar as they were expressed in the Queries — these testimonies were absolutely binding upon every true Friend. I have often thought that they were, in reality, our Quaker Ten Commandments, though no one ever said so. As a child, I certainly believed that they were special commandments given to us as Quakers, distinguishing us from all the Christians around us and making us the “peculiar people” we were proud to call ourselves.

Many of these testimonies were strict and severe, and to outsiders they must often have seemed harsh. But as all the Quakers I knew had been brought up on them from infancy, they did not press upon us as heavily as might be supposed. They served, however, to keep Quaker feet walking in a narrow way —the “strait gate and narrow way” spoken of in Scripture as the only path that “leadeth unto life.”

Every one of these testimonies had been, we devoutly believed, directly revealed by the Holy Spirit to the early Friends; and however unreasonable they might otherwise have seemed, we young Friends reverenced them as the very oracles of God.

Since these Queries have almost entirely fallen into the background among Quakers of recent years, I will record them here as a faithful exposition of the Quakerism of my youth.

First Query. — Are all our religious meetings for worship and discipline duly attended; is the hour observed; and are Friends clear of sleeping and of all other unbecoming behavior therein?

Second Query. — Are love and unity maintained among you? Are tale-bearing and detraction discouraged? And when differences arise, are endeavours used to end them promptly?

Third Query. — Are Friends careful to bring up those under their charge in plainness of speech, behavior, and apparel; in frequently reading the Holy Scriptures; and in restraining them from reading pernicious books and from corrupt conversation? And are they good examples in these respects themselves?

Fourth Query. — Are Friends careful to discourage the unnecessary distillation and use of spirituous liquors, and the frequenting of taverns; to avoid places of diversion; and to maintain true moderation and temperance at marriages, burials, and all other occasions?

Fifth Query. —Are poor Friends’ necessities duly inspected, and are they relieved or assisted in business suitable to their abilities? Do their children freely partake of learning to fit them for business, and are they and other Frie nds’ children placed among Friends?

Sixth Query. — Do you maintain a faithful testimony against oaths; a hireling ministry; bearing arms, training, and other military services; engaging in fraudulent or clandestine trade; buying or vending goods so imported; or dealing in prize goods; and against encouraging lotteries of every kind?

Seventh Query. — Are Friends careful to live within the bounds of their circumstances and to maintain moderation in their trade or business? Are they punctual in their promises and just in payment of their debts? And when any give reasonable cause for fear in these respects, are they timely laboured with for their preservation or recovery?

Eighth Query. — Do you take due care regularly to deal with all offenders in the spirit of meekness, without partiality or unnecessary delay, for their help; and when such labour is ineffectual, do you place judgment upon them in the authority of truth?

The reading of these Queries in our Monthly Meetings constituted a kind of public, monthly confessional for the whole Society, and they were seasons of solemn self-examination for both old and young. Each separate meeting belonging to the Monthly Meeting sent in its own set of answers, and the discussion of these was known as “the consideration of the state of society.”

Such answers as these linger in my memory: “Our meetings have all been duly attended by most of our members, but some Friends have not observed the hour.”

“Mostly clear of unbecoming behavior, but some sleeping has been observed.”

“ Friends generally are careful to bring up their children in plainness of speech, behavior, and apparel, but more faithfulness in this respect is desirable.”

“Our testimony against oaths, a hireling ministry, bearing arms, engaging in clandestine trade, and against encouraging lotteries, has been faithfully maintained by all our members.”

It was the custom, after each Query and answer had been read, for a period of silence to follow, giving Friends an opportunity to “relieve their minds” of any message that might have been given them concerning that particular Query. These intervals were generally times of deep searching of the heart for all who were present.

As I remember it, the Query that was preached upon most frequently and most fervently was the Third, concerning the testimony for “plainness of speech, behaviour, and apparel, and against the vain fashions of the world.” It was this testimony that most contributed to making Quakers a “peculiar people,” and that caused us young Friends the greatest heart -burnings. I remember vividly the suffering I endured each month as I sat beside my mother listening to this Query read and expounded. My constant fear was that it might make her still more strict in keeping us from the “vain fashions of the world,” which, i n spite of all our training, held a fascination we could never wholly overcome. As the Friend appointed to read the Queries approached this particular one, I would try my best to abstract my mind, even surreptitiously stopping my ears, attempting to cheat myself into thinking that if I did not hear it, my mother would not notice it either. But alas, I was always doomed to disappointment, for the preaching on this Query was the most frequent and most impassioned, and in the end, both she and I were obliged to listen.

Two incidents of my childhood, connected with this Query, come back to me with great vividness.

Our mother had bought us white China-crape shawls with lovely long fringes that seemed to us too beautiful for words, and we wore them with immense pride. One day, however, she returned from a meeting where the Queries had been read and answered, and told us that she had felt during the meeting that our long fringes were too “gay” for Friends’ children, and that she believed it her duty to cut them shorter.

I can see it all now, as she carefully spread the shawls on a large table, laid a yardstick across the fringe at what she deemed the proper length, and proceeded to cut off all the beautiful extra strands. It was like cutting into our very hearts. I remember how we pleaded and pleaded that the fatal yardstick might be moved down just a little further. Our great fear was that our fringes would be shorter than those of our intimate friends Hannah and Jane Scull, who were allowed to be a little gayer than we were. To have their fringes even a tenth of an inch longer than ours seemed a calamity beyond bearing. I cannot remember how the matter ended, but I shall never forget the agonies of mind we endured during the process.

Another experience connected with a dress left an indelible impression on me. The sleeve considered “plain” in my day was the leg -of-mutton sleeve, and all our dresses were made accordingly. But some benign influence — what it was we never knew — induced our mother one spring to allow our sleeves to be made somewhat in the fashion of the day, which happened then to be Bishop sleeves, full at both shoulder and wrist. The fashionable Bishop sleeves were very large, but ours were tiny little ones; however, they were real Bishops, and our pride in them was immense. They belonged to our new spring school dresses, of a brown-and-white striped print — “calico,” as we called it. Although the weather was still wintery, our desire to display our fashionable sleeves was so overwhelming that nothing would do but that we must put them on and take a long walk without our coats; and no two prouder little girls ever walked the streets of Philadelphia than Hannah and Sally Whitall on that morning. I remember our younger sister Mary wanting to go with us, but her sleeves were still leg-of-mutton, and we felt it would spoil the full effect if one member of our party appeared in the despised shape, so we made her walk on the opposite side of the street. I can still see her longing glances across the way as she admired our glory from afar.

She had her revenge soon enough. Ruffled “panties” (as we called drawers then), reaching to the feet, had come into fashion, and when our mother made her a new set, they were long and ruffled, while we still had to wear our plain hemmed ones, not showing below our dresses. This time, Mary too went out to walk to display her new finery, but, kinder than we had been, she invited us to accompany her. I am ashamed to say that the old Adam in us resented her favored condition so strongly that we refused to walk on the same side of the street with her, and scornfully crossed to the other side, leaving her to walk alone, with all the glory of her beautiful ruffled panties destroyed by our cruel scorn and unkindness.

The early Friends, in their testimony against the foolish changes of fashion among the “world’s people,” had adhered, as far as possible, to the style of dress in vogue when they first arose. In a very few years, this naturally became peculiar, and eventually developed into a sort of Quaker uniform which all faithful Friends felt “led” to adopt. I say “as far as possible,” because certain styles, when they ceased to be fashionable, soon disappeared from the market and could no longer be easily obtained; and also because even the strictest Friends could not help being somewhat influenced by time and habit.

Their testimony regarding plainness of apparel was not a testimony for or against any specific fashion, but simply a protest against following the “vain fashions of the world.” By th e time a style had become old-fashioned and was passing out of use, Quakers were ready to adopt it.

I recently came across a curious illustration of this in extracts from an old diary. In Queen Elizabeth’s time, before Quakers existed, the general fashion was to wear green aprons as part of a lady’s church -going dress. But when Quakers appeared, this style was beginning to die out, and stiff white aprons were becoming fashionable. In order not to follow changing fashions, Friends kept to the green aprons for their go-to-meeting dress, and their preachers denounced the fashionable white aprons as “gay and polluting.” One old preacher is recorded as having declared that the starch water used to stiffen them was “the devil’s water with which they needed to be s prinkled,” warning his hearers against its contaminating use.

Curiously enough, this Quaker objection to following worldly fashions extended even to many useful inventions, which one would suppose Friends’ practical good sense would have welcomed. I remember when sewing machines first appeared; they were considered exceedingly worldly. When I decided to buy one, I had to make the purchase in secret and hide the machine in the most inaccessible room in the house, lest anyone be grieved by my worldliness. Of course, later on, when Friends had grown used to the innovation, sewing machines became common in every well-ordered Quaker household; but for a long time, I felt an uneasy sense of having fallen from grace because of the worldly thing I had acquired.

The standard of plainness necessarily varied from generation to generation. But whatever the standard, the testimony against the vain fashions of the world remained unchanged, and each generation felt that the established costume of its day was in some sense a Divine ordinance, patterned in Heaven itself.

This conviction of the sanctity of “plain dress” arose largely, I believe, from the fact that nearly all personal religious experience seemed to come through this channel. The newly awakened Friend, whether yo ung or old, was invariably confronted with the question of “becoming plain , ” and the surrender of will involved in adopting the Quaker uniform always brought such peace and rest of soul that it was almost inevitable they should regard the plain dress as the cause of the blessing. This was especially true of our own dear father. In his diary, under the date of 1823, when he was just twenty-three, he writes: “While at home from my fifth voyage, I believed it right to adopt the plain dress and language of Friends. While under conviction of its being right, and fearing I should lose my situation if I did so, I met with Samuel Bettle, Sr., who, without knowing the distressed state of my mind, told me that if I were faithful to what I felt to be right, the Lord would make a way for me where there seemed no way; which indeed He did, giving me favour in the sight of my employer, much to my comfort. Hearing of a ship needing a chief mate, I borrowed a plain coat of my friend James Cox — my own not being ready — and applie d to the captain, telling him I could not ‘Mr.’ and ‘Sir’ him as was common. He kindly replied that it would only be a nine-day wonder, and at once engaged me as first mate. Thus, my prayer was answered, and a way was made for me where I saw no way. Praise d forever be the name of the Lord.”

This was the turning point of his religious life, followed by such an uplifting of soul and such a sense of God’s love that he could never dissociate the two experiences. All his life , he believed that if anyone adopted the same dress, the same blessing would follow. I believe he would gladly have bestowed a plain coat upon anyone who would consent to wear it, and nothing ever disturbed his profound conviction that plain coats and plain bonnets had been shaped and patterned in Heaven.

He even assured us once that he fully believed the armies of Heaven, spoken of in Revelation 19:14, who followed the King of kings on white horses, all wore “plain coats.” He was a member of the Board of a Quaker college near Philadelphia, where all students were required to wear straight-collared plain coats. But in hot weather, when students were obliged to wear linen or seersucker coats, the thin collars would wilt down in the heat. When the question came before the Board whether turned-down collars might be permitted in such circumstances, some members were inclined to allow it, but our father would not hear of it. He declared that if the collars could not otherwise be made to stand, whalebone must be used to stiffen them, for “stand they m ust.” I believe, however, that the summer heat finally proved too strong for even his stalwart principles, and he reluctantly consented to the turned-down collars.

I have no doubt similar things occur in other denominations besides Friends. They, too, have their own particular forms and ceremonies required of their members, and submission to these often results in a sense of peace and spiritual rest similar to that experienced by Friends when adopting the plain dress. And like the Friends, many have supposed these forms or ceremonies to be the cause of the blessing, and have elevated them to a place of sanctity, believing them ordained and patterned in Heaven. I was inclined to criticize the gorgeous robes of the priests, thinking that the Lord could not possibly care for such things, when suddenly it flashed upon me that there was, after all, no real difference between a robe of crimson and gold and a black coat with a stra ight collar, or between a Sister of Charity’s quaint costume and a sugar -scoop bonnet with a dove-coloured shawl. fields.body_text: Next in importance to the impression made upon my young mind by the teaching regarding the perceptible guidance of the Holy Spirit was the one made by “Friends’ testimonies,” as they were called, and by the “Queries” founded upon them. These “Queries” were a series of questions concerning the practice of Quakerism. They were solemnly asked and answered once a month in the Monthly Meetings, which had been appointed for the purpose of transacting the business of the Society. There were eight of these Queries, and they formed a noble code of morals, calculated to produce a people of unflinching uprightness and honesty in all their dealings, and of remarkable self-restraint and self-denial in their private lives. Much as I chafed under them as a child, I have never been able to forget the lessons they taught; even now, I often find myself guided by their precepts. With such monthly probing of conduct as these Queries demanded, it was almost inevitable that a high standard of righteousness became an integral part of a Quaker’s life, and I feel it to have been an invaluable element in my own religious training. Behind these Queries lay a body of “Friends’ testimonies” from which the Queries had arisen. Although unwritten — except insofar as they were expressed in the Queries — these testimonies were absolutely binding upon every true Friend. I have often thought that they were, in reality, our Quaker Ten Commandments, though no one ever said so. As a child, I certainly believed that they were special commandments given to us as Quakers, distinguishing us from all the Christians around us and making us the “peculiar people” we were proud to call ourselves. Many of these testimonies were strict and severe, and to outsiders they must often have seemed harsh. But as all the Quakers I knew had been brought up on them from infancy, they did not press upon us as heavily as might be supposed. They served, however, to keep Quaker feet walking in a narrow way —the “strait gate and narrow way” spoken of in Scripture as the only path that “leadeth unto life.” Every one of these testimonies had been, we devoutly believed, directly revealed by the Holy Spirit to the early Friends; and however unreasonable they might otherwise have seemed, we young Friends reverenced them as the very oracles of God. Since these Queries have almost entirely fallen into the background among Quakers of recent years, I will record them here as a faithful exposition of the Quakerism of my youth. First Query. — Are all our religious meetings for worship and discipline duly attended; is the hour observed; and are Friends clear of sleeping and of all other unbecoming behavior therein? Second Query. — Are love and unity maintained among you? Are tale-bearing and detraction discouraged? And when differences arise, are endeavours used to end them promptly? Third Query. — Are Friends careful to bring up those under their charge in plainness of speech, behavior, and apparel; in frequently reading the Holy Scriptures; and in restraining them from reading pernicious books and from corrupt conversation? And are they good examples in these respects themselves? Fourth Query. — Are Friends careful to discourage the unnecessary distillation and use of spirituous liquors, and the frequenting of taverns; to avoid places of diversion; and to maintain true moderation and temperance at marriages, burials, and all other occasions? Fifth Query. —Are poor Friends’ necessities duly inspected, and are they relieved or assisted in business suitable to their abilities? Do their children freely partake of learning to fit them for business, and are they and other Frie nds’ children placed among Friends? Sixth Query. — Do you maintain a faithful testimony against oaths; a hireling ministry; bearing arms, training, and other military services; engaging in fraudulent or clandestine trade; buying or vending goods so imported; or dealing in prize goods; and against encouraging lotteries of every kind? Seventh Query. — Are Friends careful to live within the bounds of their circumstances and to maintain moderation in their trade or business? Are they punctual in their promises and just in payment of their debts? And when any give reasonable cause for fear in these respects, are they timely laboured with for their preservation or recovery? Eighth Query. — Do you take due care regularly to deal with all offenders in the spirit of meekness, without partiality or unnecessary delay, for their help; and when such labour is ineffectual, do you place judgment upon them in the authority of truth? The reading of these Queries in our Monthly Meetings constituted a kind of public, monthly confessional for the whole Society, and they were seasons of solemn self-examination for both old and young. Each separate meeting belonging to the Monthly Meeting sent in its own set of answers, and the discussion of these was known as “the consideration of the state of society.” Such answers as these linger in my memory: “Our meetings have all been duly attended by most of our members, but some Friends have not observed the hour.” “Mostly clear of unbecoming behavior, but some sleeping has been observed.” “ Friends generally are careful to bring up their children in plainness of speech, behavior, and apparel, but more faithfulness in this respect is desirable.” “Our testimony against oaths, a hireling ministry, bearing arms, engaging in clandestine trade, and against encouraging lotteries, has been faithfully maintained by all our members.” It was the custom, after each Query and answer had been read, for a period of silence to follow, giving Friends an opportunity to “relieve their minds” of any message that might have been given them concerning that particular Query. These intervals were generally times of deep searching of the heart for all who were present. As I remember it, the Query that was preached upon most frequently and most fervently was the Third, concerning the testimony for “plainness of speech, behaviour, and apparel, and against the vain fashions of the world.” It was this testimony that most contributed to making Quakers a “peculiar people,” and that caused us young Friends the greatest heart -burnings. I remember vividly the suffering I endured each month as I sat beside my mother listening to this Query read and expounded. My constant fear was that it might make her still more strict in keeping us from the “vain fashions of the world,” which, i n spite of all our training, held a fascination we could never wholly overcome. As the Friend appointed to read the Queries approached this particular one, I would try my best to abstract my mind, even surreptitiously stopping my ears, attempting to cheat myself into thinking that if I did not hear it, my mother would not notice it either. But alas, I was always doomed to disappointment, for the preaching on this Query was the most frequent and most impassioned, and in the end, both she and I were obliged to listen. Two incidents of my childhood, connected with this Query, come back to me with great vividness. Our mother had bought us white China-crape shawls with lovely long fringes that seemed to us too beautiful for words, and we wore them with immense pride. One day, however, she returned from a meeting where the Queries had been read and answered, and told us that she had felt during the meeting that our long fringes were too “gay” for Friends’ children, and that she believed it her duty to cut them shorter. I can see it all now, as she carefully spread the shawls on a large table, laid a yardstick across the fringe at what she deemed the proper length, and proceeded to cut off all the beautiful extra strands. It was like cutting into our very hearts. I remember how we pleaded and pleaded that the fatal yardstick might be moved down just a little further. Our great fear was that our fringes would be shorter than those of our intimate friends Hannah and Jane Scull, who were allowed to be a little gayer than we were. To have their fringes even a tenth of an inch longer than ours seemed a calamity beyond bearing. I cannot remember how the matter ended, but I shall never forget the agonies of mind we endured during the process. Another experience connected with a dress left an indelible impression on me. The sleeve considered “plain” in my day was the leg -of-mutton sleeve, and all our dresses were made accordingly. But some benign influence — what it was we never knew — induced our mother one spring to allow our sleeves to be made somewhat in the fashion of the day, which happened then to be Bishop sleeves, full at both shoulder and wrist. The fashionable Bishop sleeves were very large, but ours were tiny little ones; however, they were real Bishops, and our pride in them was immense. They belonged to our new spring school dresses, of a brown-and-white striped print — “calico,” as we called it. Although the weather was still wintery, our desire to display our fashionable sleeves was so overwhelming that nothing would do but that we must put them on and take a long walk without our coats; and no two prouder little girls ever walked the streets of Philadelphia than Hannah and Sally Whitall on that morning. I remember our younger sister Mary wanting to go with us, but her sleeves were still leg-of-mutton, and we felt it would spoil the full effect if one member of our party appeared in the despised shape, so we made her walk on the opposite side of the street. I can still see her longing glances across the way as she admired our glory from afar. She had her revenge soon enough. Ruffled “panties” (as we called drawers then), reaching to the feet, had come into fashion, and when our mother made her a new set, they were long and ruffled, while we still had to wear our plain hemmed ones, not showing below our dresses. This time, Mary too went out to walk to display her new finery, but, kinder than we had been, she invited us to accompany her. I am ashamed to say that the old Adam in us resented her favored condition so strongly that we refused to walk on the same side of the street with her, and scornfully crossed to the other side, leaving her to walk alone, with all the glory of her beautiful ruffled panties destroyed by our cruel scorn and unkindness. The early Friends, in their testimony against the foolish changes of fashion among the “world’s people,” had adhered, as far as possible, to the style of dress in vogue when they first arose. In a very few years, this naturally became peculiar, and eventually developed into a sort of Quaker uniform which all faithful Friends felt “led” to adopt. I say “as far as possible,” because certain styles, when they ceased to be fashionable, soon disappeared from the market and could no longer be easily obtained; and also because even the strictest Friends could not help being somewhat influenced by time and habit. Their testimony regarding plainness of apparel was not a testimony for or against any specific fashion, but simply a protest against following the “vain fashions of the world.” By th e time a style had become old-fashioned and was passing out of use, Quakers were ready to adopt it. I recently came across a curious illustration of this in extracts from an old diary. In Queen Elizabeth’s time, before Quakers existed, the general fashion was to wear green aprons as part of a lady’s church -going dress. But when Quakers appeared, this style was beginning to die out, and stiff white aprons were becoming fashionable. In order not to follow changing fashions, Friends kept to the green aprons for their go-to-meeting dress, and their preachers denounced the fashionable white aprons as “gay and polluting.” One old preacher is recorded as having declared that the starch water used to stiffen them was “the devil’s water with which they needed to be s prinkled,” warning his hearers against its contaminating use. Curiously enough, this Quaker objection to following worldly fashions extended even to many useful inventions, which one would suppose Friends’ practical good sense would have welcomed. I remember when sewing machines first appeared; they were considered exceedingly worldly. When I decided to buy one, I had to make the purchase in secret and hide the machine in the most inaccessible room in the house, lest anyone be grieved by my worldliness. Of course, later on, when Friends had grown used to the innovation, sewing machines became common in every well-ordered Quaker household; but for a long time, I felt an uneasy sense of having fallen from grace because of the worldly thing I had acquired. The standard of plainness necessarily varied from generation to generation. But whatever the standard, the testimony against the vain fashions of the world remained unchanged, and each generation felt that the established costume of its day was in some sense a Divine ordinance, patterned in Heaven itself. This conviction of the sanctity of “plain dress” arose largely, I believe, from the fact that nearly all personal religious experience seemed to come through this channel. The newly awakened Friend, whether yo ung or old, was invariably confronted with the question of “becoming plain , ” and the surrender of will involved in adopting the Quaker uniform always brought such peace and rest of soul that it was almost inevitable they should regard the plain dress as the cause of the blessing. This was especially true of our own dear father. In his diary, under the date of 1823, when he was just twenty-three, he writes: “While at home from my fifth voyage, I believed it right to adopt the plain dress and language of Friends. While under conviction of its being right, and fearing I should lose my situation if I did so, I met with Samuel Bettle, Sr., who, without knowing the distressed state of my mind, told me that if I were faithful to what I felt to be right, the Lord would make a way for me where there seemed no way; which indeed He did, giving me favour in the sight of my employer, much to my comfort. Hearing of a ship needing a chief mate, I borrowed a plain coat of my friend James Cox — my own not being ready — and applie d to the captain, telling him I could not ‘Mr.’ and ‘Sir’ him as was common. He kindly replied that it would only be a nine-day wonder, and at once engaged me as first mate. Thus, my prayer was answered, and a way was made for me where I saw no way. Praise d forever be the name of the Lord.” This was the turning point of his religious life, followed by such an uplifting of soul and such a sense of God’s love that he could never dissociate the two experiences. All his life , he believed that if anyone adopted the same dress, the same blessing would follow. fields.title: The sugar-scoop Bonnet
fields.body_html:
One of the most distinctive features of the “plainness of apparel” in my day was the bonnet worn by all respectable women Friends. Because of its shape, we young people irreverently called it a “sugar - scoop,” though it often seemed almost sacrilegious to apply so flippant a name to an object we regarded as sacred. No young Quaker of my time would have thought otherwise. A writer, speaking of a period a little later than mine, described it perfectly: “To one brought up within the fold, it is no light matter to approach so awful a subject as the Quaker bonnet. There was a solemnity about it born of terror. Whether it presided at the head of the women’s meeting, or ventured into winter storms protected by its satin or oilskin case under the Friendly umbrella, or even lay alone in splendid state upon the guest-room bed — anywhere, everywhere, it was a solemn thing.”

Why this bonnet — delicate in its light silk fabric, extremely expensive, difficult to make, and decidedly uncomfortable —should have been considered “plain,” while a simple , untrimmed straw bonnet costing a fraction as much and far more comfortable was deemed “gay,” is a mys tery. But so it was. To speak of a “plain bonnet” always meant a sugar -scoop.

The rest of a woman Friend’s plain dress consisted of a soft dove -coloured silk shawl folded over a plain-waisted, low-necked dress of dove-gray or brown, with thin white muslin filling the neckline and crossed over the bosom. A muslin cap, shaped like a bonnet and tied under the chin with soft white ribbons, was worn indoors and outdoors, beneath the sugar-scoop. In cold weather, women wore larger dove-coloured cashmere shawls or cashmere Mother Hubbard cloaks pleated onto a yoke with a silk-lined hood. The shawls were always folded with exact precision: a point down the back, three neat folds at the neck fastened by a stout pin, and additional hidden pins at the shoulders to hold the fullness in place, giving the appearance that the draping arranged itself.

Men’s plain clothes were a cutaway coat with a straight clergyman’s collar and a broad -brimmed hat. The entire costume was quaint, but the women especially looked charming, and I do not think I have ever seen sweeter, more serene faces than those framed by the old Quaker caps and bonnets. The world has lost something lovely with their disappearance.

Because all Quakers — young and old —were treated as though they were already “with in the fold,” and were never exhorted to undergo conversion, the only evidence of a change in a person’s religious experience that we recognized was what we called “becoming serious” or “becoming plain.” This was marked outwardly by adopting the Society’s plain dress.

Among us, putting on the plain dress was regarded as an inevitable fate awaiting every Quaker child, one we sought to postpone as long as possible. In Philadelphia, the change usually occurred at the spring Yearly Meeting in April, when everyone appeared in new seasonal clothing. That was when the dreaded transformation was most likely to occur. Young members who had “become serious” felt obliged to appear in sugar -scoop bonnets or straight-collared coats and broad-brimmed hats — outward signs of an inward change. We who were still unclaimed would arrive early and position ourselves where we could watch the entrances, anxious to discover which friend had been taken from our ranks by this solemn calling.

We knew only vaguely of the private struggles and spiritual wrestlings preceding this public declaration, but the event carried enough weight to make us feel that our friends, once changed, belonged to a different world. And if the adoption of plain garb was accompanied by the trembling utterance of a few words in meeting, the gulf between us felt absolute — one that could not be crossed until we too fell under the same fate.

To my young mind, no words can fully convey the dreadful solemnity of this prospect. “Putting on a plain bonnet” seemed almost e quivalent to the end of ordinary human life. After that, one could never again live as other people did. If one were young, there could be no more fun — no running races, no climbing trees, no scaling hay-mows — certainly none of these while wearing a dove-coloured sugar- scoop. If older, one’s heart must turn entirely toward Friends’ meetings, testimonies, and religious concerns. One must love the Book of Discipline, Barclay’s Apology, and Friends’ Religious Journals, and turn one’s back on everything pleasant, pretty, or worldly.

Since “becoming serious” meant, to my imagination, nothing less than donning this awe - inspiring bonnet, the prospect filled my fun-loving spirit with unspeakable dread. Somehow, I had gotten the idea that our dear mother intended, in obedience to the Query concerning “plainness of apparel,” to require each of her daughters to assume the plain bonnet at age fifteen.

As a child, she herself had been made to wear one from almost babyhood. Though her heart was dutifully trained, she too had once rebelled.

She used to tell us, as a solemn warning, that when she was nine or ten, the schoolgirls teased her mercilessly for her bonnet, and she grew desperate to escape it. Her parents, unwavering, refused. One morning, crossing the lonely bridge over Woodbury Creek on her way to school, her dislike flared so strongly that she angrily kicked the bonnet ahead of her. All day, her conscience tormented her. Returning at dusk, she saw a dark shadow on the creek bank. To her excited imagination, it became a fearsome figure advancing toward her. She believed it was the Devil himself, come to seize her for her wickedness. Terrified, she fled home, vowing never again to rebel against her plain bonnet.

We, children, were profoundly impressed by this story, and we always regarded that particular bridge with the most superstitious awe. I can remember many times racing across it at breathless speed, scarcely daring to breathe for fear I might somehow evoke the awful spectre. In light of our mother’s experience, I never for a moment imagined that I could escape the fate of the “plain bonnet,” and the horror with which, as a child, I watched my years creep steadily toward the fatal age of fifteen is beyond description. Fortunately, before I reached that age, the subtle change in ideas that had quietly influenced the whole Society affected our mother as well, and the dreaded “plain bonnets” never appeared.

Instead, we wore the simplest little straw cottage bonnets that could be found. Compared with the “plain bonnets” we had so dreaded, they seemed so gay and worldly to our Quaker imaginations that we felt quite like “fashionable ladies” when we walked out wearing them , although I am now convinced we must still have looked like the primmest little Quaker maidens possible.

When the fate, as I call it, of the “plain bonnet” fell upon some young Friend, it was generally welcomed by the older Friends with a loving tenderness that made “the cross” less hard to bear.

But sometimes it descended upon a member of a family to whom it was wholly unwelcome.

There were degrees of plainness among us: some were “strict” Friends— more often called “solid” Friends— while others, who indulged more in the vain fashions of the world, were known as “gay” Friends. In one such “gay” family I knew, there was a bright, lively daughter named Elizabeth, about my own age, who went through in her early girlhood what now seems to me a truly tragic experience.

One day, when the Query about “plainness of apparel” had been read and the usual pause had followed, a travelling Minister arose and said, in an impressive manner, that she believed the Lord had given her a message for some young heart present, one who was called to take up the cross and put on the “plain dress.” For some reason, young Elizabeth was deeply moved. An inward voice seemed to tell her that the message was meant for her. She burst into tears, and at the close of the meeting, an Elder, noticing her agitation, came to her side, placed a hand on her shoulder, and said solemnly, “Precious child, I believe the Lord has spoken to thee. Mayest thou be obedient to the heavenly vision.” This confirmed the impression on Elizabeth’s mind, and she went home bowed down with a dreadful sense of a Divine call she felt she dared not resist.

Then began a fearful conflict. She knew her family would utterly disapprove, and she felt certain they would not give her the money to purchase the necessary materials to make the change of dress she believed required of her. She was afraid and ashamed to tell anyone what she was enduring. At last, she decided she must try to make a “plain dress” for herself. She saved every penny of her small allowance, and little by little she gathered enough to buy the cheapest materials she could find. At night, alone in her room after everyone had gone to bed, she began, with infinite labour and tears, to fashion the required costume. She dared not ask for instructions or patterns, and night after night she worked at her unaccustomed task until finally, in a rough and imperfect fashion, the poor little costume was finished. The day came when she laid aside her “worldly” clothes and appeared before her family dressed in the cap, handkerchief, and drab shawl worn by elderly Friends.

What this cost her, she would never tell me, and even in middle age, she could not speak of her family’s horrified reception without tears of deep pity for her own youthful martyrdom. Yet she said that, whether she had been right or wrong, she had at least been faithful to what she believed to be her duty. This faithfulness brought her such profound peace, and the radical change in her life proved of such lasting benefit to her character that she never wished to abandon it, and until her death, she continued to wear the same style of costume she had adopted in such anguish of spirit as a girl.

Perhaps an extract from my diary, written shortly after my religious awakening at sixteen, may give some insight into how similar scruples worked upon the sensitive, conscientious heart of another young girl, a close friend and confidante in all spiritual matters. Under the date 11th month, 13th, 1849, I find the following: “A. has been spending a week with me, and I do not know when I have enjoyed myself more.

The spiritual communion between us was perfect. I do not think we concealed any of our feelings from each other. She told me of the mental suffering — suffering greater than she had believed possible to bear —which preceded the making known of God’s will in her soul, and of the anguish of spirit when that will was revealed. She believed it was required of her to give up immediately all her gay dress, to burn her breastpins and her gold thimble, and many articles of clothing, even her dresses. It was a great trial; it seemed to her such a waste, and human nature shrank. And there was a still greater trial. She had done a large monochromatic picture which her parents had had framed and hung in their parlour, and which they greatly admired. She felt she must take this picture and burn it also, frame and all. She knew how grieved her parents would be, and how foolish it would seem to her sister and brother, and the conflict was immense. But the reproofs of her Divine Guide were so heartrending that at last she could bear them no longer and submitted. Her father, mother, and sister were at Cape May at the time, or she said she could never have done it. When they returned, she told them, and then, she said, the holy, heavenly calm that followed was indescribable. She scarcely felt as though she were on earth. It seemed she should never sin again, and the reward was far greater than the suffering. How nobly she has acted! I fear I should have refused to obey and would have borne any suffering rather than make such great sacrifices. And now she has consented to put on a plain bonnet —a ‘sugar - scoop,’ as I call them. Though it is a great change and will be much talked about, she scarcely dreads it, for she finds it so true that God can make hard things easy and bitter things sweet. Could I take up the cross as she has done?”

That I had been more or less influenced by my friend’s experience is shown by another diary entry written shortly afterward: “Eleventh month, 17th, 1849. Sometimes today, as I have been thinking about it, it has seemed almost as if it would be right for me to put on a plain sugar-scoop bonnet; but I hardly dare believe that so great a favour would be granted me. It is strange, even to myself, that I should long so for the time when I might make this sacrifice, though in truth it would be no sacrifice.

People generally feel so averse to these bonnets, and I, too, did, perhaps a year ago; but now I long for it so earnestly that I fear I cannot judge calmly and clearly about it. Gladly as I would make this and any other sacrifice which God might require, I know how terrible it would be to run before I was sent, and to do what God had not required. Sometimes it seems I cannot wait any longer — that I must do something to gain the salvation of my soul; and if God requires nothing, I must offer something myself. And yet that I dare not do. Oh, I feel that I could love the cross and even the shame, if only God would lay them upon me; but patience and quiet waiting are my duties now.”

It is evident from this extract that the martyr spirit had been aroused in me, and that I longed to do something difficult for the sake of my religion. But these feelings soon passed, and the “sugar - scoop” bonnet I both dreaded and desired never adorned my head. I was a healthy young creature, full of animal spirits and absorbed in the joys of outward life. My conscience was always easily quieted, and for the most part, I passed my girlhood conscious only of the ordinary claims of everyday duty, which my training and the compelling Quaker atmosphere around me had made almost second nature.

The rest of a woman Friend’s plain dress consisted of a soft dove -coloured silk shawl folded over a plain-waisted, low-necked dress of dove-gray or brown, with thin white muslin filling the neckline and crossed over the bosom. A muslin cap, shaped like a bonnet and tied under the chin with soft white ribbons, was worn indoors and outdoors, beneath the sugar-scoop. In cold weather, women wore larger dove-coloured cashmere shawls or cashmere Mother Hubbard cloaks pleated onto a yoke with a silk-lined hood. The shawls were always folded with exact precision: a point down the back, three neat folds at the neck fastened by a stout pin, and additional hidden pins at the shoulders to hold the fullness in place, giving the appearance that the draping arranged itself. Men’s plain clothes were a cutaway coat with a straight clergyman’s collar and a broad -brimmed hat. The entire costume was quaint, but the women especially looked charming, and I do not think I have ever seen sweeter, more serene faces than those framed by the old Quaker caps and bonnets. The world has lost something lovely with their disappearance. Because all Quakers — young and old —were treated as though they were already “with in the fold,” and were never exhorted to undergo conversion, the only evidence of a change in a person’s religious experience that we recognized was what we called “becoming serious” or “becoming plain.” This was marked outwardly by adopting the Society’s plain dress. Among us, putting on the plain dress was regarded as an inevitable fate awaiting every Quaker child, one we sought to postpone as long as possible. In Philadelphia, the change usually occurred at the spring Yearly Meeting in April, when everyone appeared in new seasonal clothing. That was when the dreaded transformation was most likely to occur. Young members who had “become serious” felt obliged to appear in sugar -scoop bonnets or straight-collared coats and broad-brimmed hats — outward signs of an inward change. We who were still unclaimed would arrive early and position ourselves where we could watch the entrances, anxious to discover which friend had been taken from our ranks by this solemn calling. We knew only vaguely of the private struggles and spiritual wrestlings preceding this public declaration, but the event carried enough weight to make us feel that our friends, once changed, belonged to a different world. And if the adoption of plain garb was accompanied by the trembling utterance of a few words in meeting, the gulf between us felt absolute — one that could not be crossed until we too fell under the same fate. To my young mind, no words can fully convey the dreadful solemnity of this prospect. “Putting on a plain bonnet” seemed almost e quivalent to the end of ordinary human life. After that, one could never again live as other people did. If one were young, there could be no more fun — no running races, no climbing trees, no scaling hay-mows — certainly none of these while wearing a dove-coloured sugar- scoop. If older, one’s heart must turn entirely toward Friends’ meetings, testimonies, and religious concerns. One must love the Book of Discipline, Barclay’s Apology, and Friends’ Religious Journals, and turn one’s back on everything pleasant, pretty, or worldly. Since “becoming serious” meant, to my imagination, nothing less than donning this awe - inspiring bonnet, the prospect filled my fun-loving spirit with unspeakable dread. Somehow, I had gotten the idea that our dear mother intended, in obedience to the Query concerning “plainness of apparel,” to require each of her daughters to assume the plain bonnet at age fifteen. As a child, she herself had been made to wear one from almost babyhood. Though her heart was dutifully trained, she too had once rebelled. She used to tell us, as a solemn warning, that when she was nine or ten, the schoolgirls teased her mercilessly for her bonnet, and she grew desperate to escape it. Her parents, unwavering, refused. One morning, crossing the lonely bridge over Woodbury Creek on her way to school, her dislike flared so strongly that she angrily kicked the bonnet ahead of her. All day, her conscience tormented her. Returning at dusk, she saw a dark shadow on the creek bank. To her excited imagination, it became a fearsome figure advancing toward her. She believed it was the Devil himself, come to seize her for her wickedness. Terrified, she fled home, vowing never again to rebel against her plain bonnet. We, children, were profoundly impressed by this story, and we always regarded that particular bridge with the most superstitious awe. I can remember many times racing across it at breathless speed, scarcely daring to breathe for fear I might somehow evoke the awful spectre. In light of our mother’s experience, I never for a moment imagined that I could escape the fate of the “plain bonnet,” and the horror with which, as a child, I watched my years creep steadily toward the fatal age of fifteen is beyond description. Fortunately, before I reached that age, the subtle change in ideas that had quietly influenced the whole Society affected our mother as well, and the dreaded “plain bonnets” never appeared. Instead, we wore the simplest little straw cottage bonnets that could be found. Compared with the “plain bonnets” we had so dreaded, they seemed so gay and worldly to our Quaker imaginations that we felt quite like “fashionable ladies” when we walked out wearing them , although I am now convinced we must still have looked like the primmest little Quaker maidens possible. When the fate, as I call it, of the “plain bonnet” fell upon some young Friend, it was generally welcomed by the older Friends with a loving tenderness that made “the cross” less hard to bear. But sometimes it descended upon a member of a family to whom it was wholly unwelcome. There were degrees of plainness among us: some were “strict” Friends— more often called “solid” Friends— while others, who indulged more in the vain fashions of the world, were known as “gay” Friends. In one such “gay” family I knew, there was a bright, lively daughter named Elizabeth, about my own age, who went through in her early girlhood what now seems to me a truly tragic experience. One day, when the Query about “plainness of apparel” had been read and the usual pause had followed, a travelling Minister arose and said, in an impressive manner, that she believed the Lord had given her a message for some young heart present, one who was called to take up the cross and put on the “plain dress.” For some reason, young Elizabeth was deeply moved. An inward voice seemed to tell her that the message was meant for her. She burst into tears, and at the close of the meeting, an Elder, noticing her agitation, came to her side, placed a hand on her shoulder, and said solemnly, “Precious child, I believe the Lord has spoken to thee. Mayest thou be obedient to the heavenly vision.” This confirmed the impression on Elizabeth’s mind, and she went home bowed down with a dreadful sense of a Divine call she felt she dared not resist. Then began a fearful conflict. She knew her family would utterly disapprove, and she felt certain they would not give her the money to purchase the necessary materials to make the change of dress she believed required of her. She was afraid and ashamed to tell anyone what she was enduring. At last, she decided she must try to make a “plain dress” for herself. She saved every penny of her small allowance, and little by little she gathered enough to buy the cheapest materials she could find. At night, alone in her room after everyone had gone to bed, she began, with infinite labour and tears, to fashion the required costume. She dared not ask for instructions or patterns, and night after night she worked at her unaccustomed task until finally, in a rough and imperfect fashion, the poor little costume was finished. The day came when she laid aside her “worldly” clothes and appeared before her family dressed in the cap, handkerchief, and drab shawl worn by elderly Friends. What this cost her, she would never tell me, and even in middle age, she could not speak of her family’s horrified reception without tears of deep pity for her own youthful martyrdom. Yet she said that, whether she had been right or wrong, she had at least been faithful to what she believed to be her duty. This faithfulness brought her such profound peace, and the radical change in her life proved of such lasting benefit to her character that she never wished to abandon it, and until her death, she continued to wear the same style of costume she had adopted in such anguish of spirit as a girl. Perhaps an extract from my diary, written shortly after my religious awakening at sixteen, may give some insight into how similar scruples worked upon the sensitive, conscientious heart of another young girl, a close friend and confidante in all spiritual matters. Under the date 11th month, 13th, 1849, I find the following: “A. has been spending a week with me, and I do not know when I have enjoyed myself more. The spiritual communion between us was perfect. I do not think we concealed any of our feelings from each other. She told me of the mental suffering — suffering greater than she had believed possible to bear —which preceded the making known of God’s will in her soul, and of the anguish of spirit when that will was revealed. She believed it was required of her to give up immediately all her gay dress, to burn her breastpins and her gold thimble, and many articles of clothing, even her dresses. It was a great trial; it seemed to her such a waste, and human nature shrank. And there was a still greater trial. She had done a large monochromatic picture which her parents had had framed and hung in their parlour, and which they greatly admired. She felt she must take this picture and burn it also, frame and all. She knew how grieved her parents would be, and how foolish it would seem to her sister and brother, and the conflict was immense. But the reproofs of her Divine Guide were so heartrending that at last she could bear them no longer and submitted. Her father, mother, and sister were at Cape May at the time, or she said she could never have done it. When they returned, she told them, and then, she said, the holy, heavenly calm that followed was indescribable. She scarcely felt as though she were on earth. It seemed she should never sin again, and the reward was far greater than the suffering. How nobly she has acted! I fear I should have refused to obey and would have borne any suffering rather than make such great sacrifices. And now she has consented to put on a plain bonnet —a ‘sugar - scoop,’ as I call them. Though it is a great change and will be much talked about, she scarcely dreads it, for she finds it so true that God can make hard things easy and bitter things sweet. Could I take up the cross as she has done?” That I had been more or less influenced by my friend’s experience is shown by another diary entry written shortly afterward: “Eleventh month, 17th, 1849. Sometimes today, as I have been thinking about it, it has seemed almost as if it would be right for me to put on a plain sugar-scoop bonnet; but I hardly dare believe that so great a favour would be granted me. It is strange, even to myself, that I should long so for the time when I might make this sacrifice, though in truth it would be no sacrifice. People generally feel so averse to these bonnets, and I, too, did, perhaps a year ago; but now I long for it so earnestly that I fear I cannot judge calmly and clearly about it. Gladly as I would make this and any other sacrifice which God might require, I know how terrible it would be to run before I was sent, and to do what God had not required. Sometimes it seems I cannot wait any longer — that I must do something to gain the salvation of my soul; and if God requires nothing, I must offer something myself. And yet that I dare not do. Oh, I feel that I could love the cross and even the shame, if only God would lay them upon me; but patience and quiet waiting are my duties now.” It is evident from this extract that the martyr spirit had been aroused in me, and that I longed to do something difficult for the sake of my religion. But these feelings soon passed, and the “sugar - scoop” bonnet I both dreaded and desired never adorned my head. I was a healthy young creature, full of animal spirits and absorbed in the joys of outward life. My conscience was always easily quieted, and for the most part, I passed my girlhood conscious only of the ordinary claims of everyday duty, which my training and the compelling Quaker atmosphere around me had made almost second nature.

fields.title: The Hat Testimony
fields.body_html:
Part of the testimony to “plainness of apparel” was the testimony ag ainst what was called “hat honor.” Quakers believed that since taking off the hat was an outward sign of reverence toward God, it was not right or appropriate to give that same gesture to human beings.

Barclay said, “He that uncovereth his head to the crea ture, what hath he reserved for the Creator?”

Because removing the hat was considered a mark of special respect to certain people or certain places, Friends — who believed that all people were equally worthy of respect as children of one Father, and that all places were equally holy because God’s presence was everywhere— expressed this belief by refusing to take off their hats for anyone or in any place, except when comfort required it. Not even when entering a place of worship could the rule be relaxed, because taking off the hat would imply that God was more present inside that building than outside in the open air. This idea was completely opposed to fundamental Quaker beliefs.

Prof. William James, in his valuable book The Varieties of Religious Experience, discussing early Quakers and their peculiarities, writes: “Many of these peculiarities arose from their determination to have nothing to do with shams or pretenses, but to be true and sincere in all their dealings with God and with their fellow- men.”

George Fox believed the Lord showed him that many conventional social customs were false and hypocritical. He wrote: “When the Lord sent me into the world, He forbade me to put off my hat to any, high or low; and I was required to ‘thee’ and ‘thou’ all men and women, without any respect to rich or poor, great or small. And as I traveled up and down, I was not to bid people ‘Good morning’ or ‘Good evening’; neither might I bow or scrape with my leg to anyone... Oh, the scorn, heat, and fury that arose! Oh, the blows, punchings, beatings, and imprisonments that we underwent for not putting off our hats to men! But blessed be the Lord, many came to see the vanity of that custom of putting off hats to men, and felt the weight of Truth’s testimony against it.”

All the followers of George Fox accepted these revelations as guidance for themselves as well as for him. They abandoned the worldly customs he condemned, viewing this as a sacrifice to Truth and as a way to make their actions better reflect the spirit they professed. This renunciation continued up to my own time, although I suspect many who practiced it no longer fully understood the reasons behind these peculiarities.

Some Friends in my youth went so far as to treat wearing the hat at all possible times — even during meals — as a kind of religious duty. On one occasion, a young man I knew was walking with an Elder along the streets of Wilmington, Delaware. The Elder was advising him about the importance of supporting Friends’ testimonies in every situation, and sa id: “I have noticed, my dear young friend, with great satisfaction, that thou art careful not to take off thy hat when meeting thy acquaintances in the street, nor to remove it upon entering the meetinghouse until thou hast taken thy seat. But I see room for even greater faithfulness in this matter, and I feel free to tell thee that I believe it is right for me to wear my hat at all times except when I am in bed. I put it on the moment I rise in the morning, and I do not feel at liberty to remove it until I have put on my night clothes, just before getting into bed at night.”

This practice of keeping the hat on was often a source of conflict and testing for Quakers who, because of social obligations or business, were required to appear before people who expected this gesture of respect. In the old Friends’ Journals , there are many accounts of the suffering caused by this “hat testimony.” In the Journal of Thomas Ellwood, the friend of Milton, who became convinced of Friends’ views, he describes his father’s v iolent hatred of this testimony.

He writes: “The sight of my hat upon my head when entering his presence made him so angry that, rushing at me with both hands, he violently snatched off my hat and threw it away; and then, giving me some blows on the head, he said, ‘Sirrah, get you up to your chamber.’”

On another day, he tells how he went to the dinner table wearing his hat: “As soon as I came in, I could see by my father’s expression that my hat was still an offence to him. But when I was seated, and before I had eaten anything, he made this even clearer by saying to me, ‘If you cannot content yourself to come to dinner without your Hise upon your head (so he called my hat), pray rise and go take your dinner somewhere else.’ After hearing this, I got up from the table and went into the kitchen, where I stayed until the servants sat down to dinner, and then I sat contentedly with them.”

Many years after Ellwood’s experience, a wealthy English Friend, Joseph John Gurney, described his own trial in 1810: “I was engaged long beforehand to a dinner party. For three weeks before, I was in agitation knowing that I must enter the drawing-room with my hat on. From this sacrifice, strange and unaccountable as it may seem, I could not escape. Wearing the attire of a Friend, and with my hat on, I entered the drawing-room at the dreaded moment, shook hands with the mistress of the house, then returned to the hall, deposited my hat, and came back. I went home with some degree of peace. Afterward, I had to do the same thing at the bishop’s. The result was that I found myself a decided Quaker, fully understood to have taken that position, and to dinner parties — except within the family circle —I was asked no more.”

Later still, our own dear father had a similar challenge. On one occasion, he hoped to be appointed captain of an important ship, and while preparing to apply to the owners, he struggled greatly because he believed it was his duty to enter their presence with his hat on. He feared this would prejudice them against him, but he remained steadfast in what he believed to be his religious duty and trusted that the Lord would prosper him. In his diary, he writes: “Some of my friends thought my plain dress and language would stand in my way, but I told them to wait and see whether I would not secure the position by the blessing of God, to whom I refer all my success in life. The ship New Jersey was launched on the first of Twelfth Month, 1824, and on the third, Whitton Evans, the owner, conferred on me the command.”

While reading a very interesting book recently, The Testament of Ignatius Loyola, I was struck to find that this old saint of the sixteenth century shared many of these early Quaker scruples. He writes that his custom in addressing people was to omit all titles such as “Your Lordship” or “Your Reverence,” believing that simplicity to be the practice of Christ and His Apostles. He also tells how he was tempted, out of fear of consequences, to relax this practice in the case of a certain captain, and that as soon as he recognized this as temptation, he determined: “Since so it is, I will not call him your Lordship, nor show him reverence, nor will I pull off the cap from my head.”

In fact, throughout Christian history, one of the ways devoted believers have expressed their commitment has been through peculiarities of dress or speech, and aside from the particular form it took, the early Friends were not unusual in this. But unlike many other Christian groups, they also held a particular testimony against all bright colors, which, for reasons not entirely clear, were considered worldly. Browns and drabs were considered unworldly, and most of our clothes were some variation of these colors. Occasionally a little green was allowed, and curiously, a dark purple was sometimes permitted, but red, blue, pink, or yellow were entirely forbidden as “too gay.” I even knew some conscientious Friends who did not feel free to grow scarlet geraniums in their gardens or to keep a vase of scarlet flowers in their parlors.

After I became a recognized religious teacher, people in spiritual difficulty often came to me for help. Among them was a young Friend with a very sensitive conscience, who came one day greatly troubled about scarlet geraniums. She lived in one half of a semi-detached house in the suburbs of Philadelphia. In front of both houses was a small shared garden with an oval flowerbed, which she and her neighbor took turns filling each spring. That year, it was her turn, and wishing to please her neighbor, she asked her what flowers they should plant. The neighbor preferred scarlet geraniums, and my friend was about to order them when a sudden scruple seized her against allowing such bright flowers to adorn the garden in front of her house. She struggled and prayed about it, and the more she prayed, the louder the inward voice seemed to tell her that it would not be right to plant scarlet geraniums. But how to explain this to her neighbor — who knew nothing about Friends — she could not imagine, and she came to me in great distress for help.

I have always found that nothing is more difficult to combat than scruples. Although I tried very hard to convince my poor, perplexed friend that there were matters in the Christian life far more important than the color of the flowers in our gardens — and that the Lord might well be more pleased by courtesy and kindness toward her neighbor than by any rigid rule about flower colors, which, after all, He Himself created and could not therefore find displeasing — it was all in vain.

At last, I was forced to give her a piece of advice to which I rather objected: I told her to “ask Josiah.”

Josiah was her husband, and I knew he possessed a good measure of common sense. Although I did not generally approve of letting husbands decide such matters for their wives, in this case, it seemed almost a necessity. My confidence was justified, for Josiah said — very sensibly — that he would take the responsibility for the scarlet geraniums upon his own shoulders, and that he felt sure the Lord would not be displeased to see, in front of their house, flowers which He Himself had made.

Naturally, over time, modifications of these extreme views began to appear, and in my lifetime I have seen gradual changes that, as a child, I would have thought blasphemous even to imagine.

As the young people of my generation — who regarded these old testimonies merely as “traditions of the elders” rather than personal convictions— grew to maturity, they gradually let them go. One Yearly Meeting after another became accustomed to changes that would once have bowed them to the earth with shame and sorrow.

English Friends, as far as I recall, were the first to yield; but the American Yearly Meetings, except our own in Philadelphia, were not far behind. We in Philadelphia held fast to our old customs as long as we possibly could, but even we had to yield in the end.

One of my sisters married and settled within Baltimore Yearly Meeting — a Meeting that embraced these changes far more rapidly than we did, and which we in Philadelphia regarded as lamentably “gay.” My sister, however, carried the Philadelphia spirit with her, and as her large family of daughters grew up, she tried earnestly to keep them to the Philadelphia standard of plainness. But it was all in vain; one innovation after another crept in, and she found herself powerless to prevent it.

Fortunately, she was blessed with a delightful sense of humor, and even in the midst of her struggles for plainness, she could still see the absurdity of the situation. She came to me one day to describe her difficulties and to ask my advice. When she had laid everything before me, she suddenly sprang up with a mischievous twinkle in her eye, lifted one foot into the air, and said: “Now, Hannah, please tell me where it will be safe for me to put my foot down. Once I put it down at the overskirts, but soon had to lift it again. Then I put it down among artificial flowers in the children’s hats, and once m ore had to lift it. Next, I put it down at rings on their fingers, and again it had to be lifted. Now I do not want to put it down again until I can be quite sure I will not have to take it up. Do thee think, Hannah, ”— and here she assumed an amusingly solemn expression —“that I might safely venture to put it down at nose rings?”

This was too much for my gravity. I burst into laughter, and my sister joined me. Somehow, the air was cleared, and she decided she could no longer carry on the fruitless effort to impose Philadelphia ideas upon Baltimore. She would accept the inevitable changes that were bound to come, even among such a conservative body as Friends.

The simple truth, as I have shown, was that the aim of the Quakers had always been to avoid following the “vain fashions of the world.” They only adopted a new style once it had become old and was passing away. Baltimore Friends were simply ready to do this a little sooner than Philadelphia Friends. One of my Baltimore nieces told me she remembered coming once to Philadelphia to attend a party given by her Philadelphia cousins, and feeling horribly worldly and wicked because her dress was made more in the fashion than theirs.

How little all this can be understood by the young Quakers of the present day! But how tremendously real it all was to us.
