But how to explain this to her neighbor — who knew nothing about Friends — she could not imagine, and she came to me in great distress for help. I have always found that nothing is more difficult to combat than scruples. Although I tried very hard to convince my poor, perplexed friend that there were matters in the Christian life far more important than the color of the flowers in our gardens — and that the Lord might well be more pleased by courtesy and kindness toward her neighbor than by any rigid rule about flower colors, which, after all, He Himself created and could not therefore find displeasing — it was all in vain. At last, I was forced to give her a piece of advice to which I rather objected: I told her to “ask Josiah.” Josiah was her husband, and I knew he possessed a good measure of common sense. Although I did not generally approve of letting husbands decide such matters for their wives, in this case, it seemed almost a necessity. My confidence was justified, for Josiah said — very sensibly — that he would take the responsibility for the scarlet geraniums upon his own shoulders, and that he felt sure the Lord would not be displeased to see, in front of their house, flowers which He Himself had made. Naturally, over time, modifications of these extreme views began to appear, and in my lifetime I have seen gradual changes that, as a child, I would have thought blasphemous even to imagine. As the young people of my generation — who regarded these old testimonies merely as “traditions of the elders” rather than personal convictions— grew to maturity, they gradually let them go. One Yearly Meeting after another became accustomed to changes that would once have bowed them to the earth with shame and sorrow. English Friends, as far as I recall, were the first to yield; but the American Yearly Meetings, except our own in Philadelphia, were not far behind. We in Philadelphia held fast to our old customs as long as we possibly could, but even we had to yield in the end. One of my sisters married and settled within Baltimore Yearly Meeting — a Meeting that embraced these changes far more rapidly than we did, and which we in Philadelphia regarded as lamentably “gay.” My sister, however, carried the Philadelphia spirit with her, and as her large family of daughters grew up, she tried earnestly to keep them to the Philadelphia standard of plainness. But it was all in vain; one innovation after another crept in, and she found herself powerless to prevent it. Fortunately, she was blessed with a delightful sense of humor, and even in the midst of her struggles for plainness, she could still see the absurdity of the situation. She came to me one day to describe her difficulties and to ask my advice. When she had laid everything before me, she suddenly sprang up with a mischievous twinkle in her eye, lifted one foot into the air, and said: “Now, Hannah, please tell me where it will be safe for me to put my foot down. Once I put it down at the overskirts, but soon had to lift it again. Then I put it down among artificial flowers in the children’s hats, and once m ore had to lift it. Next, I put it down at rings on their fingers, and again it had to be lifted. Now I do not want to put it down again until I can be quite sure I will not have to take it up. Do thee think, Hannah, ”— and here she assumed an amusingly solemn expression —“that I might safely venture to put it down at nose rings?” This was too much for my gravity. I burst into laughter, and my sister joined me. Somehow, the air was cleared, and she decided she could no longer carry on the fruitless effort to impose Philadelphia ideas upon Baltimore. She would accept the inevitable changes that were bound to come, even among such a conservative body as Friends. The simple truth, as I have shown, was that the aim of the Quakers had always been to avoid following the “vain fashions of the world.” They only adopted a new style once it had become old and was passing away. Baltimore Friends were simply ready to do this a little sooner than Philadelphia Friends. One of my Baltimore nieces told me she remembered coming once to Philadelphia to attend a party given by her Philadelphia cousins, and feeling horribly worldly and wicked because her dress was made more in the fashion than theirs. How little all this can be understood by the young Quakers of the present day! But how tremendously real it all was to us.

fields.title: Plainness Of Speech
fields.body_html:
The “plainness of speech” referred to in the Third Query primarily meant using thee and thou when addressing a single person, instead of the customary you . This testimony, along with the testimony of plain apparel, was one of the chief marks that set us apart as a peculiar people. To say you to one person — whether Friend or outsider — was considered the height of worldliness and insincerity. Never once, until I was married, did I dare to transgress this rule.

Naturally, it made mingling with the outside world rather difficult, since our quaint way of speaking was sure to provoke curious stares or suppressed laughter.

The roots of this testimony lay in the absolute sincerity of the early Friends. They felt it was dishonest to use a plural pronoun for a single individual. Furthermore, in their day, it was customary to address a superior as you , reserving thee and thou for inferiors. But Friends, who believed all people were equal before God — and who believed this in a very practical way — could not tolerate such distinctions. They therefore addressed everyone alike.

Those early Friends were democrats in every fiber of their being, not from political theory but from their unwavering conviction that God had made all the nations of the earth from one blood, and that all were equally His children. It was a noble foundation upon which to build their moral structure, and it helps explain many practices that might otherwise seem quaint or even foolish.

Thomas Ellwood, in his autobiography, recounts the various things he felt called to give up after becoming convinced of Quaker principles. Concerning plain language, he wrote that using you to a single person was a “corrupt and unsound form of speaking,” adopted in “later and corrupt times” as a means of flattering worldly vanity. Since God had always addressed men with thou , and men had always addressed God with thou , Ellwood considered it a moral obligation to follow that example. Under the illumination of what he called “a pure ray of divine light,” he felt required to abandon many such “evil customs” that had sprung up during the long night of spiritual darkness.

So insistent was this testimony in my childhood that it would have seemed shockingly worldly to say you to a single person, almost as “gay” as wearing silk or scarlet. Even after I grew older and went more into the world, meeting good and earnest Christians who used the forbidden word without the slightest qualm, it took great effort to shape my Quaker lips to utter it. Gradually, the difficulty faded. Now, after more than seventy years, thee and thou have become for me simply the language of intimate affection, slipping out naturally whenever someone has truly found their way into my heart. I often judge my own feelings toward a person by this test: when I hear myself saying thee , I know I have begun to love them. Many of my friends — some with no Quaker connection at all — have caught the habit from me, and use those dear old words in our private companionship. My beloved friend Frances Willard was one of them; we thee’d , and thou’d each other for many years.

The writer I quoted earlier, in A Boy’s Religion , describes how he felt as a child about plain speech.

“I said ‘thee’ and ‘thy’ to everybody,” he wrote, “and I would just as soon have used profane language as said ‘you’ or ‘yours’ to any person. I thought only Friends went to Heaven, and so I supposed that using ‘thee’ and ‘thy’ was one of the main tests of admission. Nobody ever told me such a thing, and if I had asked, I’d have been set straight— but for years that was my settled belief.”

He goes on to describe pitying his neighbors who would never, as he imagined, be “let in,” and wondering why they didn’t simply join the Meeting and learn to speak properly. He even taught one little “Gentile” friend the plain language, and the boy used it faithfully with him until the pressure of the outside world, as he put it, “got too heavy” around the age of twelve.

Another testimony related to plainness of speech was the prohibition against calling anyone Mr. , Mrs. , or Miss . These titles were believed to violate the spirit of Christ’s words, “Neither be ye called masters, for one is yo ur Master, even Christ.” No sincere Friend could give a title to a wealthy man while refusing it to a poor one; thus, Christian names were used for all — Thomas, Samuel, Abigail, Elizabeth, and so forth. (We had no Reginalds, Bertrands, Ethels, or Evelyns in those days!)

Where age demanded a touch more respect, young people were expected to use the full name — Thomas Wistar, Abigail Evans, Samuel Bettle, Elizabeth Pitfield. This practice created no end of difficulty when dealing with “the world’s people,” and b rought about many an awkward dilemma.

Our dear father was very strict on this matter, and could never be persuaded — no matter how inconvenient it might be —to use the “gay’’ titles Mr. or Mrs. I remember well the amusement we had, once we were grown, watching his ingenious methods of escaping difficulty whenever he did not know someone’s first name. In place of Mr. or Mrs. , he invented the substitute word Cummishilamus , and would say, for example, “Cummishilamus Coleman said…” or “Cummishilamus Coleman did…” When, however, he had to address a letter, he could not, of course, write such a word, and then he would turn to one of us, a merry twinkle in his dear eyes, and say, “Come, Han, thee has no scruples — thee may write the Mr. or Mrs. on this letter.”

Plainness of speech also forbade us from greeting our friends with good morning , good evening , or from saying good-bye when parting from them. Good-bye was believed to be a corruption of God be with you , and since God was always with you, it seemed a kind of unbelief to express the wish. And to say good morning or good evening — a wish that you might have a good morning or evening — implied doubt of the fact, known to every Friend, that your mornings and evenings must, in the order of Divine Providence, always be good.

I grew up with the distinct feeling that these expressions were very gay and worldly, and that the right — or, as we said, the plain — course was to greet friends with How art thou? Or how does thee do? , and to part from them with the simple word Farewell.

Why Farewell was considered more truthful than good-bye , even if good-bye did mean God be with you , I have never been able to understand.

In perfect consistency with the Quaker ideal of the absolute equality of all human beings in the sight of God, plainness of speech also forbade us to give the title Saint to any departed Christian.

We were never allowed to use it, even as a prefix. For example, we never spoke of the Gospels as the Gospel according to St. Matthew or St. Mark , but always as the Gospel according to Matthew , or Mark, Luke, or John.

I recently saw, in an old diary from the seventeenth century, an account of one very conscientious Friend who felt a “stop” against using the prefix saint even in place-names. She once had great difficulty locating St. Mary Axe because, having dropped the Saint , she asked only for “Mary Axe Street,” which no one understood.

As a testimony against idolatry, we were also forbidden to call the months of the year or the days of the week by their “heathen” names. We were taught to adhere to the “simplicity of truth” by using numbers: First Month , Second Month ; or First Day , Second Day , and so forth. This practice was so universal in my circle that it never even occurred to me to use the heathen names.

I remember being greatly shocked when I came to England in 1873 and discovered that English Friends had abandoned the practice and had returned to the old “heathen” names. For a time, I could hardly persuade myself they were truly Friends at all. And even now, when I date my letters with those names, I still feel as though I am making a forbidden little excursion into the “gay world.”

fields.title: Friends testimonies Against Fiction, Music, And Art
fields.body_html:
Another point raised in this same Third Query caused us no small amount of trouble: the question of whether Friends were careful to bring up the ir children in “frequently reading the Holy Scriptures, and to restrain them from reading pernicious books.” All fiction of every kind was considered “pernicious” by the Friends of those days. On this point , our mother was very strict, and we were not allowed to read even the most innocent and carefully chosen Sunday-school stories. As for novels, the very word was considered wicked, and to this day I never use it without a fleeting, instinctive sense of lawlessness, as if I were deliberately doing something wrong.

As we grew older, the line was naturally drawn less tightly, and when we became old enough to take a little more guidance of our lives into our own hands, we would sometimes snatch a fearful joy from a storybook borrowed from one of our school friends. One of my most vivid memories is of such an occasion, made all the more vivid because it was the first time I had dared to partake openly and boldly of the forbidden fruit.

It was a First-day afternoon, when nothing much seemed to be happening. I had borrowed a book from one of my schoolmates, who had told me it was “lovely,” and I took the book— with a plate of apples and gingerbread — and stretched myself across the outside of my bed to read and eat at my leisure.

The story I read that day, under such delightful circumstances, seemed to give me the nearest approach to perfect bliss I had ever experienced, and it remains in my memory as one of the happiest days of my life. The book was The Earl’s Daughter by Grace Aguilar. To my young American Quaker mind, an Earl was something like an archangel rather than an ordinary man, and to be an Earl’s daughter was almost akin to being a daughter of heaven. And to this day— despite all the disillusionment life has brought me regarding earls and their daughters — the old sense of grandeur that filled my soul with awe on that First-day afternoon long ago always returns for a moment whenever earls or countesses are mentioned in my presence.

But although I enjoyed this and other stories intensely, it was always with an uneasy conscience, and it took me fifty years to rid myself of the feeling that reading anything fictitious was a sin.

My diary is full of the struggles I endured because of this, and when I read them over now, I cannot help feeling deep pity for the hungry, ignorant young soul so tormented by the constant tendency to turn a perfectly innocent recreation into a moral offense.

What finally brought me deliverance was a sudden recognition that our Lord Himself constantly used parables — which are simply stories — to illustrate and enforce His teaching. Fiction, therefore, was not in itself, as I had always supposed, a synonym for sin. Its moral quality depended entirely on the kind of fiction it was, and often, fiction could be found to be an invaluable aid to virtue.

But I have known many Friends who have been tormented by scruples on this subject well into old age.

Music was another matter against which the Friends of my day had a very strong testimony. In a Philadelphia Discipline of 1873, I found the following passage concerning it, which clearly expresses the Quaker view: “We would renewedly caution to all our members against indulging in music, or having instruments of music in their houses, believing that the practice tends to promote a light and vain mind, and to disqualify for the serious thoughtfulness which becomes an accountable being, hastening to his final reckoning.… The spirit and language of the Discipline forbid the use of music by Friends, without any exception in favor of that called sacred.… Those m embers who indulge in the use of music, or who have musical instruments in their houses, bring themselves within the application of this second clause of the Discipline.… And if they be not reclaimed by further labor, so as to condemn their misconduct to the satisfaction of the meeting, it should proceed to testify our disunity with them.”

So strictly was the Discipline observed in this respect that I do not remember, in my young days, a single individual in our select circle who owned any sort of musical instrument, above all a piano, which was considered the gayest of the gay. Whenever I found myself in a room containing a piano, I felt as though I were treading the very borders of hell.

For many years after I became a woman, I never heard music anywhere without a secret, half- delicious sensation of tasting forbidden fruit. Even singing or whistling was frowned upon. I remember once, when a party of young Friends were spending a summer holiday together in Newport, a dear old Friend called us into his room and told us solemnly that he had been greatly grieved to hear some of us whistling in the garden the day before, and he hoped we would never again so transgress Friends’ testimonies.

That the Discipline on this matter was no dead letter is proved by the fact that, when I was older, and this testimony was beginning to lose its power over the less “concerned” members, I knew several instances in which Friends — though otherwise exemplary — were actually disowned simply for having a piano in their homes.

And as late as 1865, when we presented our son Frank with a cottage organ (we did not dare give him a piano, feeling that organs were somehow “plainer”), we were obliged to hide it in one of the top rooms of the house in order to spare the feelings of our Quaker relatives.

I shall never forget my astonishment when I first realized that musical instruments were not only permitted in the Bible, but that we were actually commanded to use them. One day, reading the Psalms, I could hardly believe my eyes when I came to Psalm 150: “Praise ye the Lord. Praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with the psaltery and harp. Praise Him with the timbrel and dance; praise Him with stringed instruments and organs.” I never heard a Friend explain how they justified ignoring this.

“Plainness,” in my day, also excluded pictures everywhere except in books. No respectable Quaker would hang pictures on the walls, nor did they feel free to have their likeness taken. Even daguerreotypes, when they first appeared, were consider ed “gay” by all the truly “sound” Friends. I believe the idea was that having one’s picture might encourage vanity. And for some obscure reason, pictures or statuary were felt to be spiritually dangerous — temptations to idolatry. I grew up firmly believing it was wicked to visit an art gallery or to look at a statue.

I remember clearly, at about seventeen, breaking loose from all the traditions of my upbringing and going — my heart pounding as if on some perilously wicked adventure — into the Academy of Fine Arts in Philadelphia. There stood a marble group of Hero and Leander, and Leander was not very fully clothed. I still see myself standing before it, heart in my throat, saying inwardly, “I suppose I shall go straight to hell for this, but I cannot help it. If I must go, I must — , but I will look at this statue.” No words can express how daring a sinner I felt myself to be. And I remember my astonishment distinctly to find myself afterward standing safely in Broad Street, quite unharmed, without having experienced the swift judgment of an offended Creator.

I can still see that marble group vividly, far more vividly than any sculpture I have seen since.

Though I doubt it would now be considered great art, it has lived in my memory as the acme of all art, for it marked my emancipation into an entirely unknown world. Nothing dreadful happened to me, and I gradually gained courage for more, until I learned that a gift for art is as truly a divine bestowal as a gift for mathematics, and therefore cannot be wrong to cultivate. And gradually Friends also learned this; the old scruples against art and music have almost entirely disappeared.

Another testimony included under “plainness of apparel” in my youth was one against beards.

When Friends’ customs first crystallized, smooth faces were the universal fashion. Consequently, in keeping with the principle of not following changing worldly fashions, when beards became popular, Quakers clung to the clean-shaven face. As the fashion for beards became more insistent, the Quaker resistance grew firmer, until — gradually, and without any real reason I ever heard —it became a “religious testimony.” By the time I was born, it was one of the strictest.

I vividly recall the first time I saw a “preacher” wearing a beard. He was a visit ing Friend from England, where they were less strict. Yet despite my great reverence for English Friends, his beard seemed to me so plainly the mark of the Evil One that I felt it almost sinful to listen to his preaching. In several “strict” Meetings, he w as refused entrance to the gallery because of his beard, and I remember well the grave concern expressed by the Philadelphia Elders over this sad evidence of “the gradual encroachments of a worldly spirit in London Yearly Meeting.”

This testimony against beards, I believe, is shared — though probably for different reasons — by Roman Catholic priests and by High Church clergymen of the Church of England. But Friends have long since abandoned it, along with many other strict testimonies of my childhood. They still practice moderation in dress and speech, and in the furnishing of their homes and the ordering of their lives; but they have mostly given up any idea that a special cut of clothing or the suppression of natural gifts in literature, art, or music is necessary for divine favor.

Yet one cannot help admiring the sturdy adherence to what they sincerely believed was a religious duty, even though it now seems to us a mistaken one, that characterized those dear old saints.

That the Discipline on this matter was no dead letter is proved by the fact that, when I was older, and this testimony was beginning to lose its power over the less “concerned” members, I knew several instances in which Friends — though otherwise exemplary — were actually disowned simply for having a piano in their homes. And as late as 1865, when we presented our son Frank with a cottage organ (we did not dare give him a piano, feeling that organs were somehow “plainer”), we were obliged to hide it in one of the top rooms of the house in order to spare the feelings of our Quaker relatives. I shall never forget my astonishment when I first realized that musical instruments were not only permitted in the Bible, but that we were actually commanded to use them. One day, reading the Psalms, I could hardly believe my eyes when I came to Psalm 150: “Praise ye the Lord. Praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with the psaltery and harp. Praise Him with the timbrel and dance; praise Him with stringed instruments and organs.” I never heard a Friend explain how they justified ignoring this. “Plainness,” in my day, also excluded pictures everywhere except in books. No respectable Quaker would hang pictures on the walls, nor did they feel free to have their likeness taken. Even daguerreotypes, when they first appeared, were consider ed “gay” by all the truly “sound” Friends. I believe the idea was that having one’s picture might encourage vanity. And for some obscure reason, pictures or statuary were felt to be spiritually dangerous — temptations to idolatry. I grew up firmly believing it was wicked to visit an art gallery or to look at a statue. I remember clearly, at about seventeen, breaking loose from all the traditions of my upbringing and going — my heart pounding as if on some perilously wicked adventure — into the Academy of Fine Arts in Philadelphia. There stood a marble group of Hero and Leander, and Leander was not very fully clothed. I still see myself standing before it, heart in my throat, saying inwardly, “I suppose I shall go straight to hell for this, but I cannot help it. If I must go, I must — , but I will look at this statue.” No words can express how daring a sinner I felt myself to be. And I remember my astonishment distinctly to find myself afterward standing safely in Broad Street, quite unharmed, without having experienced the swift judgment of an offended Creator. I can still see that marble group vividly, far more vividly than any sculpture I have seen since. Though I doubt it would now be considered great art, it has lived in my memory as the acme of all art, for it marked my emancipation into an entirely unknown world. Nothing dreadful happened to me, and I gradually gained courage for more, until I learned that a gift for art is as truly a divine bestowal as a gift for mathematics, and therefore cannot be wrong to cultivate. And gradually Friends also learned this; the old scruples against art and music have almost entirely disappeared. Another testimony included under “plainness of apparel” in my youth was one against beards. When Friends’ customs first crystallized, smooth faces were the universal fashion. Consequently, in keeping with the principle of not following changing worldly fashions, when beards became popular, Quakers clung to the clean-shaven face. As the fashion for beards became more insistent, the Quaker resistance grew firmer, until — gradually, and without any real reason I ever heard —it became a “religious testimony.” By the time I was born, it was one of the strictest. I vividly recall the first time I saw a “preacher” wearing a beard. He was a visit ing Friend from England, where they were less strict. Yet despite my great reverence for English Friends, his beard seemed to me so plainly the mark of the Evil One that I felt it almost sinful to listen to his preaching. In several “strict” Meetings, he w as refused entrance to the gallery because of his beard, and I remember well the grave concern expressed by the Philadelphia Elders over this sad evidence of “the gradual encroachments of a worldly spirit in London Yearly Meeting.” This testimony against beards, I believe, is shared — though probably for different reasons — by Roman Catholic priests and by High Church clergymen of the Church of England. But Friends have long since abandoned it, along with many other strict testimonies of my childhood. They still practice moderation in dress and speech, and in the furnishing of their homes and the ordering of their lives; but they have mostly given up any idea that a special cut of clothing or the suppression of natural gifts in literature, art, or music is necessary for divine favor. Yet one cannot help admiring the sturdy adherence to what they sincerely believed was a religious duty, even though it now seems to us a mistaken one, that characterized those dear old saints.

fields.title: Quaker scruples
fields.body_html:
The personal “scruples” born of Quaker testimonies seemed endless, for each individual interpreted them according to their own sense of duty. Those with particularly sensitive consciences often multiplied restrictions until life itself became a torment. One friend, burdened with such a conscience, confessed to me later in life that her mornings as a young woman were nearly unbearable. She could scarcely dress herself without being beset by doubts over every article of clothing. At times, the only way she could silence the inner voice demanding fresh sacrifices was to stuff her ears with cotton and recite poetry as quickly as possible, drowning out the relentless admonitions.

An old diary kept by my great-grandmother between 1760 and 1762 offers a vivid glimpse into the scruples of her day. She wrote with solemn conviction that laughter was madness, mirth a vanity, and that she longed to be so fixed as never to smile again. Elsewhere, she lamented the creeping fashions among Friends — the young men tying their hair with ribbons, the girls adorning their necks with black bands. To her, these were sorrowful sights, evidence that the elders had failed in their duty. She bewailed the indulgence in tobacco, tea, and calico, declaring them all equally corrupting, “as bad as the negroes,” she wrote, grouping worldly habits together as one abomination. Her words reveal how each generation found new points of conscience, yet always in the same spirit of self-denial.

Closer to my own time, another grandmother refused to wear false teeth. Though toothless and struggling to eat, she felt a “stop” in her spirit, believing them to be a vain fashion. They were placed away in a drawer beside her best silk shawl, never to be worn. We, children, admired her saintliness, even as we watched her struggle with food. A preacher friend of ours, after laying down a new carpet, feared she had yielded to pride. To humble herself, she ordered wheelbarrows of rough stones dumped upon it, stripping away its freshness. We, children, heard the tale with awe, and her preaching thereafter seemed to us like the voice of an angel.

Years later, I faced my own trial over a new Brussels carpet, patterned with delicate flowers. My husband arranged for rough working men to gather in that very room each Sunday for Bible class. I resented their heavy boots on my prized carpet, though I knew I ought not to feel so.

While praying over the matter, a v erse came to me: “Take the spoiling of your goods joyfully .” I seized upon it as a weapon of the Spirit, and from that moment I welcomed those men upon my carpet. Strangely enough, it seemed never to wear out, lasting until I grew weary of its sight. I cannot help but think my way was better than the rough stones of my dear old Friend.

After I had discovered the way of faith, a friend who had long suffered under Quaker “scruples” gave me a striking picture of the different methods of living the Christian li fe. She said, “I have noticed three ways of getting to the other side of a spiritual mountain. Some tunnel through by the sweat of their brows — that is the Quaker way, and for a long time it was mine. Others wander around the base, meandering this way and that, but because they keep their faces turned toward the goal, they gradually draw nearer. That was my way when I grew weary of tunneling. But now you tell me there is a third way — the way of faith. You say that some Christians have learned to flap the wings of faith and fly right over the mountain. I must admit, those who take your way seem to reach the other side far more quickly and easily than either the tunnellers or the wanderers. I have decided to give up tunneling and meandering, and to flap my wings too.”

Yet the dear saints of my childhood and youth did not know how to fly. For the most part, they spent their lives in steadfast, weary tunneling. Their faithfulness and self-sacrifice, even if sometimes misdirected, seemed to me then — and still seems now — worthy of all honor. The one overwhelming impression left upon my young heart was simply this: by hook or by crook, I must be good. Whatever else was lacking in Quaker teaching, there was no lack of emphasis on goodness. The necessity of being thoroughly, honestly, genuinely good was in the very air we breathed.

At times, I chafed under this atmosphere. My adventurous nature longed for a chance to be naughty, to defy expectations, but the boundaries of my life allowed only the most innocent mischief. Looking back, I cannot help but admire the remarkable shield of goodness that surrounded me, protecting me from temptations that might otherwise have enticed my free spirit.

For if ever a soul was born free, it was mine. The cry of my heart has always been for freedom.

Rules and conventions that enslave or fetter have been my lifelong abhorrence. Had my parents made many rules, I would have rebelled. But the pervasive atmosphere of goodness in which they lived constrained me with such unconscious power that I hardly knew I was being guided. I felt blissfully as though I nearly always had my own way.

No one who did not live in it could imagine the narrow range of life I knew up to the age of eighteen. I never met anyone from what was called “the gay world.” My c ompanions were only the sober Friends of our circle, and their carefully guarded children. Novels were forbidden, and I had no chance to learn what life meant outside our Quaker fold. As for the sins of the world, I had not the faintest inkling. Even at school, if anything was hinted at, I was too innocent to understand. I dare say it would be impossible today for a girl of eighteen to live in such an unreal world of ignorance, or to enter life’s responsibilities so utterly unprepared.

My inner life until sixteen was simple. I believed what little I was told and troubled myself not at all about the mysteries of the universe. My only religious thoughts were occasional fears of hellfire, which flared up during epidemics or times of danger. How I came by this fear I cannot recall, for Quakers rarely spoke of heaven or hell. Their concern was the life of God in the soul now, trusting the future to divine care. Yet sometimes I was seized with sudden dread, made great resolutions to “be good,” and tried for a few h ours to correct my faults — only to relapse into my old ways. Still, the atmosphere of goodness around me made it difficult even to think of wrongdoing, much less to act upon it. On the whole, I was as good as a lively, healthy creature could be. But up to sixteen, I was simply a good animal. My spiritual nature was unawakened; I had never consciously realized my soul.

A change was near, though I did not know it. My soul was stirring from its torpor, struggling like a butterfly in its cocoon to break free from the bonds that held it. My long search after God was about to begin.

fields.title: The First Epoch In My Religious Life (the Awakening)
fields.body_html:
In the story of my religious life, four epochs stand out clearly before me. The first dawned, as I have said, when I was sixteen. In a dim, mysterious way, I began to feel vague longings for something that would satisfy my inward nature. In my diary from the autumn of 1848, I find record of these longings — a blind reaching out for something to fill what I called, in the tragic language of youth, “the aching void in my heart.”

In the midst of this, I fell head over heels in love with one of the young teachers at the school I was attending, and her influence changed my life. I recorded in my diary every step of our acquaintance — my longing to speak to her, to beg for her love, and my hesitation from fear of troubling her. I wrote as follows: “1848. Sixteen years old. This is an important time for me. Now is the time for forming my character. I feel as I never felt before. The great and solemn duties of life have, for the first time, come before me. I was not born to be an idler; for I feel something within me which tells me: Life has more inspiring imports Than the fancies of thy youth; It has hopes as high as heaven, It has labour, it has truth.

It has wrongs that may be righted, Noble deeds that may be done.

Its great battles are unfought, Its great triumphs are unwon.

Something which points onward — far onward — into the future, beyond this life into a brighter, happier world, and tells me of the glorious reward of those who fulfill their duties.

I have not felt this long. Three months ago, I was a careless, happy child. I am still a child, but an earnest, reflective one — no longer careless or indifferent. How can I be so, when there is so much, so very much, to think about and so much to be done? What has caused this change?

There was an aching void in my heart. I felt a want of something — something I knew not what — something indefinable that would make me sit dreamily for hours and look into the sky, watching the pale stars or the moon, until my very being seemed merged into theirs. I almost forgot I was on earth while my thoughts wandered into the pathless regions over which they presided, and I strove in vain to pierce the mysteries of their existence.

Study, I thought, would fill that void, but I was mistaken. In this state of mind, at the beginning of the Ninth Month, we left our darling little cottage home and returned to the city. If at that time I had met someone I could love whose principles were bad, I shudder to think what might have happened, for I am easily influenced by those I love.

But my Heavenly Father was willing to extend a little mercy toward me. He sent across my path one in whom I found a true friend. She was a young girl employed by Miss Maryanna as a composition teacher, named Anna S — . I was prepared to love her even before I saw her, for someone dear to me had told me of her loveliness. For two weeks after she first came to school, I believe I spoke to her only once; and that was when I saw her looking for a book and handed her one, asking if it was the right one.

I thought we would never become acquainted. I would sit and watch her and wish I dared speak to her and kiss her, and this very longing made me painfully shy. I would see her put her arms around other girls, and I would turn away in sorrow to think she would not do the same to me. At last, one day — how well I remember it — I was standing at my desk when she came up and spoke to me about A. S. F. How happy I felt! How I longed to throw my arms around her neck and beg her to let me love her! My heart was in a tumult, yet I answered calmly and without emotion, and she soon left me. But the ice was broken. We began to speak more often, and one morning she kissed me. That kiss was engraved on my heart. I felt that she loved me, and the thought brought me happiness.

From that moment, I have loved — nay, almost idolized — her. The aching void in my heart is now partly filled, for I have listened to her thoughts, seen the nobility of her actions, and learned that “life is real, life is earnest,” and not to be passed in idle dreaming or wasted in frivolous amusements. She has taught me — not in so many words, but quietly through her influence — that I have a mission to fulfill on earth, and that I must straightway begin to perform it. Henceforth, I must struggle earnestly to become pure and holy and noble-hearted, so that I may be great in the world and faithfully play my part in the great battle of life. Her influence has awakened me from my dream of childhood. In one short month, I have become a woman. Oh, how blessed her friendship has been to me! I hope — earnestly hope —that I may not abuse the privilege.”

A day or two later, I wrote: “Every day , I feel grateful to my Heavenly Father for blessing me with such a friend as Anna.

This is such an important period of my life. I tremble when I think of the awful responsibility resting upon me. My character is forming, and I have the power to become what I choose. Oh, may I choose to be a good and noble woman! Today, as I walked along the street and thought of what my future destiny might be, it made me almost shrink. I may be destined for some great work. I feel something within me that tells me I could accomplish it. At any rate, I shall do a great deal of good or evil. I will choose the former.

Oh, my Father who art in Heaven, wilt Thou not help me advance in the path of self-conquest, which must be my first great battle? What a glorious triumph it will be if I succeed!”

According to my diary, each day now seemed to awaken my spiritual nature more and more, until at last a kind of climax arrived. On 11th Month 28th, 1848, I wrote: “An eventful day! Eventful, I mean, in my spiritual life. Today I have felt and thought enough for a year. My friend Anna read to us in class a book called Other Worlds , and also Future Existence from the School Boy by Abbott. It was all intensely interesting and had an almost overpowering effect on me.

As I listened to the accounts of those mighty worlds scattered everywhere around us — some so distant that the rays of light which enter our eyes had left those stars six thousand years ago! — and as I reflected that these worlds are all moving regularly, never disturbing one another, but all obedient to one mighty Creator, the grandeur of the thought was overwhelming. For a few minutes, I felt as though the very happiness of being born into a universe so limitless, so magnificent, so glorious, was almost too great to bear.

And as I heard of our future existence, of the glorious and unimaginable happiness in store for us, of the perfect bliss reserved for the good and the holy, I inwardly thanked my Creator for placing me among beings whose expectations were so blessed. But then came the awful, overwhelming thought that this eternity of endless bliss was only for the good — and the realization that I could have no share in it unless my heart was changed. Oh, I cannot describe the misery of that moment! It was almost more than I could bear. And these thoughts linger with me. Why is i t?”

The impression made upon me by this glimpse into the magnificence of the universe has never left me to this day. At the bottom of all my questionings about God, there has always been a conviction of His illimitable power — something nothing could ever withstand. But for a long time, as will be seen, I thought of this power as a selfish one, engaged not on my side but against me. And my one question for many years was how I could win the God who possessed such power over to my side.

fields.title: My Search
fields.body_html:
My awakening had come in earnest. I was then about sixteen and a half, and from that time onward, my soul thirsted to make myself worthy of the glorious destiny of which I felt I had caught a glimpse. Even deeper than this was the longing to become acquainted with the God who had created the unimaginable wonders I had been reading about. I have no recollection of feeling any particular trouble about my sins; it was the magnificence of God that had enthralled me. I felt that the grandest thing in life would be to come to know Him. And so, then and there, my search began. But alas — what a blind, ignorant search it was at first.

My only confidante was my friend Anna. Not for the world would I have said anything on the subject to my parents. Their Quaker habits of reserve on all matters of religion made it seem impossible. But to my friend, after that day of awakening, I poured out my heart in a long letter full of aspirations and yearnings. In my diary, I have a copy of her reply, with these comments: “Anna wrote me a little note in reply to my letter. Never have I received one that thrilled me more deeply than that! She begged me to give up all to my Saviour, to pray for strength, and to strive earnestly after holiness, no matter what it cost me. ‘Oh , dearest Hannah,’ she said, ‘do let us try. Let us seek to journey together toward His glorious kingdom! Let us struggle for a portion of Hi s spirit.’

“Oh, that I could follow her advice! I sat here alone in my study and tried to feel as if I could give up all. But I could not. I could not even feel repentance for the many, many sins I have committed, and far worse than all, I could not feel as though I truly loved God. It is dreadful.

What shall I do? I must repent; I must love my Heavenly Father, or I shall be eternally ruined.

But I cannot do it on my own. God alone can help me, and I know not how to pray. Oh, what shall I do? Where shall I go? It is said, ‘Ask, and ye shall receive.’ But I cannot become really righteous until I repent, and I cannot repent.”

From this time onward, my religious diary is one long record of wrestlings and agonies, with scarcely a ray of light. My friend did her best to help me, but she, like myself, supposed that the only way to find God was to search for Him within. Our Quaker education had taught us always to turn to “the light within” for teaching and guidance, and we believed that only when God revealed Himself there could we truly come to know Him. In an old Quaker tract among my papers called What Shall We Do to Be Saved? , there is a passage that clearly sets forth the kind of teaching with which we had grown up. It reads: “I cannot direct the searcher after truth who is pensively enquiring what he shall do to be saved, to the ministry of any man; but would rather recommend him to the immediate teaching of the word nigh in the heart, even the Spirit of God. This is the only infallible teacher and the primary adequate rule of faith and practice. It will lead those who attend to its dictates into the peaceable paths of safety and truth. ‘Ye need not,’ said the Apostle to the Church formerly, ‘that any man teach you, save as this anointing teacheth, which is trut h and no lie.’”

The natural result of this teaching was to turn our minds inward, upon our feelings and emotions, and to make us judge our relationship with God entirely by what we found within ourselves.

What God had said in the Bible seemed to us far less authoritative than what He might say to us in our own hearts. I have no recollection of ever, even for a moment, turning to the Scriptures for instruction. The “inward voice” was to be our sole teacher— and for me at that time, the inward voice meant only my own feelings and emotions. As there is absolutely nothing more unreliable or unmanageable than one’s inward feelings, it is no wonder that I was plunged into a hopeless struggle.

In vain I tried to work myself up into what I supposed would be feelings acceptable to God. No thought of salvation in any other way ever crossed my mind. I talked about “my Saviour,” as I called Him, but I never imagined for a moment that He could — or would — save me unless I made myself worthy to be saved. And as this worthiness consisted mostly, I believed, of inward pious emotions, I thought only of trying somehow to force these emotions into being. Anyone who has ever tried to do this will know what a weary, hopeless task it is. The records in the diary of my religious life from the age of sixteen onward are a sad illustration of the false methods of religion that were all I knew. As I read them now, I cannot help pitying the eager, hungry soul reaching out so vainly after light but finding only confusion and darkness.

One thing, however, consoles me in this retrospect: none of these religious struggles seems, as far as I remember, to have darkened the skies of my outward happiness. My times for attending to my religious life were in our Quaker meetings, or when I was alone in my study during twilight, or at night after everyone else had gone to bed — and all the tragic records in my diary were written then. Throughout the day, I was generally too happy and too full of outward interests to be troubled by what had taken place in my religious hours. I feel this was a great cause for thankfulness, for if the struggles I endured in our silent meetings or in my hours of meditation had extended into the daytime as well, I do not like to imagine what the consequences might have been.

I believe my diary was my safety valve, for I remember well that after writing there the most tragic and despairing entries, I would somehow feel as though my religious exercises were finished, and would go off to bed quite happily, sleeping the sleep of the ju st without a moment’s wakeful anxiety or worry, and waking the next morning full of the joys of a new day, having forgotten all the miseries I had so despairingly recorded the night before. I recall being occasionally surprised by this easy transition, and I find the following in my diary from this time: “I cannot understand my feelings. Such a hungering and thirsting after righteousness, and yet, except in a few moments of retirement (when I write in my diary), such lightness, gaiety, and indifference. It seems almost wrong to laugh, and yet I indulge in it continually… I know not how God can look upon me, even in pity; I am so wicked. So often have I entered into a covenant to serve Him wholly and entirely, with fervour of spirit; but when the impression of my hours of retirement has faded, and the temptations of the world have assailed me, I have yielded, and have forgotten my high and holy calling through fear of the world’s dread laugh, and through the love of sin. Oh that I could do otherwise! The mercy of God will some day be exhausted —and where shall I be then? I dare not think.”

I can see now that it was, as I have said, my salvation from an utterly morbid and false sort of religion that my naturally happy and joyous temperament continually delivered me out of its snares — even though at the time this seemed wicked to me. How morbid and false all my ideas of religion were during this period a few further extracts from my diary will reveal.

Diary: “Oh, it is a sorrowful thought that upon myself depends th e salvation of my soul, and yet I can do absolutely nothing! Wherever I turn, all looks dark and gloomy. Oh, I must renew my efforts… Oh, that I could repent! But I cannot. I know it is wrong; I dread the anger of God; but I cannot feel what I know true repentance to be. Oh, that I could! I almost wish I could be as indifferent as I once was — could forget all that I have felt — for it seems impossible for me ever to be a Christian… “This afternoon in meeting, I was favored to feel, more perhaps than ever before, the spirit of supplication. My exercise was so great that I could scarcely sit still. My head throbbed painfully, and my heart felt as though it would break with the agony. Oh, how awful to feel that I have no power of myself even to think a holy thought, and yet I must gain the salvation of my soul! I cannot repent; I cannot love my Savior; and I do not believe I ever will. What —what shall I do?”

Three months after my awakening I wrote: Diary: “It has been more than three months since I began in ea rnest to seek the salvation of my soul, and I have not advanced one step. Could I have seen then all that was before me, I would have given up in despair. I would have thought it impossible to wait, and pray, and struggle for three months — and gain nothing. Now I look forward to many, many more months of prayer and struggling and waiting, with a fear — almost a certainty — that all of that, too, will be in vain.

“If there were only some outward work, entirely distinct from the inward change that is necessary — something to be done, not something merely to be prayed for — a cutting off of a hand or a foot, or some self-inflicted austerity — then perhaps I might become a Christian, for such things I could do. But the inward change I cannot effect, and yet I am accountable if it is not effected. Accountable for not doing what I cannot do! It is a dreadful thought.

“I feel as if I were seated, sick and weary, at the base of a high and inaccessible mountain peak whose summit I must reach — alone, and in the darkness of night. Oh, Heavenly Father, wilt Thou not enable me to be faithful, to strive earnestly, and to endure to the end?… “I am so ignorant and inexperienced that I am almost afraid to do anything. There are many, many things I long to inquire about, but whom shall I ask? I cannot speak to my parents until I know for certain that I am accepted; I love them too dearly to cause them the anguish of seeing me give up in despair. My dear friend Anna says she is not a Christian, and she dares not counsel or comfort me. And there is no one. Alone, I must bear all my burdens! Alone, I must seek the entrance to the straight and narrow way! Alone, I must work out my soul’s salvation. And I can of myself do nothing. Oh, what shall I do?”

As an illustration of the sort of teaching I was receiving at this time, the following entry is valuable: Diary: “Went to Twelfth Street Meeting this morning, where I was favored to have a few moments of real prayer. But my discouragement was very great, so that I could scarcely avoid crying aloud for help; and in my despair, I besought my Father in Heaven, if it seemed good unto Him, to put a few words of encouragement into the mouth of one of His servants.

“My prayer was answered. Almost immediately Samuel Bettle rose and spoke in a manner remarkably applicable to me, bidding the poor and needy — though now they might seem to be in the depths of tribulation, in darkness seeing no light, and thirsty yet finding no water — to put their trust in the Lord Jesus and patiently abide His time; and they would be filled with the light of His Holy Spirit, and fountains of living wate r would flow from them freely.”

Of what it meant to put one’s trust in Jesus, I had not the faintest conception, and I do not remember giving it a moment’s thought. But to patiently abide God’s time seemed something I could understand, and I went home from the meeting that day with a weary sense of an interminable waiting for the light of the Holy Spirit to shine in my heart and give me the longed- for joy and peace.

And so day after day went by in a hopeless watching of my feelings and emotions, which I could never bring up to the right pitch of fervor; and my unrest and darkness of spirit only grew more and more despairing.

One final extract from my diary will suffice: Diary: “Third Month 1, 1849. Very sad. The fear that this longing for salvation may be all a delusion attends me always, and everything is so completely veiled in gloom that I can scarcely take a single step. It seems to me that I cannot bear this state much longer. But oh Father! Thy will, not mine, be done.”

fields.title: Eclipse Of Faith
fields.body_html:
This morbid self-introspection lasted, with variable degrees of earnestness, until the time of my marriage at nineteen. Nothing ever came of it, and in the nature of things, nothing ever could. It was a self-involved religion that had no relation whatever to any Divine facts. And I see now that it was a mercy my marriage, and the new life and wider interests into which I was introduced, more or less turned my attention in other directions, and made my religious emotions and feelings sink into the background for a time, so that my mind became free at a later period to take an entirely different view of the religious life.

I believe, however, that my experiences during these years have been valuable in one way, and that is in teaching me to avoid ever encouraging in the young people I have known any sort of a self-absorbed interior life. Self-absorption is always a temptation to young people, and if their religion is of a sort to add to this self-absorption, I feel that it is a serious mistake. If I had my way, the whole subject of feelings and emotions in the religious life would be absolutely ignored.

Feelings there will be, doubtless, but they must not be in the least depended on, nor in any sense be taken as the test or gauge of one’s religion. They ought to be left out of the calculation entirely. You may feel good or you may feel bad, but neither the good feeling nor the bad feeling affects the real thing. It may affect your comfort in the thing, but it has nothing to do with the reality of the thing. If God loves you, it is of no account, as far as the fact goes, whether you feel that He loves you or do not feel it; although, as I say, it materially affects your comfort. Of course, if you really believe that He loves you, you cannot help being glad about it; but if you make your belief dependent upon your f eelings of gladness, you are reversing God’s order in the most hopeless kind of way.

I like so much that story of Luther when the devil said to him: “Luther, do you feel that you are a child of God?” and Luther replied: “No, I do not feel it at all, but I know it. Get thee behind me, Satan.”

During all the years when I was struggling over my feelings, I never succeeded in making them what I thought they ought to be; and as a consequence the religious part of my life was a misery to me. But after I had learned that the facts of religion were far more important than my feelings about these facts, and had consequently given up looking at my feelings, and sought only to discover the facts, I became always happy in my religious life, and had, without any effort, the very feelings of love to God, and of rest and peace and joy in my soul that before I had so vainly tried to work up. No words can express how vital I consider this point to be, nor how much, since I have found it out for myself, I have longed to make everybody else see it.

Many years after it had all become clear to me, one of my children came to me evidently in great perplexity and said: “Mother, how long does it take God to forgive you when you have been naughty?”

“It does not take Him a minute,” I replied.

“Oh,” she said, “I can’t believe that. I think you have to feel sorry first for a good many days, and then you have to ask Him in a very pretty and nice way, and then perhaps He can forgive you.”

“But,” I said, “daughter, the Bible says that if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us right straight off.”

“Well,” she said, “I wouldn’t believe that if fifty Bibles said it, because I know that you have got to feel sorry for quite a good while, and then you have got to ask God in a very pretty way, and then you have got to wait till He is ready to forgive you.”

I found the case was really serious, so, taking the child on my lap, I opened the Bible and made her read out loud the verse I had quoted, and then explained to her that God loved us so much that He sent His Son to die for us, and that, because of His love, He was always ready to forgive us the minute we asked Him, just as mothers were always ready to forgive their children as soon as the children wanted to be forgiven.

At last the child was convinced, and putting her little hands together she said in a reverent little voice: “Dear Lord Jesus, I want you to forgive me this very minute for all my naughty, and I am certain sure you will, because you love me.” And then she jumped down off my lap and ran away shouting merrily in childish glee.

My little girl was happy because she had found out a happy fact and believed it. But in her first way of looking at the matter she was only voicing the natural idea of the human heart. We all feel, as she did, that we must come to God with great doubt and timidity, as to a Being of whom we know but little, and whom we fear much; and that His favour depends altogether upon the beauty and suitableness of our emotions, and the ceremonious order of our approach.

To come “boldly to the throne of grace to find mercy and obtain help in the time of need” is only possible to the soul that has been brought into a real acquaintance with the goodness of God.

During all the years, however, of which I speak, from the age of sixteen to twenty-six, I knew nothing of this. God was to me a far-off, unapproachable Being, whom, in spite of all my eager and painful searching, I failed utterly to find. I had not the slightest conception of what the expression “God is love” meant. My idea of Him was that He was a stern and selfish taskmaster, who might perhaps, if one could only secure the sort of feelings and conduct that would please Him, be induced to pay some little attention to the needs of His children, but who was for the most part so absorbed in thoughts of His own glory, and of the consideration and reverence due to Himself, that it was almost impossible, except by a superhuman degree of perfection, to win His regards.

He seemed to me a supremely selfish Autocrat who held my fate in His hands, but who only cared for me in proportion to my power of adding to His honour and His glory.

Of all His loving and beautiful unselfishness, which I was afterwards to discover, I had for all these years not the faintest glimpse. Moreover, the only way I knew by which one could know that this unapproachable Deity did condescend to turn even a slight ear to the cries of His children was to have some sort of an interior feeling of it. Consequently, whenever I was religious at all, the whole energy of my spirit was spent, as I have said, in the effort to acquire in some occult way this necessary inward feeling.

The sort of introspection I had imbibed from my Quaker teaching was calculated to lead to constant self-examination of the most difficult sort, because it was an examination not so much into one’s actions as into one’s emotions. And, considering what ticklish things our emotions are, and how much they depend upon the state of our health, or the state of the weather, or the influence of other minds, no more fatal occupation, in my opinion, can be indulged in than this sort of self- examination. No more unreliable gauge could possibly be found as to one’s spiritual condition than that afforded by one’s own interior emotions.

But the religion of my years between sixteen and twenty-six was nothing but a religion of trying to feel; and, as I was a very natural, healthy sort of being, my feelings were not likely to be very sentimental or pious. The agonizing, futile efforts that I have described to bring them up to the right religious pitch is something pitiful to consider.

My soul hungered after God, but I could not find Him. Even the comfort of prayer was denied me, for I had, as I have said, imbibed the idea that you could not pray acceptably unless you felt an inward sense of the Divine favour, and that any prayers offered without this sense were really a mockery, and even perhaps a sin. And, since this inward sense of God’s favour was the very thing I was seeking to secure, and yet might not pray for until I first possessed it, I seemed tossed out helpless and forlorn into dreary darkness.

What the Bible said about God’s love was altogether a secondary consideration to what I might feel about it; indeed, as far as I can recollect, I did not consider the Bible at all. “How do I feel?”

not “What does God say?” was my daily cry. I was like a criminal in the presence of a judge, who, instead of being concerned as to how the judge felt about him, should spend all his efforts in trying to see how he felt about the judge.

A more ridiculous as well as pitiful attitude of soul one can hardly conceive of. And yet no one whom I approached on the subject seemed to know any better; and I floundered on in a despairing sort of way, afraid to give up my spiritual struggles lest I should be eternally damned, and yet realizing that they brought no help; and being continually tempted to upbraid God for being deaf to my cries.

I was like a man kneeling in a dark room and praying despairingly for light, ignorant of the fact that outside the sun was shining, and that it only needed to open the windows and light would pour in. In the very nature of things, light, either in the physical world or the spiritual world, cannot be self-evolved. I had gone to work in entirely the wrong way. I was trying to feel before I knew, and, instead of basing my feelings upon my knowledge, I was seeking to base my knowledge upon my feelings.

It was just as if a man, wanting to travel to a certain place, should enter the first railway station he might come across, and, without making any enquiries, should take a seat in the first railway carriage at hand, and should then shut his eyes and try to feel whether he was in the right train or not. No man in his senses would do such an idiotic thing. And yet it was exactly this I was doing in my religious life. It never entered my head to try and find out the facts of religion. I did not even know there were any facts to find out. My relations with God seemed to me altogether a matter of my own feelings towards Him, and not in the least of His feelings towards me; and every religious energy I possessed was consequently directed towards getting up these necessary feelings.

Of course, it was an impossible task, and, as time went on, and no right feelings would come for all my striving, I became more and more discouraged. At last, when I was between twenty-three and twenty-four, I found myself being driven into absolute unbelief. I argued that, if there really was a God anywhere, some answer to all my long and earnest wrestling would surely have been vouchsafed to me; and that, since He made no sign, therefore He could not be.

Moreover, as I grew older, I had begun to learn something more of the awful condition of things in the world because of sin; and the manifest evidences I seemed to see of an imperfect creation in my own life and in the lives of others, where failure was generally the rule and success only the exception, appeared to me incompatible with the idea of a wise and sensible Creator, not to say a good One, such as I had been told I must believe in. And gradually the creation came to seem to me such a grievous failure that I felt driven to the conclusion that either it must have been a wicked God who had created us, or else we had not been created by God at all, but by some evil and malicious power opposed to Him.

In my diary under date of Eleventh month, 5th, 1855, I head my entry with the following ominous words: “The Eclipse of Faith.” *“This last year has witnessed a great change in me. Every faculty of my nature has been thoroughly aroused. I have felt my mind expanding and have been cognizant of an actual and rapid mental growth. I pass from one phase of experience to another, leave behind me one standing place after another, and am now — where! Oh Christ, that I indeed knew where!

An inevitable chain of reasoning on free will has loosened every foothold, and I know not where to rest, if indeed there is any rest. Without any apprehension on my part of the result, thoughts and reasonings have been slowly gathering around my faith, and dashing themselves against it, until at last, with a sudden shock, it has fallen; and I am lost!

It has come to me like this. Benevolence certainly is a necessary attribute of the Almighty. His love, we are told, surpasses the love of an earthly parent far more than we can imagine. But it is utterly inconsistent with this to suppose that He can have any foreknowledge of the destiny of the human beings He creates. For of course, did He know, His benevolence would not allow Him to create any but beings destined to eternal happiness. Therefore He cannot be omniscient.

Further, if He were omnipotent, as we are told, He would have made such modifications in man’s nature as would at least render the work of salvati on less difficult and of far more frequent occurrence. Therefore He cannot be both all-loving and also all-powerful. Without either of these He ceases to be a God. Either He has set in motion a creating force which He can neither control nor end, and has performed His work in the first place so imperfectly and blindly that the results are grievously disastrous; or He has nothing to do with creation, and we are created by another and an evil Power.

A further conclusion is forced upon me. Justice is another necessary attribute of a good God. But it were most utterly unjust that we now should be feeling the effects of Adam’s fall, supposing there ever was such a thing. We are driven therefore from the possibility of a just Creator making independent beings suff er eternally for each other’s sins. And on the other hand benevolence could not allow of the creation of innately wicked natures, while justice could not share in punishing them.

There is no escape! A thousand questions rush in on every side. I am a sceptic!”*

Nothing ever came of it, and in the nature of things, nothing ever could. It was a self-involved religion that had no relation whatever to any Divine facts. And I see now that it was a mercy my marriage, and the new life and wider interests into which I was introduced, more or less turned my attention in other directions, and made my religious emotions and feelings sink into the background for a time, so that my mind became free at a later period to take an entirely different view of the religious life. I believe, however, that my experiences during these years have been valuable in one way, and that is in teaching me to avoid ever encouraging in the young people I have known any sort of a self-absorbed interior life. Self-absorption is always a temptation to young people, and if their religion is of a sort to add to this self-absorption, I feel that it is a serious mistake. If I had my way, the whole subject of feelings and emotions in the religious life would be absolutely ignored. Feelings there will be, doubtless, but they must not be in the least depended on, nor in any sense be taken as the test or gauge of one’s religion. They ought to be left out of the calculation entirely. You may feel good or you may feel bad, but neither the good feeling nor the bad feeling affects the real thing. It may affect your comfort in the thing, but it has nothing to do with the reality of the thing. If God loves you, it is of no account, as far as the fact goes, whether you feel that He loves you or do not feel it; although, as I say, it materially affects your comfort. Of course, if you really believe that He loves you, you cannot help being glad about it; but if you make your belief dependent upon your f eelings of gladness, you are reversing God’s order in the most hopeless kind of way. I like so much that story of Luther when the devil said to him: “Luther, do you feel that you are a child of God?” and Luther replied: “No, I do not feel it at all, but I know it. No words can express how vital I consider this point to be, nor how much, since I have found it out for myself, I have longed to make everybody else see it. Many years after it had all become clear to me, one of my children came to me evidently in great perplexity and said: “Mother, how long does it take God to forgive you when you have been naughty?” “It does not take Him a minute,” I replied. “Oh,” she said, “I can’t believe that. At last the child was convinced, and putting her little hands together she said in a reverent little voice: “Dear Lord Jesus, I want you to forgive me this very minute for all my naughty, and I am certain sure you will, because you love me.” And then she jumped down off my lap and ran away shouting merrily in childish glee. My little girl was happy because she had found out a happy fact and believed it. But in her first way of looking at the matter she was only voicing the natural idea of the human heart. We all feel, as she did, that we must come to God with great doubt and timidity, as to a Being of whom we know but little, and whom we fear much; and that His favour depends altogether upon the beauty and suitableness of our emotions, and the ceremonious order of our approach. To come “boldly to the throne of grace to find mercy and obtain help in the time of need” is only possible to the soul that has been brought into a real acquaintance with the goodness of God. During all the years, however, of which I speak, from the age of sixteen to twenty-six, I knew nothing of this. God was to me a far-off, unapproachable Being, whom, in spite of all my eager and painful searching, I failed utterly to find. I had not the slightest conception of what the expression “God is love” meant. My idea of Him was that He was a stern and selfish taskmaster, who might perhaps, if one could only secure the sort of feelings and conduct that would please Him, be induced to pay some little attention to the needs of His children, but who was for the most part so absorbed in thoughts of His own glory, and of the consideration and reverence due to Himself, that it was almost impossible, except by a superhuman degree of perfection, to win His regards. He seemed to me a supremely selfish Autocrat who held my fate in His hands, but who only cared for me in proportion to my power of adding to His honour and His glory. Of all His loving and beautiful unselfishness, which I was afterwards to discover, I had for all these years not the faintest glimpse. Moreover, the only way I knew by which one could know that this unapproachable Deity did condescend to turn even a slight ear to the cries of His children was to have some sort of an interior feeling of it. Consequently, whenever I was religious at all, the whole energy of my spirit was spent, as I have said, in the effort to acquire in some occult way this necessary inward feeling. The sort of introspection I had imbibed from my Quaker teaching was calculated to lead to constant self-examination of the most difficult sort, because it was an examination not so much into one’s actions as into one’s emotions. And, considering what ticklish things our emotions are, and how much they depend upon the state of our health, or the state of the weather, or the influence of other minds, no more fatal occupation, in my opinion, can be indulged in than this sort of self- examination. No more unreliable gauge could possibly be found as to one’s spiritual condition than that afforded by one’s own interior emotions. But the religion of my years between sixteen and twenty-six was nothing but a religion of trying to feel; and, as I was a very natural, healthy sort of being, my feelings were not likely to be very sentimental or pious. The agonizing, futile efforts that I have described to bring them up to the right religious pitch is something pitiful to consider. My soul hungered after God, but I could not find Him. Even the comfort of prayer was denied me, for I had, as I have said, imbibed the idea that you could not pray acceptably unless you felt an inward sense of the Divine favour, and that any prayers offered without this sense were really a mockery, and even perhaps a sin. And, since this inward sense of God’s favour was the very thing I was seeking to secure, and yet might not pray for until I first possessed it, I seemed tossed out helpless and forlorn into dreary darkness. What the Bible said about God’s love was altogether a secondary consideration to what I might feel about it; indeed, as far as I can recollect, I did not consider the Bible at all. “How do I feel?” not “What does God say?” was my daily cry. I was like a criminal in the presence of a judge, who, instead of being concerned as to how the judge felt about him, should spend all his efforts in trying to see how he felt about the judge. A more ridiculous as well as pitiful attitude of soul one can hardly conceive of. And yet no one whom I approached on the subject seemed to know any better; and I floundered on in a despairing sort of way, afraid to give up my spiritual struggles lest I should be eternally damned, and yet realizing that they brought no help; and being continually tempted to upbraid God for being deaf to my cries. I was like a man kneeling in a dark room and praying despairingly for light, ignorant of the fact that outside the sun was shining, and that it only needed to open the windows and light would pour in. In the very nature of things, light, either in the physical world or the spiritual world, cannot be self-evolved. I had gone to work in entirely the wrong way. I was trying to feel before I knew, and, instead of basing my feelings upon my knowledge, I was seeking to base my knowledge upon my feelings. It was just as if a man, wanting to travel to a certain place, should enter the first railway station he might come across, and, without making any enquiries, should take a seat in the first railway carriage at hand, and should then shut his eyes and try to feel whether he was in the right train or not. No man in his senses would do such an idiotic thing. And yet it was exactly this I was doing in my religious life. It never entered my head to try and find out the facts of religion.
