Many a time, when some new insight into His goodness overwhelmed me, I would take my Bible, open it to the passages declaring that we belong to Him, and put my fingers on the verses, reading them aloud just to reassure myself that they really did say — freely and without limitation — that He was indeed my Owner. The phrase, “Remember thy Creator,” suddenly took on a wholly different character. I had always thought of it as a warning meant to frighten us into good behavior. Now it shone with comfort — a delightful assurance that everything must be well with the creatures of such an unselfish Creator. I saw that God was good not merely in a religious sense, but in the truest, most practical sense of the word. And a good Creator was, of course, bound to make everything go right with His creation. The fact that nothing was hidden from His eyes — once so terrifying — became the most comforting truth in the universe, because it meant He knew all about us and could therefore do His best for us. My own experience as a mother — once a source of conflict with my beliefs about God — now came into perfect harmony. My children have been the joy of my life. I cannot imagine bliss more exquisite than the moments when my arms have been around them. Those moments have seemed nearer to the joy of Heaven than anything else on earth. And I think this joy has taught me more about God’s feelings toward His children than anything else. If I, a finite human being with limited capacity, could find such joy in my children, what must God — with His infinite heart — feel for His? Most of my understanding of the love of God has come from this very experience. I could not believe that God had created me with a greater capacity for unselfish love and self-sacrifice than He possessed Himself. Since discovering the mother-heart of God, I have answered every doubt about God ’s love simply by looking into my own heart as a mother. To me, it is impossible that a true mother could be selfish toward her children. A mother who puts her own comfort and welfare before her children is, in my mind, an unnatural mother, one who has failed in her highest calling. And if one looks at what we call the lower creation, even the animals teach us the supreme duty of maternal self-giving. The mother tiger will die before she lets harm come to her young. She will starve so they may eat. Could God do less? I speak of self-sacrifice, but in truth I cannot really call it sacrifice. No true mother — one who knows the reality of motherhood — would ever regard her care for her children as a sacrifice. It may involve exhaustion or hardship, but not sacrifice in the ordinary sense. The real sacrifice would be if she were not allowed to care for them. For this reason, I believe that many disappointed mothers — who do not receive the gratitude they desire — have only themselves to blame, because they demanded gratitude rather than inspired it. This understanding has revealed to me God’s feelings toward us: that what we call Christ’s “self - sacrifice” was simply the natural and necessary expression of His love; and that the astonishing thing is not that He did it, but that He could not have done otherwise . Since discovering the mother-heart of God, I have never been able to feel the slightest anxiety for any of His children — and by His children, I do not mean only the good ones, but the bad ones equally. Did not Jesus tell us that the Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine safe sheep to search for the one that is lost, and does not rest until He finds it? Viewed in the light of motherhood, the word “lost” becomes profoundly comforting. Nothing can be “lost” unless it is owned by someone. To be lost means only, “not yet found.” The lost coin is still gold, bearing the king’s image. The lost sheep is still a sheep, not a wolf. The lost son is still a son, with his father’s blood in his veins. So if a person is a “lost sinner,” it simply means he is owned by the Good Shepherd, and that the Shepherd, by the very duties of ownership, must go after that which is lost — and keep going until He finds it. To me, the word “lost” contains the strongest possible proof of ownership. Who can imagine a mother with a lost child having one moment of rest until the child is found? And who could imagine God being less concerned than a mother? I believe that all the problems of the spiritual life , which so often distress conscientious souls, would disappear like morning mist before the rising sun if only the full blaze of the mother-heart of God were allowed to shine upon them. I came to see that, since Scripture declares we were created in the image of God, we are obliged to believe that the best in us — not the worst — is what reflects that image. Anything that, in our highest and most unselfish moments, appears selfish, unkind, unjust, or self-seeking must never be attributed to God, no matter how things may “seem.” If God is unselfish, then He must be at least as unselfish as the noblest ideal we can conceive — and of course infinitely more. All the biblical texts about God’s goodness suddenly shone with new meaning. I realized that His goodness is not a condescending benevolence but a genuine, wholehearted goodness — one that includes true unselfishness, deep consideration, and above all, justice. Justice has always seemed to me one of the first essentials of goodness; I cannot imagine calling anyone “good” who is unjust, no matter how impressive their outward appearance of virtue may be. In short, I had, such an overwhelming revelation of God’s intrinsic and inherent goodness and unselfishness that nothing since has been able to shake it. Many aspects of His dealings with the world have been,, and still are, mysterious to me; but I am convinced that every one of them could be explained through the lens of His love and justice, if only I could see deeply enough. And I believe that one day I will see clearly what I now hold by faith: that His loving kindness truly reaches over all His works. I do not mean that all this understanding came to me at once. But I do mean that on that day, riding a tramcar in Philadelphia, a light broke across the character of God — a light that has never dimmed in the slightest and has only grown brighter with each passing year. For me, it is enough to say, “God is,” and the answer to every difficulty is already present. What amazes me is that I, along with so many other Christians, had failed to see this, even with the open Bible before us —and that all sorts of distortions of God’s character, even outright slanders against His goodness, can find a ready welcome in Christian hearts. To me, such misrepresentations became almost unbearable. I could listen patiently — even with interest — to almost any strange or unorthodox idea that did not malign God’s character. But the one thing I could not endure, the one thing I could not sit quietly through, was anything that — even under a cloak of piety —suggested the faintest insult to God’s love or His unselfishness. I will never forget a memorable incident in our home when a distinguished preacher from Boston was visiting us. At breakfast, the conversation turned to God’s love. He insisted that you must not rely on it too much, for there were limits to what God could endure — just as, he said, there were limits to a mother’s love. He claimed that a daughter might commit certain sins a mother could never forgive, sins that would forever close her heart and her home, and he argued that God was the same. To believe otherwise, he said, was to hold a “grandmotherly religion.” I have no doubt he meant to undermine my views on Restitution, though we were not discussing that topic. He simply wished to convince me that God was not as “foolishly loving” as I believed. But to hear mothers, and the God who created mothers, so misrepresented was more than I could bear. Though he was my guest, I burst out in fierce indignation, declared that I would not sit at the table with anyone who held such slanderous ideas of God, and left the room in tears. I refused to see him again. I do not claim that this reaction was courteous or even Christ- like, but it shows how overwhelmingly I felt about the matter. To me, the honor of God outweighed every rule of social etiquette. I see now that I might have defended that honor just as strongly, but in a far more Christ-like way. Still, to this day, the one thing I find extremely hard to tolerate is anything that maligns the character of God. Nothing else compares to this in importance, for our entire salvation depends absolutely on who God is. Unless he can be shown to be wholly good, wholly unselfish, and wholly just, then our case is utterly hopeless. God alone is our salvation, and if He fails us — even in the smallest degree — we have nowhere else to turn.

fields.title: Effect Of My Views On My Public Work
fields.body_html:
As could be expected in those days, my views on Restitution — views I announced rather quickly — met with considerable disapproval from the Plymouth Brethren and many of my other orthodox friends. I had to endure a fair amount of what might be called persecution, though in truth I took a certain satisfaction in it, for I felt it was a grand thing to know so much more of God than those who opposed me.

I often compared my feelings to those of a civilized traveler trying to explain the marvels of his world to people in a remote, “savage” country— people who could neither understand nor believe what he described. His sense of superior knowledge would make their disapproval and opposition only a reason to pity their ignorance and to bear with it patiently. On that same principle, I almost enjoyed being regarded as a heretic, and I never wanted anyone’s endorsement. To be endorsed felt, to me, like being bound; and I preferred to be a free lance, unhindered in my absolute mental and spiritual freedom.

At that time the discovery I had made was not as widely known as it is now, and it seemed likely that holding what many considered a grave heresy might hinder my Christian work. And perhaps it did in some circles. But as I always had far more invitations to speak than I could possibly accept, I never truly suffered any difficulty. I tried to be courteous enough not to place on others — especially those who found my views abhorrent — the burden of endorsing me. Still, the revelation I had received was too glorious to withhold whenever a door opened. And since I refused to sail under false colors, and insisted that any place I spoke should know beforehand exactl y what a “heretic” I was, I generally enjoyed all the freedom I desired.

In fact, these very views — and my open confession of them under rather trying circumstances — opened the way for some of our most important and fruitful work. It happened in this way.

In 1873, my husband came to England to hold meetings in the interests of the Higher Life, or what I prefer to call the Life of Faith. I followed soon after, and upon my arrival in London I was invited to meet a gathering of leading Evangelical ladies who were to decide whether it would be safe for them to support me and lend their influence to the work.

Lady Mount Temple, one of the women present, later described the meeting in her life of Lord Mount Temple: “I think it was in 1873 that Mr. Pearsall Smith cam e to England from America, followed a few months later by his dear, beautiful wife. It was a time long to be remembered. They came, one may say, full of the new wine of the Spirit, longing to help others onward in the Divine life. A friend invited us to lunch to meet them. I shall never forget my first sight of Hannah Smith. We called her the ‘angel of the Churches,’ and she looked like one, with her golden hair and clear, beautifully cut face, in a dress all her own, yet as simple as that of the Friends among whom she had been raised.

“What especially drew me to her that day was this. I must confess that I was only a seeker after truth. Hannah was sitting in a small circle of excellent orthodox friends, gathered to hear the good things she had to share, and she was, in fact, on trial. She had seen a funeral procession in the street, and when she mentioned it, we all adopted the conventional expression of sorrow.

‘Oh,’ she said, ‘when I see a funeral I always give thanks for a brother or sister delivered from the trials and pains of this mortal state.’ I thought, How wonderful! And I could not help asking, ‘Is that possible? Do you feel this about everyone?’ I was indeed an enfant terrible.

“She paused for a moment and glanced around. She was among evangelicals, at a time when the universal hope was considered a heresy, and this was her examination. She later said she experienced a brief inner struggle. But truth prevailed, and with her bright, fearless look she said, ‘Yes— about everyone. For I trust in the lov e of God.’ I surrendered my heart immediately to this trust, love, and candor.”

I remember the occasion perfectly, and the thoughts running through my mind. I knew I was being tested, and I suspected that my answer might shock the entire company. But I felt that loyalty to God required me to say what honored Him, and to leave the consequences in His hands.

The moment I finished speaking, Lady Mount Temple — then Mrs. Cowper Temple — rose from her seat, came straight to me, and, though I was a stranger, gave me a warm, affectionate kiss.

“You must come and hold some meetings at Broadlands,” she said at once. I don’t know what the others felt, but not a word of disapproval was spoken, and they later became some of my dearest friends.

The result was that, within a few weeks, Broadlands — the country home of Lord and Lady Mount Temple in Hampshire — was opened to us for our first conference. It was a time of extraordinary blessing, and it became the doorway to all the later conferences and to our entire subsequent work in England and beyond.

When a conference was planned at Brighton in 1874, some members of the organizing committee became anxious about my “heresies,” fearing they might hinder the work. They persuaded my husband — who had arrived in England before I did — to write to me in America and tell me that unless I promised to keep my views quiet, they would strongly oppose my participation in the meetings. Recently, while looking through an old bundle of letters, I found my reply, which reveals precisely how I felt at the time: “Philadelphia, April 6, 1874.

Thy letters from London have arrived. Thee need not think I would be troubled at not being allowed to speak in the meetings, for nothing would suit me better. I am not in the least anxious to preach. Indeed, I consider it quite a favor on my part to be willing to do it at all, and just as much of a favor on others’ part to listen to me. If your committee should say, ‘We do not want to hear you speak at Brighton,’ I would have thanked them heartily. No one need feel any delicacy about this. But it must be thoroughly understood that I will make no compromises for anyone, and that I believe in Restitution more firmly than ever. I do not think I could bear the misery I see in this poor, sad, sin-stricken world without it. Our temperance work brings us face to face with such helpless suffering that my heart would break if I did not know that God loves all His creatures and has something gracious in store for everyone.”

Since I would not compromise — and since it was still considered important to have me at the meetings — the committee dropped the matter and decided to take me as I was, heresies and all.

When my husband wrote to tell me this, I replied: “Philadelphia.

I am very glad thee has escaped thy difficulty about thy heretical preaching wife with so little trouble. But the idea of B — , with his shaky views, undertaking to excommunicate me! I do not think it honest. I will not sail under false colors, and my conviction about Restitution grows stronger every single day. If they leave me alone in England, I will probably say little about it; but if there is even the slightest hint of compromise or secrecy on my part, I will blaze out into a perfect conflagration. I cannot endure anything of that sort. So please remember this, ye Lords of Creation.

Seriously, though, I do not feel drawn to preach or teach Restitution over there, and if the dear, frightened orthodox friends make no fuss about it, I am unlikely to do so. Their worries about me do not annoy me in the least. I believe I actually enjoy being the target of the odium theologicum.

I suppose there is som ething of the war horse in my constitution.”

Whether the committee’s fears were well founded or not, I cannot say; I only know that not once, during all my work in England, did I ever feel that my views on Restitution hindered the reception of my message or closed even a single door. In fact, I believe they opened doors that might otherwise have remained shut. The deeper truth was that my underlying belief in the absolutely unlimited justice and love of God enabled me to speak with a far more courageous faith than I could ever have managed without it. I am convinced that without this conviction I would have been deprived of half my power.

Whatever others may think, the revolution this discovery worked in my own experience was immense — beyond words. The spiritual romance of my life became more captivating than ever.

Every day brought some deeper and more radiant insight into the unimaginable goodness and unselfishness of God. I felt at last that I was beginning to enter into the meaning of the Apostle’s prayer for the Ephesians: that we might comprehend, with all the saints, the breadth and length and depth and height of Christ’s love, and know— even if only faintly — the love that surpasses knowledge.

Such love truly does surpass knowledge; it could arise only from the heart of a wholly unselfish God. I stood in awe before its breadth and length and depth and height, and I marveled — endlessly — that I could ever have imagined a Divine love with boundaries.

For a long time the joy of it all was so wonderful that I thought there could be nothing more to discover about God — that I had reached the final revelation.

But a further unveiling awaited me, and the fourth epoch of my soul’s life— its most entrancing chapter yet — was about to begin.

fields.title: The Fourth Epoch In My Religious Life (the Life Of Faith)
fields.body_html:
It was in 1865 that the fourth, and by far the most captivating, epoch of my spiritual journey dawned upon my soul. I had been a Christian for nine years — years filled with delight and enchantment — but what now came to me was so far beyond all that preceded it that it felt as though an entirely new and magical world had opened before me.

During those earlier years, my faith had been thoroughly satisfying in everything relating to God.

Every discovery I made about His character and His ways brought me only joy. But when it came to my own part in the Christian life, the satisfaction was far less complete. I was happy, yes, but I was not the person I longed to be.

I had found a religion that promised perfect deliverance for the future, but it did not seem to offer deliverance now . I had found an unselfish and just God whom I could worship without fear of disappointment — but I was continually disappointed in myself. I knew I was not what I ought to be. My life felt full of failure — not so much outward sin, but inward sins: coldness, spiritual deadness, lack of Christian love, roots of bitterness, all those hidden failings over which God’s children so often grieve. When I wanted to do good, evil was present. The good I desired, I did not do; and the evil I despised, I still did. I found myself constantly sinning and repenting, making resolutions and breaking them, hating what was wrong yet yielding to it, longing for victory but more often failing than overcoming.

Yet Scripture seemed to teach that Christ came to bring a real and present victory to His followers. It implied that Christians were meant to be free from anxious cares and fears, and to enjoy even now a peace that surpasses understanding. But I knew painfully little of that. My heart was at rest about my future , but my present was torn by a thousand daily worries and anxieties. The very fruits of the Spirit — which I believed I had received — were love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, meekness, goodness; yet these were the very qualities in which I felt most deficient.

This was not what I had expected when I first became a Christian. Raised among the Quakers — whose lives radiated peace — and taught from childhood that goodness was essential, I had assumed that becoming a Christian necessarily meant becoming peaceful and good. I expected victory over sin and over worry as naturally as I expected the sun to rise. But in the secret depths of my soul, I had to admit that I was disappointed.

At first, the joy of my newfound salvation had swept everything else aside. I thought temptation and fear and sin were gone forever. But when the initial glow faded, the old temptations returned with their old power. It became as easy as ever to be anxious, worried, burdened, irritable, unkind, critical, and severe — to do and be all the things from which I believed religion would deliver me. None of this ever shook my conviction that I was God’s child and an heir of heaven, but it often made me feel miserably ashamed. To be a child of God and yet unable to live like one made me wonder whether I had missed something in the Christian life — something that could have brought me victory.

Determined to discover what that missing element was, I questioned several older Christians. But they all gave me the same answer: No, you have not missed anything. The life of sinning and repenting is all we can expect in this world, because of the weakness of the flesh. They explained that the old Adam, inherited at birth, and the new Adam, received at conversion, constantly warred against each other — sometimes one prevailing, sometimes the other — and that only in death would we find true deliverance from the old nature.

N othing could have described my condition better than Paul’s own lament in Romans 7:14– 23. It seemed written for me. Again and again I cried out with him, “O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” But I could not understa nd why Paul even asked that question if, as everyone said, there was no deliverance in this life. Surely he knew the old nature was destined to remain until death. Yet he not only asked the question — he answered it triumphantly: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

What could he have meant? I had entered into salvation through Jesus Christ, yet I knew nothing of such triumphant deliverance. I was still bound by the “body of death” within me.

Why? Where lay the difficulty?

These questions grew even more pressing after I discovered the unlimited love of God. It felt so ungenerous — almost ungrateful — to respond to His boundless unselfishness with such lack of spiritual fruit. Since He had shown Himself so mighty to save in the future, how could He be powerless in the present?

The Quaker lives around me also suggested there must be deliverance, for they claimed to have experienced it — even though they could never explain clearly what it was or how it worked.

Another influence strengthened this conviction. I owned a book that taught not only that God’s children were commanded to bear the fruits of the Spirit, but that they could do so — and that also offered hints of the mystical pathway toward it. The book was Spiritual Progress , a collection of selections from Fenelon and Madame Guyon. It was especially precious because it had been a gift from my adored father and always lay on my desk beside my Bible.

My father had discovered it when he was only eighteen. As he walked through Philadelphia on his way to board a ship for a long voyage to China, he passed a second-hand bookstall. Though he had only recently begun the spiritual life, he was drawn to the title Spiritual Progress .

Knowing nothing of its contents, he bought it on impulse — guided unconsciously, no doubt, by the Lord in whom he had begun to trust. He wrote in his Reminiscences: “This book proved to be of the greatest comfort to me. I carried it in my pocket and read it in spare moments, to my everlasting profit, I trust. I cannot but thank a kind Providence for placing this blessed book in my hands.”

My father valued that book so highly that as soon as each of us children was old enough, he gave us our own copy and asked us to study it carefully. Because we loved him so dearly, we always wanted to please him, and during the years of my first hungry and despairing search for God, the book became my constant companion.

But since it was written more to guide souls who were already progressing in the spiritual life than to help seekers enter that life in the first place, it wasn’t of much definite help to me during those early, blind years of searching. And when, in 1858, I came to believe I had discovered “the plan of salvation”— settled, as I imagined, in the councils of Heaven, revealed in the life and death of Christ, and neatly formulated by the Apostle Paul — I filled the margins of my copy with what I thought were decisive critiques proving the book’s unsoundness.

Still, without my realizing it, its teachings made a profound impression on me. Even while I criticized it, I felt an underlying hunger for the mystical side of religion that the book expressed.

Throughout the years that followed, I was pulled back and forth between the claims of Plymouth Brethren doctrine on one side and the claims of mysticism on the other.

The practical, businesslike part of my nature leaned toward the Brethren; my Quaker upbringing and the influence of my cherished book pulled me toward the mystical.

At times, doctrines seemed supr emely important and one’s actual life almost insignificant; at other times, doctrines felt worthless unless they resulted in a righteous life. Sometimes Paul held sway in my thinking — teaching salvation by faith — and sometimes James, insisting that faith without works is dead. My Plymouth Brethren friends exalted Paul and justification by faith; my Quaker friends and the Catholic saints in my book exalted James and justification by works. The practical part of me leaned to the first; the mystical side leaned to the second. The result was an ongoing restlessness of soul which, combined with my distress over my continual spiritual failures, often made me question whether what I had learned about the salvation of Christ could really be the whole story.

With no be tter remedy, I turned increasingly to “sound doctrine” to quiet my unrest. Under Plymouth Brethren influence, these doctrines had become very clearly defined, each one neatly labeled and stored away in the mental pigeonholes of my mind. Nothing could have been more orderly — at least as far as doctrines were concerned. I had become quite a successful teacher of these doctrines, and I looked down pityingly on anyone who was not as clear and definite as I was.

I often wished I could seat all the religious teachers I knew in a row of baby high chairs before me, so that I could explain to them the doctrines they seemed so confused about — especially justification by faith and the judicial standing of the believer . I regularly declared that if one simply understood these two points and believed them fully, then everything was all right and nothing else mattered much.

I remember saying something like this to a cousin who came to me distressed about her shortcomings in the Christian life. She said, “But Hannah, according to what you’re saying, all our sins — past, present, and future — are forgiven if we simply believe. It makes very little difference what we do.”

“Yes,” I answered in my ignorance, “and that is exactly the beauty of it! We wear the robe of Christ’s righteous ness, and that robe covers all the vileness underneath. When God looks at us, He sees not our unrighteousness but Christ’s righteousness, and He accepts us because of that.”

Another time, a Quaker preacher who had heard me expound these crude ideas said, “ It seems to me, Hannah Smith, that you talk as if you could walk into a ready-made clothing shop, buy garments of salvation, put them on immediately, and come out fully clothed in righteousness and ready for heaven.”

“Yes!” I replied. “That is exactly how it is —except I don’t have to buy the garments; Christ gives them to me! Thank you for such a beautiful illustration; I shall certainly use it in my preaching.”

I have no doubt I interpreted Plymouth Brethren teaching in a far more literal and external way than they ever intended. But I liked to have everything defined with absolute clarity, and this seemed the logical outcome of their views. Strangely, I failed to see how inconsistent it was to believe in a righteous God who supposedly covered up our unrighteousness with the robe of His own righteousness, and then pretended to Himself that we were fit for heaven — when He certainly knew that beneath the robe our “filthy garments” were still there.

Whenever my Quaker friends hinted at this inconsistency, I silenced my uneasiness by telling myself that although they were dear, good people, they were not doctrinal at all and knew very little about the “plan of salvation,” “justification by faith,” or the “judicial standing of the believer.” Their objections, there fore, were not worth considering.

However, after the discovery I had made of the vastness of God’s love , as described in my previous chapters, I began to feel increasingly uneasy. It seemed a most ungrateful response to such boundless love that we — its recipients — should fail so miserably in living the kind of life God clearly intended for us. The more I thought, the more inconsistent it seemed that salvation, which was ultimately to be so magnificent and complete, should fail so obviously now , in this present life, to provide the victory over sin and over worry that the gospel so plainly promises as its immediate result.

Why was it, I asked myself again and again, that the God who had planned such a glorious deliverance for us in the future had not also planned a better deliverance for us in the present?

I had found a religion that promised perfect deliverance for the future, but it did not seem to offer deliverance now . I had found an unselfish and just God whom I could worship without fear of disappointment — but I was continually disappointed in myself. I knew I was not what I ought to be. My life felt full of failure — not so much outward sin, but inward sins: coldness, spiritual deadness, lack of Christian love, roots of bitterness, all those hidden failings over which God’s children so often grieve. When I wanted to do good, evil was present. The good I desired, I did not do; and the evil I despised, I still did. I found myself constantly sinning and repenting, making resolutions and breaking them, hating what was wrong yet yielding to it, longing for victory but more often failing than overcoming. Yet Scripture seemed to teach that Christ came to bring a real and present victory to His followers. It implied that Christians were meant to be free from anxious cares and fears, and to enjoy even now a peace that surpasses understanding. But I knew painfully little of that. My heart was at rest about my future , but my present was torn by a thousand daily worries and anxieties. The very fruits of the Spirit — which I believed I had received — were love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, meekness, goodness; yet these were the very qualities in which I felt most deficient. This was not what I had expected when I first became a Christian. Raised among the Quakers — whose lives radiated peace — and taught from childhood that goodness was essential, I had assumed that becoming a Christian necessarily meant becoming peaceful and good. I expected victory over sin and over worry as naturally as I expected the sun to rise. But in the secret depths of my soul, I had to admit that I was disappointed. At first, the joy of my newfound salvation had swept everything else aside. I thought temptation and fear and sin were gone forever. But when the initial glow faded, the old temptations returned with their old power. It became as easy as ever to be anxious, worried, burdened, irritable, unkind, critical, and severe — to do and be all the things from which I believed religion would deliver me. None of this ever shook my conviction that I was God’s child and an heir of heaven, but it often made me feel miserably ashamed. To be a child of God and yet unable to live like one made me wonder whether I had missed something in the Christian life — something that could have brought me victory. Determined to discover what that missing element was, I questioned several older Christians. But they all gave me the same answer: No, you have not missed anything. The life of sinning and repenting is all we can expect in this world, because of the weakness of the flesh. They explained that the old Adam, inherited at birth, and the new Adam, received at conversion, constantly warred against each other — sometimes one prevailing, sometimes the other — and that only in death would we find true deliverance from the old nature. N othing could have described my condition better than Paul’s own lament in Romans 7:14– 23. It seemed written for me. Again and again I cried out with him, “O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” But I could not understa nd why Paul even asked that question if, as everyone said, there was no deliverance in this life. Surely he knew the old nature was destined to remain until death. Yet he not only asked the question — he answered it triumphantly: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” What could he have meant? I had entered into salvation through Jesus Christ, yet I knew nothing of such triumphant deliverance. I was still bound by the “body of death” within me. Why? Where lay the difficulty? These questions grew even more pressing after I discovered the unlimited love of God. It felt so ungenerous — almost ungrateful — to respond to His boundless unselfishness with such lack of spiritual fruit. Since He had shown Himself so mighty to save in the future, how could He be powerless in the present? The Quaker lives around me also suggested there must be deliverance, for they claimed to have experienced it — even though they could never explain clearly what it was or how it worked. Another influence strengthened this conviction. The book was Spiritual Progress , a collection of selections from Fenelon and Madame Guyon. It was especially precious because it had been a gift from my adored father and always lay on my desk beside my Bible. My father had discovered it when he was only eighteen. As he walked through Philadelphia on his way to board a ship for a long voyage to China, he passed a second-hand bookstall. Though he had only recently begun the spiritual life, he was drawn to the title Spiritual Progress . Knowing nothing of its contents, he bought it on impulse — guided unconsciously, no doubt, by the Lord in whom he had begun to trust. He wrote in his Reminiscences: “This book proved to be of the greatest comfort to me. I carried it in my pocket and read it in spare moments, to my everlasting profit, I trust. I cannot but thank a kind Providence for placing this blessed book in my hands.” My father valued that book so highly that as soon as each of us children was old enough, he gave us our own copy and asked us to study it carefully. Because we loved him so dearly, we always wanted to please him, and during the years of my first hungry and despairing search for God, the book became my constant companion. fields.title: The Way Of Escape
fields.body_html:
This unrest and questioning came to a head in 1865. Because of family circumstances, we had to leave our delightful home in Germantown — along with all our wide circle of interests — and move to a remote village in New Jersey, where we were almost completely cut off from any congenial society. Financially, it was an advantage, but in every other respect it was a tremendous trial, especially for me. I confess that my spirit rebelled bitterly against the change.

Little did I imagine that in this very place, which felt so desolate and isolated, a glorious new light would dawn, ushering in the fourth and crowning epoch of my spiritual life.

It happened this way. As I’ve said, I was deeply rebellious about the move. Yet I had enough spiritual insight to know that this rebellion was wrong. Since the move was clearly a providential arrangement beyond my control, the only right response was to accept it cheerfully and genuinely say, “Thy will be done.” But although I scolded myself constantly, I couldn’t bring myself to accept God’s will—and in truth, I didn’t want to acc ept it. I felt it was harsh treatment to be forced to leave my happy Germantown home and my sphere of usefulness to live in such a lonely, remote place as Millville. It seemed to me that God ought not to have allowed it, and that I had every right to grumble and fret.

As a result, I fell into a deeply uncomfortable state of mind. Even my clear doctrines could no longer help me, and I began to fear that I was going to lose whatever spirituality I had left.

In the face of a need so real, it was no comfort to know I was forgiven. I wanted more than forgiveness — I wanted deliverance. But I had no idea how to obtain it.

Because we frequently had Mission preachers visit us, I explained my case to several of them and asked for help, but no one could tell me anything useful. At last, a very successful religious teacher came for a few days, and to him I poured out my trouble fully, begging him to suggest some path to deliverance. He considered my situation seriously and finally said he believed what I needed was to engage in some Christian work. If I would go out the next morning to visit the poor in our neighborhood and see how I could help them, he thought my spiritual life would be renewed and everything would come right.

So the next day, I tried his suggested remedy. But I quickly discovered how futile it was. Almost in the first house I entered I found a woman struggling with the very same spiritual difficulty as my own, and she desperately needed help — and I had none to give. I felt like someone trying to feed the hungry out of an empty bowl. It was a silly and impossible task. I returned home more discouraged than ever, convinced that before I could help anyone else, I would have to find deliverance for myself.

There was a local dressmaker who often came to sew for me, and since I had so little companionship in the village, I would sometimes sit and talk with her while we worked. She seemed unusually spiritually minded, and I was fascinated by her experiences. I discovered that she believed in an actual victory over temptation — that it was not necessary, as I had thought, to go through life sinning and repenting, sinning and repenting, but that a Christian could truly be delivered. She told me that among the Methodists there was a doctrine called “Holiness,” and an acc ompanying experience called “sanctification,” or “the second blessing,” which brought people into a place of victory. I was intensely interested in everything she said, and began to hope that perhaps here might be the solution to my struggles.

She also told me that a small meeting was held in the village on Saturday evenings where this doctrine was taught and where people shared their experiences. She urged me to attend. I thought I might go someday, but allowed other things to interfere. I was convinced that poor, uneducated factory workers could not possibly have anything to teach me. I had studied and taught the Bible extensively and had a high opinion of my own religious attainments. I felt that if I did go to the meeting, I would likely have far more to teach them than they would have to teach me.

Eventually, however, one evening I decided to grant them the favor of my presence — and I confess, I did feel it was a great favor. I went to the meeting full of my own importance and superiority, expecting to astonish them with my biblical knowledge.

When I entered, a factory woman with a shawl over her head —she likely didn’t own a bonnet— was speaking. I heard her say: “My whole horizon used to be filled with this great big Me of mine, but when I got a glimpse of Christ as my perfect Savior, that great big Me shriveled down to nothing.”

Those words were a revelation to me. I realized I knew nothing whatsoever of such an experience. My own “Me” was very large and very self - assertive, and I couldn’t imagine how it c ould possibly “shrink to nothing.” But a deep conviction came over me that this must be real Christianity — and perhaps the very thing I had been longing for.

Needless to say, I did not attempt any teaching that night. I sat instead as a learner at the feet of these humble Christians, who knew little of book learning but whose souls were clearly taught by the Holy Spirit in depths of spiritual truth I had never touched. I began attending the meeting regularly as a learner, and took every opportunity I could to talk with those who understood this way of life. I found that its essence was exactly what Paul meant when he wrote, “Not I, but Christ”— that the victory I sought would come through ceasing to live my own life and allowing God’s power to “work in me to will and to do His good pleasure.”

In my diary, dated October 18, 1866, I wrote: “The Lord has been teaching me in many ways lately my utter weakness in the face of temptation. I have grown much in knowledge, but not in grace, and I find that I have no more real power over sin than I did when I was first converted. This has not led me to doubt that I am a child of God — justified, forgiven, possessing eternal life, and heir to a heavenly inheritance.

But even with this assurance, I cannot be happy while my heart condemns me. I long for more holiness, more power over sin, more unbroken communion with God. But I do not know how to attain it. Resolutions are useless; my efforts in vain. My prayers go unanswered. A thousand times I have been ready to give up in des pair and conclude that it is not God’s will for me ever to gain victory over sin. And yet the Bible presents such a different picture —‘blameless, harmless, without rebuke’; with every temptation a ‘way of escape’; ‘purified’; ‘conformed to the image of Chr ist’; ‘holy as He is holy.’”

Then I wrote: “I find there are Christians who say that by receiving Christ by faith for our sanctification, just as we received Him by faith for our justification, all this work I long for is accomplished — that is, the method of accomplishing it is discovered. They claim that the Bible teaches that the Lord can deliver from the power of sin as well as from its guilt, and that the soul learns to trust Him to do this, ceasing to rely on its own resolutions or efforts at holiness, and committing the entire work of being kept from evil to the Lord alone.”

And finally: “I am beginning to see more clearly that the Lord is worthy of the most unlimited and boundless confidence; and perhaps this is the first dawning of the light I have been seeking. It is a Methodist doctrine, and I have long been accustomed to hearing Methodists criticized for it, but it seems to be the only thing that meets my need, and I feel compelled to try it.”

On February 11, 1867, I recorded my early efforts to grasp this conquering faith, and wrote: “My soul’s present posture is one of trusting the Lord. And I’ve discovered that this is a practical reality — He actually does deliver. When temptation comes, if I turn to Him at once with the prayer, ‘Lord, save me. I cannot save myself from this sin, but You can and will,’ He never fails.

Either He completely changes my feelings or He makes me forget the whole matter — and the victory, or rather His victory, is complete. This is a secret of the Christian life I never knew before.

But why did I not know it? Why has my path been so halting and miserable when I might have lived in victory? I am a striking example of the inherent legalism and unbelief of the human heart. While trusting the Lord entirely for my justification, I have always trusted myself for my sanctification.

I have relied on my own efforts, resolutions, watchfulness, fervor, and striving to accomplish holy living. This was legalism — just as truly legalism as if I had trusted these things to save my soul in the first place. I was ‘frustrating’ the grace of God as fully in sanctification as those whom I had condemned as legalists were frustrating it in justification. I could easily see how they nullified Christ’s death by their legal efforts, but I was blind to th e fact that I was doing the same thing. Their striving and mine differed in the goal, but in both cases it was self and not Christ. For ‘if righteousness comes by the law, then Christ died in vain.’

But now how different everything is! Now I entrust my daily life to Him just as I entrust my eternal destiny. I trust Him just as nakedly in one as in the other. I am equally powerless in both.

I can do nothing —not even I, the ‘new man’— and if the Lord does not do everything, nothing will be done.

And oh, glorious truth — He does do it! When I trust Him, He gives deliverance from the power of sin as well as from its guilt. I can place everything in His care — my troubles, my temptations, my growth, my service, my daily life, moment by moment. Oh, the rest and calm of living this way!

And this is the Methodist ‘blessing of holiness.’ Expressed by them in terms I do not fully endorse, and surrounded by what seems to me a mixture of error — but still genuinely experienced and enjoyed by them. I am truly grateful for their testimony to its reality. And I now see that it is far better to have the experience — even if mixed with error — than to live without it and be doctrinally correct, as I formerly was.”

My diary from this period is full of the astonishing discoveries I was making, but these extracts are enough. From then on, the possibilities of faith opened before me in ways I had never dreamed. I saw that faith was truly the victory that overcomes the world, and I marveled at my blindness in never having understood it.

Once again, it felt as if a veil had been stripped from the Bible, and it became a new book to me: “The truth that was mine yesterday Is larger truth today; Its face has grown more divine, Its kingship fuller sway.

For truth must grow as ages roll, And God loom larger in the soul.”

One day I was at a meeting where the speaker read John 15, and the words “Without Me you can do nothing” struck me with breathtaking force. I had read and quoted these words hundreds of times — even preached on them. But now they blazed with such meaning that it seemed as though they must have been newly added to the Bible. Here was the Lord saying plainly, “Without Me you can do nothing,” and yet all the while I had been thinking I could— and must — do so much.

What meaning ha d I previously given the word “nothing”? I tried to recall, but there was only a blank. I had never truly noticed it.

Another day I read the passage in Matthew 6 where Jesus tells us to “take no thought for your life,” because our Heavenly Father cares for us — citing the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and reminding us that we are of far greater value. I read the passage repeatedly in utter astonishment. Could it possibly be true? Had it really been in the Bible all these years? If so, how had I never seen it? And yet not only had I seen it — I had memorized it and recited it often. But in the only sense that matters, I had never seen it before.

Now I saw — and at that sight, my cares, worries, fears, and anxieties vanished like mist before the sun.

The same happened with all the familiar Scriptures — they were illuminated with entirely new meaning. Every page proclaimed, as if with a trumpet, the reality of a victorious Christian life lived by faith in Jesus Christ. My whole soul burned with the discovery. I could think and speak of little else. I had found something about the salvation of Christ I had never imagined — something that proved Him a far more complete Savior than I had ever conceived.

I saw that He was not only my Savior for the future but my all-sufficient Savior for the present.

My Captain to fight my battles so I need not fight them myself. My Burden-Bearer so I could roll my burdens off my weak shoulders. My Fortress from my enemies. My Shield, my Guide, my Comforter, my Shepherd. No longer did I need to protect, defend, or fight for myself. Everything was in the hands of One mighty to save — and what else could I do but trust Him?

No words can express the fullness and sufficiency I found stored up in the Lord. I could not keep such glorious news to myself. Everyone who came near me was obliged to hear my story.

One of the first I told was the cousin I had mentioned earlier — the one who had once been puzzled by my teaching that although our sins were forgiven, we must remain lifelong slaves to sin’s power. I seized the earliest opportunity to invite her for a visit, and as soon as she arrived, I exclaimed: “Oh, Carrie, I have something wonderful to tell you. We mustn’t lose a minute!”

As soon as we were alone, I poured out my discovery — that in Christ there is not only forgiveness for sin but deliverance from its power , and that we need no longer live as slaves to sin but may be more than conquerors through Him.

She listened with astonished, perplexed interest, her expression growing more amazed at every sentence. Finally she burst out: “But Hannah, what do you mean? You always told me that even though you were a child of God, you couldn’t expect deliverance from sin or from worry— that the old Adam was too strong and the new nature too weak. When I was converted, I fully expected to be delivered from sin and unrest, but when I asked you about it, you said it was impossible in this life. And I believed you!

And now you say the opposite. It’s terribly confusing—I don’t know what to think!”

I agreed it was confusing, but it had been ignorance, not malice, that had enabled me to teach such a distorted view. Now that I had discovered something far better in the gospel, all we needed to do was abandon the old error and embrace the new truth shown us.

My cousin — who all along had instinctively felt the old view could not possibly represent the best Christ had to offer — embraced the new teaching with eagerness and lived it out far more faithfully than I did.

The practical working of my discovery amazed me. I surrendered my entire rebellious spirit to the Lord and told Him I could not conquer it but believed He could conquer it for me. Then I stepped aside, so to speak, and left the battle to Him. To my indescribable joy, He removed all my rebellion and replaced it with such peaceful acceptance of His will that the life which had seemed so distasteful now appeared pleasant —even desirable. I could say “Thy will be done” with genuine gratitude.

My discovery proved itself a practical success, and I was delighted. I tested it in countless ways — and it never once failed. One instance in particular remains vivid in my mind.

There came a time when I was treated in a way I felt was utterly unfair — unjustifiable then, and still unjustifiable now when I look back on it. I felt deeply wronged and was strongly tempted to retreat into a long, simmering sulk, letting my silence and coldness express the indignation I felt so keenly.

But the moment the temptation came, I saw at once the way of escape. I hurried off to be alone, prac tically running to my bedroom because I was so full of provocation that I couldn’t even walk calmly. I slammed the doors behind me, desperate for privacy to fight the battle out.

Once alone, I knelt down and prayed: “Lord, I am provoked. I want to be provo ked. And honestly, I think I have good reason.

But I know I shouldn’t give in to this, and I want victory. I give this whole matter to You. I cannot fight this battle —You must fight it for me. Jesus saves me now.”

I said those words while my heart still felt completely rebellious. Outwardly, it probably looked as though I was declaring a lie. I didn’t feel saved from my anger, and it didn’t seem at all likely that I could be. But by faith I clung to the truth, insisting — even in the midst of turmoil — that the Lord could and did save me now.

And then it happened.

Instantly, a calm as bright as a summer morning settled over me. All my resentment vanished.

My anger dissolved. I felt as carefree and joyful as a bird in the sunshine, delighting in the very situation that only moments before had enraged me. My faith had seized hold of a divine reality: God was able to deliver, and He did deliver the soul that trusted Him.

I realized what a remarkable truth it was that I did not need to fight my own battles at all. The Lord would fight for me, and I could simply be still. Since that day, hundreds of such battles have been fought — and won — for me by the Captain of my Salvation. The secret I learned then, of placing the battle entirely in His hands and stepping aside to let Him fight, has never once failed when I have practiced it. It has proven again and again to be a living demonstration of Christ’s words: “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world.”

He has overcome it — not we — and He always will, if only we will surrender the matter into His hands.

Never once, when I have done this, have I been disappointed. It is gloriously true — though so few seem to realize it — that He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him , because He lives forever to intercede for them. He was able when the Epistle to the Hebrews was written, and He is just as able now, for He is not dead — He still lives to intercede for us.

I had discovered that faith is the governing law of the universe . God spoke, and it was done; and when we rely on Him, we too may speak, and it shall be done. fields.body_text: This unrest and questioning came to a head in 1865. Because of family circumstances, we had to leave our delightful home in Germantown — along with all our wide circle of interests — and move to a remote village in New Jersey, where we were almost completely cut off from any congenial society. Financially, it was an advantage, but in every other respect it was a tremendous trial, especially for me. I confess that my spirit rebelled bitterly against the change. Little did I imagine that in this very place, which felt so desolate and isolated, a glorious new light would dawn, ushering in the fourth and crowning epoch of my spiritual life. It happened this way. As I’ve said, I was deeply rebellious about the move. Yet I had enough spiritual insight to know that this rebellion was wrong. Since the move was clearly a providential arrangement beyond my control, the only right response was to accept it cheerfully and genuinely say, “Thy will be done.” But although I scolded myself constantly, I couldn’t bring myself to accept God’s will—and in truth, I didn’t want to acc ept it. I felt it was harsh treatment to be forced to leave my happy Germantown home and my sphere of usefulness to live in such a lonely, remote place as Millville. It seemed to me that God ought not to have allowed it, and that I had every right to grumble and fret. As a result, I fell into a deeply uncomfortable state of mind. Even my clear doctrines could no longer help me, and I began to fear that I was going to lose whatever spirituality I had left. In the face of a need so real, it was no comfort to know I was forgiven. I wanted more than forgiveness — I wanted deliverance. But I had no idea how to obtain it. Because we frequently had Mission preachers visit us, I explained my case to several of them and asked for help, but no one could tell me anything useful. At last, a very successful religious teacher came for a few days, and to him I poured out my trouble fully, begging him to suggest some path to deliverance. He considered my situation seriously and finally said he believed what I needed was to engage in some Christian work. If I would go out the next morning to visit the poor in our neighborhood and see how I could help them, he thought my spiritual life would be renewed and everything would come right. So the next day, I tried his suggested remedy. But I quickly discovered how futile it was. Almost in the first house I entered I found a woman struggling with the very same spiritual difficulty as my own, and she desperately needed help — and I had none to give. I felt like someone trying to feed the hungry out of an empty bowl. It was a silly and impossible task. I returned home more discouraged than ever, convinced that before I could help anyone else, I would have to find deliverance for myself. There was a local dressmaker who often came to sew for me, and since I had so little companionship in the village, I would sometimes sit and talk with her while we worked. She seemed unusually spiritually minded, and I was fascinated by her experiences. I discovered that she believed in an actual victory over temptation — that it was not necessary, as I had thought, to go through life sinning and repenting, sinning and repenting, but that a Christian could truly be delivered. She told me that among the Methodists there was a doctrine called “Holiness,” and an acc ompanying experience called “sanctification,” or “the second blessing,” which brought people into a place of victory. I was intensely interested in everything she said, and began to hope that perhaps here might be the solution to my struggles. She also told me that a small meeting was held in the village on Saturday evenings where this doctrine was taught and where people shared their experiences. She urged me to attend. I thought I might go someday, but allowed other things to interfere. I was convinced that poor, uneducated factory workers could not possibly have anything to teach me. I had studied and taught the Bible extensively and had a high opinion of my own religious attainments. I felt that if I did go to the meeting, I would likely have far more to teach them than they would have to teach me. Eventually, however, one evening I decided to grant them the favor of my presence — and I confess, I did feel it was a great favor. I went to the meeting full of my own importance and superiority, expecting to astonish them with my biblical knowledge. When I entered, a factory woman with a shawl over her head —she likely didn’t own a bonnet— was speaking. I heard her say: “My whole horizon used to be filled with this great big Me of mine, but when I got a glimpse of Christ as my perfect Savior, that great big Me shriveled down to nothing.” Those words were a revelation to me. I realized I knew nothing whatsoever of such an experience. My own “Me” was very large and very self - assertive, and I couldn’t imagine how it c ould possibly “shrink to nothing.” But a deep conviction came over me that this must be real Christianity — and perhaps the very thing I had been longing for. Needless to say, I did not attempt any teaching that night. I sat instead as a learner at the feet of these humble Christians, who knew little of book learning but whose souls were clearly taught by the Holy Spirit in depths of spiritual truth I had never touched. I began attending the meeting regularly as a learner, and took every opportunity I could to talk with those who understood this way of life. I found that its essence was exactly what Paul meant when he wrote, “Not I, but Christ”— that the victory I sought would come through ceasing to live my own life and allowing God’s power to “work in me to will and to do His good pleasure.” In my diary, dated October 18, 1866, I wrote: “The Lord has been teaching me in many ways lately my utter weakness in the face of temptation. I have grown much in knowledge, but not in grace, and I find that I have no more real power over sin than I did when I was first converted. This has not led me to doubt that I am a child of God — justified, forgiven, possessing eternal life, and heir to a heavenly inheritance. But even with this assurance, I cannot be happy while my heart condemns me. I long for more holiness, more power over sin, more unbroken communion with God. But I do not know how to attain it. Resolutions are useless; my efforts in vain. My prayers go unanswered. A thousand times I have been ready to give up in des pair and conclude that it is not God’s will for me ever to gain victory over sin. And yet the Bible presents such a different picture —‘blameless, harmless, without rebuke’; with every temptation a ‘way of escape’; ‘purified’; ‘conformed to the image of Chr ist’; ‘holy as He is holy.’” Then I wrote: “I find there are Christians who say that by receiving Christ by faith for our sanctification, just as we received Him by faith for our justification, all this work I long for is accomplished — that is, the method of accomplishing it is discovered. They claim that the Bible teaches that the Lord can deliver from the power of sin as well as from its guilt, and that the soul learns to trust Him to do this, ceasing to rely on its own resolutions or efforts at holiness, and committing the entire work of being kept from evil to the Lord alone.” And finally: “I am beginning to see more clearly that the Lord is worthy of the most unlimited and boundless confidence; and perhaps this is the first dawning of the light I have been seeking. It is a Methodist doctrine, and I have long been accustomed to hearing Methodists criticized for it, but it seems to be the only thing that meets my need, and I feel compelled to try it.” On February 11, 1867, I recorded my early efforts to grasp this conquering faith, and wrote: “My soul’s present posture is one of trusting the Lord. And I’ve discovered that this is a practical reality — He actually does deliver. When temptation comes, if I turn to Him at once with the prayer, ‘Lord, save me. I cannot save myself from this sin, but You can and will,’ He never fails. Either He completely changes my feelings or He makes me forget the whole matter — and the victory, or rather His victory, is complete. This is a secret of the Christian life I never knew before. But why did I not know it? Why has my path been so halting and miserable when I might have lived in victory? I am a striking example of the inherent legalism and unbelief of the human heart. While trusting the Lord entirely for my justification, I have always trusted myself for my sanctification. I have relied on my own efforts, resolutions, watchfulness, fervor, and striving to accomplish holy living. This was legalism — just as truly legalism as if I had trusted these things to save my soul in the first place. I was ‘frustrating’ the grace of God as fully in sanctification as those whom I had condemned as legalists were frustrating it in justification. I could easily see how they nullified Christ’s death by their legal efforts, but I was blind to th e fact that I was doing the same thing. Their striving and mine differed in the goal, but in both cases it was self and not Christ. For ‘if righteousness comes by the law, then Christ died in vain.’ But now how different everything is! Now I entrust my daily life to Him just as I entrust my eternal destiny. I trust Him just as nakedly in one as in the other. I am equally powerless in both. I can do nothing —not even I, the ‘new man’— and if the Lord does not do everything, nothing will be done. And oh, glorious truth — He does do it! When I trust Him, He gives deliverance from the power of sin as well as from its guilt. I can place everything in His care — my troubles, my temptations, my growth, my service, my daily life, moment by moment. Oh, the rest and calm of living this way! And this is the Methodist ‘blessing of holiness.’ Expressed by them in terms I do not fully endorse, and surrounded by what seems to me a mixture of error — but still genuinely experienced and enjoyed by them. I am truly grateful for their testimony to its reality. And I now see that it is far better to have the experience — even if mixed with error — than to live without it and be doctrinally correct, as I formerly was.” My diary from this period is full of the astonishing discoveries I was making, but these extracts are enough. From then on, the possibilities of faith opened before me in ways I had never dreamed. I saw that faith was truly the victory that overcomes the world, and I marveled at my blindness in never having understood it. Once again, it felt as if a veil had been stripped from the Bible, and it became a new book to me: “The truth that was mine yesterday Is larger truth today; Its face has grown more divine, Its kingship fuller sway. For truth must grow as ages roll, And God loom larger in the soul.” One day I was at a meeting where the speaker read John 15, and the words “Without Me you can do nothing” struck me with breathtaking force. I had read and quoted these words hundreds of times — even preached on them. But now they blazed with such meaning that it seemed as though they must have been newly added to the Bible. Here was the Lord saying plainly, “Without Me you can do nothing,” and yet all the while I had been thinking I could— and must — do so much. What meaning ha d I previously given the word “nothing”? I tried to recall, but there was only a blank. I had never truly noticed it. Another day I read the passage in Matthew 6 where Jesus tells us to “take no thought for your life,” because our Heavenly Father cares for us — citing the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and reminding us that we are of far greater value. I read the passage repeatedly in utter astonishment. Could it possibly be true? Had it really been in the Bible all these years? If so, how had I never seen it? And yet not only had I seen it — I had memorized it and recited it often. But in the only sense that matters, I had never seen it before. Now I saw — and at that sight, my cares, worries, fears, and anxieties vanished like mist before the sun. The same happened with all the familiar Scriptures — they were illuminated with entirely new meaning. Every page proclaimed, as if with a trumpet, the reality of a victorious Christian life lived by faith in Jesus Christ. My whole soul burned with the discovery. I could think and speak of little else. I had found something about the salvation of Christ I had never imagined — something that proved Him a far more complete Savior than I had ever conceived. I saw that He was not only my Savior for the future but my all-sufficient Savior for the present. My Captain to fight my battles so I need not fight them myself. My Burden-Bearer so I could roll my burdens off my weak shoulders. My Fortress from my enemies. My Shield, my Guide, my Comforter, my Shepherd. No longer did I need to protect, defend, or fight for myself. Everything was in the hands of One mighty to save — and what else could I do but trust Him? No words can express the fullness and sufficiency I found stored up in the Lord. I could not keep such glorious news to myself. Everyone who came near me was obliged to hear my story. One of the first I told was the cousin I had mentioned earlier — the one who had once been puzzled by my teaching that although our sins were forgiven, we must remain lifelong slaves to sin’s power. I seized the earliest opportunity to invite her for a visit, and as soon as she arrived, I exclaimed: “Oh, Carrie, I have something wonderful to tell you. We mustn’t lose a minute!” As soon as we were alone, I poured out my discovery — that in Christ there is not only forgiveness for sin but deliverance from its power , and that we need no longer live as slaves to sin but may be more than conquerors through Him. She listened with astonished, perplexed interest, her expression growing more amazed at every sentence. Finally she burst out: “But Hannah, what do you mean? You always told me that even though you were a child of God, you couldn’t expect deliverance from sin or from worry— that the old Adam was too strong and the new nature too weak. When I was converted, I fully expected to be delivered from sin and unrest, but when I asked you about it, you said it was impossible in this life. And I believed you! And now you say the opposite. It’s terribly confusing—I don’t know what to think!” I agreed it was confusing, but it had been ignorance, not malice, that had enabled me to teach such a distorted view. Now that I had discovered something far better in the gospel, all we needed to do was abandon the old error and embrace the new truth shown us. My cousin — who all along had instinctively felt the old view could not possibly represent the best Christ had to offer — embraced the new teaching with eagerness and lived it out far more faithfully than I did. The practical working of my discovery amazed me. I surrendered my entire rebellious spirit to the Lord and told Him I could not conquer it but believed He could conquer it for me. Then I stepped aside, so to speak, and left the battle to Him. To my indescribable joy, He removed all my rebellion and replaced it with such peaceful acceptance of His will that the life which had seemed so distasteful now appeared pleasant —even desirable. I could say “Thy will be done” with genuine gratitude. My discovery proved itself a practical success, and I was delighted. I tested it in countless ways — and it never once failed. I felt deeply wronged and was strongly tempted to retreat into a long, simmering sulk, letting my silence and coldness express the indignation I felt so keenly. But the moment the temptation came, I saw at once the way of escape. I slammed the doors behind me, desperate for privacy to fight the battle out. Once alone, I knelt down and prayed: “Lord, I am provoked. I want to be provo ked. And honestly, I think I have good reason. But I know I shouldn’t give in to this, and I want victory. I give this whole matter to You. I cannot fight this battle —You must fight it for me. Jesus saves me now.” I said those words while my heart still felt completely rebellious. Outwardly, it probably looked as though I was declaring a lie. I didn’t feel saved from my anger, and it didn’t seem at all likely that I could be. Instantly, a calm as bright as a summer morning settled over me. All my resentment vanished. My anger dissolved. I felt as carefree and joyful as a bird in the sunshine, delighting in the very situation that only moments before had enraged me. My faith had seized hold of a divine reality: God was able to deliver, and He did deliver the soul that trusted Him. I realized what a remarkable truth it was that I did not need to fight my own battles at all. The Lord would fight for me, and I could simply be still. Since that day, hundreds of such battles have been fought — and won — for me by the Captain of my Salvation. It has proven again and again to be a living demonstration of Christ’s words: “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world.” He has overcome it — not we — and He always will, if only we will surrender the matter into His hands. Never once, when I have done this, have I been disappointed. fields.title: A Discovery, Not An Attainment
fields.body_html:
Again I want once more to make this absolutely clear: what came to me was a discovery , not an attainment . I did not suddenly become a better woman. I simply realized that Christ was a far better Savior than I had ever imagined. I was no more capable of conquering my temptations than before — but I had discovered that He was able, and that He was willing, to conquer them for me. I had no more wisdom or righteousness of my own, but I had finally learned that He could truly become for me — just as the Apostle declared — wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption .

I will never forget the first time I discovered that this was not merely a beautiful saying, but an actual, practical fact.

Not long after I first began to grasp the fullness of Christ’s salvation, I learned that someone particularly antagonistic toward me was coming to stay at our house for two weeks. She had always been provoking and difficult. As the time drew near, I felt certain that if I were to treat her in a Christlike manner, I would need far more patience than I normally possessed.

Still being new in the life of faith, I assumed the only way to obtain enough patience was to wrestle for it in prayer . My days were too busy, so I decided to devote an entire night to this spiritual struggle. After the family went to bed, I shut myself in my room, brought along a plate of biscuits in case I grew hungry, and knelt by my bed prepared for an all-night battle. I felt almost heroic, for long hours in prayer had always exhausted me; but since I desperately needed a storehouse of patience, I thought this was the only way to secure it. I expected something like a large “lump” of patience to be deposited into my heart— a reserve from which I could break off pieces whenever needed.

But no sooner had my knees touched the floor than the familiar Scripture flashed into my mind: “But of Him are ye in Christ Jesus , who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption… that he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”

“Yes!” I cried inwardly. “And that must surely include patience as well!”

Immediately I rose from my knees with absolute confidence that I did not need to acquire a stockpile of patience ahead of time. Instead, I could simply look to the Lord for a present supply whenever the need arose. I saw Christ as a vast, inexhaustible storehouse, always open, always full — offering exactly the grace required at exactly the moment it was required. And suddenly it seemed absurd for me to carry about packages of grace in my spiritual pockets, which — even if I could gather them — would be misplaced the very moment I needed them most.

Naturally, that faith was fully answered. My visitor proved even more aggravating than usual, yet patience came to me moment by moment — always exactly enough for the moment at hand.

Even more wonderful than the patience itself was the discovery I had made: the storehouse of God’s grace is always open , and His supplies are always available to His children.

Some people might call my patience an “attainment.” But I had not attained anything. I had simply discovered God’s supply and taken hold of it by faith, hour by hour, as each hour required.

When reduced to its simplest form, my discovery was this: In Christ there is a perfect supply for every need, and faith alone is the channel through which that supply flows. Struggling cannot bring it. Wrestling cannot bring it. Worrying and agonizing cannot bring it. Faith always will. Faith always does.

It seems such a simple realization — one would think that any believer who reads the Bible would immediately know it. But I did not know it, not even after nine years of careful study and earnest striving. And when at last I discovered it, it revolutionized my life.

There was nothing mysterious about it. It wasn’t something added to the gospel— it was the true meaning of the gospel. Christ came, according to Scripture, to accomplish certain things; my discovery was simply that He could actually be depended on to accomplish them . And if that is true, then surely those who desire these things accomplished should hand them over to the One who has undertaken the work.

To me, this seemed — and still seems — not some extraordinary spiritual attainment, but simple, practical common sense . When I hire a builder to construct a house, it is because he knows how to build and I do not. I don’t consider handing the job to him to be some great “attainment” on my part — it is merely sensible. If I come to a roaring river and find a bridge, I do not consider crossing it an accomplishment — I merely take advantage of what has been provided.

For this reason, I much prefer the word gifts to attainments . Attainments imply my own work and effort; but Christian graces are free gifts from God. Those who “reign in life” are not those who rise to great heights by their own efforts, but those who receive abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness. If God did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, how shall He not with Him freely give us all things?

To discover that all things are truly ours is not an attainment — it is a magnificent discovery. And any soul that discovers such riches would be profoundly lacking in common sense not to take possession of whatever it needs.

No angel could fully describe what this discovery meant to me. But it is enough to say that life was transformed. Where defeat and failure once ruled, victory and triumph became my daily and hourly experience — whenever I chose to take hold of them by faith. I was no longer a slave to sin, forced to obey it even when I hated it, but had entered into the liberty Christ gives, no longer bound by the old chains.

I had thought myself happy before, but now my joy was beyond words. At times it seemed to me that even Heaven itself could scarcely offer more. Yet this joy was not rooted in myself, nor in any achievement of my own — for I had none. It was joy in the Lord.

I understood, at last, t he prophet’s words: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories, glory in this: that he understands and knows Me.”

I had no wisdom, no strength, no riches in myself — but I was learning to know the Lord, and in Him I could glory with all my heart.

“Where, then, is boasting?” asks the Apostle.

“It is excluded… by the law of faith.”

A soul that has no attainments cannot boast in itself; and a soul that receives everything freely from the Lord cannot help but boast in Him.

“For by grace you are saved through faith… not of yourselves… not of works, lest any man should boast.”

“They did not gain the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them; but Your right hand, O Lord, and the light of Your countenance.”

This was my experience. And with all my heart I could echo the Psalmist: “In God we boast all day long, and praise His Name forever.”
