I understood, at last, t he prophet’s words: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories, glory in this: that he understands and knows Me.” I had no wisdom, no strength, no riches in myself — but I was learning to know the Lord, and in Him I could glory with all my heart. “Where, then, is boasting?” asks the Apostle. “It is excluded… by the law of faith.” A soul that has no attainments cannot boast in itself; and a soul that receives everything freely from the Lord cannot help but boast in Him. “For by grace you are saved through faith… not of yourselves… not of works, lest any man should boast.” “They did not gain the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them; but Your right hand, O Lord, and the light of Your countenance.” This was my experience. And with all my heart I could echo the Psalmist: “In God we boast all day long, and praise His Name forever.”

fields.title: The Secret Of A Happy Life
fields.body_html:
This new spiritual life I had entered had been given many different names. The Methodists called it “the Second Blessing” or “the Blessing of Sanctification.” The Presbyteri ans preferred “the Higher Life” or “the Life of Faith.” The Friends spoke of it as “the life hidden with Christ in God.” Whatever the terminology, the truth behind each phrase was exactly the same, and it could be reduced to four simple words: “Not I, but Christ.”

In every case, the heart of the matter was surrender — turning ourselves over to the Lord so that He might work within us, shaping both our desires and our actions according to His will. It meant taking Him at His word: trusting Him not only to save us from sin’s punishment but also from sin’s power, and believing His promise to give us grace and help in every moment of need.

Personally, I prefer to call this simply “the life of faith,” because that is the plainest description.

But in the book where I explained it most fully, I called it The Secret of a Happy Life , because for so long it truly had been a secret to me — and because I fear it is still a secret to hundreds of God’s children who are staggering under the same heavy burdens I once carried. It was not a secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it. It has always been an open secret — spread clearly across the pages of Scripture — if only I had possessed the spiritual perception to see it.

“The secrets of the gods are from of old, Guarded forever, and forever told; Blabbed in all ears, but published in a tongue Whose purport the gods only can unfold.”

An ox and a philosopher may look at the same field, yet see entirely different things. In the same way, before and after this glorious discovery, I looked at the same Bible and even read the same verses — but I saw them with entirely different eyes. Scripture, like nature, lies open to all, but not all truly see it. The law of gravitation operated plainly before humankind for ages, but only Newton recognized it. Likewise, the law of faith had been written plainly in the Bible, though I had failed to discern it. The forces we harness in nature were not created by us, only discovered; they existed just as truly before discovery as afterward. And I am certain that no scientific discoverer ever felt gre ater delight in uncovering nature’s secrets than I felt when I uncovered the “secrets of God.”

My joy was so great that I felt compelled to speak of it to everyone — to insist upon their listening. At first, my husband — an earnest and successful Christian worker — was somewhat alarmed. He feared I might be rejoicing in some error that would harm me and perhaps others.

He frequently returned to the argument that the “old man” within us could never be completely conquered in this life, and must always hold us in some degree of bondage.

One morning, as we were discussing this, I said, “Well, impossible or not, the Bible certainly says it. What does thee make of this passage in Romans 6: ‘Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.’ What else can that mean but that sin’s power is truly to be conquered, so that we need no longer serve it?”

Startled by the sudden light that seemed to flash from those words, he said, “There is no such passage in the Bible.”

“Oh yes, there is,” I replied. I opened my Bible and showed it to him. It was a verse he had, of course, known for years, yet in that moment it appeared to him with such a new and striking meaning that he felt as if he had never seen it before. It brought with it a deep conviction, and from that moment he did not rest until he had discovered the truth for himself.

His own account of this discovery, published in 1868, was as follows. After describing the lack he had been feeling in his Christian life, he continued: “I knew that the Bible seemed to promise a better life for the Christian than the one I knew, and for years the conviction had grown in me that there was some part of God’s truth that I had yet to discover. I felt that something essential was missing in the way I understood Scripture — something that would supply that spirit of love which the Bible declares is greater than all knowledge and all faith. I had often expressed my growing sense that some truth was waiting to bre ak forth from God’s Word— something that would fill our hearts with a love that could bear all things. My feeling was so strong that I arranged a meeting with several brethren well-versed in Scripture so that we might examine, carefully and in detail, what part of God’s Word we had failed to understand and to teach.

Circumstances delayed that meeting, but in the meantime — through a completely unexpected channel — I received the secret that taught me the joy of Christian liberty and the power of true service. That secret was faith . How strange that I, who had constantly taught faith as the channel for the forgiveness of sins, had failed to see that faith alone is also the means of deliverance from the inward power of sin. Not only the sinner, but the Christian also, must receive everything by faith.

“At this time, I met some Christians whose inner life, as they described it, seemed utterly different from mine. They declared that practical sanctification was obtained, just like justification, by simple faith; that it could be realized at any moment when one’s faith could fully grasp it; and they insisted that they themselves had experienced it. The subject continued to confront me, and again and again passages of Scripture were presented to me — passages to which I sincerely believed myself completely submissive. Yet I regarded the entire matter with profound unease, for it seemed to me that what they sought and claimed to possess was nothing less than perfection in the flesh —and that, I knew, was impossible.”

I can hardly describe the depth of prejudice I felt against this teaching. Few ideas had ever stirred such instinctive resistance in me, and I spent many anxious hours worrying over what I believed were the dangerous consequences of this “heresy” creeping in among us. My opposition was so determined that even familiar passages of Scripture — texts I had known for years — seemed strange and almost unrecognizable when someone quoted them to prove that sanctification was by faith, and that it was possible to “walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing.”

One morning, Romans 6:6 was read to me: “Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” My friend added, “Surely these words must m ean something — and something that makes it possible for a believer to cease being a slave to sin.”

I was so startled by the force of the verse that I blurted out emphatically, “That passage is not in the Bible!”— even though, in truth, it was one of the most familiar passages in all of Scripture to me. When I was forced to admit that it really was there, I took refuge in the explanation that it was merely judicial truth: something true “in God’s sight,” but never actually true in a Christian’s experience.

But from that moment, I began to wonder whether there might be some truth in what these people were teaching. Slowly it dawned on me that I had misunderstood them. They were not talking about perfection in the flesh, but about the death of the flesh — and a life hidden in Christ.

A life of abiding in Him, walking in Him, living through His power — a life of victory and joy that was truly pleasing to God.

“So that is all you mean?” I asked once, when this truth had been pressed upon me with unusual force. “That is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“But have you lived it?” came the reply.

“Yes,” I answered, “I have lived so at times. Often I have given myself wholly into the Lord’s care and realized that I was dead, and that He alone lived in me.”

“You have kno wn this as an occasional experience,” my friend said gently. “But have you ever known it as a life ? You say you sometimes take refuge in the Lord — but have you ever made your home in Him?”

I saw at once that I had not. My faith in this matter had been intermittent. In moments of unusual difficulty, or whenever I felt especially weak, I had turned exclusively to the Lord and had always found Him sufficient for my need. But that this occasional experience might become — and ought to become — the experience of my whole life had never occurred to me.

“What would you think,” my friend continued, “of people who trusted Christ in such an intermittent way for the salvation of their souls? Suppose one week they felt powerless and cast themselves entirely on Him, only to spend the next week trying to earn salvation partly themselves, merely asking Him to make up what they lacked. Would you not think such a course inconsistent and foolish? And yet is it not just as inconsistent — and just as dishonoring to Christ — to trust Him in this on-again, off-again way for your daily life? Sometimes walking by faith, sometimes relying on your own strength?”

I could not deny the truth of this, and the possibility — and beauty — of a life of continuous faith began to open before me.

Such was my husband’s account of his discovery. To my great joy, from that time forward we were entirely united in the matter. It was not that either of us believed we had become sinless, or that we never failed again. Rather, we had discovered the secret of victory — that we were no longer slaves to sin, compelled to yield to its power, but could, if we chose, become “more than conquerors through Him who loved us.”

This did not mean temptations ever ceased. But we had learned that the Lord is both able and willing to deliver us out of every temptation — if only we would trust Him. We saw that our old belief —that we were doomed to be lifelong “servants of sin”— was contrary to Scripture and a slander upon the completeness of Christ’s salvation, for He died precisely to free us from sin’s bondage. “For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under grace.”

We learned further that faith — faith alone — was the road to victory, and that effort and self- struggle accomplished nothing in this battle. Our part was surrender and trust; God’s part was everything else.

For the third time, as I have said, a veil seemed to lift from the pages of Scripture, and everywhere we saw the “secret of victory” shining in letters of light. Old texts blossomed with new fullness. Take, for instance: “For whatsoever is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he that believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Formerly we thought this referred only to a future victory, after death. Now we saw it spoke of a present victory, by a present faith, while still living in the world.

Or this: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” We had always taken it to mean the rem oval of sin’s penalty . Now we saw it meant the removal of its power — that we need no longer serve it or be enslaved by it.

I could give countless examples of this unveiling of Scripture, but these must suffice. We had made a transforming discovery, and it filled our every thought. Whenever I met a friend, my first question was, “How much time do you have? I have something wonderful to tell you.” And I would pour out my story of the great salvation I had discovered.

To most, it was as new and delightful as it had been to me, and many immediately embraced it as an experiential reality. But one friend — the same who had awakened me to religious things at sixteen, and who had been my closest spiritual confidante ever since — listened and then said, “But Hannah, that is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“Then why,” I cried indignantly, “did you never tell me? You knew how I have struggled all these years — winning a few battles, losing far more — and all the while you had this secret of victory and never told me! How could you be so unkind?”

“But I thought everyone knew it,” she said. “It is what the Quakers have always taught. Their preaching is almost entirely about it.”

“Well,” I said, “everyone does not know it. Very few know it. Most Christians believe they must remain ‘servants of sin’ all their lives because of the weakness of the flesh. And most think that if they are ever to gain victory, they must fight for it themselves, and only if defeat seems imminent may they call the Lord to help. They do not understand that the battle is to be handed over to Him from the beginning — just as the Israelites stood still at the Red Sea and saw the salvation of the Lord.”

“And,” I added with conviction, “I intend to tell this to everyone I can.”

And I did. Young or old, whether mature Christians or beginners — no one escaped hearing the story if I dared speak. Nearly all who heard it embraced it and began to live in its power.

One of them was my little daughter, about seven or eight years old. She had begun to develop a strong willfulness that I found almost impossible to manage. She herself recognized it as wrong and tried hard to conquer it, but she seemed almost possessed by it. One day she came to me, puzzled, and said, “Mother, why am I so naughty? I know I’m a little C hristian girl, and I thought Christian children were always good. But no matter how hard I try to make myself good, I just can’t help being naughty.”

From my own experience, I understood her perfectly. I said, “I think, darling, the reason is that you are trying to make yourself good. We never can make ourselves good, try as we may. Only our Heavenly Father can do that. Whenever you feel tempted to be naughty, tell Him all about it, ask Him to make you good, and then trust Him to do it. He will surely take the naughtiness away.”

She thought a moment and said, “Oh, I didn’t know that. I thought you had to use your will and just do it yourself.”

She walked away quietly, clearly considering this new idea. Soon I noticed a great change. Her willfulness seemed entirely gone; she was gentle and obedient as a lamb. I said nothing, wanting to respect the delicacy of the moment. A few days later, I heard her playing softly with her dolls and murmuring with quiet delight, “Oh, I am so glad Heavenly Father is making me so good. It feels so nice to be good.”

Still I said nothing. But a few nights afterward, as I tucked her into bed, she burst out, “Oh, Mother, aren’t you glad Heavenly Father is making me so good? He’s going to make me a great deal gooder, but aren’t you glad He has made me as good as I am now?”

As I hugged and kissed her, rejoicing with her, she added earnestly, “Mother, do you tell everybody about this?”

I said I tried to, but she insisted, “You mustn’t only try— you must really do it every time you preach. I think lots of people are like I was — wanting to be good but not knowing how. You must tell every single person you meet.”

I have always taken that as a kind of divine call to my work.

In truth, our hearts were so full that we hardly needed encouragement. Everyone we knew heard the story eventually, and soon a great stir arose — not only in our own community, but throughout the American church and even in England. Letters poured in from all directions asking what this “new doctrine taught by the Pearsall Smiths of Millville, New Jersey” might be. Meetings and conferences sprang up that continue even to this day, many known as “meetings for the deepening of the spiritual life.”

This discovery was the beginning of a great revival in the spiritual life of the Church everywhere. It reached its height in the meetings of 1873 and 1874 on the Continent, and later at Oxford and Brighton, where thousands came to hear the message. Its effects are still felt in countless lives. Wherever I go, people tell me their whole lives were changed by what they learned there.

It was not a new religion they discovered, but the vitality of the old one. Truths they had long professed became living realities. They had called Christ their Savior; now they learned that He truly saves , and trusting Him, they found Him faithful.

There was nothing sectarian in the teaching. No one had to change creed or denomination.

Across all churches — Methodist, Quaker, Catholic, and more — there have always been those who truly understood and lived the life of faith. It lies, I believe, at the heart of every Christian creed. All that is needed is for believers to stop merely professing their faith and begin actually believing it — and they will always find it true.

The life of faith fits every creed and every denomination. The story is the same everywhere.

fields.title: The Life Of Faith Quaker Doctrine
fields.body_html:
Among those especially interested in these new spiritual discoveries were the Friends. As I mentioned in the last chapter, one of them — after hearing my story — expressed surprise that any of it was new to me. She insisted it was exactly what the Quakers had always taught.

Her comment suddenly cast a new light on Quakerism, one I had never imagined.

My mother said something similar after he aring me speak one day. “But Hannah,” she asked, “why do you call this doctrine new? You’re only preaching what the old Friends always preached.”

“Yes,” I replied, “I’m beginning to see that. But they have never preached it in a way that ordinary people could grasp. Unless one already knew the secret, their words could hardly give it. Certainly I never understood it, though I listened to their preaching all my life. For my part,” I added, “I am determined to speak plainly enough that no one can fail to understand.”

But I eventually concluded that my mother and my friend were right: what we had discovered really was genuine Quaker doctrine. With my eyes newly opened, I reread their writings and listened again to their sermons. I realized that the heart of true Quakerism is this “life hid with Christ in God,” and that their central teaching was that Christ is a present and complete Savior — One who keeps His people’s feet, as He promised, and makes them more than conquerors through His strength.

I saw that a life of absolute consecration, full obedience, and simple trust was the life they had always urged upon us. I had not understood them before because they were preaching about the building of the Christian life, while I was still searching for the foundations of that life.

Alexander Knox says that the Christian faith has “foundation truths” and “superstructure truths,” both necessary to form a complete whole. The foundation and the building are different, yet perfectly harmonious. Foundation truths introduce us to the Christian life; superstructure truths teach us how to live once we are in it. Without superstructure, the foundation remains bare and unfinished; without foundations, the superstructure is unstable.

The early Friends were, from the beginning, a society devoted to building the superstructure.

Their message was directed chiefly to Christians. Their early history shows that most of them had already been serious believers within the denominations of their day, yet had not found there what fully satisfied their spiritual hunger.

One writer describes them this way: for years they had sought the Lord with deep longing, trying every teacher, every practice, every form of devotion, yet still craving something more. They wanted the inward presence and power of the Spirit — something beyond what they could gather merely from Scripture’s letter. They longed for life, for communion with Christ, for an entrance into His kingdom and His reign within. When the light of the Spirit finally broke upon them, it came with such joy and power that they never forgot it — a sense of life poured into their hearts, drawing them into divine rest and setting them apart for God’s service.

My own dear father, a genuine and wonderfully delightful Friend, lived this early Quaker experience. We had long known that he lived a life of steady trust and simple obedience. But in our more evangelical days, we thought him unclear on doctrines such as justification by faith or the believer’s legal standing before God. We often tease d him that although he was certainly good, he was also rather “unsound.”

After discovering the life of faith for ourselves, however, we became convinced that this was the secret of his steadiness. At the first opportunity I asked him, “Now, Father, isn’t t his the secret of your life and the source of your strength? Haven’t you always lived this way?”

I will never forget his answer.

“Why, of course it is, daughter,” he said with a joyful triumph in his voice. “I know no other way to live. And I certainly know what it is, when the enemy comes in like a flood, for the Lord to raise His standard against him and drive him off.”

It now seems clear to me that Friends were meant to be workers on the interior life — not primarily to convert sinners, but to lead believers into a deeper walk with God and a life of abiding trust. Yet in recent days it seems to me they have drifted from this calling, striving more to do foundational work than to build the superstructure. Their traditions and methods, suited for the latter, are less suited for the former. The results, unsurprisingly, do not compare with denominations whose chief aim has long been the foundation work of evangelism.

A thoughtful Friend recently said to me that they were meant to be a strong mystical society, but feared they were becoming a weak evangelical one. I could not deny the truth in his words.

If only the Friends would again proclaim with the old clarity and power that glorious message of a full and present salvation in Christ — available here and now — the blessing to thousands of hungry souls would be immeasurable.

One of their early preachers once said: “I bring you good news. Not that the day of your redemption is near, but that it has already come. Many are already blessing God that they are redeemed and delivered from corruption’s bondage, and have more joy in His service than they ever had in the world’s. Oh, the conquering faith, the overcoming life and power of the Spirit!

We cannot help but speak of these things, and exalt the perfect gift and power of Him who not only can complete His work in the heart, but delights to do so — yes, even to tread down Satan under the feet of those who trust Him.”

No matter how vague Quaker preaching had become in my time, the early Friends spoke plainly enough. Small wo nder their message spread so widely. And if today’s Friends were to sound that same clear trumpet again, I believe multitudes would respond — for the children of God are as hungry now as ever to know the fullness of Christ’s salvation.

fields.title: Holiness Camp Meetings
fields.body_html:
As may be imagined, we eagerly seized every opportunity to learn more about the truths we had discovered. And though the Friends did indeed teach them, it was among the Methodists that we found the clearest light. The Methodists spoke with great certainty: they taught that the Christian life involved two distinct experiences — the first, justification; the second, sanctification. They urged believers not to rest content with justification (that is, forgiveness), but to press on to sanctification, the “second blessing,” as they called it. I would not now express the truth in quite that way, but at the time it was profoundly helpful.

Not all Methodists embraced this teaching; many considered it too extreme. Those who did were known as “Holiness Methodists,” and it was from them that we received the greatest help. They held special “Holiness Meetings” devoted to the subject, and we delighted in attending whenever possible. Most of all, we cherished their “Holiness Camp Meetings,” held in summer in secluded forests or by the sea. These gatherings —“Meetings for the Promotion of Holiness”— were in fact great open-air conferences, drawing Christians of many denominations from across the country, all intent on seeking deeper communion with God. Living in tents beneath the trees, we spent a week or more waiting upon God and sharing together the profound things of the Kingdom.

No words can capture the extraordinary power, solemnity, and yet overwhelming joy of those meetings. We were cut off from our ordinary occupations and cares, with nothing to do but yield ourselves to the spiritual influences around us and open our hearts to what we believed to be the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Such a company of earnest Christians, all intent on drawing nearer to God, created an atmosphere of spiritual intensity that was unforgettable. Testimonies of joy resounded in every meeting, songs of praise echoed through the forest, and the radiant faces of those we met made it seem as though we stood on the very threshold of Heaven. I cannot help but pity any Christian who has never known such seasons of pure delight. For me, they were the culmination of the grand spiritual romance that religion has always been, and I count them among the most entrancing experiences of my life. Even now, the sight of a camp chair or a tent beneath the trees brings back something of that supreme happiness that filled every hour of those blessed gatherings.

On one occasion, a friend of ours — unaware of the true purpose of the meetings — came to see what they were like. Arriving early in the morning, he met worshippers returning from prayer.

Struck by their radiant expressions, he asked us, “What is the matter with all these people, that their faces shine so? Nearly everyone I have seen here has a shining face; but I met a few whose faces did not shine, and I want to know the difference.” We explained that the shining faces reflected hearts at rest in the Lord, while those without such radiance had not yet discovered the blessed secret. He listened intently, then declared , “I am determined that I too will get a shining face, and I will stay here until I do.” And indeed, within days his face shone with the joy of God’s salvation.

I shall never forget my first Camp Meeting, nor the first prayer gathering I attended there. It was an early morning meeting in a tent. Having known only the small Methodist meetings at Millville, I had no conception of the emotional atmosphere into which I had stepped. I realized, too late, that I had forgotten my handkerchief — but having never shed tears in a meeting before, I thought little of it. Yet in that gathering the fountains of my being were broken open, and floods of sweet tears poured from my eyes. In desperation I lifted my dress and used the white underskirt to dry them. Ever since, I have carried at least two handkerchiefs to every meeting, though I have never again been so overwhelmed with emotion as I was then.

That morning was my first taste of the entrancing joys of spiritual emotion, and I reveled in it. As I left the tent, a Metho dist “Holiness Sister,” seeing my tears, put her arm around me, shared her own experience of sanctification, and began to guide me. Under her care, I soon learned how to receive the full benefit of the meetings. Much was said about the “blessing of sanctification,” and at every gathering we were urged to come forward to the “altar”— a simple bench set apart — to seek it. I did not fully understand what this “blessing” was, but it seemed something tangible, born of complete consecration and simple faith, and it filled people with rapturous joy. My Holiness Sister soon had me going forward to the altar myself, determined to receive whatever God had to give. The thrilling testimonies I heard continually fired my enthusiasm, and I embraced every opportunity to seek the blessing. I enjoyed it immensely, for it seemed to bring me to the very edge of unknown spiritual possibilities ready at any moment to unfold.

Apart from those moments of standing, as it were, on the threshold, no special “blessing” ever came to me from my visits to the altar. I am not naturally emotional, and the overpowering feelings others described as the essence of the blessing never fell to my share. What I did receive was the grand truth taught at those meetings — that the Lord Jesus Christ is a Savior not only from the guilt of sin but also from its power. That truth became increasingly real and effective to me. But as for any blessing apart from the truth itself, I experienced nothing. In time, I came to see that the knowledge of the truth was al l the blessing I needed. Much of what was called “the blessing” seemed to me simply the emotional response of emotional natures to the discovery of a magnificent truth. For me, it came with intellectual conviction and delight; for others, with emotional conviction and delight. But in both cases the truth was the same, and it was the truth — not the emotion — that set the soul free.

My husband, however, being of a more emotional nature, did at one of these Camp Meetings receive the blessing in true Methodist fashion. He returned home radiant, filled with a divine glow that touched everyone he met. He could not speak of the meeting without moving us to tears, and it was clear he had undergone a remarkable spiritual experience. He told us of a special gathering devoted to prayer for the Baptism of the Spirit. Afterwards, he withdrew alone into the woods to continue in prayer. Suddenly, from head to foot, he was shaken by what felt like a magnetic thrill of heavenly delight. Floods of glory poured through him, body and soul, with the inward assurance that this was indeed the longed-for Baptism of the Holy Spirit. The whole world seemed transformed: every leaf and blade of grass shimmered with exquisite color, heaven opened before him as a present possession, and everyone he saw appeared beautiful, for he seemed to perceive the Divine Spirit within them. This ecstasy lasted for weeks and marked the beginning of a life of extraordinary spiritual power and blessing.

I confess I was jealous that I did not receive a similar blessing, for I felt I needed it as much as he did. I renewed my efforts to obtain it, but all in vain. I never passed from the realm of conviction into the realm of emotion. My experiences remained intellectual rather than emotional. At last I became con vinced that the difference lay not in God’s favor but in the differing natures of the recipients. Emotional natures received the truth with floods of delight; I received it calmly, with intellectual joy. The truth was the same, only the manner of reception differed.

Over time I observed that emotional experiences were often less solid and permanent than intellectual ones. Emotions, by their nature, fluctuate, while true convictions remain. Once a person is convinced that two and two make four, no amount of ill health or adverse weather can shake that conviction. Feelings, however, are at the mercy of countless influences. I learned, therefore, not to seek emotions but convictions. To my surprise and delight, convictions brought me a more stable and lasting joy than many of my emotional friends seemed to know. In times of stress, their emotions flagged or vanished, and they struggled to avoid despair. Some were grateful at last to return to the stable ground of conviction, which in their emotional days had seemed barren.

This lesson took me years to learn. Meanwhile, the joy and power of the glorious secret we had discovered grew ever more practical. My soul learned to rest in absolute confidence in the keeping and saving power of the Lord. Temptations did not cease, nor d id we attain “sinless perfection.” Temptations arose, failures occurred. But we had discovered a way of escape— the way of faith. We learned that Christ is a Deliverer not only from the future punishment of sin but from its present power. We realized we need no longer be slaves to sin. As far as we laid hold of this deliverance by faith, so far we were delivered. We had not pocketed holiness as a permanent possession, but we had discovered the highway of holiness and learned the secret of walking in it. When we walked there, we had victory; when we strayed, we met failure. After years of wilderness wandering, we had entered the promised land, and found it true, as God said to Israel of old: “Every place the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given you.” The whole land was ours; we need only go up and possess it.

We discovered that the Bible’s words were fact: “God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work.” And we proved in experience that God truly was able — if only we were willing. Christ was revealed to us not merely as our future Savior, but as our present and complete Savior, able to keep us from falling and to deliver us from all our enemies.

For me, this was the beginning of a romance before which all others paled. It was like exploring the courts of heaven itself. Each day brought fresh revelation. Words fail me. I often called it the “bird life,” for I felt like a bird set free, soaring upward into the bl ue of an unfathomable sky.

Once I had been a caged bird, content because I knew nothing of the freedom beyond. Now all barriers were gone, and my soul was free to comprehend with all saints the breadth, length, depth, and height of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge. What once seemed unfathomable now opened into an abyss of delight.

I found that God Himself was enough. Even His promises paled beside the comfort of His presence. What did it matter if I could not find a promise to fit my case? I had found the Promiser, and He was infinitely more than all His promises. As a child, when in trouble, the mere presence of my father or mother brought instant relief. They did not need to explain or promise; their presence was assurance enough. How much more true is this of our Heavenly Father, whose very name is Love. His presence is all we need. Over and over in Scripture He settles His people’s fears with the simple words, “I will be with thee.” That means all His wisdom, love, and power are engaged on our behalf.

I learned that God’s character is our resting place. His ways or promises we may misunderstand, but His goodness cannot be mistaken. If He is good, loving, wise, just, omnipotent, and omnipresent, then all must be ordered rightly for us. Appearances may deceive, but the deeper reality is secure. As George MacDonald said, we need “eyes that can see below surfaces.” Once we discover God’s utter unselfishness, those eyes are opened, and all mysteries of His dealings are answered forever.

No wonder th e Psalmist rejoiced again and again in God’s goodness: “Oh, give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, trust in the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good.” Surrounded by nations whose gods were cruel, selfish, and indifferent, Israel’s triumph was to declare without fear that their God was good. And I feel it is no less a triumph today, in a world that misunderstands and maligns Him, to be able to say with absolute conviction: “Come, taste and see that the Lord is good!”

No wonder th e Psalmist rejoiced again and again in God’s goodness: “Oh, give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, trust in the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good.” Surrounded by nations whose gods were cruel, selfish, and indifferent, Israel’s triumph was to declare without fear that their God was good. And I feel it is no less a triumph today, in a world that misunderstands and maligns Him, to be able to say with absolute conviction: “Come, taste and see that the Lord is good!”

fields.title: The Lovely Will Of God
fields.body_html:
With my eyes newly opened to the absolute goodness and selflessness of God, my entire attitude toward His will was transformed. In the past, I had viewed God’s will as something set against me; now I discovered it was wholly for me. I had feared it as something harsh; now I saw it as something to embrace with joy. I once thought His will was the terrible weapon of His severity, descending upon me to punish. Now I saw it as the tender instrument of His love, bringing into my life only what was kindest and best.

I realized that the will of perfect, unselfish love could only be good, and that since God possesses all knowledge and all wisdom, His will must — by its very nature — be the best thing the universe could offer. No greater bliss could come to any of us than to have that beautiful, selfless will perfectly done both in us and for us.

Sometimes hiding myself in God’s will felt like retreating into an impregnable fortress of love and protection, where no harm could reach me. At other times it felt like sinking into the softest bed of down, resting in perfect peace. I can never fully put into words all that I began to see of the loveliness, tenderness, generosity, and infinite goodness of the will of God. I truly reveled in its sweetness.

This did not mean life would be free of trials; a wise and loving will might see trials as necessary gifts of love. Nor was it essential that I perceive the divine hand in every difficulty. My common sense told me that if God is omnipresent, He must be present in my trials as well — and, being there, He must be there to help and bless.

We are not wise enough to judge whether our experiences are truly joys or sorrows, but the Lord knows. And because He loves us with limitless, unselfish love, He cannot fail — literally cannot fail — to make even the things that appear hard, or cruel, or wicked, work together for our greatest good. I say “cannot fail” because it is unimaginable that such a God could act otherwise.

It does not matter who begins the trial — whether human malice, spiritual evil, or our own foolishness. If God allows it to reach us, then by that very permission He makes the trial His own, transforming it into a chariot of love that carries our souls to blessings we never could have reached otherwise. For the Christian who dwells in the fortress of God’s will, there are no “second causes”; nothing can enter that fortress unless th e Divine Keeper of it opens the door.

And when He does, it means He has adopted that thing for our eternal good.

Joseph was sold into Egypt through the wickedness of his brothers, yet God made their cruelty the very chariot that carried him to triumph. So we may be more certain of this than we are that the sun will rise tomorrow: God’s will is the loveliest thing in the universe for us— not because it always looks best, but because it cannot be anything but best, being the will of infinite love.

I found myse lf continually singing Faber’s beautiful hymn: “I worship Thee, sweet will of God, And all Thy ways adore; And every day I live it seems I love Thee more and more.”

One verse delighted me especially because I so often found it true in experience: “I know n ot what it is to doubt, My heart is always gay; I run no risks, for, come what will, Thou always hast Thy way.”

The first time I realized this in a deeply practical way was three days after the birth of my beloved baby girl — a child I had longed for with unspeakable yearning, who felt to me like the most exquisite treasure ever entrusted to human care.

My nurse had suddenly fallen ill and was forced to leave, so we had to bring in a stranger whose looks I mistrusted and whose ignorance seemed obvious. At that time trained nurses were far less common, and I felt this one was wholly unqualified. I could hardly bear to have her touch my precious child, yet I was not allowed to care for my baby myself.

It was winter, and a bright wood fire burned on the hearth of my room. On the nurse’s first evening, after settling me in bed, she sat close to the fire with my baby on her lap. Soon she fell into a deep sleep, snoring loudly, and I awoke to see my infant lying perilously near the blaze on her slanting knees, while the nurse’s head drooped dangerously above her.

My voice was weak, and I could not rouse her. I expected at any moment to see my little one roll into the fire. I could make no one hear me, and to rise from bed and cross the cold floor might have seriously harmed my health. Yet my anxiety drove me upright, and I was struggling to stand when suddenly these words flashed through my mind: “I run no risks, for, come what will, Thou always hast Thy way.”

With those words came a deep conviction that my child was u tterly safe in God’s care. A profound peace settled over me. My head sank back onto my pillow and my soul sank back into the sweetness of God’s will. I saw that my baby was cradled in the arms of almighty love. I fell asleep without a trace of fear and woke to find her being tucked beside me for her feeding.

It was beyond words beautiful to have experienced such a practical revelation of the loveliness and blessedness of the will of God.

Since that first awakening, I have had many similar insights, and I have come to know — beyond even the faintest shadow of doubt — that the will of God is the most delicious, delightful reality in the universe. This is not because life always unfolds according to my preferences, nor because of any special piety in me, but simply because plain common sense tells me that the will of perfect, unselfish love could only be delightful. Heaven is heaven precisely because God’s will is done perfectly there; and earth would inevitably resemble heaven if His will were perfectly done here.

For years I had heard Christians describe consecration to God’s will as a spiritual achievement so lofty that only a few exceptionally devout souls could hope to reach it. But once I discovered the infinite unselfishness of God, I realized that consecration is not an attainment at all — it is a priceless privilege. I am convinced that if people truly understood the beauty of His will, not only the particularly devout but every soul in existence would rush to choose it gladly for every moment of their lives.

This is not a higher degree of piety; it is simply a higher degree of good common sense. If I were lost in a trackless wilderness, unable to see any way out, and an experienced guide offered to lead me to safety, would it feel difficult or sacrificial to pl ace myself in his hands and say, “Your will be done”? And if not, how could it feel burdensome to entrust myself to my heavenly Guide and say, “Thy will be done”? It cannot— it is impossible. Surrender to God, or consecration as many call it, is the greates t privilege offered to any soul in this life. To say “Thy will be done” is one of the most delightful sentences a human being is permitted to utter.

An old writer once said that God’s will is not a burden to carry, as so many imagine, but a pillow on which to rest. I found this profoundly true. My soul sank into His will with an indescribable sweetness of peaceful content. At other times, saying “Thy will be done” felt like a magnificent cry of victory — like raising a triumphant banner before the entire universe and daring it to oppose me. So vivid was this feeling that I found myself repeating, day and night, as a victorious soldier might sing after battle: “Thy wonderful, grand Will, my God, With triumph now I make it mine; And Love shall cry a joyous Yes T o every dear command of Thine.”

But I could never fully tell all that my soul discovered when I discovered the goodness and unselfishness of God. To say that He is enough is to give a complete and unshakeable answer to every doubt and question that can ever arise. My feelings may not always confirm that prayers are answered or promises fulfilled — but what of that? Behind every prayer and every promise stands God Himself — the sheer God, if I may put it so — and if He exists at all, then He must be enough.

For years I had sung the familiar words: “Thou, O Christ, art all I want; More than all in Thee I find.”

But until now, I had never understood what they truly meant. They had sounded beautiful, but only as a poetic sentiment. Now I saw that they state a fact. I had begun to discover that He really was everything I needed — and that infinitely more than all I could ask or imagine was stored up for me in Him.

In a certain sense, my search for God ended there, for I had found that He was enough. I have discovered many other beautiful and precious truths about Him since, but at that moment I had reached Himself — the real God behind all appearances — and my heart entered into its rest. I saw that nothing else ultimately mattered: not creeds, nor ceremonies, nor doctrines, nor dogmas.

fields.title: Old Age And Death
fields.body_html:
Now that I am seventy years old and life is swiftly moving toward its close, I can say without hesitation that discovering the unselfishness of God has transformed the way I feel about both old age and death. Knowing — utterly and securely — that God is , and that God is enough , makes old age a joy in the present and death a delicious prospect for the future.

Without Him, old age — with its diminishing strength and frequent infirmities — could only be dreary and exhausting. But with God, our beautiful, unselfish God, behind it all, old age becomes a gentle resting place. Reaching seventy gives me permission to step aside from the pressures of life, to put down the burden of keeping the world running, and I gladly accept that release.

I did my part to carry the responsibilities of my own generation, and now that it has nearly passed away, I rejoice that the weight of today’s world rests, not on me, but on younger and stronger shoulders — those whom God has called to their own appointed work. I laugh to myself with real pleasure at the thought, and I even enjoy the infirmities of age as they arrive. Each one frees me from some task or duty and allows me the peaceful leisure to watch the younger wrestlers in the world’s arena. I may not always think they wrestle in the best way, judging with my old eyes, but I admire the divine order that assigns to each generation its own work, to be done in its own way. Whether it seems wise or foolish to us, the passing generation must make room for the rising one, and must refrain from interfering.

We older people may offer advice and share the fruits of our experience, but we must hold ourselves completely content when our advice is ignored. If we did this — truly did it — I am convinced the young would gladly seek our counsel far more often. But they hesitate because they fear that asking for advice obliges them to follow it, and that we will feel wounded if they do not. True freedom in seeking guidance can only exist alongside true freedom not to take it.

I am not speaking of children, but of adults in two different generations. And in general, when the older insist that their advice must be followed, they put themselves in the unfortunate position of obstructing the world’s progress. In almost every field today, businesses employ younger and younger workers because older ones tend to settle into ruts and resist being urged out of them. It is striking, in this regard, that by divine command the Israelites retired from public service at the age of fifty —whether in the Tabernacle or the army. “From the age of fifty years they shall cease their service… and serve no more.” If they step ped back at fifty, then at seventy I am surely free to withdraw from the world’s work and enjoy the blissful sense of release from responsibility that belongs to old age.

We often hear about the duty the young owe to the old. But I believe it is far more important for us to consider the duty the old owe to the young. I do not mean that the young owe us nothing; but at seventy, I see clearly that the greater burden lies on our side. We brought the younger generation into the world without consulting them. Therefore we are obligated to pour ourselves out for their good — just as God, who created us, has poured Himself out for ours through the sacrifice of Christ. I cannot see how God could have done less, and I cannot see how we should do less either.

Having discovered the unselfishness of God — as everyone who reaches seventy ought to have done — our attitude toward others should reflect, in our measure, the same unselfishness. Surely this is what Jesus meant when He urged us to love our enemies, bless those who curse us, and do good to those who hate us, so that we might be “children of our Father in Heaven,” who does exactly these things. And Jesus ends with, “Be perfect, therefore, as your Father in Heaven is perfect.” Our perfection is the perfection of unselfish love. The older we are, the more deeply we should understand this and live it.

Everything is safe when guided and controlled by unselfish love. And so my old heart rests quietly. I can lay down my arms with joyful confidence. Since God is in His Heaven, all must ultimately be right with His world, whatever appearances may suggest. I can peacefully wait to understand what now seems mysterious until that glorious day of revelation that draws closer with every hour.

One of my most comforting discoveries is that God can manage His universe by Himself, even without my assistance. Whenever I look at the sun, the moon, or the stars —“the work of His fingers”— I feel the deep satisfaction of knowing they are His responsibility, not mine. Because of this, I can gladly die and leave the whole universe in His care, without the slightest fear that things will fall apart when I depart. God is the housekeeper of His own creation. Just as it would be foolish for me to trouble myself about the housekeeping of my neighbors in Grosvenor Road, it is even more foolish to worry about God’s housekeeping. So with a quiet mind I look forward to death. The thought of leaving this life and entering the larger, grander life beyond is pure joy.

It feels like standing on the threshold of a new country full of unknown wonders — and knowing that nothing and no one can prevent me from going there fills my heart with secret, continual delight.

Often, when some pleasant earthly plan is spoiled, I say to myself with triumph, “Well, there is one thing I will never be disappointed about — and that is dying. No one, not even an enemy, can take that from me.” Whenever I see a funeral, I laugh inwardly at the renewed realization that such a happy future awaits every one of us. I hardly dare write condolence letters anymore, for they almost always turn into letters of congratulation at the blessed escape of another soul from this earthly prison-house.

In the organizations to which I belong, my companions never dare ask me to lead a memorial service, lest I b e tempted to give thanks for the departed person’s release. Even when someone I dearly love dies, I can rejoice. It seems to me nothing but selfishness to let my own loss overshadow their immeasurable gain.

I love Walt Whitman’s incomparable death song, an d I always long to send it to every dying friend: “Joy, shipmate, joy… Our life is closed, our life begins…” This passing life, with all its affairs — once so important — shrinks into insignificance when set beside the life beyond. I am glad to be almost finished with it. Its pull upon me is gone. I, who once craved every new place and every new experience, now care for them no longer. I feel a deep, satisfying sense of being done with this earth. Every place looks the same to me; every experience feels tame compared to what lies ahead.

What that life will be, I can only imagine vaguely. I feel like a butterfly preparing to slip out of its cocoon, longing for the life outside but with no experience to tell me what that life will be like. Yet I believe with all m y heart the Apostle’s words: “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him.” What more glorious prospect could the soul desire?

I remember the joy I once felt at the thought of exploring the unknown wonders of Yellowstone Park and the Hoodoo Mountains of Wyoming — a joy heightened precisely because they were unknown and seemed full of possibility. But that joy is nothing compared to what I feel now, looking toward the things God has prepared that have not even entered my imagination.

The one thing I know for certain is this: the prayer of Jesus will be fulfilled — “Father, I will that they whom You have given Me be with Me where I am, that they may behold My glory.” That glory is not blinding light or dazzling gold, but the glory of unselfish love, the greatest glory there is. I have had faint glimpses of it here, and even those glimpses have ravished my heart.

But there I will see Him as He is, in the full splendor of an infinite unselfishness no human mind has ever conceived — and I await that moment with joy.

END

fields.title: Personal Profile
fields.body_html:
Gareth, and his wife Anne, were both born and raised in Wales. They married in 1961 after he had received his Bachelors of Science with honors in Physics as well as a Diploma of Education from the University of Wales. In 1975 they immigrated to Canada where Gareth continued in his chosen profession as a secondary school physics teacher. In 1979 he was invited to pastor a church in Kitchener, Ontario with the Christian and Missionary Alliance.

Four years later, he received a call to Victoria, British Columbia where he pastored for the next eight years, and where they still reside. In 1990 Gareth was invited to serve as the chaplain on board the Mercy Ship, M/V Anastasis, working between Europe and West Africa. There he and Anne ministered to the crew and had many opportunities to speak at churches, pastors’ seminars, and missionary conferences.

Since leaving the ship in 1994 Gareth has traveled extensively, teaching at discipleship training schools and various conferences. Gareth and Anne have three daughters and nine grandchildren.

fields.title: Foreword by Keith Price
fields.body_html:
There can surely be no better recommendation for a book than its having stood the test of clinical trial. That such a test has been applied to the principles enunciated here is surely adequate endorsement.

As you read these pages you will sense a shepherd’s heart.

Though a man of science, this man of God has no time for ivory towers. Having gone through the fires of life’s uphill experiences himself, he understands what others feel in times of struggle.

Gareth Evans has proved these principles not only in pastoral work in Victoria, British Columbia, but also further afield in places as diverse as Mexico, Africa, Europe, and Australia where he has been invited to present the material to many different groups of churches and Christian leaders.

Because of his high view of the inspiration of the scriptures from which he draws these lessons, I am confident that they will retain their value until we, being made perfect, no longer need to take the initiative to restore broken relationships.

Keith Price Victoria, British Columbia March, 1996

fields.title: Priorities
fields.body_html:
The Covenant Feast It was a hot, dusty day as Peter and John, disciples of Jesus, entered the city of Jerusalem. They had come to celebrate Pesach, the Feast of the Passover, and were even now following a man, carrying a pitcher of water, who would lead them to the place where the feast was to be prepared.

As the Lord had told them, it had not been difficult to find their guide, for the sight of a man carrying a pitcher of water was uncommon. That was a task usually done by the women.

He led them to a pleasant two-story house where the host greeted them warmly. When they had told him their errand, they were ushered into a large, furnished room on the upper floor.

It did not take them long to prepare the low-lying table since the requirements for the feast were well known to both. Bowls of bitter herbs were alternated with plates of apples, cinnamon, and almonds. A flask of salt water and some boiled eggs were placed beside the vessels of wine and there were several portions of the unleavened bread they called “matzah.” Soon the hour arrived and Jesus came with the rest of the disciples.

There was a buzz of excitement and animated conversation as they entered the upper room. This was to be a celebration time, the happiest time of the year for all Jews; when they were reminded again of the great faithfulness of Jehovah. Had He not delivered them from the bondage of Egypt so many years ago? Could He not still deliver them from the present oppression of the Romans?

To the disciples of Jesus this time was probably even more exciting. They were wondering if the day was near when their master would reveal Himself to the nation as the long-awaited Messiah who came to set them free as prophesied by the prophets of old. They felt they were at a strategic time in the history of their people. Indeed, this past week had been rather unusual, and things were coming to a head. It was obvious that the religious leaders were very shaken by both the teachings and popularity of Jesus.

I can imagine that the conversation of the disciples was centered entirely around the events of this past week and wondering just what significance they had. I’m sure Peter couldn’t stop talking about the triumphal entry into Jerusalem just five days earlier, when the crowds had laid their garments on the dusty road and torn branches from the palm trees to wave, as they cried out, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, even the king of Israel” (John 12:13).

I can imagine him, head held high, chest out, as he led the donkey’s colt, upon which the master sat. John and James, the Zealots (sons of thunder), would have been more impressed with the way their master had turned over the tables of the money changers and driven them from the temple. “Did you see the look on the High Priest’s face? Brother, was he mad!”

They all lowered themselves to a reclining position alongside the table, still happy in their celebratory mood: it was party time. Jesus looked on with pleasure as His friends celebrated, but He knew something that had eluded their understanding: tomorrow He would die.

What would you do if your doctor told you that you only had a short time to live? Of course, you’d ask for a second opinion! And if that also confirmed that you would soon leave this world, your constant companions, and friends? I know what I would do. I would quickly finish my present activities and arrange to be with those most precious to me: my wife, our daughters, and their families.

I would want to tell them how much I love them and how proud I am of them. I would encourage them to go on with Jesus, serving Him and living a life to the praise of His glory.

I would ask them if there is anything for which I need to apologize to them, any hurts, any unkind words or thoughtlessness. I would want to make very sure that there was nothing left undone that could be done in bonding our relationship one with the other.

I would find very little time to talk about trivial things such as the latest sports scores or gossip, which occupy so much of my time otherwise. Indeed, all I’d be doing would be dealing with priorities . And that night, at the paschal feast, that is just what the Lord was going to do with His disciples - deal with priorities !

His Requirements As was customary, they had all removed their shoes as they entered this upper room. Their feet were dusty, and the sand between their toes made them feel rather uncomfortable.

Soon a murmur of discontent could be heard. The bowls of water were on a table near the door and there were towels available, but where was the servant girl whose job it was to wash their feet to refresh them? She should have been here when they arrived!

I can imagine that it must have been Peter who would be the first to speak out what they were all thinking. He is so much like me - always putting his foot in his mouth! “Where’s the girl? My feet are itching. Has someone made a mistake and forgotten to tell her? Who planned this feast? Who’s on the committee?” An embarrassed whispering would be heard as the others tried to tell him to be quiet. After all, it was the Master who had made the arrangements! And He doesn’t make mistakes; even when we cannot understand His purposes.

Jesus rose from the table and walked toward the bowls of water.

“Oh good,” thought Peter, “He’s going to call the girl.”

Jesus removed His outer garment, clothed Himself with a towel, picked up a bowl of water, and turned… towards Peter!

“Oh no,” thought Peter, “He’s going to ask me to do it!”

Instead, Jesus washes the dusty feet of Peter and then, those of all the others, including Judas Iscariot who would betray Him and bring about the suffering He was anticipating that night. Can you imagine the Lord looking up into the eyes of Judas as He washed his feet? What did He see in those eyes?

Fear? Or guilt? What did Judas see in His master’s eyes? I wonder, was he able to look? Such love!

Jesus returned the bowl and towel to their place by the door, put on His outer garment ,and turned toward the disciples.

“I give you an example,” He said, “as I have done to you, so do you to one another” (John 13:1-20).

The first priority of discipleship is servanthood . We are charged by the Lord to be servants. It is essential if we desire to be like Him, who came not to be served, but to serve (Matthew 20:28). It is the condition of greatness in the Kingdom of Heaven and an evidence of being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18,21).

I do not think that the Lord meant for us to follow Him literally in washing one another’s feet (though that is a great blessing to experience), but rather, that we are to seek to refresh one another from the dust and dirt of walking in this world. It is impossible to live in this world without some of its dirt rubbing off on you. How seldom can one read a newspaper, watch the television, or chat with neighbors or colleagues without being infected by its poison? Gossiping and grumbling, so common even among believers, soon rob us of the joy of walking the Christian way. We need the cleansing words, the refreshment and encouragement of other believers. We need to have our feet washed! That is the purpose of Christian fellowship; however, there is often just as much ‘dirt’ thrown about among believers as among those of the world!

Not only are we called to serve one another in the Body of Christ, but we are also challenged to be servants to those who would even betray our Lord and not be one of His followers.

Jesus washed the feet of Judas knowing all that was in his heart. He saw his doubts and frustrations, knew his politicking and deceit, yet He did not hesitate to wash his feet.

When He finished this task He invited all those who would recognize Him as master, to do the same.

To have the attitude of a servant is not easy in our self- centered world. It requires humility - knowing oneself as one truly is - and acceptance of oneself. When we see ourselves ‘in Christ’ we are not threatened by what others may think of us. Who cares what others may say when we know we are pleasing to the Lord? Our confidence is in Him and in His promises.

Jesus knew what His commission was, where He had come from, and what His destiny was (John 13:3). This confidence was the foundation of His servanthood. The Father had given Him authority, had sent Him into the world, and would receive Him back again.

We have the same commission and the same destiny! The World may call us weak or spineless, trying to manipulate our servant attitude to their own ends. They will take your coat, compel you to go with them a mile, and make you their slave.

Jesus told us, if that should happen, to give them also your shirt and go the second mile! In doing so, you are removing yourself from their slavery and making yourself a voluntary servant (Matthew 5:40-41).

Shortly after Judas had left the room to do his dirty work, Jesus taught His disciples a second requirement. “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34-35). Note that this is a commandment, not an option! Have you ever tried to measure just how much He loves you? That is the only scale by which He will measure how much you love “one another!”

It would be impossible if it were not for His grace and the indwelling Holy Spirit He gives.

“To live above with those I love, O, that will be glory! To live below with those I know - well, that’s a different story!”

(Unknown Author).

We may not like one another, but we are commanded to love one another! That means no gossiping and no backstabbing, but instead honoring, preferring one another, bearing one another’s burden, and so much more… A third requirement was placed before the disciples. “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). He calls us to be obedient to His word. The Old Testament prophet, Samuel, rebuked the disobedient King Saul saying, “Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.

For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has also rejected you from being king” (1 Samuel 15:22-23).

Because Saul did not obey the word of the Lord God, he lost his kingdom and authority. When Jesus spoke to the multitudes, those who heard Him were filled with amazement for He spoke as one having great authority (Matthew 7:28- 29).

We who recognize Him as Saviour must also acknowledge that He is Lord. What He says has the greatest of authority.

We need to be sensitive to hear and recognize His voice day by day. He said that we, His sheep, should recognize His voice. Above all, we should hear Him speak to us through the Scriptures and obey what He says. All believers should be students of the written Word, living in obedience to its precepts.

Jesus’ requirements for His disciples are that we serve one another, love one another, and obey His Word.

His Promises Besides the three requirements He placed before His disciples, Jesus also promised them rich blessings. He would come again and receive them to Himself having prepared a place “in [His] Father’s house” (John 14:2) for them. They would do greater works than He did as He would send them another Helper and would answer the prayers they asked according to His will. They were to know the blessing of being in Christ , and to experience the Father’s love.

The Helper, the Holy Spirit, would come to dwell in them and would lead them to the truth and knowledge of God’s will; He would bring to their remembrance all they had been taught by Jesus.

“Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1).

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27).

“These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11).

He promised them - and us - a peace that the world cannot give or take away, a joy whose measure is fullness, and a presence who is none other than the Spirit Himself, never to leave us or forsake us (Deuteronomy 31:6).

Have you experienced these in your walk with the Lord? I certainly have, but I long for more!

The experience of these promises is contingent on us being servants , lovers , and obedient to His Word.

fields.title: A Covenant People
fields.body_html:
The Agape Feast “Jesus took bread and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, ‘This is My Body, broken for you. Take and eat!’”

(1 Corinthians 11:23-24). They all did and, in so doing, identified themselves with the Body of Christ.

“In the same way He took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me’” (1 Corinthians 11:25-26). I am struck that none of those present asked Him what He meant when He said this. I can only assume that they all understood.

A covenant is an agreement between two parties. “You do this for me, and I’ll do that for you!” Today, when men make covenants it is essential that proof be available in the form of signatures attached to the written agreement. Sadly, the word of a gentleman is no longer acceptable. In the time of Jesus, covenants were sealed over a common drink. It would not have been blood, as more recently among the Native Indians of North America and the tribesmen of Africa, though all the covenants of the Old Testament days would have been signified by the shedding of blood in the slaying of a sacrificial animal. Indeed, one was said to ‘cut the covenant’ rather than make one.

An interesting story is told concerning Dr. Livingstone, the great pioneer missionary to Africa. He, with his guides and bearers, was often taken captive by warrior tribesmen as they journeyed through the dark continent.

On one occasion, the captives were brought before a hostile chief who began to berate them for trespassing on his territory. As he was getting angrier at Livingstone’s silence, a guide leaned over to the missionary and urged him to ‘cut the covenant.’ Livingstone did not understand what was being requested, but he soon recoiled in dismay as he watched his Christian servant and a chosen young man from the hostile tribe, perform what was to him, a pagan act. They made a small cut in their forearms, gathered the blood into a bowl and drank it together!

The chief then stepped forward and took hold of the string by which Livingstone was leading a goat, the source of the milk he so enjoyed. Livingstone was dismayed and then surprised as the chief pressed a gift into his hands - the copper-tipped staff with which he had met the trespassing party. They were then led to a hut where they would spend the night after receiving a meal from their captors.

Some time later, while journeying through another region of Africa, Livingstone was captured again and brought before another hostile chief. This time, however, the chief fell on his knees before the missionary. It was only then that understanding came. When the young guide had ‘cut the covenant’ on behalf of Livingstone, and had sealed it by the drinking of blood, an agreement was made between them and the tribe, especially between Livingstone and the chief.

As a token of that covenant agreement, the chief had given his staff, a symbol of his commitment and support. The second hostile chief had recognized the staff, understood that Livingstone had a blood brother and had yielded to that superior power and authority.

Jesus has made such a covenant with us! We can now walk tall in this crippled world by His authority! We have a blood brother Who shed His blood, drank it to the bitter dregs on our behalf, and gave us the authority of His name (Acts 3:16)!

Our enemy, Satan, and his henchmen, sin and death, should have no dominion over us (Romans 6:14)!

When Jesus invited His disciples to drink the ‘covenant cup,’ they knew they were indicating their agreement to the terms of a new covenant. So it is every time we take the emblems at the Lord’s table. As we eat the bread, we are declaring ourselves to be the body of Christ . As we drink the cup, we are covenanting again to be servants to one another, lovers of one another, and obedient to His Word .

An Unworthy Manner In his letter to the Corinthians, Paul exhorts us to be very careful in taking these emblems. If we drink the Lord’s cup “in an unworthy manner” we may well drink judgment to ourselves, not recognizing the Lord’s body. “For this reason many among you (believers) are weak and sick” (1 Corinthians 11:30).

If I bear animosity in my heart to another, or am not living as a servant , lover , or in obedience , my taking of the bread and cup is hypocrisy. I am failing to recognize the other as one with me in the Body of Christ. This may well result in weakness and sickness coming upon me. This is not from the Lord - He is not the author of sickness, but I have given the devil a foothold (2 Corinthians 2:11), and he certainly knows how to manipulate such footholds for his advantage!

Praying for the Sick Now I have an understanding of what James meant when he wrote, “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven” (James 5: 14-15).

I do not now believe that calling the elders has anything to do with their prayer power, but rather their authority . This verse must be linked with Paul’s warning above, as they are the only verses that give any reference to reasons why believers may be sick or weak. Of course, we also are subject to germs, diseases, and sickness just as anyone in the world, but Paul’s warning must be strongly expressed to believers.

Should the elders discern that the believer’s sickness may be associated with a wrong attitude to others in the Body of Christ, they must exercise their authority as elders in the church, to charge that one to be reconciled. Only then can they pray, anointing him with oil (a symbol of the Holy Spirit’s blessing and protection) in the name of the Lord. The sick one - the guilty one - will be restored and forgiven.

One should take time to read John 17 to hear the cry of Jesus’ heart on the night before He died. Let me walk with you through these wonderful words, emphasizing a major theme.

“Father, I have finished the work You gave Me to do… I have manifested Your name (attributes) to these men… and they have kept Your word. I ask on their behalf… for they are Yours. They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. As You have sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world. I do not only ask for these but also for all who will believe in Me through their word (which includes you and I). That they may all be one … that the world may believe. I have given them Your glory… that they may be one … as We are One. That they may be perfected in unity , that the world may know that You sent Me and that You love them even as You love Me… I have made Your name (attributes) known to them… that the love with which You love Me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17).

God’s name was revealed to Moses when they met on Mount Sinai; therefore, we can be certain that He is “ The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:6-7).

Truly, Jesus manifested these same attributes to all He met.

God’s Gospel Tract I cannot take even one page out of the Bible and use it as an evangelical tract to give to an unbelieving friend. I can quote from John 3 or follow “The Romans Road” which explains to them the way of salvation. I can give them the “Four Steps” or “God’s Wonderful Plan of Salvation,” but I cannot tear one page out of the Bible and give it away as a gospel tract.

However, I can take whole chapters and even books, to point out God’s priorities to the believer: His way of salvation. He has declared that when His people are walking in unity as servants , as lovers and in obedience , the world will know and believe !

We are His Gospel tract! It’s time we got our priorities right and in line with His priorities! We are quick to speak when we detect heresy of doctrine in one another - isn’t it time we were just as quick to act against heresy of practice, seeing the many divisions among believers, so evident to the world?

“For the anxious longing of all creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the Sons of God” (Romans 8:19).

They all did and, in so doing, identified themselves with the Body of Christ. “In the same way He took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me’” (1 Corinthians 11:25-26). A covenant is an agreement between two parties. “You do this for me, and I’ll do that for you!” Today, when men make covenants it is essential that proof be available in the form of signatures attached to the written agreement. He, with his guides and bearers, was often taken captive by warrior tribesmen as they journeyed through the dark continent. On one occasion, the captives were brought before a hostile chief who began to berate them for trespassing on his territory.
