fields.title: The Body of Christ
fields.body_html:
One Body “So we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Romans 12:5).

The apostle Paul takes up the theme of the Lord’s upper room prayer to teach us that the relationship called for in one-to- the-other serving and loving, is best demonstrated in the example of a living body. He sees the church as the living Body of Christ instituted by God. It is not a man-made organization, but a God-made organism - a living, vital reality. It is the training and exercise ground for serving and loving. This is why Christian fellowship is so important.

John Donne, a sixteenth century Anglican priest, wrote, “No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as if a manor of thy friend’s or of thine own were: any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind, and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”

His sentiments could well be those of a member of the Body of Christ, recognizing his interdependence on all other parts of that body.

Islam teaches that Mohammed was called by God to complete what Jesus failed to do! Muslims recognize Jesus as a great prophet, second only to Mohammed, but they believe He failed in that He was not able to make all people into one nation. Islam calls peoples of all nations to be one as Muslims. They have failed to understand that the unity Jesus came to bring was for those who are members of His kingdom, and not one of this world. How tragic that there is such obvious disunity in that kingdom. No wonder Islam is growing so rapidly!

At conversion, the new birth, we were, “by one Spirit all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). This includes Baptists, Anglicans, Pentecostals, and whatever group you belong to. Not the denominations, but the individuals within all such groups who know the Lord as a personal Savior, and know their sins are forgiven through the work finished on Calvary. The baptism into the Body must not be confused with the baptism into the Spirit, experienced by the disciples on the day of Pentecost, and by many since that day. The former is “by the Spirit into the Body” whereas the latter is “by the Lord Jesus into the Spirit” (Luke 3:16). We are to be “in Christ” for justification, and Christ is to be “in us” for sanctification.

Fullness of the Spirit One major division in the body is due to various doctrines concerning this baptism of the Spirit.

Are tongues the initial evidence of being so filled? Are they evidence at all? I am not getting into that argument except to say that, whichever view we hold, we should not make our disagreement a cause for division, that way we are certainly not exhibiting the reality of any fullness of the Holy Spirit!

He comes to make the presence of Christ, and His will, real to us. He leads us into truth. I find it rather striking that, when Paul exhorts us to be “filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), he follows by giving us three evidences of a life so filled: 1. A worshiping attitude speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19).

2. A thankful attitude always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father (Ephesians 5:20).

3. A servant attitude and be subject to one another in the fear of Christ (Ephesians 5:21).

Don’t tell me that you are a Spirit-filled Christian unless these three are evident in your life!

Paul then continues in his letter to the Ephesians by showing how this third evidence is worked out in our relationships as: husband and wife, children and parents, and workers and masters (Ephesians 5:22-6:9).

The Local Church I am not among those who consider denominations as such to be evil. I believe that the Lord established most of them to enable us to mature as believers within a group of people most like us in personality and persuasion; however, when our groupings cause us to be divided from those within the Body of Christ who do not share our opinions concerning styles of worship, interpretation of Scriptures, and emphases, we are in danger of bringing condemnation upon ourselves. We may not like one another, but we are commanded to love one another!

There are three major Scripture portions where the apostle outlines his understanding of the Body of Christ.

1. Ephesians 4:1-16 → We are challenged to walk in a manner worthy of our calling showing humility, gentleness, patience, love, and being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For, he declares, “There is ONE BODY” (Ephesians 4:4). He continues by writing about some of the grace gifts in verse seven given to that Body. They are ministry gifts of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, which are given “for the equipping of the saints… unto maturity” (Ephesians 4:13).

2. Romans 12:1-8 → We are challenged again to give ourselves as living sacrifices with renewed minds. All members of the Body do not have the same function, but we are all interdependent on one another. We all have different grace gifts (Romans 12:6) with which to serve one another.

Therefore, we must, “Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:9-10).

3. 1 Corinthians 12-14 → We cannot separate chapters 12 and 14 from that great chapter on love, chapter 13! The first chapter deals with the doctrines of the Body and the charismata given to that Body. Note that these charismata are given to the individual, not for their own use, but for the benefit of the whole Body!

Then Paul expands on his teaching concerning the Body by showing just how foolish it is for one part of the Body to claim that they do not need the other parts! The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you” (1 Corinthians 12:21). We need one another!

At the end of this chapter, he gathers together the lists of grace gifts he recorded in Ephesians and Romans showing them all to be among his long list of charismata .

Such gifts are of little value unless exercised with love (1 Corinthians 13) and properly in an orderly manner (1 Corinthians 14).

Are you fully functioning in the Body of Christ? Are you grounded in a local church, serving others, loving others, and obedient to His Word? If your ministry is wider than the local church, are you in the right relationship with God to appoint leaders, and be accountable to them as a member of the same local expression of the Body?

Some might seek to be an arm reaching out, others a voice speaking to this world, but I often see myself as nothing more glamorous than a big toe! As a former pastor, I was often working in dark and smelly places, feeling under pressure, dealing with peoples’ problems (sand between the toes).

However, I feel I am privileged when asked to minister because I get to bring balance to the Body. That surely, is the main function of the big toe!

fields.title: The Tragic Truth
fields.body_html:
God’s desire, and the priority on the heart of Jesus, is that He will have a people whose love for one another, and attitude of servanthood will be such a witness to this world that men and women will be crying out to know our Lord. They will want to know the secret of our peace, joy, and harmony. They will watch our marriages, homes, children, and workplaces, not to criticize, but to know our secrets.

Having urged his readers to be “filled with the Spirit,” and expressing one evidence of being so filled, as being “subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21),Paul gives examples of how this should be in our relationships.

Christian Marriage → Ephesians 5:22-33 If Christian marriages were what they are supposed to be, with both parties Spirit-filled and submitted to one another, honoring, and preferring the other, they would be the mystery revealed to a watching world. Men would see the relationship that Jesus has with His bride, the church, and would be drawn to know Him as the foundation for his marriage also. There would be a steady path of seekers coming to our home or church door, rather than rushing, as they now do, to the divorce courts!

Women would want to honor their own husband above all other men, because of the love they receive, and men would want to love their wives because of the honor they receive.

Rather than a vicious circle of abuse and retaliation which is so common in the world, there would be a delicious circle of blessing one another in Christ.

It is so tragic that divorce is so common among Christian believers. What kind of witness is that?

The Christian Home → Ephesians 6:1-4 Where parents are in the right relationships with the Lord and with one another, their children mature in a secure, loving home. Most of the counseling I do as a pastor has to do with wounds received by children growing up in a rather different situation, though often “Christian” fathers fail to disciple (or discipline) their children and, instead, provoke them to anger (Colossians 3:21).

Christian counselors today speak of dysfunctional families where the child’s ‘love tank’ is not filled with the love it was created to receive, because the dysfunctional parents are incapable of providing that love. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self- esteem, acceptance, and encouragement. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self- esteem, acceptance, and encouragement.

Instead of growing up emotionally and spiritually healthy, they become just like their parents, dysfunctional. They never learn to walk tall in a world of bowed shoulders and broken hearts. The empty space in their love tank is filled with one thing: anger, which produces a life of rebellion to God’s purposes. Such children never learn to obey their parents in the Lord.

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Colossians 3:21).

It is so tragic that so many rebellious children are the product of “Christian” homes. What kind of witness is that?

The Workplace → Ephesians 6:5-9 The Spirit-filled believer is called to be a witness in his workplace by displaying the attitude of a servant before his co-workers and employers and should be trustworthy to do his work well.

I am familiar with a teacher whose school was to be amalgamated with two others in a major reorganization. All the teachers from the three schools gathered together to form a Staff Association to speak on the teachers’ behalf to the School Governors, expressing their desires for the design of the new school buildings and their terms of employment.

One man was nominated and seconded for the position of president for this new association. Another was nominated and seconded. Then, much to his surprise, my friend was nominated. Immediately, the two others who had been nominated withdrew their names in order to second my friend’s nomination. No other names were presented and he was elected unanimously to represent all the staff. As he left the room he expressed amazement to a colleague. “Just wait till I tell my wife,” he said. “She’ll never believe me!” “Why not?” replied the colleague, “We all know you’re the only one we can trust to always speak the truth!”

My friend was the only Christian on the senior staff of those schools.

Sadly, I am often told by business men (Christians among them) that the worst people to do business with are Christians.

They want the most out of you for the least payment. They are the poorest at giving tips, and often the last in settling debts! Of course, it may well be that we are judged more harshly by the world than non-believers are, but that is to be expected!

We are called to have the attitude of servants. We should be living at a higher level of commitment and workmanship than the world! Sadly, we all know of Christian employers and workers who do not display a Spirit-filled work ethic or relationship with their colleagues. What kind of witness is that?

Worker Attrition Most relevant research reveals that the number one reason for missionaries to leave the field is poor interpersonal relationships! They have studied for many years in Bible Schools and language seminaries, interned in home churches, invested a large portion of their lives in preparation, and, after one term overseas, have returned home bitter, disillusioned, embarrassed, and hurt. This ought not to be!

In North America, the average tenure for a pastor in a local church is fewer than five years. The first year is honeymoon, the second, familiarity. In the third year, disillusionment sets in with rumblings of discontent; both the pastor and the church members have unfulfilled expectations of one another.

The fourth year sees the discontent come to the surface, often with acrimony and accusations. People take sides, a lot of heat is generated, and the pastor leaves, usually saying, “I don’t have to put up with this!” What kind of witness is that?

Church Fights Have you ever been involved in a church fight? It is not a pleasant thing! I know of one church, once over three hundred people, now non-existent. Everyone in that town seems to know some aspect of the story, and there are many people, once faithful in attendance, who say that they will never attend a church again!

The wounds are real because the fighting was bitter. Believers would fire ‘gunshots’ at one another assassinating one another, which reverberated all around the town. Satan gloated, and the Lord wept!

Of course, most of our fighting is kept indoors, or is more subtle. I read an interesting newspaper article where it told of a group of ministers establishing support groups for pastors who had grievances against their church or church organization. It told of ministers in one denomination, who were “suing for big money,” and then added that churches are a lot more brutal to their pastors than businesses are to their employees, and that the most vicious are in the evangelical tradition (Christian Week (Canada), June 21, 94).

Look at the Saturday evening church ads in your local newspaper to see how we compete with one another in the arena of winning more people to our church - usually from some other church! It is well documented that most church growth is transfer growth, not conversion growth. Personal anecdotes are not to be commended, but I once had an interesting experience worth recounting.

It was early in the university year and all the local pastors were invited to meet with the students to tell them about our churches. We were given two minutes each to make our pitch.

I listened as, one after the other, pastors extolled the virtues of their churches. “We have a wonderful ‘College and Career Group’ and can send our bus to pick you up.” “You’ll really enjoy our music - it’s up-beat, just as young people like it!”

“Most of your fellow students attend our church since we are located near the campus.” I was roughly the 30th pastor in the line-up, and was pastoring a small, struggling work. When I stood, I told the students that we were a small church with no special programs. We had nothing to offer them, except work if they wanted to help us reach our neighborhood for Christ.

I sat down - and the students broke into applause!

As the church grew, a substantial number of our congregation were university students. Why do we compete with one another for the sheep when we all serve the same Great Shepherd? What kind of witness is that?

Why do we find it so difficult to honor one another, to love , and serve one another? Is it simply our pride getting in the way while, at the same time, we speak about being filled with the Spirit? Or are we just ignorant of the fact that we are in a battle, and that the enemy is very cunning?

Be very sure of this! If it is the Lord’s priority to have a people in right relationships with one another in obedience to His Word, it certainly is Satan’s priority to mar such relationships! “Divide and conquer,” might as well be his motto.
fields.body_text: God’s desire, and the priority on the heart of Jesus, is that He will have a people whose love for one another, and attitude of servanthood will be such a witness to this world that men and women will be crying out to know our Lord. They will want to know the secret of our peace, joy, and harmony. They will watch our marriages, homes, children, and workplaces, not to criticize, but to know our secrets. Having urged his readers to be “filled with the Spirit,” and expressing one evidence of being so filled, as being “subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21),Paul gives examples of how this should be in our relationships. Christian Marriage → Ephesians 5:22-33 If Christian marriages were what they are supposed to be, with both parties Spirit-filled and submitted to one another, honoring, and preferring the other, they would be the mystery revealed to a watching world. Men would see the relationship that Jesus has with His bride, the church, and would be drawn to know Him as the foundation for his marriage also. There would be a steady path of seekers coming to our home or church door, rather than rushing, as they now do, to the divorce courts! Women would want to honor their own husband above all other men, because of the love they receive, and men would want to love their wives because of the honor they receive. Rather than a vicious circle of abuse and retaliation which is so common in the world, there would be a delicious circle of blessing one another in Christ. It is so tragic that divorce is so common among Christian believers. What kind of witness is that? The Christian Home → Ephesians 6:1-4 Where parents are in the right relationships with the Lord and with one another, their children mature in a secure, loving home. Most of the counseling I do as a pastor has to do with wounds received by children growing up in a rather different situation, though often “Christian” fathers fail to disciple (or discipline) their children and, instead, provoke them to anger (Colossians 3:21). Christian counselors today speak of dysfunctional families where the child’s ‘love tank’ is not filled with the love it was created to receive, because the dysfunctional parents are incapable of providing that love. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self- esteem, acceptance, and encouragement. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self- esteem, acceptance, and encouragement. Instead of growing up emotionally and spiritually healthy, they become just like their parents, dysfunctional. They never learn to walk tall in a world of bowed shoulders and broken hearts. The empty space in their love tank is filled with one thing: anger, which produces a life of rebellion to God’s purposes. Such children never learn to obey their parents in the Lord. “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Colossians 3:21). It is so tragic that so many rebellious children are the product of “Christian” homes. What kind of witness is that? I am familiar with a teacher whose school was to be amalgamated with two others in a major reorganization. All the teachers from the three schools gathered together to form a Staff Association to speak on the teachers’ behalf to the School Governors, expressing their desires for the design of the new school buildings and their terms of employment. One man was nominated and seconded for the position of president for this new association. Another was nominated and seconded. Then, much to his surprise, my friend was nominated. Immediately, the two others who had been nominated withdrew their names in order to second my friend’s nomination. No other names were presented and he was elected unanimously to represent all the staff. As he left the room he expressed amazement to a colleague. “Just wait till I tell my wife,” he said. “She’ll never believe me!” “Why not?” replied the colleague, “We all know you’re the only one we can trust to always speak the truth!” My friend was the only Christian on the senior staff of those schools. Sadly, I am often told by business men (Christians among them) that the worst people to do business with are Christians. They want the most out of you for the least payment. They are the poorest at giving tips, and often the last in settling debts! Of course, it may well be that we are judged more harshly by the world than non-believers are, but that is to be expected! fields.title: The Devices of Satan
fields.body_html:
When Jesus died on the cross and then rose again, He conquered Satan and his demonic hosts, taking away all their power, “having disarmed the powers and authorities He made a show of them openly” (Colossians 2:15). They now wage war through lies, deceit, and fear which he works into all areas of our lives: our attitudes, emotions, thoughts, and even the physical.

However, they only have power in these areas as we give it to them! The apostle Paul declared that we are not ignorant of his devices (2 Corinthians 2:11), but unfortunately that is just not true for the majority of believers today!

The Devil’s Opportunity Have you ever been angry? Of course you have. Me too. And so was Jesus when He saw the money changers in the temple.

I’m sure He was also angry when He saw the multitudes in deep poverty and with much sickness. His heart grieved when He saw the results of the disobedience of Adam falling on all mankind. The feeling of anger is not sin. Feelings are not moral or immoral - they are amoral. What we do with our feelings, however, does matter, greatly. Paul exhorts us that when we are angry we must not sin. Then continues to add, “and do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26).

We must deal with the situation right away. If we allow the anger within to fester, it will produce a bitterness that will rob us of God’s best. As long as we are in this world, people will do us wrong, and offenses will come. Jesus warned us of that (Luke 17:1). There might be a ‘good’ cause behind our anger within us, but He has given us His Holy Spirit to enable us to know grace in those times.

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12: 15).

If we do not deal with the anger in the appropriate way (which we will discuss later), we are playing right into the hands of the enemy! Paul continues by saying “and do not give the devil an opportunity” (Ephesians 4:27). Later, in the same portion of Scripture dealing with our conversations with one another, he warns us that we may be grieving the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:30).

When we bear anger (or other wrong attitudes), the enemy has access to our thoughts, spreading his lies and deceit to drive a wedge further in. Soon it appears that reconciliation is impossible, and he has won that battle.

Jesus warned us to be on our guard (Luke 17:3) and Paul charged us to be sure that no advantage be taken of us by Satan (2 Corinthians 2:11). Both are in the context of forgiveness to those whom we perceive as having wronged us. An attitude of unforgiveness (like anger) gives the enemy an advantage - an opportunity - a foothold in our life. The opposite attitudes of forgiveness and peace defeat him.

The Roaring Lion Have you ever seen a lion stalking its prey? I haven’t, but I assume it is much like my cat stalking the birds or mice in our garden. He crouches very low and moves very slowly so as not to warn his intended prey of his intentions. He certainly doesn’t let them know he is coming by making a loud meow!

What, then, does the apostle Peter mean when he tells us to “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8)?

In “Pilgrim’s Progress” by John Bunyan, we read that Pilgrim was approaching the Palace Beautiful which was built for the relief and security of believers. He now understood why Timorous and Mistrust, others seeking the Celestial City, had fled past him in great fear, for the entranceway was guarded by two lions.

Immediately, Pilgrim’s heart sank and he also became afraid.

If a lion came bounding into your room and roared at you, I imagine you would react like them - full of fear! I would!

Roaring lions have that effect on us - they are very frightening.

Soon, Pilgrim noticed that both lions were chained and that, so long as he walked a narrow path between them, neither could reach him to cause him harm. We need to understand that the lion, Satan, has had his teeth pulled and is chained.

He cannot harm the people of God so long as we keep to the narrow way. Even when we step off the narrow way, the Father’s love reaches out to bring us back before the enemy can destroy us. However, he will roar, and many are defeated by their emotions reacting to the roar.

His roar is often that of the accuser, bringing condemnation.

It was the first time Mary had sung the solo parts in the youth choir. It went well except for that high note in the chorus where she was a little weak and wobbly. It was only a quiet voice whispering in her ear that told her, “You made a fool of yourself,” but it was the roar of the lion. She vowed never to sing in public again.

Pastor John had such high hopes when he began ministry at St. Peter’s church. Now, just two years later he was leaving.

The youth group had not grown in numbers as the senior pastor had expected, so John was invited to leave. The lion roared, “you’ll never be successful as a pastor. You’re a failure!” A week later, he reapplied for the secular job he had left when he first believed that God had called him into the pastorate.

Alec had slipped again. He so longed to be free from this filthy habit of smoking, but it was too tempting when he’d been offered this cigarette. Now he was feeling guilty, and the lion roared, “God can’t use you. You’re always letting Him down!”

Not only does the lion roar at every slip or failure, but he knows which of our emotions are the most likely to be affected by the roar. For some it is the emotion of guilt, for others, it’s fear. Many react to his roar in the emotions of low self-esteem, lacking confidence. Where do you react?

How sad when the roar of the lion comes through the thoughtless comment of another believer! It is important in the Body of Christ to affirm one another to counteract the lies - the roar of the devil!

The Archer When one is about to wage a battle, it is good to occupy the high ground. This enables you to see their moves so that you can take the appropriate steps to counteract them. We need to understand as believers, the tremendous privilege we have of being “in Christ.” Paul declares that God has “exalted Jesus, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21).

To the Jews, these are the names of the ranks of the demonic army of Satan, but all of them are far beneath His feet. He has crushed the head of their master and has all authority over them. He wills us to exercise that authority so that we may learn to be overcomers. Those that would reign with Him must be worthy to wear a crown, and crowns are only to be given to the overcomers.

“[Christ has] raised us up with him and seated us with him in the Heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6).

We must live on that higher ground where the only way Satan can reach us is by firing his fiery arrows. We have also been provided with a sure defense against those flaming missiles when Paul writes, “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16) As the enemy would throw his lies and accusations against us, we hold up our shield of faith, remembering that “faith comes by hearing… the Word of God” (Romans 10:17).

We need to know who we are and the privileges of being “ in Christ .”

I am… ● A child of God (John 1:12).

● A friend of Jesus (John 15:15).

● A joint-heir with Christ (Romans 8:17).

● Joined to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:17).

● A member of His Body (Ephesians 5:30).

● Reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:18).

● God’s handiwork (Ephesians 2:10).

● A citizen of Heaven (Philippians 3:20).

● A new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

● Chosen by God (Colossians 3:12).

● A saint (Ephesians 1:1).

● A stranger to this world (1 Peter 2:11).

● What I am (1 Corinthians 15:10).

● Satan’s enemy (1 Peter 5:8).

● Clothed in righteousness (Ephesians 4:24).

● God’s dwelling place (1 Corinthians 3:16).

● A member of a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for God’s own possession (1 Peter 2:9- 10).

In Christ I… ● Am completely forgiven (Romans 5:1).

● Am greatly blessed (Ephesians 1:3).

● Am chosen to be holy (Ephesians 1:4).

● Am sealed by His Spirit (Ephesians 1:13).

● Am predestined to be His child (Ephesians 1:5).

● Have Christ within me (Colossians 1:27).

● Am made complete (Colossians 2:10).

● Am bought back from Satan (Ephesians 1:7).

● Am seated in Heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).

● Am free from condemnation (Romans 8:1).

● Have direct access to God (Ephesians 2:18).

● May come to God confidently (Ephesians 3:12).

For a more complete list, read your Bible!

It used to be that there was a simple remedy for most minor ailments, “Just take two aspirins and go to bed!” Today, I have a simple remedy for most of the minor attacks of the enemy to offer.

Take two of the above Scriptures each day and meditate on them. Your faith will soon grow strong, and the fiery arrows will be less effective against you.

fields.title: Unneeded Baggage
fields.body_html:
“Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

Many are hindered in the battle, not because of the roaring lion or the arrows of lies, but because they have taken upon themselves a burden that they should not be carrying; they have been offended by someone and have taken umbrage.

I was at a viewing place, looking down on Gibraltar. There were many signs warning viewers not to feed the small monkeys that lived in the surrounding trees. Of course, some people chose to ignore the signs with the result that soon, a monkey would land on one’s shoulders. While cameras were in action, the monkey would begin to tangle its fingers in the hair so that, when it became painful, the recipient found difficulty in its removal.

Satan has an army of trained ‘monkeys’ ready to jump on one’s shoulder to tangle their fingers in their victim’s hair.

We need to recognize the monkey of offense and quickly remove it before it robs us of our peace.

Many are hindered in the battle, not because they have been ‘wounded’ by others, but because they have taken upon themselves a burden that they should not be carrying. They have been offended by someone and have ‘taken umbrage.’

We must realize that offense and sin are very different.

Though the former may be a ‘fruit’ of the sinful life, it is not a deliberate sinful act of the one who offends. Indeed, we are told that Jesus was an ‘offense’ to the religious leaders of His time, and He was without sin. It is my belief that He deliberately caused offense on more than one occasion, as I shall present to you shortly.

There may be many causes for offense, but the following are the most common: ● Personality clashes : People will often use this phrase as an ‘excuse’ for not getting along with one another!

● False expectations : Probably, the number one reason pastors and churches separate. We are not very good at making our expectations known before offense occurs.

● Misunderstandings : Poor communication.

● Gifts and talents : I often see people envy others’ prominence, instead of feeling secure in their own ministry or ‘calling.’

● Pride : An affront to one’s ‘ego.’ (for example: a father who is angered (offended) by his son’s average grades in school, believing it reflects poorly on himself).

● Rebellion : The ‘old man’ refuses to die!

A great example of these offenses at work was when a church was undergoing a renovation - they were rebuilding their sanctuary. It had been two long years of hard work for the congregation who were building this church, but God had proven Himself to be faithful.

There were many stories of ‘miracles’ of provision from Jehovah Jireh. It was now time to decide the color scheme for the interior of the sanctuary, so a small committee was formed of members of the church and John, art master at the local school, was asked to lead the group. At their first meeting, John arrived with a portfolio outlining his suggestions (some say ‘decisions’) for the color scheme. It was not long before others present expressed their disagreement with his proposals, having some opinions of their own.

Finally, a vote was taken and a consensus decision made - that did not reflect the art teacher’s views. John was offended and the reverberations of his offense were felt in that church for some time afterwards. Indeed, some even said that that was when the ‘miracles’ ceased.

John is no different than all of us! It is so easy to be offended without realizing the terrible negative impact this can have on ourselves and on the work of Christ. It is a major weapon used by Satan in defeating us in the battle. Be sure of this - offenses will come (Luke 17:1). Jesus told us of their certainty and warned us how we can be kept from stumbling at the offense: by responding to His requirements for discipleship, made in the Upper Room Let us look at some Biblical examples of people who were offended. We shall seek the cause and note the results of their offense. Hopefully, we shall also discern the Lord’s purposes in allowing the offenses to come. He has promised to deliver us from the ‘evil one,’ but has never promised to deliver us from offenses! He would, however, teach us to recognize the offense and to receive His grace in such times of testing.

The various translations of the New Testament can confuse us on this topic, so let us understand that the Greek word, “skandalon” is variously translated as “a stumbling block.” In other words, “an offense,” or “a falling away.”

The Sower and the Seed → Matthew 13:18-21 In the verses above, Jesus teaches a crowd this well known parable as well as interprets the parable for them, likening the four types of soil to four types of hearers of the God’s Word.

The ‘stony places’ describes the person who “hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away” (Matthew 13:20-21).

This is a believer who doesn’t like what the Bible teaches him. He had anticipated that being a Christian would be easy!

He wanted joy and peace, but wasn’t prepared to take up his cross (Matthew 16:24), to pay the price of servanthood. By and by, he is offended and falls away, the result being no fruit !

A Prophet Without Honour → Matthew 13:54-57 Jesus came to His own town of Nazareth where He taught in the synagogue. His neighbors were astonished at His teaching, questioning where He received such wisdom. “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” they said. “We’ve known him since childhood! Who does he think he is?” There is a common phrase, ‘familiarity often breeds contempt’ and as we read in verse 57, those from Jesus’ hometown “took offense at Him.”

How many young men and women, responding to God’s call on their lives, have tried to answer that call, but have been hindered by the greater ‘wisdom’ of their neighbors:family, friends, and church leaders! I am reminded of the old prophet in 1 Kings 13 who was offended because God was using another young man to proclaim His word. Because of his offense, the old prophet deceived the young man, the result being the silencing of his witness, through death!

As a result of their offense in Nazareth, “he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:58). A sure way to stop the Lord moving in miraculous ways in your life, is to take offense. The result of their being offended was no miracles !

The Betrayer → Matthew 26:6-14 Jesus was at the home of Simon, a leper, when a woman came in with an expensive box of perfumed ointment. She broke it over the Lord’s feet and began to wipe them with her hair, so that the fragrance filled the house. Matthew tells us that the disciples were offended when they saw this ‘waste,’ declaring that the perfume could have been sold for a high price and the money given to the poor (Matthew 26:8).

Just after this, Judas Iscariot went to the chief priests in order to betray his master (Matthew 26:14-16). In John’s account of this event, we are told it was Judas himself, who made the complaint, being offended, “not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the money bag he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6).

I remember when a well-known international charity spent over one million dollars to make a documentary film about their work. Many of their supporters expressed indignation at such ‘waste’ and withheld their monthly contributions. They felt themselves to be justly indignant; however, within one year, the proceeds from the showing of that film, exceeded five times the cost of making it! I believe we should rather be on the cautious side when we come to spend the Lord’s money, but taking offense could be a greater source of embarrassment!

Judas was offended, so he went out to betray his master. The potential for betrayal was already there, but the offense stirred that potential into action. The result of his offense was that he no longer trusted the Lord to do what He said He would. Judas would goad Him into action. If He were the promised Messiah who would establish His kingdom in place of the Roman empire, now was the time to prove it! But only one thing was proved - that he, Judas, was a poor politician and an even poorer friend!

Judas had lost confidence in the Lord! Where is your confidence placed? What do you place your trust and your hope in? Christian ‘hope’ is an eager expectation that what He has promised, He will complete! The hymnist declares “My hope is built on nothing less than Jesus’ blood and righteousness!” (My Hope is Built On Nothing Less, Robert Critchley).

The writer of Hebrews encourages us to “not throw away [our] confidence, which has a great reward” (Hebrews 10:35).

When we are offended, a lack of hope will be the result, and therefore, we will have no confidence !

Peter’s Denial → Matthew 26:31-35, 69-75 Jesus had just come to the Mount of Olives, having instituted the communion covenant with His disciples. He now teaches them that He is about to be taken away from them.

Jesus tells His disciples, that “You shall all be offended because of Me tonight.” But Peter, being brave and foolish, says, “I will never be offended in You, even if everyone else is!” (Matthew 26:31-33). How he must have regretted those words just a few hours later! I feel for Peter because he is so much like me! How wonderful a Savior we have who, feeling his pain, would appear first to Peter after His resurrection, and before the others saw Him (Luke 24: 34). I can only imagine that scene as the two of them were reconciled through the Saviour’s love.

John and Peter entered the house of the High Priest where Jesus was being tried. As Peter passed through the doorway a slave girl said to him, “Aren’t you one of His disciples?” He responded, “I am not!” Then two more times he denies his Lord, adding some choice oaths before the roosters crow.

I like to imagine that young slave girl and her question. Could it have been possible that she was interested in the Lord and wanted to know more about Him? If Peter had acknowledged his discipleship, would she have asked him to tell her about his friend since she wanted to love Him also? However, Peter was offended , and the result of his offense was no testimony !

Many Turn Away → John 6:53-61 In this passage, Jesus is speaking some hard things to His followers. He is calling them to “eat of My flesh and drink of My blood” (John 6:53). Today, in retrospect, we understand this in terms of the communion cup and the new covenant He has called us into, but to them it was a hard saying which was difficult to understand.

Jesus asked them, “Are you offended?”

Are you offended by His call to the discipleship demanded in the communion covenant? The discipleship which is the core challenge of this book? The result of their offense was that many of His disciples went back and walked no more with Him (John 6:66). The result of their offense was no community.

So we have five Biblical examples of those who were offended, with the result that they lost their fruit , confidence , and testimony . Within them there was disunity, and God didn’t do any miracles among them! Therefore we can be sure Satan must have gloated.

fields.title: The Rock of Offense
fields.body_html:
Jesus was the cause of much offense! Both Peter and Paul quote the Old Testament in calling Him “a rock of offense” (Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8).

The Pharisees were offended by Him, demons were offended by Him, and even His family was offended by Him!

But to some He deliberately avoided offending such as the despised tax gatherers. He told Peter to go to the sea where he would find the required tax in the mouth of a fish, “so that we do not give them any offense” (Matthew 17: 24) But to others He seems to deliberately offend!

John the Baptist - Jesus’ Cousin John the Baptist was second cousin to Jesus and had been born just a few months before Him. He was full of the Holy Spirit even while in his mother’s womb and was the first to show any response to the promised Messiah. He had leapt in Elizabeth’s womb when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had first come to tell the remarkable story of her baby’s conception.

I’m sure the two boys must have spent many hours together during childhood. They had probably played and worked together, run and fought together, and talked and argued together. Perhaps they even talked together about the burden that was growing in each of their hearts.

Finally, John leaves home to answer a strange compulsion. It could have been possible that Jesus was the only one who understood when he announced that he must “prepare the way of the Lord” (Matthew 3:3), and then he left for the desert.

There, John began to preach to all who would listen to him.

“The Messiah is coming soon” he would proclaim, “and we are not ready! Repent and be baptized. Return to your God!”

(Matthew 3:2-12) The people responded, seeking to be reconciled to Jehovah and indicating their new resolve by being baptized in the local stream, the River Jordan. Theirs was a baptism of repentance and a return to orthodoxy.

One day Jesus came to the Jordan River and John cried out to the people, “Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sin of the World!” (John 1:29). John gave witness that he saw a dove descending upon Jesus and remaining upon him.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit had already told John that this would be the sign of the coming Messiah in John 1:34 where it’s written “I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”

John was not a popular preacher who ‘tickled men’s ears.’

Most of those who came to hear and see him were looking for a curiosity, hoping that they would be there to hear his condemnation of the self-righteous leaders of the synagogue.

He had some choice things to say to such leaders and the people loved it; however, Herod did not. He was the ruler of the Roman Empire at the time, and was a wicked man who was having an affair with his sister-in-law - an affair that John openly condemned. To silence his voice Herod had John sent to prison.

I can imagine the thoughts of John while in those dungeons.

“Herod, you old fool! You think you are in control and that putting me in prison will silence my voice. But my cousin is the Messiah and He has come to overthrow your little empire and to establish His own kingdom! He’ll get me out of this prison soon, and you will be the one locked away! He has declared that He has come to set the captive free. I can hardly wait to see your face when He does it!” And with that, John sits back in his cell and waits… and waits… and waits… Meanwhile, Jesus continues with His ministry in the nearby villages, not even finding the time to visit John in prison!

Surely, He would at least come to visit him! But because He doesn’t come, John gets offended and subsequently was beheaded! John’s disciples are sent to Jesus to ask a pointed question. “Are you truly the Messiah or should we wait for another?” (Matthew 11:3). “You do not meet our criteria since You are not doing what we expected You to do!”

Jesus replies, “And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (Luke 7:22- 23).

Jesus’ Dear Friend Mary Jesus had some very special friends who lived in the small town of Bethany. He was just a few miles away when He received news that His friend Lazarus was dying and that his sisters Mary and Martha were grieving for him. “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was” (John 11:5-6).

We do not read of any miracles, any teaching, or anything that He did during those two days! And Lazarus died! When Jesus finally came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days and his sisters were in deep sorrow. It is Martha who comes out to greet Him. That is noteworthy, for she was the one we often think of as ‘the drudge’ - the one who was kitchen-bound - while her sister Mary would leave everything to sit at Jesus’ feet, washing them with precious perfume and wiping them with her hair while absorbing everything He said. Today, Mary would be prominent in Christian activity - president of the local Women’s Adoration Group while her sister would be in the background making coffee and serving cookies.

Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here my brother would not have died” (John 11:21). Jesus assures her that her brother will live again, for He is the resurrection and the life.

I do not hear any condemnation in Martha's comment, just sadness. She then goes to Mary, to ask her to come to Jesus.

But why isn’t Mary already there? Surely, she knows that He is coming? Everyone would be aware of that, but Mary sat still in the house. Why? May I suggest that she was pouting!

She was offended ! When she comes to Jesus, she falls before Him weeping and says the same words as Martha had. “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:32).

Note that Jesus does not say the same comforting words to Mary that He expressed to her sister. Could this have been because of the tone of her voice? Accusing? Judgemental?

Instead of comforting Mary, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), but not because Lazarus was dead - He had known that for some time and also that, in a short while, all would be rejoicing at his resurrection. He didn’t weep because Mary, Martha, and their friends were in sorrow - He had known that they would be for that was natural at the death of a loved one.

He wept because Mary was offended.

Jesus would die for our “offenses,” but He still grieves when we take offense.

On the journey to Bethany, Jesus had told His disciples that people are often offended when they cannot understand. They are walking in the dark (John 11:10). Had He known how Mary would react?

Why Offenses Come Why does the Lord allow offenses to come? Could it be that His purpose is to reveal to us something about ourselves? Did John have to realize that, though he had declared that, “He must increase, and I must decrease” (John 3:30), that the timetable has to be the Lord’s not his.

It’s easy for us to fall into the trap of trying to manipulate God into doing things our way. It’s too easy to cross the line between accomplishing His will, versus our will. We must not get offended when He doesn’t do things ‘our way’ because only He knows what is best for us, even when we cannot see the reasons for the valleys we experience.

Did Mary need to learn that obedience and trust is far better than prominence and popularity, even in the Lord’s ‘service?’

Greatness in the Kingdom comes to those who would be least, even as servants (Luke 9:48).

What to Do With Offenses First, you must own it ! The offense is yours! Another has not sinned against you - you ‘took the monkey’ on your own shoulders, so throw it off - or carry it!

Next, examine it ! The Lord allowed it to come that it may teach you something about yourself.

I have had to learn some hard things this way, and I have given you some of the reasons for offenses in the previous chapter. You must study your personality types and learn to major on your strengths. For example, most pastors tend to be melancholics. One gift of the melancholic is the ability to see problems long before others do. This can cause them to be critical of others, offended by their inability to see ‘the obvious,’ and to do something about it. Thank God you are not all like me!

Everybody’s giftings are different. For many years I was offended by others’ failure to recognize my teaching as a ‘gift.’ Everyone thinks they can teach, and I have had to learn to be ‘thick skinned’ when people ignore my giftings and calling as a pastor.

Once you have owned it and examined it , discard it !

By choice, pray about it and bury it! Bless those who have offended you and seek the empowering of the Holy Spirit if the offense seems too heavy - He has promised to be sufficient for all your trials.

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:14-15).

Then, the last step to take when the monkeys are on your shoulders, is to forget it ! Do not let the offense dwell in your heart any longer. Hand it off to the Lord, and let it off of your mind and heart.

Finally, do not be the one who causes offense , for, “woe to him through whom they come!” (Luke 17:1)!

John’s disciples are sent to Jesus to ask a pointed question. “Are you truly the Messiah or should we wait for another?” (Matthew 11:3). “You do not meet our criteria since You are not doing what we expected You to do!” Jesus replies, “And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (Luke 7:22- 23). Jesus’ Dear Friend Mary Jesus had some very special friends who lived in the small town of Bethany. He was just a few miles away when He received news that His friend Lazarus was dying and that his sisters Mary and Martha were grieving for him. “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was” (John 11:5-6). We do not read of any miracles, any teaching, or anything that He did during those two days! And Lazarus died! When Jesus finally came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days and his sisters were in deep sorrow. It is Martha who comes out to greet Him. That is noteworthy, for she was the one we often think of as ‘the drudge’ - the one who was kitchen-bound - while her sister Mary would leave everything to sit at Jesus’ feet, washing them with precious perfume and wiping them with her hair while absorbing everything He said. Today, Mary would be prominent in Christian activity - president of the local Women’s Adoration Group while her sister would be in the background making coffee and serving cookies. Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here my brother would not have died” (John 11:21). Jesus assures her that her brother will live again, for He is the resurrection and the life. I do not hear any condemnation in Martha's comment, just sadness. She then goes to Mary, to ask her to come to Jesus. But why isn’t Mary already there? Surely, she knows that He is coming? Everyone would be aware of that, but Mary sat still in the house. Why? May I suggest that she was pouting! She was offended ! When she comes to Jesus, she falls before Him weeping and says the same words as Martha had. “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:32). Note that Jesus does not say the same comforting words to Mary that He expressed to her sister. Could this have been because of the tone of her voice? Accusing? Judgemental? Instead of comforting Mary, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), but not because Lazarus was dead - He had known that for some time and also that, in a short while, all would be rejoicing at his resurrection. He didn’t weep because Mary, Martha, and their friends were in sorrow - He had known that they would be for that was natural at the death of a loved one. He wept because Mary was offended. Jesus would die for our “offenses,” but He still grieves when we take offense. On the journey to Bethany, Jesus had told His disciples that people are often offended when they cannot understand. They are walking in the dark (John 11:10). Had He known how Mary would react? Why Offenses Come Why does the Lord allow offenses to come? Could it be that His purpose is to reveal to us something about ourselves? Did John have to realize that, though he had declared that, “He must increase, and I must decrease” (John 3:30), that the timetable has to be the Lord’s not his. It’s easy for us to fall into the trap of trying to manipulate God into doing things our way. It’s too easy to cross the line between accomplishing His will, versus our will. We must not get offended when He doesn’t do things ‘our way’ because only He knows what is best for us, even when we cannot see the reasons for the valleys we experience. Did Mary need to learn that obedience and trust is far better than prominence and popularity, even in the Lord’s ‘service?’ Greatness in the Kingdom comes to those who would be least, even as servants (Luke 9:48). What to Do With Offenses First, you must own it ! The offense is yours! Another has not sinned against you - you ‘took the monkey’ on your own shoulders, so throw it off - or carry it! Next, examine it ! The Lord allowed it to come that it may teach you something about yourself. I have had to learn some hard things this way, and I have given you some of the reasons for offenses in the previous chapter. You must study your personality types and learn to major on your strengths. For example, most pastors tend to be melancholics. One gift of the melancholic is the ability to see problems long before others do. This can cause them to be critical of others, offended by their inability to see ‘the obvious,’ and to do something about it. Thank God you are not all like me! Everybody’s giftings are different. For many years I was offended by others’ failure to recognize my teaching as a ‘gift.’ Everyone thinks they can teach, and I have had to learn to be ‘thick skinned’ when people ignore my giftings and calling as a pastor. Once you have owned it and examined it , discard it ! By choice, pray about it and bury it! Bless those who have offended you and seek the empowering of the Holy Spirit if the offense seems too heavy - He has promised to be sufficient for all your trials. “Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:14-15). Then, the last step to take when the monkeys are on your shoulders, is to forget it ! Do not let the offense dwell in your heart any longer. Hand it off to the Lord, and let it off of your mind and heart. Finally, do not be the one who causes offense , for, “woe to him through whom they come!” (Luke 17:1)!

fields.title: The Wounded Soul
fields.body_html:
The Bible clearly presents to us the devices of Satan as seen in: ● The roaring lion affecting our emotions.

● The arrows of lies affecting our thoughts.

● The ‘monkeys’ of offense affecting our peace.

However, his most effective device is not so clearly understood. He has targeted you from before your birth. He is not omniscient, so he doesn’t know if you will become a believer and an opponent in the battle, so he has tried to wound you before you were aware of any battle. This is evident in the large number of ‘dysfunctional’ people in our churches, but it is my belief that there are many more who struggle, but are unaware of their wound.

A New Creation When I became a believer I was taught that “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). This verse was used to challenge me concerning the little things of the old nature that still were present in my life. Naturally, I was made to feel guilty. I eased my guilt by reasoning that my old habits weren’t as bad as some of those I saw in others. We were very quick to condemn those who were not so able as we were to overcome their old habits, particularly those obvious “sins” such as smoking and drinking, not to mention dancing and keeping company with those who do such things! I’m glad I have come to understand this verse better, and to understand something more of the grace of God.

Thank God that in Christ we are fully accepted and reconciled to the Father - that we are justified, forgiven, and made new creatures. However, my teeth did not shed their fillings and return to the undecayed brightness of my youth when I was converted. Indeed, my body has not been made a new creation, rather, it continues to die day by day.

The ‘new creation’ refers to that part of me which once was dead - my spirit. I am aware that there is much confusion about the difference between the soul and the spirit but, for the purpose of this book, I shall call the spirit that part of me which, now being alive to God, differentiates me from an unconverted person, whose spirit is dead however noble or religious they may be. They, like me, have a body with varying degrees of health, but which will surely die one day, unless the Lord comes before.

We also have souls - our minds, our wills, and our emotions.

Even the non-Christian man has a living soul. At conversion, these are not made a new creation; they carry many wounds from the past and provide a fertile battlefield for Satan. He knows the wounds - after all, his hosts were very active in causing them! For too long we have made many new (and some older) believers feel incompetent in the battle by charging them to be more mature than their wounded souls have allowed them to be. We have urged them to run when their soul is crippled - to fight when their muscles have atrophied! Instead, we should have been ministering to their hurts and wounds, bringing healing through Biblical teaching since the Lord has committed unto us the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).

Bruises of the Soul Many people have been subject for most of their lives to continuous criticism and verbal abuse perhaps from a parent or siblings. Their retiring personality invites others to continue this abuse at school or at work, then they enter adulthood with great ‘bruises’ on their soul. They are often accused of being too sensitive, and indeed they are, as a result of the abuse. They function well enough until criticized again when they find themselves unable to handle the pain. New bruises are formed and each new criticism, real or imagined, is like a punch on the bruise.

Peter had been raised in a somber, though Christian home. He was an only child and had few friends. He was not allowed to bring friends home from school because they were ‘worldly’ and there were no other youth his age that attended the small church his family went to. He could never quite meet his father’s expectations or demands and was unable to hold a job for very long. He was never made to feel good enough to be accepted. In his mid-thirties he left home and went to work for a Christian mission where he was befriended by three other men. He began to enjoy his work and friends and became a well-accepted part of that ministry until, just over a year of working there, each of his three friends announced that they would soon be leaving to work elsewhere.

Instead of the usual sorrow one would expect, Peter began to act in a strange way. He deliberately set out to make himself disliked by his departing friends. For example, he would borrow something from one of them, and deliberately break it, claiming that it was an accident. Each of the friends left the mission offended by Peter.

Just why did he act like this? He told me that it had started just after he had returned from holidays - at home. That had not been a good time and he had been glad to return to the mission. When I suggested that his experience of more criticism at home had produced renewed bruising on his soul, and that the departure of his friends had been like punches on the bruising, Peter broke down and cried. “That’s exactly how I feel,” he declared, “their leaving just added to my feelings of being unworthy of love and acceptance.” Today, Peter is walking in a new freedom, knowing his worthiness in Christ.

Stab Wounds For others, the wound may have been created by a single act - a wound similar to being stabbed. A classic example, of course, is the child who is sexually abused by a trusted, loved one. In this example, the child does not understand that they are the victim and not the guilty one. They are afraid to speak about the incident, choosing rather, to bury it in their memory.

Sometime afterwards, the wound is covered over and not easily brought to the surface to be faced, even in adulthood.

The ‘bandage’ with which the wound was covered has become a bondage affecting other areas of the adult’s personality. Such a soul needs healing!

When I asked Alec why he couldn’t read or write, he told me a sad story. For four years his mother had doted on him, her only child, after his father had walked out on them. Then another father came on the scene - one who did not like or want Alec around him. He soon knew the deep pain of rejection.

At the age of five, Alec started primary school where he would sit in the back of the room, daydreaming. He remembers well the occasion when an unthinking teacher shouted at him. “Alec, you’re nothing but a dumbo!” The hurting, little soul said to himself, “If that’s what you think I am, that’s what I’ll be!” He resolved, as a young child, never to study to please that teacher… and therefore grew into a teenage illiterate!

Was Alec bright enough to have learned? Just one month after we talked, Alec was reading all the sports news in the daily newspaper! He had an interest in a young lady and was motivated to walk out healing. I used his knowledge of sports personalities and their photographs in the newspapers, to encourage him in reading the words explaining the pictures.

Soon, he needed no pictures and I watched his self-esteem grow as he began to read with understanding. So many teachers, parents, and others will never know the negative significance of the stabbing wounds their unthinking words have had on so many young souls. Many adults today are still carrying the scabs and scars from those wounds on their souls!

Grazes Then there’s the grazing kinds of wounds. They usually leave no scar or permanent bondage, but can bleed profusely at the time of injury. If not treated correctly, however, they can fester and then produce far worse injury. I see such wounds of the soul occurring when one experiences discouragement or a great disappointment. It is accompanied by feelings of inadequacy and loneliness, and spiritual defenses are down.

This is the time when we need to come around in tender support for the hurting one. It is the time for empathy and understanding.

Mary had become ill with “Epstein Barr” or “Yuppie Flu” which was widely known as the disease of the nineties. It was hard not knowing how long she was likely to be ill, for the doctors had no ready cure. The members of her church were praying for her, but she wished someone would come to visit her. No one came, giving their reason that they were unsure if such a disease was contagious. That was hard to accept, but Mary did so with grace. Then one day, she received a telephone call which caused much ‘bleeding’ of her soul. Her closest friend called to tell her that the church had stopped praying for Mary since it was obvious she was not exercising faith. Her reasoning being, that if she had been so doing, she would have been well by then.

Fractures Let us continue with our metaphors. Are there such wounds as fractures in the soul? Yes, and there are many believers who are limping through life because of some traumatic experience. It may be the death of a loved one, a broken engagement, or some accident of life. They were crippled by the experience and have never learned to walk again.

Melinda had an argument with her mother during which she had pushed her away with some force. Some months later, mother was diagnosed as having developed breast cancer, and within a year, had died. No amount of argument could convince Melinda that her push had not created the cancer in her mother. She would not forgive herself and could not accept the Lord’s forgiveness. She was a broken woman when I met her, and to this day, remains crippled.

“He Restores My Soul” I am convinced that many believers today have wounded souls. I am also convinced that the Lord wants to heal those wounds - to restore the soul. The psalmist David was guilty of adultery and murder; he carried terrible soul wounds, but he could still say, “The Lord is my shepherd… He restores my soul” (Psalm 23:3).

There are also wounds created by our own doings. It seems to me that when we deliberately act contrary to the explicit Word of God, we create our own wounds. Sex outside of marriage and divorce will always create wounded souls that need healing through the grace of God. Be very sure that it is His desire to bring such healing. Indeed, I see this as the true work of sanctification - the second part of salvation.

Justification is when one has been set free from the penalty of sin: salvation for one’s spirit. The Holy Spirit has already completed this work.

Sanctification is when one has been set free from the power of sin: salvation for one’s soul. This is the present work of the Holy Spirit.

Glorification is when one has been set free from the presence of sin: salvation for the body. This is the work that the Holy Spirit has yet to do.

For these reasons we call Him Savior!

The Angler We have likened Satan to a roaring lion and an archer; however, it seems to me that his most effective warring device is like an angler’s hook and rod -he knows exactly where our soul wounds are. After all, he was instrumental in creating them. When we get ready to enter the battle in the heavenlies, he then casts his line, hooks it into the wound, and manipulates the soul into ineffectiveness.

A Personal Story Early in 1990 I became closely involved in a new work of God among the native peoples of western Canada. The spiritual battle was intense. I also stopped sleeping at the same time. My doctor tried many different medications to get me to sleep, but it was several weeks before a way was found for me not to lie awake all night. Many thought I was under an Indian curse and I would receive letters and telephone calls of encouragement from throughout the north-west of America and Canada. I asked Charles and Claudia, another pastor and his wife, to pray for me, at which time she told me that she was aware of a “terrible spirit of abandonment” upon me. I had no understanding of what she meant.

Shortly afterwards, I was invited to spend a week at an Anglican Retreat for clergymen and wives. There I was told that there was an area of my emotions missing and it had much to do with my mother’s death. My mother had died when I was a teenager, and though I had not cried at the time in a normal mourning, I thought I had dealt with her death very well. Now I was being told that this had something to do with my sleeplessness? I still did not understand.

After four months I offered to resign my position at the church, but the elders and members would not let me. Instead, much love was shown to me by them and the greater church body of our city.

After eight months, I entered Vancouver University Hospital as a patient in the sleep clinic where it was diagnosed that there had been a physical breakdown in my body’s production of the sleep-inducing neurochemicals. The specialist put this down to stress. The next week, I was able to resign from the church, which had now decreased to sixty percent the attendance rate it had been at the beginning of the year.

The following Tuesday I was with a group of my closest friends, other pastors who met together weekly for prayer. As we finished our breakfast, one of them said to me, “Gareth, I sense an awful spirit of abandonment upon you!” These were the same words I had heard almost nine months earlier. When I got back home, I called Claudia to ask her to explain to me just what she had meant by her comment. She told me to sit down that evening and to go back over my life, looking for the times when the little boy in me might have felt abandoned.

My wife Anne and I were amazed as we considered the different periods of my life - there were so many times when I had felt the pain of abandonment, not least of which was my mother’s death when I was just fourteen. I had not cried then, but for some time afterwards, I had grieved. Later that same evening I relaxed to read a novel about the Crusades of the thirteenth century.

Two knights were leading their men into battle on the fields of France. Suddenly, they were face to face; however, Sir Rufus had been wounded and was slumped over in his saddle, his sword hanging by his side. His enemy, Sir Nigel, quickly rode toward him, raising his mighty sword to slay his opponent. Just as he would strike the fatal blow, nine arrows from Sir Rufus’ bowmen flew through the air to find their target in Sir Nigel’s armpit. They were ineffective against his armor, but very effective at his weak spot, where no armor could be worn. I sensed that the Spirit of the Lord was speaking to me.

“Gareth, you might be putting on the armor of God, but when you go into battle against the enemy, be aware that he knows exactly where your weakest spots are - and yours is that of abandonment. They must be healed if you would be effective in the battle!”

I now began to understand why people had been drifting away from our church over the past two years. Three elders had left because of job relocation and had been replaced by three other good men; however, the new elders’ board did not have the gifts necessary to maintain the programs initiated by the former men and soon there began a slow exodus from the church. I would meet people on the street who would rush up to me to tell me that they loved me, but had started to go to another church “because our children enjoy their youth work so much.” There were many reasons, but few had displayed the grace to come and tell me of their intentions. I would have gladly given them letters of introduction if I had known they wanted to transfer.

Then, as I grew more weary, I was not feeding and leading my flock as they were used to, so more began to leave. Instead of the fulfillment I was used to, I had the pain, almost every week, of seeing another vacant pew. Since I was very committed to my people, each departure was like a mini divorce. I’m sure that none of those people would have deliberately hurt me, but their actions were used by the enemy as hooks in my wounds of abandonment. No wonder the doctor called it stress, even though I would boast that I never took my church problems home with me!

A personal note for readers potentially planning on leaving your local church: do it the right and ethical way. Let your pastor know of your intentions, because you’d be surprised if you knew exactly how easily we wound one another.
