After four months I offered to resign my position at the church, but the elders and members would not let me. Instead, much love was shown to me by them and the greater church body of our city. After eight months, I entered Vancouver University Hospital as a patient in the sleep clinic where it was diagnosed that there had been a physical breakdown in my body’s production of the sleep-inducing neurochemicals. The specialist put this down to stress. The next week, I was able to resign from the church, which had now decreased to sixty percent the attendance rate it had been at the beginning of the year. The following Tuesday I was with a group of my closest friends, other pastors who met together weekly for prayer. As we finished our breakfast, one of them said to me, “Gareth, I sense an awful spirit of abandonment upon you!” These were the same words I had heard almost nine months earlier. When I got back home, I called Claudia to ask her to explain to me just what she had meant by her comment. She told me to sit down that evening and to go back over my life, looking for the times when the little boy in me might have felt abandoned. My wife Anne and I were amazed as we considered the different periods of my life - there were so many times when I had felt the pain of abandonment, not least of which was my mother’s death when I was just fourteen. I had not cried then, but for some time afterwards, I had grieved. Later that same evening I relaxed to read a novel about the Crusades of the thirteenth century. Two knights were leading their men into battle on the fields of France. Suddenly, they were face to face; however, Sir Rufus had been wounded and was slumped over in his saddle, his sword hanging by his side. His enemy, Sir Nigel, quickly rode toward him, raising his mighty sword to slay his opponent. Just as he would strike the fatal blow, nine arrows from Sir Rufus’ bowmen flew through the air to find their target in Sir Nigel’s armpit. They were ineffective against his armor, but very effective at his weak spot, where no armor could be worn. I sensed that the Spirit of the Lord was speaking to me. “Gareth, you might be putting on the armor of God, but when you go into battle against the enemy, be aware that he knows exactly where your weakest spots are - and yours is that of abandonment. They must be healed if you would be effective in the battle!” I now began to understand why people had been drifting away from our church over the past two years. Three elders had left because of job relocation and had been replaced by three other good men; however, the new elders’ board did not have the gifts necessary to maintain the programs initiated by the former men and soon there began a slow exodus from the church. I would meet people on the street who would rush up to me to tell me that they loved me, but had started to go to another church “because our children enjoy their youth work so much.” There were many reasons, but few had displayed the grace to come and tell me of their intentions. I would have gladly given them letters of introduction if I had known they wanted to transfer. Then, as I grew more weary, I was not feeding and leading my flock as they were used to, so more began to leave. Instead of the fulfillment I was used to, I had the pain, almost every week, of seeing another vacant pew. Since I was very committed to my people, each departure was like a mini divorce. I’m sure that none of those people would have deliberately hurt me, but their actions were used by the enemy as hooks in my wounds of abandonment. No wonder the doctor called it stress, even though I would boast that I never took my church problems home with me! A personal note for readers potentially planning on leaving your local church: do it the right and ethical way. Let your pastor know of your intentions, because you’d be surprised if you knew exactly how easily we wound one another.

fields.title: Our Response
fields.body_html:
God’s Priority is Satan’s Priority!

We can be certain of this! Whatever God’s purposes are for mankind, Satan will do his utmost to hinder that work. If it is the Lord’s desire that believers live in unity, the enemy works very hard to hinder such unity.

As we study the Bible it is very evident that relationships are high on God’s priority list. He created us for Himself, and for one another. From cover to cover, the Bible emphasizes relationship: man with God, and man with man.

In Genesis, God created man in His own image - that they might have fellowship together (1 John 1:3). Then for the man, He created a woman, because “it is not good for man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18).

Later, He chose one man from whom would come a special nation. He called Himself, “The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” becoming a Father and husband to their descendants.

Satan did all he could to break these relationships with a lot of help from men themselves! Know that today he is still working frantically to draw men from God, to break up families, and to destroy the Jews.

The Old Testament ends with a wonderful promise concerning relationships, “He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction” (Malachi 4:6).

The emphasis of the New Testament is the same as the old with the added responsibility for the believers of being in unity as a foundation for their witness.

Major sections of the New Testament emphasize this truth, ending with the invitation of the last chapter, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17). “Bride,” like “Body” is a relationship word!

Dysfunctional Wounds If the Lord would mature a man or woman to become a mighty warrior who is effective in the battle against evil, the enemy will try to ‘cripple’ that soldier even before he enters the army as a cadet.

Satan is not omniscient, and therefore, does not know your future. He is neither omnipresent, to wrestle with you every moment, so he must use ‘guerrilla’ tactics in the warfare, with his soldiers (demons) using a ‘hit or miss’ policy. Clear ‘hits’ are seen in the high proportion of people classified as coming from ‘dysfunctional’ families.

Counselors, both secular and Christian, spend many hours trying to teach people how to deal with their wounds - their dysfunction. They hope to bring their patients to a place of ‘maintenance’ where they learn to effectively use the ‘crutches’ the counselors offer them. For example, the goal of Alcoholics Anonymous is to enable their members to maintain their sobriety rather than bringing them to healing.

Sadly, many Christian counselors have adopted worldly methods and tools in dealing with these wounds, seldom bringing their people to the place of healing that Jesus obtained on the cross. “With His wounds, we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Satan’s devices wound many who will never even enter the army against him, since they will never avail themselves of the salvation offered to them in Christ. However, when one is recognized as being in the Body of Christ, then Satan concentrates his efforts on that person, especially if they begin to come on the offensive against him.

The Ministry of Reconciliation Jesus came to defeat Satan’s power in the life of men. In Him, our new relationship should be manifested in our unity as believers: as one Body. Satan has no power to destroy this unity or these relationships, but through ignorance, carnality, and the unhealthy wounds of our souls, we have given him strongholds.

What can we do to correct this situation? Of course, we can pray! After all, without the help and guidance of the Holy Spirit, we can do nothing! However, we must realize that the Father will seldom answer prayer in those areas where He has already given the authority and responsibility to us. The responsibility for reconciliation between people, is no longer His, it is ours. “All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).

We need to deal with our offenses, seek to understand our ‘wounds,’ and use Biblical principles to obtain healing, restoration, and reconciliation. If you are wounded, I trust that this section of the book will give you some assistance in bringing you to a place of wholeness in Christ, knowing as David did, that “He restores the soul” (Psalm 23:3) and that those, “whom the Son sets free, are free indeed” (John 8:36).

The Offended Sheep For those who are counselors, elders, or pastors, I would charge you that this is your ministry. A passage of Scripture that greatly challenges me as a pastor and counselor is found in Matthew 18. The entire context of this chapter is dealing with offense, restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness.

I am particularly challenged by Matthew’s account of the parable of the shepherd and the hundred sheep where it is written, “If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray? And if he finds it, truly, I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray” (Matthew 18:12- 14).

It is a sheep that has left the fold, not a goat. In the New Testament, believers are usually referred to as “sheep” whereas the word “goat” is used for non-believers.

This picture is of the believer who has been offended, and has walked out of the church, possibly with a little poison ready to spread to whomever will listen. All of us have had this happen in our congregations and very often we are tempted to rub our hands together saying, “Good riddance! He was such a miserable man!” Instead, we are urged to go after that sheep, seeking to understand him and to minister to him without condemnation, trusting that the Lord will bring about a reconciliation and restoration. If we did, maybe we would have far fewer ‘miserable men’ in our church!

Sometimes the sheep leaves feeling deeply wounded. I remember a young lady who came to me, deeply hurt because the leaders of her ‘ministry’ had disciplined her, having received some bad reports concerning her; however, no one would tell her what the reports said. I went to see her leaders and was told by her chief judge that they were “letting her stew in her own juice to teach her a lesson.” I told that leader, who considered himself a pastor, that we have no permission to treat the sheep that way.

“If a sheep is caught in a bramble bush, I must crawl in to set it free, even though I may get scratched with thorns and possibly bitten by the hurting sheep. Then I pour in oil and wine and bind up the wounds, before releasing the sheep with the admonition not to go into a bramble bush again. If I hear the bleating again and see the sheep in another bush a little while later, I repeat the process. This continues with more admonition and possible use of a leash, but I can never stand outside the bush, wag my finger and say, ‘Serve you right!

Stew in your own juice!’ The Great Shepherd gave me no such permission when He called me to serve as an under- shepherd!”

That young lady was dismissed from that ministry, though I had clearly shown her leaders that the reports against her were based on a lie! No wonder she was so badly wounded and needed lengthy professional counseling!

fields.title: The Key to Release
fields.body_html:
Much of the counseling I do is to help people deal with their offenses. How many hours would be saved if they knew their personal responsibility and acted according to Biblical principles!

I am of the opinion that one of the major ploys used by the enemy to hinder us in the battle, is the large number of hours spent by pastors (especially in North America), dealing with counseling matters that believers could handle themselves if they were more active in studying the Word.

The role of a pastor should be to do away with most counseling needs of his people, by teaching them Biblical principles. It’s his role, as a shepherds, to lead them to ‘green pastures’ where the sheep feed themselves; however, we have come to the place where the sheep still need to be bottle fed (counseled), every time there is a ‘crisis!’ Satan has robbed the church of many of its shepherds by overloading them with counseling ‘needs.’

A natural analogy is that, if we eat and exercise properly, we will stay in good health; however, one recognizes that there will come times whether through an accident or chronic sickness, that one needs the assistance of another. When there are terrible wounds and the patient is handicapped in some way, the empathy, comfort, and help of another is appreciated. This is the same with spiritual wounds.

There are many Christian books on the market dealing with wounds to the soul. They speak of ‘healing the memories’ of dysfunctional families and codependency. Many of them are very good and have given a lot of help to people seeking a new perspective of life and themselves. The ‘12-step’ program by Alcoholics Anonymous has become the basis for much of this teaching, with the goal of bringing the wounded person to a place of ‘maintenance.’ They are then able to deal with their problem in a practical way, with the use of support groups, ongoing counseling, and prescribed plans or a ‘formula’ of action. Each day, they have a prescription to ‘walk out’ their healing. I have used these books and continue to do so in part. What bothers me about most of them is that few of them mention the releasing effect of forgiveness .

I do not believe that the Lord’s intention is to bring His wounded people to ‘maintenance,’ but that He wishes to restore their souls, and bring them healing. The main purpose of this book is to teach how we can be set free from the bondage of our wounds, so that we can be most effective in the warfare against our enemy, Satan. The key of healing is found in forgiveness.

The Keys to the Kingdom → Matthew 16:19 For three years the disciples had walked with the Lord through the regions of Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. They had watched Him perform many miracles and had heard Him teaching the multitudes, but He had seldom sat down just to talk with them. Now, after a very busy time, He leads them to the far north of the country, to the regions around Caesarea Philippi, on the lower slopes of Mount Hermon. As they walk, the master turns to His disciples and asks them two questions.

The first question is concerning men’s opinions of Jesus, whereas the next question is concerning the disciples opinion of Jesus.

After the disciples answer the first question, He again turns to them, and asks, “But who do you say I am?” (Matthew 16:15). Had they come to understand that Jesus was more than just a good man or a miracle worker?

“Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in Heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 16:16-19).

For centuries, the Roman Catholic Church taught that this is the mandate given to all popes, as successors of Peter, the head of the church, to excommunicate kings, countries, and peoples who do not support their edicts, or grant indulgences.

Wouldn’t it be wonderful if you had the key to the kingdom for your loved ones? For your spouse? For your unsaved child? For your parents? If only you could open up the way to eternal life for them! Well, I believe we have that possibility!

It is certain that many are being kept away from the joys of seeing and entering the kingdom by our failure to be the witnesses we ought to be. Much of that failure is in our attitudes of unforgiveness. There are many parents today who pray, with weeping, for their wayward child, not realizing that the unforgiveness they bear against that child is the greatest hindrance to God answering the prayer!

What did Jesus mean by the latter part of the verse above? I have been given many explanations, from the popes ‘authority,’ to ‘deliverance from the demonic,’ but I see neither here.

It is good exegesis when considering an obscure verse, to look for parallel verses, particularly from the same author. In this case, we do not have to go very far, for just two chapters later, Matthew writes it again.

“Truly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

This time the Lord is speaking to all the disciples, not just to Peter. If the keys were given to loose and to bind (a common use of keys!), then they were given to all the disciples - including you and me!

A second principle of good exegesis is to study the context, so we will consider what the Lord was teaching in the rest of Matthew 18. We soon see that the entire chapter is dealing with restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness. The small scenarios speak of being like children, having no guile and holding no bitterness - such believers do not offend or wound, and we should be careful not to cause them offense or wounds.

The second thing I notice is that if one is wounded or hurt, and as a result, goes away, a good shepherd will leave the others to restore that ‘sheep’ to the fold. Note again, that the story is about ‘sheep’ not ‘goats.’ It is about believers, not the ‘lost.’ How often, when a ‘problem person’ leaves the church, we wipe our hands saying, “good riddance!” God’s demand of servant shepherds, and the rest of the sheep, is that we seek their restoration, not their dis-fellowship.

“If a brother sins against you, you are to go to him, privately at first, with the one purpose of seeking understanding and reconciliation” (Matthew 18:15). Note the word “sin . ” Too often we leave when we are offended, which in turn, creates an even greater offense. We have no such injunction to go to them when we are offended - only when we are sinned against. The only exception would be, when the church pastor or elders feel it necessary to approach someone who they believe to consistently be a cause of offense, or who has sinned against others. In that case, the purpose of approaching them is always for reconciliation.

When Jesus is giving the teaching of Matthew 18:18-20, a question comes to Peter asking the Lord how many times he should forgive. “Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18:22). Peter probably thought his question was going to be good, but the Lord used it to emphasize that forgiveness is to be unlimited.

Love demands that we always forgive.

The entire context of chapter 18 is to do with restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness, all without causing offense yourself… the theme of this book!

John 20:23 This verse is another parallel verse to the two above, though it is written by John in John 20:23.

In this verse, the disciples are all in a locked room because they are afraid that the Jewish leaders would soon come to take them, just as they had taken their Lord. Their emotions are running high, and some there claimed that they had seen the Lord, risen from the dead! The story was going around that Jesus had appeared to Peter and Mary Magdalene as well as two others on the Emmaus Road. Others would not believe unless they also saw the risen Lord.

Suddenly, even though the doors were locked, Jesus stood in their midst! He said, “Peace be with you! As the Father has sent Me, I also send you… receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:21-22).

The Greek tense of “receive,” is the aorist imperative which always demands an immediate response. At that moment, the disciples received their new life in the Spirit. Then later, on the day of Pentecost, they would receive His fullness to empower them for service. They had been given a new authority! “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld” (John 20:23). Allow me to paraphrase, “Those you loose (set free) are loosed; those you bind, are bound.”

“Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7) asked the Pharisees. In a sense, they were correct because the Lord’s mandate to us does not ‘forgive’ sins to the same measure as His forgiveness. When He forgives it is “as far as the east is from the west to the depths of the sea, never to be remembered anymore” (Psalm 103: 12) . You and I cannot do that - for our own sins, let alone anyone else’s. The only sins we can ‘forgive’ are those committed against ourselves - sins that have likely caused the soul-wounds we bear, by which Satan has hindered us.

Removing the Barrier of Sin Should I sin against you, I also sin against God. Immediately, a barrier comes between me and my Lord. I find it more difficult to pray, the Word loses its interest, and fellowship is not so sweet -my sin has become a cloud above my head!

There are two ways in which that ‘cloud’ can be removed.

First, is to “confess my sin, [because] He is faithful and just to forgive me my sin and to cleanse me from all unrighteousness!” (1 John 1:9). Hallelujah! I have found that promise to be true.

However, I have also discovered that the Lord has this little ‘habit’ of talking to me about the sin. Having forgiven me, He then whispers to my soul, “Now, go to your brother and for him to forgive you. I don’t just desire to cleanse you from the sin, but I want to see you reconciled.” His priority is not forgiveness - it is reconciliation! The confession is not complete unless it brings about reconciliation. That is not His responsibility - it is mine, for “Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5: 18-19).

The second way that my ‘cloud’ can be removed, so that Heaven is once more opened to me, is if you remove it by your forgiveness. The King James Version of the Bible uses a special word in its translation of John 20:23, which writes, “Whosoever’s sins you remit…” The word “remit” speaks of ‘setting aside.’ You can remit my sin, which was committed against you, and in doing so, open Heaven up to me. As you ‘set aside’ my sin, you move the ‘cloud’ away, and the way is open for the Father to speak to me just as when I sought His forgiveness for myself. He again will move upon my heart, in order to bring about our reconciliation!

You might choose to forgive me because you know the Scripture demands that, but it is essential if we are to be reconciled, that you also loose me from God’s judgment upon me by seeking to set aside the ‘cloud’ of sin above me.

I always speak of “forgiveness and release” - they must be preached together! A good example would be Stephen, the first martyr. He had just been appointed as a leader in the early church when the Jewish leaders took him and stoned him to death. Saul of Tarsus stood by, in hearty agreement with their actions, for he had a great hatred for these followers of Jesus.

As Stephen died, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge!” (Acts 7: 60) . He did not pray on behalf of himself for courage, strength, or even to be released, but rather, he released them of their guilt.

I wonder, would Saul have ever become the great apostle Paul, if Stephen had not prayed that prayer? It is my conviction that he ‘opened Heaven’ for Saul! Jesus also prayed a similar prayer where He cried out, “Father, forgive them for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34) as He died for you and me.

One wonderful result of releasing others is that we are also released! It’s like having a horse on the end of a rope - we might say that the horse is bound as it runs around us in the paddock; however, should the horse decide to gallop off across the muddy field, we are going to get dragged along through the mud unless we let go of the rope!

That knot you feel in your stomach after someone has sinned against you, is just like that rope. You are emotionally bound to those who hurt you . That pain is part of the wound they caused. Though you have forgiven them, the knot is there whenever you meet them or hear someone talk about them.

You, and they, need to be released!

Jesus in the Midst It is sad how often Matthew 18:18-20 is quoted out of context! These verses are referring to forgiveness, release, and reconciliation, not God’s presence when multiple people come together! The promises of Jesus given there, are for those who actively seek to be reconciled.

“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in Heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:19-10). The emphasis here is not His presence, for He is always with each of us who are believers, but instead His blessing for reconciliation - His priority!

We have been given a key that will open Heaven for others and that will set us free from the wounds, the bondages they have caused in our soul! Let us learn how to use that key!

There are many Christian books on the market dealing with wounds to the soul. They speak of ‘healing the memories’ of dysfunctional families and codependency. Many of them are very good and have given a lot of help to people seeking a new perspective of life and themselves. The ‘12-step’ program by Alcoholics Anonymous has become the basis for much of this teaching, with the goal of bringing the wounded person to a place of ‘maintenance.’ They are then able to deal with their problem in a practical way, with the use of support groups, ongoing counseling, and prescribed plans or a ‘formula’ of action. Each day, they have a prescription to ‘walk out’ their healing. I have used these books and continue to do so in part. What bothers me about most of them is that few of them mention the releasing effect of forgiveness . I do not believe that the Lord’s intention is to bring His wounded people to ‘maintenance,’ but that He wishes to restore their souls, and bring them healing. The main purpose of this book is to teach how we can be set free from the bondage of our wounds, so that we can be most effective in the warfare against our enemy, Satan. The key of healing is found in forgiveness. The Keys to the Kingdom → Matthew 16:19 For three years the disciples had walked with the Lord through the regions of Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. They had watched Him perform many miracles and had heard Him teaching the multitudes, but He had seldom sat down just to talk with them. Now, after a very busy time, He leads them to the far north of the country, to the regions around Caesarea Philippi, on the lower slopes of Mount Hermon. As they walk, the master turns to His disciples and asks them two questions. The first question is concerning men’s opinions of Jesus, whereas the next question is concerning the disciples opinion of Jesus. After the disciples answer the first question, He again turns to them, and asks, “But who do you say I am?” (Matthew 16:15). Had they come to understand that Jesus was more than just a good man or a miracle worker? “Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in Heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 16:16-19). For centuries, the Roman Catholic Church taught that this is the mandate given to all popes, as successors of Peter, the head of the church, to excommunicate kings, countries, and peoples who do not support their edicts, or grant indulgences. Wouldn’t it be wonderful if you had the key to the kingdom for your loved ones? For your spouse? For your unsaved child? For your parents? If only you could open up the way to eternal life for them! Well, I believe we have that possibility! It is certain that many are being kept away from the joys of seeing and entering the kingdom by our failure to be the witnesses we ought to be. Much of that failure is in our attitudes of unforgiveness. There are many parents today who pray, with weeping, for their wayward child, not realizing that the unforgiveness they bear against that child is the greatest hindrance to God answering the prayer! What did Jesus mean by the latter part of the verse above? I have been given many explanations, from the popes ‘authority,’ to ‘deliverance from the demonic,’ but I see neither here. It is good exegesis when considering an obscure verse, to look for parallel verses, particularly from the same author. In this case, we do not have to go very far, for just two chapters later, Matthew writes it again. “Truly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 18:18). This time the Lord is speaking to all the disciples, not just to Peter. If the keys were given to loose and to bind (a common use of keys!), then they were given to all the disciples - including you and me! A second principle of good exegesis is to study the context, so we will consider what the Lord was teaching in the rest of Matthew 18. We soon see that the entire chapter is dealing with restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness. The small scenarios speak of being like children, having no guile and holding no bitterness - such believers do not offend or wound, and we should be careful not to cause them offense or wounds. The second thing I notice is that if one is wounded or hurt, and as a result, goes away, a good shepherd will leave the others to restore that ‘sheep’ to the fold. Note again, that the story is about ‘sheep’ not ‘goats.’ It is about believers, not the ‘lost.’ How often, when a ‘problem person’ leaves the church, we wipe our hands saying, “good riddance!” God’s demand of servant shepherds, and the rest of the sheep, is that we seek their restoration, not their dis-fellowship. “If a brother sins against you, you are to go to him, privately at first, with the one purpose of seeking understanding and reconciliation” (Matthew 18:15). Note the word “sin . ” Too often we leave when we are offended, which in turn, creates an even greater offense. We have no such injunction to go to them when we are offended - only when we are sinned against. The only exception would be, when the church pastor or elders feel it necessary to approach someone who they believe to consistently be a cause of offense, or who has sinned against others. In that case, the purpose of approaching them is always for reconciliation. When Jesus is giving the teaching of Matthew 18:18-20, a question comes to Peter asking the Lord how many times he should forgive. “Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18:22). Peter probably thought his question was going to be good, but the Lord used it to emphasize that forgiveness is to be unlimited. Love demands that we always forgive. The entire context of chapter 18 is to do with restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness, all without causing offense yourself… the theme of this book! John 20:23 This verse is another parallel verse to the two above, though it is written by John in John 20:23. In this verse, the disciples are all in a locked room because they are afraid that the Jewish leaders would soon come to take them, just as they had taken their Lord. Their emotions are running high, and some there claimed that they had seen the Lord, risen from the dead! The story was going around that Jesus had appeared to Peter and Mary Magdalene as well as two others on the Emmaus Road. Others would not believe unless they also saw the risen Lord. Suddenly, even though the doors were locked, Jesus stood in their midst! He said, “Peace be with you! As the Father has sent Me, I also send you… receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:21-22). The Greek tense of “receive,” is the aorist imperative which always demands an immediate response. At that moment, the disciples received their new life in the Spirit. Then later, on the day of Pentecost, they would receive His fullness to empower them for service. They had been given a new authority! “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld” (John 20:23). Allow me to paraphrase, “Those you loose (set free) are loosed; those you bind, are bound.” “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7) asked the Pharisees. In a sense, they were correct because the Lord’s mandate to us does not ‘forgive’ sins to the same measure as His forgiveness. When He forgives it is “as far as the east is from the west to the depths of the sea, never to be remembered anymore” (Psalm 103: 12) . You and I cannot do that - for our own sins, let alone anyone else’s. The only sins we can ‘forgive’ are those committed against ourselves - sins that have likely caused the soul-wounds we bear, by which Satan has hindered us. Removing the Barrier of Sin Should I sin against you, I also sin against God. Immediately, a barrier comes between me and my Lord. I find it more difficult to pray, the Word loses its interest, and fellowship is not so sweet -my sin has become a cloud above my head! There are two ways in which that ‘cloud’ can be removed. First, is to “confess my sin, [because] He is faithful and just to forgive me my sin and to cleanse me from all unrighteousness!” (1 John 1:9). Hallelujah! I have found that promise to be true. However, I have also discovered that the Lord has this little ‘habit’ of talking to me about the sin. Having forgiven me, He then whispers to my soul, “Now, go to your brother and for him to forgive you. I don’t just desire to cleanse you from the sin, but I want to see you reconciled.” His priority is not forgiveness - it is reconciliation! The confession is not complete unless it brings about reconciliation. That is not His responsibility - it is mine, for “Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5: 18-19). The second way that my ‘cloud’ can be removed, so that Heaven is once more opened to me, is if you remove it by your forgiveness. The King James Version of the Bible uses a special word in its translation of John 20:23, which writes, “Whosoever’s sins you remit…” The word “remit” speaks of ‘setting aside.’ You can remit my sin, which was committed against you, and in doing so, open Heaven up to me. As you ‘set aside’ my sin, you move the ‘cloud’ away, and the way is open for the Father to speak to me just as when I sought His forgiveness for myself. He again will move upon my heart, in order to bring about our reconciliation! You might choose to forgive me because you know the Scripture demands that, but it is essential if we are to be reconciled, that you also loose me from God’s judgment upon me by seeking to set aside the ‘cloud’ of sin above me. I always speak of “forgiveness and release” - they must be preached together! A good example would be Stephen, the first martyr. He had just been appointed as a leader in the early church when the Jewish leaders took him and stoned him to death. Saul of Tarsus stood by, in hearty agreement with their actions, for he had a great hatred for these followers of Jesus. As Stephen died, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge!” (Acts 7: 60) . He did not pray on behalf of himself for courage, strength, or even to be released, but rather, he released them of their guilt. I wonder, would Saul have ever become the great apostle Paul, if Stephen had not prayed that prayer? It is my conviction that he ‘opened Heaven’ for Saul! Jesus also prayed a similar prayer where He cried out, “Father, forgive them for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34) as He died for you and me. One wonderful result of releasing others is that we are also released! It’s like having a horse on the end of a rope - we might say that the horse is bound as it runs around us in the paddock; however, should the horse decide to gallop off across the muddy field, we are going to get dragged along through the mud unless we let go of the rope! That knot you feel in your stomach after someone has sinned against you, is just like that rope. You are emotionally bound to those who hurt you . That pain is part of the wound they caused. Though you have forgiven them, the knot is there whenever you meet them or hear someone talk about them. You, and they, need to be released! Jesus in the Midst It is sad how often Matthew 18:18-20 is quoted out of context! These verses are referring to forgiveness, release, and reconciliation, not God’s presence when multiple people come together! The promises of Jesus given there, are for those who actively seek to be reconciled. “Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in Heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:19-10). The emphasis here is not His presence, for He is always with each of us who are believers, but instead His blessing for reconciliation - His priority! We have been given a key that will open Heaven for others and that will set us free from the wounds, the bondages they have caused in our soul! Let us learn how to use that key!

fields.title: Heaven is Opened
fields.body_html:
I have seen several miracles in my time - including a number of physical healings. I was present when a 12 year old deaf- mute girl received hearing and could talk for the first time. I saw a woman, crippled from birth, walk after prayer. I have seen a large goiter disappear from a woman’s neck as she was being prayed for.

However, as much as these miracles thrilled and encouraged me, they were no more spectacular than the miracles of soul- healing I have witnessed in recent years as wounded believers have used the “key to the kingdom of heaven” to release those who have wounded them, and to release themselves.

The following stories are based on true experiences with the exception of altered names and locations to maintain confidentiality; however, I have not exaggerated the outcome in any way, and have tried to be faithful in reporting the miraculous work of the Lord.

Marie I first met Marie when she was 28. Her counselors were trying to place her under psychiatric care, and she was deeply depressed and withdrawn. She told me of her sad childhood, having been brought up in a strict Jehovah’s Witness home in Canada where they never celebrated any birthdays or Christmas. There were no memories of affection from either parent, and she had never heard her father tell her that he loved her, nor had she ever felt his embrace or received his kisses.

At the age of 16, Marie ran away from home. Several years later, she heard the wonderful news of the Gospel and immediately yielded her life to Christ, desiring to serve Him.

A small local church nurtured her in those early years as she wrestled with her identity and emotions. On one occasion an attempt was made to be reconciled with her family, but the experience was very painful since arguments arose about their differing understandings of Scripture. The parting was acrimonious, and Marie decided that she would never see her parents again. “I hate them,” she told me at our first meeting.

Over the next months, I spent many hours with Marie. She looked to me as her father, and I saw in her the little girl who had never grown up. Many of her actions were those of the adolescent, though she was well educated and even bilingual.

She was a hard worker and very competent at her designated task, but her emotions and attitudes were those of an insecure teenager. We talked about many things, but whenever her parents were mentioned, a barrier grew between us.

Finally, I was able to explain that God had created her as a ‘heart-shaped’ vessel, designed to receive love from her mum and dad. Such love is demonstrated, not so much in the giving of sweets and presents, but in nurturing security, self-worth, identity, comfort, and acceptance by encouraging ambitions and goals, and so much more - things that she never received.

Marie was eager to agree that her parents had sinned against her in failing to pour this love into her, but it was much harder to explain to her that her parents were no different to the great majority of us. They are walking in darkness, bearing their own wounds - their own dysfunction - as victims of Satan’s attacks. They had no desire to hurt Marie and were probably ignorant of the wounds she was carrying.

“I want you to write a letter to your parents,” I said. “Don’t worry! You won’t have to send it, but I do want you to think about what you’d say in such a letter. Tell them specifically, just how they have hurt you, with examples. Also tell them how much you long for their love.”

This is a practice I often use in my counseling since it enables the patient to bring the subconscious to the conscious surface.

The letter will not be sent, but it enables them to have something concrete on which to concentrate. It took Marie three tear-filled weeks to complete the letter. As we prayed for the Lord to direct her thinking, she was amazed at the memories He brought back to her.

When the letter was finished, I was invited to read it. This is not essential for the counselor, and I make it quite clear to all I counsel that they do not have to show me what they have written. There was obviously a great deal of pain in this letter, and my heart ached for this lost, little girl hidden inside a woman’s body.

I folded the paper and returned it to its envelope. “Marie, will you choose now to forgive your parents and to release them?”

I asked. “I cannot!” she cried through her tears. I told her I could do no more, the remedy for her hurts was now in her hands, the “key to the kingdom” was hers should she choose to use it.

Three more weeks passed before Marie knelt in my office, and with much weeping, told the Lord that she was forgiving her parents and wanted Him “not to lay their sin to their charge.” She then promised me that she would pray a blessing upon her parents each day.

A few weeks later, as I saw Marie grow in confidence, I told her that I wanted her to go home to visit her parents for a few days. She protested strongly, but finally agreed to write to see if they would receive her.

It was two weeks later that she rushed into my office, full of excitement. She had received an envelope containing two letters, a brief one from mum saying that she was welcome, and a longer one from dad. The latter was quite clinical and cold, telling her that they had changed homes and that, should she come, it would now be a long journey. She would need to catch an early train in Toronto, change at Montreal, and would then arrive at their home quite late at night. He wasn’t sure if he would see her since he had so much work to do; however, what excited Marie the most was that he ended his letter with, “Hugs and kisses, Dad!”

As I saw Marie onto the train at Toronto, I told her I would be praying for her and encouraged her not to get into any religious arguments. “Before you leave” I said, “make sure you ask your dad for those ‘hugs and kisses.’” She doubted that she would have the courage, but I assured her of my prayers toward that end.

Late that evening I received a telephone call. “Gareth, it’s me, Marie.” She sounded so excited and could hardly contain herself as she told me what had happened. As she was changing platforms in Montreal, she suddenly noticed her mother and father standing there! They had journeyed some distance to meet her. Marie was walking toward them when suddenly, her father stepped forward, threw his arms around her and kissed her! O how the angels of Heaven must have rejoiced!

But what had happened? I believe that Marie had opened heaven for her father by her prayer of release. That morning, her Heavenly father had spoken down through that ‘opened door’ to her earthly father, prompting him to take a day off work and take his wife on a trip to meet their daughter. Then, He had moved upon his heart, causing him to reach out in love to kiss Marie for the very first time. Of course, dad was unaware that his plans and actions were being directed by God.

After two years, Marie had grown into a wholesome, beautiful young lady. She fully reconciled to her family and even moved to their city. She became active in her evangelical church and was even appointed a deaconess. It didn’t take long for Marie to find a husband in the church with the plan to serve the Lord as missionaries. God is so good!

Angela “What’s wrong with me, Gareth?” Angela cried, when she had settled into my office chair. “I wake up each morning so full of fear that I will be making a mistake if I marry John.”

She went on to explain that each morning she was determined to finish the relationship, but, as the day progressed, she knew that she could not, since John was a fine young man whom any girl would be proud to marry. He was a committed Christian and he treated her with courtesy and love. Their interests were similar and both had a desire to serve the Lord in missionary work.

Angela knew that the problem was hers since this was not the first relationship in which she had felt such fear. Twice, she had ended good relationships and then cried for weeks afterwards wondering why she had been ‘so foolish.’

In our counseling, she told me of a father who was an elder in a healthy evangelical church. She respected him greatly, but felt she could never satisfy him. He had made it known that, for his first child, he had wanted a boy instead of a girl. As she grew up, Angela would play cricket with her father and her younger brothers. She was good, but never quite as good as her brothers were so she never received the plaudits that they did. When she received an A grade at school, she was asked why it wasn’t an A+. When she took her first job in a bank, she was told that she should have applied to another, better, bank. She had never heard her father’s commendation or affirmation though she had tried so hard to please him.

I suggested to her that her dad had failed to give her identity and worth, that her self-confidence was low because she constantly saw herself as unable to satisfy the men in her life.

Satan was using the wounds produced by her father’s lack of acceptance of her, to hinder her in developing a Godly relationship with John. Angela saw the pattern and understood how she could break the bondage by healing the wounds through release of her father. We prayed together as she asked the Lord “not to lay this sin to my father’s charge.”

Some weeks later, Angela developed some kidney stones.

She left the area where we were working together to return to her home state, where she would enter a hospital for surgery.

Two months later, when I met her for the first time since the operation, she ran up to me, threw her arms around me, and with great excitement, told me an amazing story.

When she had arrived home, her father announced that he was taking five weeks off work so that he could spend it with his daughter! He took her out to meals and to visit local places of interest. They talked together and discovered so many things about one another that neither had known before. There were many visits to the places where her father worked, and at each, she was embarrassed because he would boast about his daughter and the wonderful things she was doing. He was so proud of her!

“Gareth,” she said, “I’ve fallen in love with my father!” Then she added, “and I could hardly wait to get back to see John.”

John and Angela happily got married and together, served the Lord with joy.

What had prompted her dad to take five weeks off work to spend with his daughter? Could it have been the Lord speaking to him through the door opened by Angela’s prayer of release? I certainly believe so.

Tony It took quite an effort for Tony to pluck up courage to visit me. He did not relate very well to any man, having been brought up by his mother after an angry divorce.

Since leaving school, there had been a succession of jobs, but he had failed to keep any of them. I listened as he gave me his excuses and soon saw a pattern that it was always “my supervisor’s fault.”

We talked together about his childhood, loneliness, and dislike of school. It soon emerged that he had a great fear of one of his teachers. He had not been a brilliant student and this particular teacher had been quite cruel in some of the things he had done and said. His teacher seemed to delight in making his students uncomfortable in class and would embarrass the more sensitive ones by mocking them in front of the class. Tony was often the target of his barbs.

Then there were the threats. Hardly a week went by without Tony being threatened with a trip to see the headmaster because his work was not “up to standard.” Even though he worked harder, he could never satisfy this teacher, and was often given extra work to do. He was so glad when he was old enough to leave school and to start earning money; however, it soon became evident that wounds remained since Tony was unable to relate to any dominant man in a position of authority. Whenever he was given an unpleasant task to do, he took it as punishment meted out by a supervisor who must have disliked him. He could not see that it was a task normally expected of any young employee of that company.

I explained how we often get wounded by the actions or words of others and how those wounds hinder us in walking out a life in the freedom Jesus bought for us on the cross.

Tony understood how his teacher had been used by Satan to wound his soul. Together we prayed as he chose to forgive and to ask the Lord to forgive that teacher. He committed himself to prayer for his family, and in particular, for his sons who were quite rebellious which had been causing much heartache to their parents.

Soon another work opportunity was opened, and Tony applied. He was given the job and started within a few days.

A year later he was promoted to foreman because he had developed such a good relationship with his colleagues. Also, as the company owner declared, “You can give him any task to do and you know it will be done well. He’s a man I can trust!” God had done a good work.

I suggested to her that her dad had failed to give her identity and worth, that her self-confidence was low because she constantly saw herself as unable to satisfy the men in her life. Satan was using the wounds produced by her father’s lack of acceptance of her, to hinder her in developing a Godly relationship with John. Angela saw the pattern and understood how she could break the bondage by healing the wounds through release of her father. We prayed together as she asked the Lord “not to lay this sin to my father’s charge.” Some weeks later, Angela developed some kidney stones. She left the area where we were working together to return to her home state, where she would enter a hospital for surgery. Two months later, when I met her for the first time since the operation, she ran up to me, threw her arms around me, and with great excitement, told me an amazing story. When she had arrived home, her father announced that he was taking five weeks off work so that he could spend it with his daughter! He took her out to meals and to visit local places of interest. They talked together and discovered so many things about one another that neither had known before. There were many visits to the places where her father worked, and at each, she was embarrassed because he would boast about his daughter and the wonderful things she was doing. He was so proud of her! “Gareth,” she said, “I’ve fallen in love with my father!” Then she added, “and I could hardly wait to get back to see John.” John and Angela happily got married and together, served the Lord with joy. What had prompted her dad to take five weeks off work to spend with his daughter? Could it have been the Lord speaking to him through the door opened by Angela’s prayer of release? I certainly believe so. Tony It took quite an effort for Tony to pluck up courage to visit me. He did not relate very well to any man, having been brought up by his mother after an angry divorce. Since leaving school, there had been a succession of jobs, but he had failed to keep any of them. I listened as he gave me his excuses and soon saw a pattern that it was always “my supervisor’s fault.” We talked together about his childhood, loneliness, and dislike of school. It soon emerged that he had a great fear of one of his teachers. He had not been a brilliant student and this particular teacher had been quite cruel in some of the things he had done and said. His teacher seemed to delight in making his students uncomfortable in class and would embarrass the more sensitive ones by mocking them in front of the class. Tony was often the target of his barbs. Then there were the threats. Hardly a week went by without Tony being threatened with a trip to see the headmaster because his work was not “up to standard.” Even though he worked harder, he could never satisfy this teacher, and was often given extra work to do. He was so glad when he was old enough to leave school and to start earning money; however, it soon became evident that wounds remained since Tony was unable to relate to any dominant man in a position of authority. Whenever he was given an unpleasant task to do, he took it as punishment meted out by a supervisor who must have disliked him. He could not see that it was a task normally expected of any young employee of that company. I explained how we often get wounded by the actions or words of others and how those wounds hinder us in walking out a life in the freedom Jesus bought for us on the cross. Tony understood how his teacher had been used by Satan to wound his soul. Together we prayed as he chose to forgive and to ask the Lord to forgive that teacher. He committed himself to prayer for his family, and in particular, for his sons who were quite rebellious which had been causing much heartache to their parents. Soon another work opportunity was opened, and Tony applied. He was given the job and started within a few days. A year later he was promoted to foreman because he had developed such a good relationship with his colleagues. Also, as the company owner declared, “You can give him any task to do and you know it will be done well. He’s a man I can trust!” God had done a good work.

fields.title: Jesus - The Healer
fields.body_html:
Generational Sins Through my years of counseling, I have learned that wounds hindering my patients in their walk with the Lord, often go back to causes many years earlier. Sometimes, there is evidence of a line of similar wounds through several previous generations. It is a Biblical truth that, “the sins of the father may come upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exodus 20:5) .

Further, there was a barrier to the children of illegitimacy coming into full fellowship with the congregation of the Lord “even to the tenth generation” (Deuteronomy 23:2)! These are Old Testament judgements showing how sin can affect, not just the sinner, but many of his descendants. Thankfully, Jesus came to remove the curse of sin and to set us free from its effects, therefore, we do not have to continue in bondage to the wounds of our parents’ sin.

The Lord wants us to walk free, but how can we release those who caused the wounds if they have already died? If we cannot release them, can we be released ourselves? These are the types of questions I am often asked as the counselees recognize the wounds of the past and the patterns of the present. We do not believe that praying for the dead will change in any way, their standing before God, the Great Judge, therefore, we unfortunately cannot open the kingdom of heaven for them.

Even though we cannot use the key to the kingdom that has been given to us, the Lord still will set us free by the healing He purchased on Calvary, because it was “by His wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Hidden Memories Whenever I counsel someone, we always start by asking the Holy Spirit to direct our thoughts. We want Him to reveal to us the areas of the soul where wounds may be found.

It constantly amazes me (though it shouldn’t) how often memories of long-forgotten events come flooding back! On one occasion, I was counseling a middle-aged lady who was having some relational problems. She started to quietly sob for no apparent reason.

My assistant, Debbie, moved over and put her arms around her, at which the counselee began to weep uncontrollably.

Debbie took her onto her lap and hugged her as a mother would a small child. After a few moments of deeply emotional tears, the patient began to beat upon Debbie with her fists, crying out “Why did you do it? Why did you do it?”

As she calmed down, she told us that she had thought she was beating her mother for throwing out her favorite rag doll when she was just four years old! The little girl had carried that wound for over 40 years even though she had not remembered it! It had been buried in the subconscious.

Many times patients have returned to tell me of a sudden recall of memory of some traumatic event of the past. I do not automatically assume that these recalls are all accurate. There is a great danger today because many people want to blame others for imagined sins of the past, and they want to excuse themselves from blame for present weaknesses and attitudes.

That is not my purpose in writing this book. I want to see people take responsibility for their own actions, to exercise the key to the kingdom of Heaven, to set themselves free, and to release those who may have wounded them. Both are victims of Satan - both need to be set free. Recrimination never produces freedom, only forgiveness does!

The Same Yesterday, Today and Forever As the Holy Spirit reveals wounds, we must take time to present that wound before the Lord, for His touch of healing.

He is the “alpha and omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 1:8). He is “the same yesterday, today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8) . He knows your wound - He was there when it happened - and He wept for you. As we present the wound to Him, with forgiveness for the one who caused it, He begins to heal and to restore the soul. Even though we cannot release the one who wounded us, the Lord is faithful to heal and to release us.

The Letter When the patient and I have talked, and they have recognized the hurts, wounds, and patterns, I invite them to write a letter to the person who wounded them outlining the perceived wound and the pain it caused. I encourage them to express their feelings and longings.

“If only you understood how much you hurt me when you… Oh how much I longed to hear you tell me you loved me!”

The letter can be very detailed because it will not be sent. Its purpose is to bring to the surface all the subconscious feelings and pain. When the time for forgiveness and release (if possible) comes, this letter becomes the ‘contract’ of forgiveness. “Are you willing to forgive for all that you have written down here?” I ask them. Then when I am confident that they have fully understood what I have taught, and that they have truly forgiven (and released) the offender, I invite them to destroy the letter making note of the location and date of their action. They are then encouraged to pray blessings upon their offender, if they are still alive.

In order to complete their release, I have known of people who took the letter to a local cemetery, where they have sprinkled its ashes and placed flowers upon the grave of the departed. For some, this has been the first time they have truly mourned over the death of a family member, even a parent, and have known the healing touch that follows true mourning.

Our conscious act of forgiveness breaks the power of Satan.

As the Lord does His work of healing in our lives, we learn to walk in the power of His Spirit.

As we take upon ourselves the whole armor of God, the enemy finds that we have no area of weakness in our lives by which he can hinder us in the battle.

Of course, forgiveness is not a one-time event or even a seven-time commitment. As Jesus taught Peter, it is a “seventy-times-seven” (Matthew 18:22) requirement. In other words, we are to have a continuous forgiving attitude.

We must always be quick to be reconciled with those whose actions or words may cause a division between us. One must recognize that there could very well be a need to ‘cool-off,’ but there can be no excuse for ongoing animosity.

May we become so committed to exercising the key in our hands that we will be known as ‘peacemakers,’ those who are known as the children of God (Matthew 5:9).

fields.title: Walking Out Your Healing
fields.body_html:
In many ways, this is the most difficult chapter to write. I have taught the principles outlined in the earlier chapters, to many different groups of people. There have been youth groups and seniors, to liturgical congregations and non-conformist, to Bible colleges and home groups. In almost all of them, there has been an emotional response, with many weeping people coming to me seeking counsel.

I am saddened that I am usually just passing through, and am unable to commit myself to the long process of walking out the healing so many of them require. I am aware that I have often ‘opened a wound’ - a memory long suppressed - that now needs healing.

Sometimes their response is quite unexpected. I remember one Episcopalian congregation made up of mature adults, who broke into applause as the pastor and I embraced as we acted out the reconciliation that follows release. They were very conscious of their need to forgive and release a former pastor of that church, and excitement at their new understanding of how they could be relieved of the pain they bore, caused them to break out into spontaneous applause. We immediately lifted that applause as a praise offering to the Lord.

I hope that this book will awaken many pastors and counselors to the tremendous responsibility we have to bring reconciliation and healing to the broken relationships and wounded souls that are so prevalent in our churches. I further hope that many believers will learn how to operate the keys that open the kingdom of Heaven for their loved ones, and bring release to themselves from the wounds that they have carried for too long.

It’s about time Satan was put in his place and the people of God were able to walk in wholeness and power, rather than limping along as so many do!

For those who may have recognized themselves as wounded as they have read this book, I am closing with some guidelines that will enable them to ‘walk out’ their own healing. If it is possible to find a good counselor who will walk through this with you, such a companion would be of utmost value. I would encourage you to urge them to become familiar with this book before you start.

Ask the Lord to Direct Your Thoughts Be assured that the Lord wants to heal your soul wounds. He is aware of them, but has given you the key to being healed, and wants you to use it! He will not answer prayer in the areas of our lives where He has already won the victory on the cross, and where He has given the authority or mandate to us.

Take Your Time Healing rarely comes quickly. Most of the stories I can tell relate to many months of counseling. It takes time to walk again after a bad wound.

Just as physiotherapy is essential if we are to walk again after a bad accident-causing leg injuries, so spiritual therapy is essential to walk out our healing after long-standing soul- wounds.

Talk About Your Past I usually encourage the counselee to break their past down into short time periods. For example, preschool, junior school, teenage years, young adult, etc. I prompt them with questions about their home, school, friends, things they love, and things they hate, meanwhile assessing for patterns of attitudes or hurts. “How did the little child inside you feel?”

Ask the Lord to touch each wound as it is revealed.

Write Down Anything You Feel Is Relevant I always have a pen and paper handy to note any patterns that may be emerging or any thoughts that strike me. During the days when no counselor or friend is with you, you will become surprised as memories come of things long forgotten, but why should you be surprised when you have already asked the Lord to be actively involved in your healing process? Make a note of these memories.

Recognize if You Have Been Wounded by Another’s Sin Do not blame another if the sin is your own. If you have taken offense, you must deal with it as described in chapter nine.

Do not go into denial if the one who has wronged you is someone you love, and certainly do not make excuses for them. God sees they as a sinner, just like you and me - and sinner’s sin! There’s no need to beat around the bush - just call it as it is - sin! He may be a redeemed sinner, but he is still capable of wounding you.

Most often, the wounds were created unintentionally, but they are real wounds, and if the offender were not a sinner, they would not have been so injurious to you.

As I came to understand this principle, I saw how I had probably wounded my own daughter through ignorance.

Anne was in hospital for a few weeks before the birth of our first daughter, Corinne, so when she began labor, I was at home, unaware of what was happening. Two friends were the first to tell me of her labor since they had called the hospital just before departing on vacation. The nursing staff told them that the baby was born, but would not be specific about the birth details, especially the sex of the child - the father would be the first to be so informed. They urged me to phone the hospital so that they could know the details before beginning their vacation. I told them that I would do so after finishing the Agatha Christie novel I was reading! Of course, I was joking, just to keep them in suspense, and we quickly went together to the public call-box to hear the exciting news that I was now the father of a lovely baby girl.

However, that story was repeated many times to visiting friends over the years, and sometimes, in the presence of my daughter. I never thought about how she was hearing the story - that daddy didn’t really care when she was born. Perhaps he did not want her?

Just two years after first publishing this book, I wrote to Corinne asking her forgiveness for the wounds caused by my thoughtlessness.

Write a Letter, Being Specific About Your Hurts You do not have to show this letter to anyone, though you may choose to confide in your counselor. However, this should only be if they can be trusted with confidentiality, and you know that he will not allow your information to affect his attitude toward you or the one who wounded you. Try to be comprehensive and objective in the letter, writing down how you felt when wounded: rejected, belittled, embarrassed, etc.

Try to also add any positive things you can say.

Being objective may be very difficult as this letter can raise strong emotions and pain. Its purpose is to enable you to bring emotions you have suppressed for years to the surface.

Bandages that have become bondages have to come off! Take your time!

Choose to Forgive Recognize that the one who wounded you is a sinner walking in darkness. They are blind to what they have done to your soul. Your real adversary is Satan whose army has targeted you from birth, and your offender is but an agent, ignorant of Satan’s devices. Get angry at Satan, and forgive the blind man. Make sure you are prepared to forgive for every item mentioned in the letter you wrote.

Do not expect the Lord to heal where you are not prepared to forgive.

Choose to Release Why not use the prayer of St. Stephen? “Father, do not lay these sins to their charge! Today, I choose to release them from all guilt.”

After praying that prayer, I suggest you make a note of the date, recording it in your memory just as you would a birthday.

Burn the Letter!

The matter has been dealt with - why keep it hanging around?

This should be recorded in your memory only as the day on which you started to walk out your healing - a day for celebrating!

Pray for the One Who Wounded You Commit yourself to pray each day for God to bless the one who wounded you. Are his children far from the Lord? Pray for them. Is his business in difficulty? Pray for its success. As you continue to pray in this way, God will work through the channel between Himself and them - a channel that you opened by your forgiveness and release. In doing this, you will be delivering yourself from slavery to the emotional bondage of your wounds and becoming the servant Jesus called you to be.

If one wrongs you by taking your shirt, he makes you his slave, but by giving him your coat also, you make yourself his servant. If he wrongs you by forcing you to go a mile, he makes you his slave, but by going two miles, you make yourself his servant (Matthew 5:40-41). If he wounds your soul, you become an emotional slave, but by praying for him, you become his servant.

The first call of discipleship is to become a servant , just as Jesus was for you.

Be Open to Reconciliation Should there be an opportunity to be reconciled to the one who wounded you, do not let apprehension or fear hinder you.

The Lord’s priority is not just the healing, which blesses you, but the reconciliation which blesses Him!

Walk Out Your Healing Each day, take upon yourself all the armor of God of God as found in Ephesians 6:10-18. Make this a conscious action, even speaking out as you do it. “I take on the belt of truth so that my ‘inner man’ may not be wounded by the lies of the enemy. I take on the breastplate of righteousness so that the enemy may never cause my heart to be divided in its commitment and love for the Lord” and so forth. Only the “pure in heart” shall see God - those whose hearts are unalloyed with the dross of this world (Matthew 5:8).

Give Each Wound to the Great Physician Just as surely as the enemy knows where your wounds are, so does the Lord. He felt your pain when you were hurt and longs for your healing; however, He has given the key to you.

As you begin to use it, He is very willing to assist in the walking out of the healing. As He has revealed the wounds to you, so He removes the bondages and brings wholeness in their place, after all, He is the “Great Physician,” the healer, who took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows and, by whose wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:4-5).

Lastly, thank Him for His healing!
