fields.title: The Ploughman
fields.body_html:
The Lord ploughs the human heart with patience and power. Unless His grace tills us, no holiness grows. Persevere, yield, and let God’s plough prepare your soul for eternal fruit.

“Does the ploughman plough all day to sow?” — Isaiah 28:24 (ESV) Unless fields are cultivated, they yield nothing but briers and thistles. In this we see ourselves.

Unless the great Husbandman tills us by His grace, we will produce nothing good, but only what is evil. If one day I hear that a country has been found where wheat grows without the work of the farmer, perhaps then I may hope to find someone who will bring forth holiness without the grace of God. So far, every land where the foot of man has trodden has required labour and care; and in men the need for gracious tillage is universal.

Jesus says to all of us, “You must be born again.” Unless God the Holy Spirit breaks up the heart with the plough of the law and sows it with the seed of the gospel, not a single ear of holiness will be produced by any of us, even if we are children of godly parents or regarded as morally excellent by those around us.

Yes, the plough is needed not only to produce what is good, but to destroy what is evil. There are diseases that, over the course of ages, wear themselves out and do not reappear; and there may be forms of vice which under changed circumstances do not abound as they once did. But human nature remains the same, and therefore there will always be plentiful crops of the weeds of sin in humanity’s field. Only spiritual husbandry carried out by the Spirit of God can keep these weeds down.

You cannot destroy weeds by exhortations, nor can you tear out the roots of sin from the soul by moral persuasion. Something sharper and more effective must be brought to bear on them. God must put His own right hand to the plough, or the hemlock of sin will never give way to the wheat of holiness. Good never arises spontaneously in unrenewed humanity, and evil is never cut out until the ploughshare of almighty grace is driven through it.

The text guides our thoughts in this direction and helps us practically by asking a simple question: “Does the ploughman plough all day to sow?” This question may be answered in two ways. First, in the affirmative: “Yes, in the proper season he does plough all day to sow.” Secondly, in the negative: “No, the ploughman does not plough every day to sow; he has other work to do according to the season.”

I. The Affirmative Answer: “Yes, the ploughman does plough all day to sow.” When it is ploughing time, he continues until his work is finished. If it takes one day or twenty, he perseveres while the weather allows. The ploughman’s perseverance is instructive, teaching us two lessons.

First, when the Lord comes to plough the human heart, He ploughs all day — and here we see His patience. Secondly, so ought the Lord’s servants to labour with people’s hearts, showing perseverance in their work.

“Does the ploughman plough all day?” So God ploughs the heart of man, and here lies His patience. For some of us, the team was in the field very early in the morning of life; our first recollections involve conscience and the furrows of pain it made in our youthful minds. As little children, we walk in the night conscious of sin. Our parents’ teaching and prayers made deep and painful impressions, and though we did not then yield our hearts to God, we were greatly stirred, and indifference to religion became impossible.

At school, reading a chapter of God’s Word, the death of a playmate, an address at a Bible class, or a solemn sermon often affected us deeply, leaving us uneasy for weeks. The Spirit of God within urged us to think of higher and better things. Though we quenched the Spirit and stifled conviction, we still bore the marks of the ploughshare. Furrows were made in our souls, and certain foul weeds of evil were cut up by the roots, although no seed of grace had yet been sown in our hearts. Some have remained in this state for many years — ploughed but not sown. Blessed be God, it was not so with others of us, for we had not left boyhood before the good seed of the gospel fell on our hearts.

Alas, many do not yield to grace, and with them the ploughman ploughs all day to sow. I have seen young men come to London in their youth, yielding to its temptations, drinking in its poisoned pleasures, violating conscience, yet unhappy all the while. Fearful and restless, they were stirred within, like soil turned up by the plough. In many cases this work goes on for years without result.

I have known men reach middle age without receiving the good seed, their hard hearts never thoroughly broken up. They go on in business without God; day after day they rise and sleep with no more religion than their horses. All the while warnings of judgment and the chidings of conscience ring in their ears, so they lack peace.

After a powerful sermon they cannot enjoy meals or sleep, asking themselves, “What shall I do in the end of this?” The ploughman has ploughed all day, until evening shadows fall and the day comes to a close. What a mercy it is when the furrows are finally ready and the good seed is cast in to be received, nurtured and multiplied a hundredfold. It is sad to remember how often this ploughing continues until the sun touches the horizon and night dews begin to fall. Even then, the long-suffering God continues His work — ploughing and ploughing until darkness ends all.

Do I address any aged ones whose time is short? Consider your position. What! Sixty years old and yet unsaved? Forty years God bore with Israel in the wilderness; He has borne with you for sixty years. Seventy years old and still unregenerate! How little time remains to serve your Saviour before you go to heaven. But will you go there at all? Is it not terribly likely that you may die in your sins and perish forever?

How happy are those brought to Christ in early life; yet remember: “While the lamp holds out to burn, The vilest sinner may return.”

It may be late, very late, but it is not too late. The ploughman ploughs all day; and the Lord waits to be gracious to you. I have seen many aged people converted, and therefore I encourage other older souls to believe in Jesus.

I once read a sermon in which a minister claimed he had seldom known anyone converted over the age of forty who had been a Gospel hearer all their lives. We must caution against delay, but we must not invent facts.

Whatever that minister thought, my observation leads me to believe that, accounting for the greater number of young people, about as many are converted to God at one age as at another. It is dreadful to remain an unbeliever for so many years; yet God’s grace does not stop at a certain age. Those who enter the vineyard at the eleventh hour shall receive their pay, and grace shall be glorified in both the old and the young.

Come along, old friend — Jesus Christ invites you to come to Him even now, though you have resisted so long. You have been a tough piece of ground, and the ploughman has ploughed all day.

But if at last the sods are turned and your heart lies in ridges, there is still hope for you.

“Does the ploughman plough all day?” I answer — Yes. However long the day may be, God in mercy still ploughs; He is patient, tender, full of mercy and grace. Do not reject such patience, but yield to the Lord who has shown you gentle love.

Perseverance in Seeking God The text not only shows God’s patience but also teaches perseverance on our part. “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Yes, he does. Then if I am seeking Christ, should I be discouraged because I do not find Him immediately? The promise is: “For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8, ESV).

There may be reasons the door does not open at the first knock. What then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will knock all day. I may not find at first; what then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will seek all day. I may not receive at first; what then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will ask all day.

Friends, if you have begun to seek the Lord, the short way is: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV). Do it at once. In the name of God, do it at once, and you are saved at once. May the Spirit of God bring you to faith in Jesus, and you enter the kingdom of Christ immediately. But if, in seeking the Lord, you are unsure of this or do not see your way, never give up seeking. Go to the foot of the cross, hold on to it and cry, “If I perish, I perish here.

Lord, I come to You in Jesus Christ for mercy; and if You are not pleased to look on me immediately and forgive my sins, I will cry to You until You do.”

When God’s Holy Spirit brings a person to earnest prayer that will not be denied, they are not far from peace. Careless indifference and half-hearted devotion hold people in bondage. They find peace when their hearts are roused to strong resolve; to seek until they find. I like to see people study the Scriptures until they learn the way of salvation, and hear the gospel until their souls live by it. If they are determined to drive the plough through doubts, fears and difficulties until they reach salvation, by God’s grace they will soon find it.

The same is true in seeking the salvation of others. “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Yes, when it is ploughing-time. Then I will work on and on — pray and preach, or pray and teach — however long the day God appoints me, for — “’Tis all my business here below The precious Gospel seed to sow.”

Brother worker, are you becoming a little weary? Never mind. Stir yourself and keep ploughing on for the love of Jesus and for dying people. Our workday has only its appointed hours, and while they last, let us fulfill our task. Ploughing is hard work, but there will be no harvest without it. So let us put forth all our strength and not grow tired until we have done our Lord’s will and, by His Holy Spirit, brought conviction to people’s hearts.

Some soils are very hard and cling together, making the labor discouraging. Others are like uncultivated wasteland, full of roots and tangled brambles. They need a steam plough, and we must pray that the Lord makes us equal to such work, for we cannot leave them untilled. Therefore, we must exert even greater effort so that the task may be completed.

I once heard of a minister who tried to visit a dying man but was refused entry. He returned the next morning, and another excuse prevented him from seeing the man. He came again and was still refused. He continued until he had called twenty times without success. But on the twenty- first visit, he was finally admitted, and by God’s grace, a soul was saved from death.

“Why do you tell your child something twenty times?” someone once asked a mother. “Because,” she replied, “nineteen times is not enough.” When a soul needs to be ploughed, even hundreds of furrows may not be enough. What then? Keep ploughing all day until the work is done. Whether you are ministers, missionaries, teachers, or personal soul-winners, do not grow weary.

Your work is noble, and its reward is eternal. The grace of God is seen in allowing us to engage in such holy service. It is magnified in sustaining us in it, and it will be most clearly displayed when He enables us to persevere until we can say, as Jesus did, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4, ESV).

We value what costs us labor and service, and we will treasure even more those who are saved through our efforts. It is good for us to learn the value of our harvest by going out weeping at the time of sowing. When you think of the ploughman working all day, let it move you to steady, earnest effort in winning souls. Seek— “With cries, entreaties, tears to save And snatch them from the fiery wave.”

Does the ploughman plough all day for a little oats or barley? And will you not plough all day for souls who will live forever—either to adore the grace of God if saved, or to remain in outer darkness if not? By the reality of coming judgment and the glory yet to be revealed, strengthen yourselves and keep ploughing all day.

I urge every member of our churches to keep their hands on the gospel plough and their eyes straight ahead. Does the ploughman plough all day? Then let Christians do the same. Start close to the hedge and go all the way to the end of the field. Plough as near to the ditch as possible, leaving as little untouched ground as you can. Even if there are fallen women, thieves, and drunkards in the surrounding slums, do not neglect them. If you leave any stretch of land to weeds, they will soon spread into the wheat.

When you have gone from one end of the field to the other, what next? Turn around and go back to where you began. And after that? Go up and down again. And again. You have visited that district with tracts—do it again, fifty-two times a year. Multiply your furrows. We must learn to continue in doing good. Your eternal calling is to go on doing good forever, and it is wise to rehearse that calling now. So keep ploughing and expect results as the reward of faithful perseverance.

Ploughing is not done with sudden bursts of energy. It requires steady, consistent effort. Flash and excitement may be suitable elsewhere, but not in ploughing.

The work must be regular and persistent. Some give up quickly—it wears out their gloves, blisters their soft hands, tires their bodies, and makes them earn their bread with more sweat than they prefer. But those whom the Lord fills with His grace will continue year after year, and truly, they will receive their reward. Does the ploughman plough all day? Then let us do the same, confident that one day every hill and valley will be tilled and sown, every desert and wilderness will yield a harvest for our Lord, the angel reapers will descend, and the shouts of harvest joy will fill both earth and heaven.

But now, briefly, the question may also be answered differently: Does the ploughman plough all day in order to sow? No. He does not plough forever. After ploughing, he breaks up the clods, sows, reaps, and threshes. As the chapter shows, there are many other tasks in farming. The ploughman has more to do than plough. There is progress in his work. This teaches us that there is progress in God’s work—and there should be progress in ours.

First, consider God’s work. Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He moves on to other tasks.

It may be that the Lord has been using painful means to plough your heart. You feel the terrors of the law, the bitterness of sin, the holiness of God, the weakness of the flesh, and the shadow of coming judgment. Will this continue forever? Will it last until your spirit fails?

Listen: Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in preparation for sowing. So the Lord deals with you. Be encouraged—there is an end to the wounding and the humbling, and better things lie ahead.

You may feel poor and needy, seeking water and finding none, your tongue parched with thirst.

Yet the Lord says, “The poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst; I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them” (Isaiah 41:17, ESV). He will not contend forever, nor will He always be angry (see Psalm 103:9, ESV). He will turn again and have compassion. He will not always make furrows by rebuke. He will sow the precious seed of comfort, water it with the dew of heaven, and shine upon it with the sunlight of His grace. Then there will be growth—first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear (Mark 4:28, ESV). In due season, you will rejoice as at harvest.

You who feel deeply wounded, does God always send terror and conviction? Hear this: “If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land” (Isaiah 1:19, ESV).

And what is God’s call? “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV).

You will be saved now. You can find peace now, if you stop relying on yourself and your own works and turn instead to the One who paid your ransom on the cross.

The Lord is gentle and compassionate. “He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9, ESV). Many of your fears arise from unbelief, from Satan, or from your own weakness—not from God. Do not blame Him for what He has not sent. His purpose is your peace, not your distress. He says, “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1, ESV). And again, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22, ESV).

He has struck, but He will heal. He has wounded, but He will bind up. He has brought low, but He will raise up. Therefore, turn to Him and receive comfort. The ploughman does not plough forever, or he would never reap a harvest. God is not always breaking hearts; He also comes to heal them.

There is progress in God’s work. He moves from painful preparation to fruitful growth. The furrows will not always remain visible—the corn will cover them with beauty. As a woman forgets her anguish for joy that a child is born, so you who are under conviction will forget your sorrow when grace bears fruit in your soul. You will also advance to joy. The ploughman may not own much, yet he whistles as he works because he looks forward to harvest. He ploughs in hope. And dear soul, God will rejoice over you when you believe in Jesus Christ, and you too will be filled with joy. Be encouraged—the better portion is ahead. Gospel sorrow leads to gospel hope, faith, and rejoicing, and that rejoicing has no end.

God will not discipline all day. He will lead you from strength to strength, from glory to glory, until you are made like Him. This is the progress in God’s work among people: from painful preparation, to fruitful grace, to joyful experience. But what if the ploughing never leads to sowing? What if your conscience is stirred, yet you continue resisting? Then God will move forward—but in judgment. He may set aside the plough and command the clouds to withhold their rain. The land will be left barren, and its end will be to be burned. There is nothing more terrifying than for a soul to be abandoned—to be left uncultivated by God Himself. Surely that is hell. “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy” (Revelation 22:11). Character becomes fixed forever. The merciful hand will no longer till the soil of the heart. What could be worse than that?

This progression is also a lesson for us, because we too must move forward. Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in order to sow, and in due time he sows. Some churches seem to think their whole duty is ploughing—or at least talking about ploughing. There is much discussion, much planning, much outlining of grand programs. It sounds impressive. But does the ploughman plough all day?

You may create large plans and promise great results—but do not stop there. Do not spend all your time making furrows. Move on to sowing. Those who promise the most often accomplish the least.

People who truly accomplish much often begin without elaborate plans. By God’s grace, their work grows out of inward conviction and action. They do not merely propose—they perform. They are like the servant in the parable: “A sower went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3, ESV).

Ministers of Christ must also follow this pattern of progress. We must move from preaching the law to preaching the gospel. The ploughman does plough—he would not sow without preparing the soil first. Robbie Flockhart, who preached for years in the streets of Edinburgh, said, “It is in vain to sew with the silk thread of the gospel unless you use the sharp needle of the law.” Some shrink from preaching about eternal judgment and its terrors. But that is a false kindness. To hide danger is to ruin souls.

You cannot sew without a needle, and you cannot reap without disturbing the soil. You cannot save souls if you never warn them of hell. We must declare what God has revealed about sin, righteousness, and judgment to come. Yet we must not plough forever. The law prepares; the gospel saves. The heart of our ministry is the proclamation of good news. We are followers of Jesus Christ, not merely prophets of warning. We are heralds of grace.

Do not be content only with revival meetings and emotional appeals. Teach the doctrines of grace fully and faithfully. After ploughing comes planting and watering. After reproof comes consolation. First make disciples, then teach them to observe all that Christ has commanded (see Matthew 28:19–20, ESV). Move from foundations to building upward, from basic truths to deeper instruction.

Now let me speak to those who are only hearers. You must move forward as well—from hearing and fearing to believing. Some of you have heard the gospel for years. Will you remain in that state forever? You have been stirred deeply. Recently you nearly left broken-hearted.

Surely your heart has been ploughed enough. Yet you have not received the seed of eternal life because you have not believed in the Lord Jesus.

It is dreadful to stand on the brink of eternal life and never enter it. To be almost in heaven and yet shut out forever—that is terrifying. It is like arriving at a train station just as the train pulls away.

To miss it by a second is deeply frustrating. If you continue as you have for years, you may have your hand on the latch of heaven and still be shut out. Within a hair’s breadth of glory—yet covered in eternal shame. Beware of being near the kingdom and yet lost. Almost saved, but not saved.

May God forbid that you be among those who are ploughed again and again but never sown.

It will not help at the last day to say, “We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” (Luke 13:26, ESV). You may say, “We attended church, joined prayer meetings, participated in Bible classes, distributed tracts, gave generously, gave up open sins, prayed daily, read Scripture faithfully.” All these things may be true; yet without saving faith in Christ. Take care lest the Lord reply, “I tell you, I do not know you. Depart from me” (Luke 13:27, ESV). If Christ truly knows a person, He always knows them. He will never say that to one who has come to Him in humble dependence. Some of you have done many good things—but you have never truly trusted Christ, never rested in Him, never known Him personally. How tragic your condition.

Will it always remain so?

Finally, to those who are being ploughed and feel deeply troubled about your souls: move at once to believing. If people only understood how simple faith is, surely they would believe. Yet its very simplicity makes it seem difficult. The difficulty of believing lies in the fact that there is no difficulty in it. “If the prophet had commanded you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” (2 Kings 5:13, ESV). Yes, you would have done it gladly. But when the command is simple “Wash, and be clean”—pride resists. If you are willing to lay aside pride and do whatever the Lord commands, then there is nothing more to prepare. Believe in Jesus now.

May the Holy Spirit make you weary of self and ready to accept the gospel. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Romans 10:8, ESV). Let it be believed. With your heart believe in Jesus, and with your mouth confess Him, and you will be saved (see Romans 10:9, ESV).

A vital part of faith is giving up all other confidences. Abandon every false hope. I once tried to explain faith by quoting Isaac Watts: “A guilty, weak, and helpless worm, On Your kind arms I fall; Be my strength and righteousness, My Jesus and my all.” I described faith as falling into Christ’s arms. Afterward, a young man said to me, “Sir, I cannot fall into Christ’s arms.” I answered, “Then tumble into them. Collapse into them. Faint into them.

Even die into them—only get there.”

Many people talk endlessly about what they can or cannot do, and they miss the central point. Faith means stopping all talk of what you can do and leaving everything to Christ. He can do all things.

You can do nothing.

Does the ploughman plough all day in order to sow? No. He moves forward from ploughing to sowing. Go and do likewise. Sow to the Spirit the precious seed of faith in Christ, and the Lord will give you a joyful harvest.

If one day I hear that a country has been found where wheat grows without the work of the farmer, perhaps then I may hope to find someone who will bring forth holiness without the grace of God. So far, every land where the foot of man has trodden has required labour and care; and in men the need for gracious tillage is universal. Jesus says to all of us, “You must be born again.” Unless God the Holy Spirit breaks up the heart with the plough of the law and sows it with the seed of the gospel, not a single ear of holiness will be produced by any of us, even if we are children of godly parents or regarded as morally excellent by those around us. Yes, the plough is needed not only to produce what is good, but to destroy what is evil. There are diseases that, over the course of ages, wear themselves out and do not reappear; and there may be forms of vice which under changed circumstances do not abound as they once did. But human nature remains the same, and therefore there will always be plentiful crops of the weeds of sin in humanity’s field. Only spiritual husbandry carried out by the Spirit of God can keep these weeds down. You cannot destroy weeds by exhortations, nor can you tear out the roots of sin from the soul by moral persuasion. Something sharper and more effective must be brought to bear on them. God must put His own right hand to the plough, or the hemlock of sin will never give way to the wheat of holiness. Good never arises spontaneously in unrenewed humanity, and evil is never cut out until the ploughshare of almighty grace is driven through it. As little children, we walk in the night conscious of sin. Our parents’ teaching and prayers made deep and painful impressions, and though we did not then yield our hearts to God, we were greatly stirred, and indifference to religion became impossible. At school, reading a chapter of God’s Word, the death of a playmate, an address at a Bible class, or a solemn sermon often affected us deeply, leaving us uneasy for weeks. The Spirit of God within urged us to think of higher and better things. Though we quenched the Spirit and stifled conviction, we still bore the marks of the ploughshare. Furrows were made in our souls, and certain foul weeds of evil were cut up by the roots, although no seed of grace had yet been sown in our hearts. Some have remained in this state for many years — ploughed but not sown. You feel the terrors of the law, the bitterness of sin, the holiness of God, the weakness of the flesh, and the shadow of coming judgment. Will this continue forever? Will it last until your spirit fails? Listen: Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in preparation for sowing. So the Lord deals with you. Be encouraged—there is an end to the wounding and the humbling, and better things lie ahead. You may feel poor and needy, seeking water and finding none, your tongue parched with thirst. Yet the Lord says, “The poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst; I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them” (Isaiah 41:17, ESV). He will not contend forever, nor will He always be angry (see Psalm 103:9, ESV). He will turn again and have compassion. He will not always make furrows by rebuke. He will sow the precious seed of comfort, water it with the dew of heaven, and shine upon it with the sunlight of His grace. Then there will be growth—first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear (Mark 4:28, ESV). In due season, you will rejoice as at harvest. You who feel deeply wounded, does God always send terror and conviction? Hear this: “If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land” (Isaiah 1:19, ESV). And what is God’s call? “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV). You will be saved now. You can find peace now, if you stop relying on yourself and your own works and turn instead to the One who paid your ransom on the cross. The Lord is gentle and compassionate. “He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9, ESV). Many of your fears arise from unbelief, from Satan, or from your own weakness—not from God. Do not blame Him for what He has not sent. His purpose is your peace, not your distress. He says, “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1, ESV). And again, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22, ESV). He has struck, but He will heal. He has wounded, but He will bind up. He has brought low, but He will raise up. Therefore, turn to Him and receive comfort. The ploughman does not plough forever, or he would never reap a harvest. God is not always breaking hearts; He also comes to heal them. There is progress in God’s work. He moves from painful preparation to fruitful growth. The furrows will not always remain visible—the corn will cover them with beauty. As a woman forgets her anguish for joy that a child is born, so you who are under conviction will forget your sorrow when grace bears fruit in your soul. You will also advance to joy. The ploughman may not own much, yet he whistles as he works because he looks forward to harvest. He ploughs in hope. And dear soul, God will rejoice over you when you believe in Jesus Christ, and you too will be filled with joy. Be encouraged—the better portion is ahead. Gospel sorrow leads to gospel hope, faith, and rejoicing, and that rejoicing has no end. God will not discipline all day. He will lead you from strength to strength, from glory to glory, until you are made like Him. This is the progress in God’s work among people: from painful preparation, to fruitful grace, to joyful experience. But what if the ploughing never leads to sowing? What if your conscience is stirred, yet you continue resisting? Then God will move forward—but in judgment. He may set aside the plough and command the clouds to withhold their rain. The land will be left barren, and its end will be to be burned. There is nothing more terrifying than for a soul to be abandoned—to be left uncultivated by God Himself. Surely that is hell. “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy” (Revelation 22:11). Character becomes fixed forever. The merciful hand will no longer till the soil of the heart. What could be worse than that? This progression is also a lesson for us, because we too must move forward. Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in order to sow, and in due time he sows. Some churches seem to think their whole duty is ploughing—or at least talking about ploughing. There is much discussion, much planning, much outlining of grand programs. It sounds impressive. But does the ploughman plough all day? You may create large plans and promise great results—but do not stop there. Do not spend all your time making furrows. Move on to sowing. Those who promise the most often accomplish the least. People who truly accomplish much often begin without elaborate plans. By God’s grace, their work grows out of inward conviction and action. They do not merely propose—they perform. They are like the servant in the parable: “A sower went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3, ESV). Ministers of Christ must also follow this pattern of progress. We must move from preaching the law to preaching the gospel. The ploughman does plough—he would not sow without preparing the soil first. Robbie Flockhart, who preached for years in the streets of Edinburgh, said, “It is in vain to sew with the silk thread of the gospel unless you use the sharp needle of the law.” Some shrink from preaching about eternal judgment and its terrors. But that is a false kindness. To hide danger is to ruin souls. You cannot sew without a needle, and you cannot reap without disturbing the soil. You cannot save souls if you never warn them of hell. We must declare what God has revealed about sin, righteousness, and judgment to come. Yet we must not plough forever. The law prepares; the gospel saves. The heart of our ministry is the proclamation of good news. We are followers of Jesus Christ, not merely prophets of warning. We are heralds of grace. Do not be content only with revival meetings and emotional appeals. Teach the doctrines of grace fully and faithfully. After ploughing comes planting and watering. After reproof comes consolation. First make disciples, then teach them to observe all that Christ has commanded (see Matthew 28:19–20, ESV). Move from foundations to building upward, from basic truths to deeper instruction. Now let me speak to those who are only hearers. You must move forward as well—from hearing and fearing to believing. Some of you have heard the gospel for years. Will you remain in that state forever? You have been stirred deeply. Recently you nearly left broken-hearted. Surely your heart has been ploughed enough. Yet you have not received the seed of eternal life because you have not believed in the Lord Jesus. It is dreadful to stand on the brink of eternal life and never enter it. To be almost in heaven and yet shut out forever—that is terrifying. It is like arriving at a train station just as the train pulls away. To miss it by a second is deeply frustrating. If you continue as you have for years, you may have your hand on the latch of heaven and still be shut out. Within a hair’s breadth of glory—yet covered in eternal shame. Beware of being near the kingdom and yet lost. Almost saved, but not saved. May God forbid that you be among those who are ploughed again and again but never sown. It will not help at the last day to say, “We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” (Luke 13:26, ESV). You may say, “We attended church, joined prayer meetings, participated in Bible classes, distributed tracts, gave generously, gave up open sins, prayed daily, read Scripture faithfully.” All these things may be true; yet without saving faith in Christ. Take care lest the Lord reply, “I tell you, I do not know you. Depart from me” (Luke 13:27, ESV). If Christ truly knows a person, He always knows them. He will never say that to one who has come to Him in humble dependence. Some of you have done many good things—but you have never truly trusted Christ, never rested in Him, never known Him personally. How tragic your condition. Will it always remain so? Finally, to those who are being ploughed and feel deeply troubled about your souls: move at once to believing. If people only understood how simple faith is, surely they would believe. Yet its very simplicity makes it seem difficult. The difficulty of believing lies in the fact that there is no difficulty in it. “If the prophet had commanded you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” (2 Kings 5:13, ESV). Yes, you would have done it gladly. But when the command is simple “Wash, and be clean”—pride resists. If you are willing to lay aside pride and do whatever the Lord commands, then there is nothing more to prepare. Believe in Jesus now. May the Holy Spirit make you weary of self and ready to accept the gospel. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Romans 10:8, ESV). Let it be believed. With your heart believe in Jesus, and with your mouth confess Him, and you will be saved (see Romans 10:9, ESV). A vital part of faith is giving up all other confidences. Abandon every false hope. I once tried to explain faith by quoting Isaac Watts: “A guilty, weak, and helpless worm, On Your kind arms I fall; Be my strength and righteousness, My Jesus and my all.” I described faith as falling into Christ’s arms. Afterward, a young man said to me, “Sir, I cannot fall into Christ’s arms.” I answered, “Then tumble into them. Collapse into them. Faint into them. Even die into them—only get there.” Many people talk endlessly about what they can or cannot do, and they miss the central point. Faith means stopping all talk of what you can do and leaving everything to Christ. He can do all things. You can do nothing. Does the ploughman plough all day in order to sow? No. He moves forward from ploughing to sowing. Go and do likewise. Sow to the Spirit the precious seed of faith in Christ, and the Lord will give you a joyful harvest.

fields.title: Ploughing The Rock
fields.body_html:
The ploughman cannot till rock, nor can ministers break hearts unwilling to yield. God’s Word pierces receptive soil, yet stubborn hearts resist. Let us learn patience, discernment, and the necessity of divine grace in fruitful spiritual labor.

“Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” — Amos 6:12 These expressions are proverbs drawn from common sayings of the Eastern countryside. A proverb is like a sword with two edges — or rather, with many edges. It can be turned in different directions, and each angle still cuts sharply. A proverb often carries several meanings, and it is not always easy to determine the exact sense intended by the one who first spoke it. In this case, the context allows more than one interpretation. An ancient commentator even claimed the verse contains seven meanings, each consistent with its setting. I cannot dismiss that possibility; indeed, it would simply be another example of the manifold wisdom of the Word of God. Like those intricately carved Chinese ivory balls, where one sphere rests within another, so many passages of Scripture contain meaning within meaning, teaching within teaching — each layer worthy of the Spirit who inspired it.

The first sense I will briefly mention is this: the prophet is confronting ungodly people about their attempt to find happiness where it cannot be found. They were striving to become rich, powerful, and secure through oppression. As the prophet says, “You have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.” Justice among them was bought and sold; the book of the law was used as an instrument of fraud. Yet, the prophet insists, there is no true gain in such a path, no real profit, no lasting happiness. It is as absurd as horses running upon solid rock or oxen attempting to plough stone. It is labor wasted. If any of you try to satisfy yourselves with this world alone, if you hope to find heaven in your business and family life without looking upward to God, you labor in vain.

If you expect pleasure in sin and imagine that it will go well with you while you despise God’s law, you are gravely mistaken. You might as well search for roses in the depths of the sea or look for pearls on the city pavement. You will find what your soul truly needs nowhere but in God.

To seek happiness in evil is to plough granite. To pursue real prosperity through dishonesty is as useless as tilling the sandy shore. “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” Young man, you are exhausting yourself with ambition, chasing honor and advancement. These are poor goals for an immortal soul. And you, sir, are wearing out both mind and body in the pursuit of wealth, as though life consisted in possessions. You are ploughing rock. Your anxieties will not produce peace; your toil will not bring contentment.

And you who attempt to weave a righteousness from your own works apart from Christ — who imagine that by diligent outward ceremonies you can accomplish the work of the Holy Spirit within your heart — you too are ploughing thankless rock. The full strength of fallen human nature can never save a soul. Why, then, continue this futile labor? Abandon the task.

So far, I believe this interpretation faithfully reflects the text. Yet another meaning suggests itself, equally suitable, and upon that I will now dwell, with God’s help. It is this: God will not always send His ministers to call people to repentance. When hearts remain stubborn — when people refuse to repent — God does not strive with them forever. “My Spirit shall not always strive with man.” There is a season of ploughing, but when it becomes clear that the heart is willfully hardened, wisdom itself may counsel mercy to withdraw her efforts.

“Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” No. There is a limit even to patient kindness. In due time, the labor ceases, and the rock remains unploughed forever.

I. Ministers Labor to Break Up the Heart Taking this meaning, we observe first that ministers labor to break up the hearts of people. A wise preacher, by the power of the Holy Spirit, seeks to break apart the hardened clods of the heart so that it may receive the heavenly seed. Many truths serve as sharp ploughshares. People must be made to feel that they have sinned and must be led to repentance.

They must receive Christ not merely with intellectual agreement but with the heart, “for with the heart one believes and is justified.” There must be genuine emotion and conviction. The ploughshare of the law must cut into the heart.

A farmer who is too tender-hearted to tear and harrow his field will never see a harvest. This is the failure of certain preachers: they fear hurting anyone’s feelings and therefore avoid truths that might awaken fear or grief. They keep no sharp ploughshare in their shed and are therefore unlikely to gather a harvest into their barn. They fish without hooks so as not to injure the fish. They fire guns without bullets out of respect for the birds’ feelings. This kind of love is cruelty to souls. It is like a surgeon who allows a patient to die rather than cause pain with a necessary incision or amputation. Such tenderness is dreadful — it leaves people to perish rather than disturb them. It may be pleasant to speak only smooth words, but woe to the one who does so at the cost of truth.

Was this Christ’s spirit? Did He hide the sinner’s danger? Did He cast doubt upon the unquenchable fire and the undying worm? Did He soothe souls with flattering speech? No. With honest love and deep concern, He warned of wrath and urged people to repent or perish. Let Christ’s servants follow their Master. Let them plough deeply with a sharp blade that will not be turned aside by hard soil. If we truly love souls, we must prove it through faithful speech. The hard heart must be broken, or it will continue to reject the Savior who binds up the brokenhearted.

There are certain things people may or may not experience and still be saved. But the realities associated with this ploughing are indispensable. There must be holy fear and humble trembling before God. There must be acknowledgment of guilt and a penitent plea for mercy. In short, there must be a thorough ploughing of the soul before we can expect the seed to bear fruit.

II. At Times Ministers Labor in Vain The text also teaches that sometimes ministers labor without visible success. “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” A ploughman quickly senses whether his plough can cut the ground. So does a minister. He may preach the same words in two different places. In one setting he feels hope and joy; in another, heaviness and resistance. The plough seems to leap out of the furrow.

The blade chips against the stone. He says to himself, “I do not understand why I make no progress here,” and realizes he has been assigned particularly hard soil.

All who labor for Christ know this experience. You may have felt it in a Sunday school class, in a cottage meeting, or in any setting where you have tried to teach Christ. At one time you turned up rich soil that yielded easily under the oxen. At another time, though the horse strains and the oxen labor until their shoulders are sore, no furrow can be cut. The rock resists to the very end.

Such hearers exist in every congregation. They may sit beside tender hearts. A sister, brother, son, or daughter may respond readily to the gospel, yet they remain unmoved. They listen respectfully.

They allow the message to pass in one ear and out the other. They would not abandon public worship, and so they attend — but only to refuse the message inwardly. They are hard rock; the plough does not touch them.

Others are equally hard, but in a different way. The impression made upon them is shallow and temporary. They receive the word with joy, yet do not hold fast to it. They listen attentively, but never put it into practice. They hear about repentance but never repent. They hear about faith but never believe.

They are capable judges of gospel preaching, yet have never personally accepted it. They insist that good bread be served, yet refuse to eat it. They strongly defend truths which they themselves reject. They may be moved to tears, yet their hearts remain unbroken. They leave unchanged and forget what kind of people they are. They are rocky ground throughout. All efforts to plough them seem to fail.

Now this is all the worse, because certain of these rocky-hearted people have been ploughed for years and have grown harder instead of softer. Once or twice ploughing — with a broken share or two and a disappointed ploughman or two — we might not mind, if at last they would yield; but these people have known the gospel since childhood and have never surrendered to its power. And for some of them, childhood is long past. Their hair is turning gray; they themselves are growing weak with age. They have been urged and persuaded times beyond number, yet all that labor has been lost on them.

In fact, years ago they felt the Word in a way they do not feel it now. The sun that softens wax hardens clay; and the same gospel that has brought others to tenderness and repentance has had the opposite effect on them, making them more careless about divine things than they were in their youth. This is a mournful condition, is it not?

Why are some people so extremely rocky? Some are so because of a certain natural stolidity. There are many people whom you simply cannot easily move. There is a great deal of granite in their constitution; they are more closely related to Mr. Obstinate than to Mr. Pliable. Yet I do not altogether think badly of such people. Anyone who has preached to highly excitable hearers knows what it is to stir them greatly, only to discover in the end that they are none the better for it. By contrast, when some of these more immovable people are truly moved, they are moved indeed.

When they feel, they feel deeply, and they retain the impression made upon them. A small chip struck from granite by heavy blows will remain there, while the lashing of water — though easy enough — leaves no trace at all. It is a noble thing to take hold of a solid piece of rock and exercise faith concerning it. The Lord’s hammer has mighty power to break, and in that breaking great glory comes to the Most High.

Worse still, some are hard because of infidelity — not always open rejection of the heart, but a kind of unbelief that springs from a desire not to believe, and that desire helps them discover difficulties. These difficulties do exist, and they were meant to exist; for if everything were as plain as the nose on one’s face, there would be no room for faith. Such people gradually come to doubt — or at least to think that they doubt — essential truths, and this renders them resistant to the gospel of Christ.

A far more numerous group are orthodox enough in doctrine, yet hard-hearted all the same.

Worldliness hardens a person in every way. It dries up charity toward the poor because the man must make money, and he thinks the taxes he pays are excuse enough for neglecting compassion.

He has no time to think of the next world; all his thoughts are absorbed with this one. Money is scarce, he says, and so he must hold it tightly; and when money yields little interest, he finds even more reason to be stingy. He has no time for prayer — he must get to the office. He has no time to read his Bible — his ledger demands attention. You may knock at his door, but his heart is not at home; it is in the counting-house, where he lives and moves and has his being. His god is gold, his joy is business, his all-in-all is himself. What is the use of preaching to such a man? You might as well have horses run upon a rock, or oxen drag a plough across a field covered with iron a mile thick.

With others, hardness comes from the opposite of stern worldliness — a constant levity. They are like butterflies, flitting about and accomplishing nothing. They never think, nor do they wish to think. Half a serious thought exhausts them; they must be amused, or their shallow minds grow weary. Their life is a circle of entertainment. To them the world is a stage, and all men and women merely actors. It is of little use to preach to such people. There is no depth of soil in their nature.

Beneath a thin layer of shifting, worthless sand lies an impenetrable rock of stupidity and senselessness. I could multiply reasons why some are harder than others, but the fact is certain — and there I leave it.

I now ask you to consider whether horses should always run upon a rock, and whether oxen should always plough there. Is it reasonable to expect that God’s servants should labor in vain forever?

These people have been preached to, taught, instructed, warned, pleaded with, and advised. Shall this unrewarded work continue endlessly? They have been given a fair trial. What do reason and prudence say? Are we bound to persevere until we are worn out by fruitless effort? Ask those who plough their own fields — do they recommend continuing when failure is certain? Shall horses run upon the rock? Shall one plough there with oxen? Surely not forever.

Consider the ploughman. He may not seek much consideration, but his Master does not overlook him. See how weary he becomes when his work discourages him. He cries, “Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” “Why have You sent me,” he asks, “to a people who have ears but do not hear? They sit as Your people sit, they hear as Your people hear, but then they go their way, forget every word, and do not obey the voice of the Lord.” Observe how disappointed the preacher becomes. It is hard work to see no progress, though one has done his utmost. No one likes to be assigned a task that seems a complete waste of time and effort. It begins to feel almost absurd, and he fears he will be despised for attempting the impossible.

Shall it always be the lot of God’s ministers to be trifled with? Will the great Husbandman command His ploughmen to spend their strength for nothing? Must His preachers continue to cast pearls before swine? If their Lord commands it, they will persevere; yet their Master is considerate.

I ask you to consider whether it is reasonable to expect a zealous heart to be forever occupied with the salvation of those who never respond. Shall the horses always plough upon the rock? Shall the oxen always labor there?

And what of the Master Himself? Is the Lord always to be resisted and provoked? Many of you have had eternal life set before you as the result of believing in Jesus, and yet you have refused to believe. It is a wonder that my Lord has not said, “You have done your duty with them; never present Christ to them again; My Son shall not be insulted.” If you offer a beggar a coin and he refuses it, you simply put it back in your pocket and walk away. You do not plead with him to accept relief. Yet our God, in mercy, pleads with sinners to come to Him and implores them to receive His Son. In gracious condescension He stands, as it were, like a merchant in the marketplace, crying, “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” And elsewhere He says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

When the Lord of mercy has been refused for so long, does not some righteous indignation mingle with your pity? While you long for sinners to be saved, do you not feel there must be an end to such insult? I ask even the careless to consider this. If they do not respect the ploughman, let them at least consider his Master.

Moreover, there are so many others who need the gospel and would receive it, that wisdom seems to suggest leaving those who despise it. Did not our Lord say that if the mighty works done in Bethsaida and Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented? Even more astonishing, He said that if the same works had been done in Sodom and Gomorrah as were done in Capernaum, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Should we not then take the word to those who will receive it and leave the despisers to their willfulness? Does not reason say, “Send the medicine where there are sick people who value it”?

Thousands are willing to hear the gospel. See how they gather wherever the preacher goes — how they press upon one another in their eagerness. If those who hear daily will not receive the message, “then in God’s name,” says the preacher, “let me go where there is hope of soil that can be ploughed.” “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” Must I always labor where nothing results? Does not reason say, let the word go to China, to India, to the farthest ends of the earth — where people will receive it — rather than remain where it is despised in the streets?

I will not extend the argument further, but I ask the question again solemnly: Would any of you continue pursuing an object once it proved hopeless? When the Lord has sent His servants with kind, gracious, tender words and people refuse to hear, do you marvel that He says, “They are joined to their idols; let them alone”? There is a limit to human patience, and we reach it quickly.

Surely there is also a limit — though we reach it slowly — to the patience of God. At last He says, “It is enough. My Spirit shall no longer strive with them.” If the Lord declares this, can we complain? Is this not wisdom? Does not prudence itself affirm it? Any thoughtful mind will agree: a rock cannot be ploughed forever.

There must, then, be a change — and that soon. The oxen will be taken away from such labor. This can be done easily and quickly, and in three ways.

First, the unresponsive hearer may be removed so that he no longer hears the gospel from the lips of the minister most fitted to reach him. There may be a preacher who has some measure of influence over him; but since he rejects the message and remains unrepentant, he may be relocated to another place where he hears monotonous discourses that do not touch his conscience. He will go where he is no longer urged and pleaded with, and there he will sleep himself into hell. That can be done easily enough. Some of you may even now be arranging your own removal from the field of hope.

Another possibility is this: the plowman may be taken away. He has done his work as faithfully as he could, and he will be released from his difficult task. He is weary. Let him go home. The soil would not break up, but that was not his fault. Let him receive his wages. His plow has been damaged in the effort; let him go home and hear his Lord say, “Well done.” He was willing to continue the discouraging labor as long as his Master commanded him, but if it is clearly fruitless, then let him go home, for his work is finished. He has been seriously ill—let him die and enter into his rest. This is not unlikely.

Or something else may happen. The Lord may say, “That field will trouble the plowman no more.

I will remove it.” And he may remove it in this way: the man who has heard the gospel but rejected it may die. I pray that my Master will not allow any of you to die in your sins, for then we can no longer reach you or hold even the faintest hope for you. No prayer of ours can follow you into eternity.

There is one name by which you must be saved, and that name has been proclaimed to you—the name of Jesus. But if you reject him now, even that name will not save you. If you refuse to receive Jesus as your Savior, he will appear as your Judge. I plead with you: do not destroy your own soul by stubbornly resisting almighty love.

God grant that something better may happen. Is there nothing else that can be done? This soil is rock—can we sow it without breaking it up? No. Without repentance there is no forgiveness of sins. Is there some way of saving people without the grace of God? The Lord Jesus never suggested such a thing. Instead, he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16, ESV). He did not hint at a middle path or suggest a “larger hope.” He plainly declared, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Do not imagine there is a hidden back door into heaven. The Lord has provided none.

What then? Should the preacher continue his seemingly fruitless labor? If even half a hope remains, he is willing to go on and cry, “Hear, you deaf, and see, you blind, and live, you dead.” He will speak that way today, because his Master commands him to preach the gospel to every creature.

But it is heavy work to repeat words of appeal for years to those who refuse to listen.

Yet there is still one more possibility. There is a God in heaven—let us pray that he would stretch out his power. Jesus is at his right hand—let us ask for his intervention. The Holy Spirit is almighty—let us call on him for help. Brothers who plow and sisters who pray, cry out to the Master for aid. The horse and the ox may fail, but there is One above who can accomplish mighty wonders. Did he not once speak to the rock and turn flint into a flowing stream? Let us ask him to do the same now.

And if there is someone who feels and grieves that his heart is like a rock, I am glad he feels it.

The very awareness that your heart is hard is a sign that the stone may already be softening. O hard heart, instead of striking you—as Moses struck the rock in the wilderness and sinned in doing so— I would speak to you. Would you become like wax? Would you melt into streams of repentance?

Listen to God’s voice. Break with holy desire. Melt with longing for Christ, for God may even now be at work within you. Who knows? At this very moment you may begin to crumble. Do you feel the power of the Word? Does the sharp blade of truth pierce you now?

Break and break again, until through true sorrow you are softened. Then the good seed of the gospel will enter your heart, and you will receive it, and we will see its fruit.

So I will cast one more handful of good seed before I finish. If you desire eternal life, trust in Jesus Christ, and you are saved at once. “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22). Whoever believes in him has eternal life. And as Jesus said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15).

O Lord, break up the rock. Let the seed fall into the broken ground and bring a harvest even from hardened stone, for the sake of Jesus Christ. Amen.
