They were striving to become rich, powerful, and secure through oppression. As the prophet says, “You have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.” Justice among them was bought and sold; the book of the law was used as an instrument of fraud. Yet, the prophet insists, there is no true gain in such a path, no real profit, no lasting happiness. It is as absurd as horses running upon solid rock or oxen attempting to plough stone. It is labor wasted. If any of you try to satisfy yourselves with this world alone, if you hope to find heaven in your business and family life without looking upward to God, you labor in vain. If you expect pleasure in sin and imagine that it will go well with you while you despise God’s law, you are gravely mistaken. You might as well search for roses in the depths of the sea or look for pearls on the city pavement. You will find what your soul truly needs nowhere but in God. To seek happiness in evil is to plough granite. To pursue real prosperity through dishonesty is as useless as tilling the sandy shore. “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” Young man, you are exhausting yourself with ambition, chasing honor and advancement. These are poor goals for an immortal soul. And you, sir, are wearing out both mind and body in the pursuit of wealth, as though life consisted in possessions. You are ploughing rock. Your anxieties will not produce peace; your toil will not bring contentment. And you who attempt to weave a righteousness from your own works apart from Christ — who imagine that by diligent outward ceremonies you can accomplish the work of the Holy Spirit within your heart — you too are ploughing thankless rock. The full strength of fallen human nature can never save a soul. Why, then, continue this futile labor? Abandon the task. So far, I believe this interpretation faithfully reflects the text. Yet another meaning suggests itself, equally suitable, and upon that I will now dwell, with God’s help. It is this: God will not always send His ministers to call people to repentance. When hearts remain stubborn — when people refuse to repent — God does not strive with them forever. “My Spirit shall not always strive with man.” There is a season of ploughing, but when it becomes clear that the heart is willfully hardened, wisdom itself may counsel mercy to withdraw her efforts. “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” No. There is a limit even to patient kindness. In due time, the labor ceases, and the rock remains unploughed forever. I. Ministers Labor to Break Up the Heart Taking this meaning, we observe first that ministers labor to break up the hearts of people. A wise preacher, by the power of the Holy Spirit, seeks to break apart the hardened clods of the heart so that it may receive the heavenly seed. Many truths serve as sharp ploughshares. People must be made to feel that they have sinned and must be led to repentance. They must receive Christ not merely with intellectual agreement but with the heart, “for with the heart one believes and is justified.” There must be genuine emotion and conviction. The ploughshare of the law must cut into the heart. A farmer who is too tender-hearted to tear and harrow his field will never see a harvest. This is the failure of certain preachers: they fear hurting anyone’s feelings and therefore avoid truths that might awaken fear or grief. They keep no sharp ploughshare in their shed and are therefore unlikely to gather a harvest into their barn. They fish without hooks so as not to injure the fish. They fire guns without bullets out of respect for the birds’ feelings. This kind of love is cruelty to souls. It is like a surgeon who allows a patient to die rather than cause pain with a necessary incision or amputation. Such tenderness is dreadful — it leaves people to perish rather than disturb them. It may be pleasant to speak only smooth words, but woe to the one who does so at the cost of truth. Was this Christ’s spirit? Did He hide the sinner’s danger? Did He cast doubt upon the unquenchable fire and the undying worm? Did He soothe souls with flattering speech? No. With honest love and deep concern, He warned of wrath and urged people to repent or perish. Let Christ’s servants follow their Master. Let them plough deeply with a sharp blade that will not be turned aside by hard soil. If we truly love souls, we must prove it through faithful speech. The hard heart must be broken, or it will continue to reject the Savior who binds up the brokenhearted. There are certain things people may or may not experience and still be saved. But the realities associated with this ploughing are indispensable. There must be holy fear and humble trembling before God. There must be acknowledgment of guilt and a penitent plea for mercy. In short, there must be a thorough ploughing of the soul before we can expect the seed to bear fruit. II. At Times Ministers Labor in Vain The text also teaches that sometimes ministers labor without visible success. “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” A ploughman quickly senses whether his plough can cut the ground. So does a minister. He may preach the same words in two different places. In one setting he feels hope and joy; in another, heaviness and resistance. The plough seems to leap out of the furrow. The blade chips against the stone. He says to himself, “I do not understand why I make no progress here,” and realizes he has been assigned particularly hard soil. All who labor for Christ know this experience. You may have felt it in a Sunday school class, in a cottage meeting, or in any setting where you have tried to teach Christ. At one time you turned up rich soil that yielded easily under the oxen. At another time, though the horse strains and the oxen labor until their shoulders are sore, no furrow can be cut. The rock resists to the very end. Such hearers exist in every congregation. They may sit beside tender hearts. A sister, brother, son, or daughter may respond readily to the gospel, yet they remain unmoved. They listen respectfully. They allow the message to pass in one ear and out the other. They would not abandon public worship, and so they attend — but only to refuse the message inwardly. They are hard rock; the plough does not touch them. Others are equally hard, but in a different way. The impression made upon them is shallow and temporary. They receive the word with joy, yet do not hold fast to it. They listen attentively, but never put it into practice. They hear about repentance but never repent. They hear about faith but never believe. They are capable judges of gospel preaching, yet have never personally accepted it. They insist that good bread be served, yet refuse to eat it. They strongly defend truths which they themselves reject. They may be moved to tears, yet their hearts remain unbroken. They leave unchanged and forget what kind of people they are. They are rocky ground throughout. All efforts to plough them seem to fail. Now this is all the worse, because certain of these rocky-hearted people have been ploughed for years and have grown harder instead of softer. Once or twice ploughing — with a broken share or two and a disappointed ploughman or two — we might not mind, if at last they would yield; but these people have known the gospel since childhood and have never surrendered to its power. And for some of them, childhood is long past. Their hair is turning gray; they themselves are growing weak with age. They have been urged and persuaded times beyond number, yet all that labor has been lost on them. In fact, years ago they felt the Word in a way they do not feel it now. The sun that softens wax hardens clay; and the same gospel that has brought others to tenderness and repentance has had the opposite effect on them, making them more careless about divine things than they were in their youth. This is a mournful condition, is it not? Why are some people so extremely rocky? Some are so because of a certain natural stolidity. There are many people whom you simply cannot easily move. There is a great deal of granite in their constitution; they are more closely related to Mr. Obstinate than to Mr. Pliable. Yet I do not altogether think badly of such people. Anyone who has preached to highly excitable hearers knows what it is to stir them greatly, only to discover in the end that they are none the better for it. By contrast, when some of these more immovable people are truly moved, they are moved indeed. When they feel, they feel deeply, and they retain the impression made upon them. A small chip struck from granite by heavy blows will remain there, while the lashing of water — though easy enough — leaves no trace at all. It is a noble thing to take hold of a solid piece of rock and exercise faith concerning it. The Lord’s hammer has mighty power to break, and in that breaking great glory comes to the Most High. Worse still, some are hard because of infidelity — not always open rejection of the heart, but a kind of unbelief that springs from a desire not to believe, and that desire helps them discover difficulties. These difficulties do exist, and they were meant to exist; for if everything were as plain as the nose on one’s face, there would be no room for faith. Such people gradually come to doubt — or at least to think that they doubt — essential truths, and this renders them resistant to the gospel of Christ. A far more numerous group are orthodox enough in doctrine, yet hard-hearted all the same. Worldliness hardens a person in every way. It dries up charity toward the poor because the man must make money, and he thinks the taxes he pays are excuse enough for neglecting compassion. He has no time to think of the next world; all his thoughts are absorbed with this one. Money is scarce, he says, and so he must hold it tightly; and when money yields little interest, he finds even more reason to be stingy. He has no time for prayer — he must get to the office. He has no time to read his Bible — his ledger demands attention. You may knock at his door, but his heart is not at home; it is in the counting-house, where he lives and moves and has his being. His god is gold, his joy is business, his all-in-all is himself. What is the use of preaching to such a man? You might as well have horses run upon a rock, or oxen drag a plough across a field covered with iron a mile thick. With others, hardness comes from the opposite of stern worldliness — a constant levity. They are like butterflies, flitting about and accomplishing nothing. They never think, nor do they wish to think. Half a serious thought exhausts them; they must be amused, or their shallow minds grow weary. Their life is a circle of entertainment. To them the world is a stage, and all men and women merely actors. It is of little use to preach to such people. There is no depth of soil in their nature. Beneath a thin layer of shifting, worthless sand lies an impenetrable rock of stupidity and senselessness. I could multiply reasons why some are harder than others, but the fact is certain — and there I leave it. I now ask you to consider whether horses should always run upon a rock, and whether oxen should always plough there. Is it reasonable to expect that God’s servants should labor in vain forever? These people have been preached to, taught, instructed, warned, pleaded with, and advised. Shall this unrewarded work continue endlessly? They have been given a fair trial. What do reason and prudence say? Are we bound to persevere until we are worn out by fruitless effort? Ask those who plough their own fields — do they recommend continuing when failure is certain? Shall horses run upon the rock? Shall one plough there with oxen? Surely not forever. Consider the ploughman. He may not seek much consideration, but his Master does not overlook him. See how weary he becomes when his work discourages him. He cries, “Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” “Why have You sent me,” he asks, “to a people who have ears but do not hear? They sit as Your people sit, they hear as Your people hear, but then they go their way, forget every word, and do not obey the voice of the Lord.” Observe how disappointed the preacher becomes. It is hard work to see no progress, though one has done his utmost. No one likes to be assigned a task that seems a complete waste of time and effort. It begins to feel almost absurd, and he fears he will be despised for attempting the impossible. Shall it always be the lot of God’s ministers to be trifled with? Will the great Husbandman command His ploughmen to spend their strength for nothing? Must His preachers continue to cast pearls before swine? If their Lord commands it, they will persevere; yet their Master is considerate. I ask you to consider whether it is reasonable to expect a zealous heart to be forever occupied with the salvation of those who never respond. Shall the horses always plough upon the rock? Shall the oxen always labor there? And what of the Master Himself? Is the Lord always to be resisted and provoked? Many of you have had eternal life set before you as the result of believing in Jesus, and yet you have refused to believe. It is a wonder that my Lord has not said, “You have done your duty with them; never present Christ to them again; My Son shall not be insulted.” If you offer a beggar a coin and he refuses it, you simply put it back in your pocket and walk away. You do not plead with him to accept relief. Yet our God, in mercy, pleads with sinners to come to Him and implores them to receive His Son. In gracious condescension He stands, as it were, like a merchant in the marketplace, crying, “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” And elsewhere He says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and contrary people.” When the Lord of mercy has been refused for so long, does not some righteous indignation mingle with your pity? While you long for sinners to be saved, do you not feel there must be an end to such insult? I ask even the careless to consider this. If they do not respect the ploughman, let them at least consider his Master. Moreover, there are so many others who need the gospel and would receive it, that wisdom seems to suggest leaving those who despise it. Did not our Lord say that if the mighty works done in Bethsaida and Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented? Even more astonishing, He said that if the same works had been done in Sodom and Gomorrah as were done in Capernaum, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Should we not then take the word to those who will receive it and leave the despisers to their willfulness? Does not reason say, “Send the medicine where there are sick people who value it”? Thousands are willing to hear the gospel. See how they gather wherever the preacher goes — how they press upon one another in their eagerness. If those who hear daily will not receive the message, “then in God’s name,” says the preacher, “let me go where there is hope of soil that can be ploughed.” “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” Must I always labor where nothing results? Does not reason say, let the word go to China, to India, to the farthest ends of the earth — where people will receive it — rather than remain where it is despised in the streets? I will not extend the argument further, but I ask the question again solemnly: Would any of you continue pursuing an object once it proved hopeless? When the Lord has sent His servants with kind, gracious, tender words and people refuse to hear, do you marvel that He says, “They are joined to their idols; let them alone”? There is a limit to human patience, and we reach it quickly. Surely there is also a limit — though we reach it slowly — to the patience of God. At last He says, “It is enough. My Spirit shall no longer strive with them.” If the Lord declares this, can we complain? Is this not wisdom? Does not prudence itself affirm it? Any thoughtful mind will agree: a rock cannot be ploughed forever. There must, then, be a change — and that soon. The oxen will be taken away from such labor. This can be done easily and quickly, and in three ways. First, the unresponsive hearer may be removed so that he no longer hears the gospel from the lips of the minister most fitted to reach him. There may be a preacher who has some measure of influence over him; but since he rejects the message and remains unrepentant, he may be relocated to another place where he hears monotonous discourses that do not touch his conscience. He will go where he is no longer urged and pleaded with, and there he will sleep himself into hell. That can be done easily enough. Some of you may even now be arranging your own removal from the field of hope. Another possibility is this: the plowman may be taken away. He has done his work as faithfully as he could, and he will be released from his difficult task. He is weary. Let him go home. The soil would not break up, but that was not his fault. Let him receive his wages. His plow has been damaged in the effort; let him go home and hear his Lord say, “Well done.” He was willing to continue the discouraging labor as long as his Master commanded him, but if it is clearly fruitless, then let him go home, for his work is finished. He has been seriously ill—let him die and enter into his rest. This is not unlikely. Or something else may happen. The Lord may say, “That field will trouble the plowman no more. I will remove it.” And he may remove it in this way: the man who has heard the gospel but rejected it may die. I pray that my Master will not allow any of you to die in your sins, for then we can no longer reach you or hold even the faintest hope for you. No prayer of ours can follow you into eternity. There is one name by which you must be saved, and that name has been proclaimed to you—the name of Jesus. But if you reject him now, even that name will not save you. If you refuse to receive Jesus as your Savior, he will appear as your Judge. I plead with you: do not destroy your own soul by stubbornly resisting almighty love. God grant that something better may happen. Is there nothing else that can be done? This soil is rock—can we sow it without breaking it up? No. Without repentance there is no forgiveness of sins. Is there some way of saving people without the grace of God? The Lord Jesus never suggested such a thing. Instead, he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16, ESV). He did not hint at a middle path or suggest a “larger hope.” He plainly declared, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Do not imagine there is a hidden back door into heaven. The Lord has provided none. What then? Should the preacher continue his seemingly fruitless labor? If even half a hope remains, he is willing to go on and cry, “Hear, you deaf, and see, you blind, and live, you dead.” He will speak that way today, because his Master commands him to preach the gospel to every creature. But it is heavy work to repeat words of appeal for years to those who refuse to listen. Yet there is still one more possibility. There is a God in heaven—let us pray that he would stretch out his power. Jesus is at his right hand—let us ask for his intervention. The Holy Spirit is almighty—let us call on him for help. Brothers who plow and sisters who pray, cry out to the Master for aid. The horse and the ox may fail, but there is One above who can accomplish mighty wonders. Did he not once speak to the rock and turn flint into a flowing stream? Let us ask him to do the same now. And if there is someone who feels and grieves that his heart is like a rock, I am glad he feels it. The very awareness that your heart is hard is a sign that the stone may already be softening. O hard heart, instead of striking you—as Moses struck the rock in the wilderness and sinned in doing so— I would speak to you. Would you become like wax? Would you melt into streams of repentance? Listen to God’s voice. Break with holy desire. Melt with longing for Christ, for God may even now be at work within you. Who knows? At this very moment you may begin to crumble. Do you feel the power of the Word? Does the sharp blade of truth pierce you now? Break and break again, until through true sorrow you are softened. Then the good seed of the gospel will enter your heart, and you will receive it, and we will see its fruit. So I will cast one more handful of good seed before I finish. If you desire eternal life, trust in Jesus Christ, and you are saved at once. “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22). Whoever believes in him has eternal life. And as Jesus said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15). O Lord, break up the rock. Let the seed fall into the broken ground and bring a harvest even from hardened stone, for the sake of Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: The Parable Of The Sower
fields.body_html:
The sower scatters seed freely, yet not all soil receives it. Hearts may be hardened, distracted, or entangled, preventing growth. God’s Word calls for receptive ground, patience, and perseverance, reminding us that fruit depends on divine grace, not human effort.

“And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: ‘A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.’ As he said these things, he called out, ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’” Luke 8:4–8.

In our country, when a farmer goes out to sow, he usually works in an enclosed field, scattering seed from his basket along every ridge and furrow. But in the East, near small towns, farmland was often an open stretch of ground. It was divided into different properties, but there were no visible fences—only ancient boundary markers or perhaps small ridges of stones.

Footpaths ran through these open fields. The most traveled paths were called highways, though they were nothing like our paved roads—just well-worn tracks, hardened by constant use. There were also smaller side paths, made by travelers seeking safer routes or shortcuts. Over time, these too became worn and firm.

When the sower went out to sow, he worked soil that had been scratched by a simple, primitive plow. He aimed to scatter most of his seed there. But since a path ran through the middle of the field, unless he left a wide strip unused, some seed would fall on the path. In another place, a rock might rise close to the surface, covered only by a thin layer of soil. Seed would fall there as well.

In yet another corner, the ground might be tangled with the roots of nettles and thistles.

The farmer would scatter seed there too, and both the grain and the weeds would grow together— until the stronger thorns choked the young plants so that they produced no mature fruit.

Remembering that the Bible was written in the East, and that its images come from that setting, often helps us understand its meaning more clearly than if we picture only English farming customs. The preacher of the Gospel is like that sower. He does not create the seed; it is given to him by his divine Master. No one can create even the smallest grain that grows in the earth, much less the heavenly seed that gives eternal life. The minister goes to his Master in private prayer and asks to be taught the gospel. In that way, he fills his basket with the good seed of the kingdom.

Then he goes out in his Master’s name and scatters the precious truth. If he knew exactly where the best soil was—where hearts had already been prepared by conviction—he might focus only there. But since he cannot see into human hearts, he must preach the gospel to every creature. He must scatter seed on hardened hearts, on distracted minds, and on those entangled in the cares and pleasures of this world.

He must leave the results to the Lord who gave him the seed. He is not responsible for the harvest; he is responsible only for faithfully and diligently doing his work. Even if not a single ear of grain should ever make the reaper glad, the sower will still be rewarded by his Master if he has planted the right seed with careful hands. Without this assurance, how could we avoid crying out with the prophet, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1, ESV).

Our duty is not determined by the character of our hearers but by the command of our God. We must preach the gospel whether people listen or refuse. We must sow beside all waters. Whatever condition hearts may be in, the minister must preach—to the rock as well as the furrow, to the path as well as the plowed field.

Now I will speak about the four kinds of hearers described in our Lord’s parable. First, those like the path—hearers only. Second, those like rocky ground—briefly moved, but without lasting fruit. Third, those among thorns—where the word begins to grow, but is choked by life’s cares, the deceitfulness of riches, and worldly pleasures.

And lastly, that small group—may God greatly increase it—the good soil, in whom the Word produces abundant fruit.

I. The Path “Some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.” Many of you do not come to worship seeking a blessing. You do not intend to worship God or to be changed by what you hear. You are like the path, never meant to be a field of grain. If even one seed of truth were to grow in you, it would be as surprising as wheat growing in the middle of a busy street.

If the seed is skillfully scattered, some may rest briefly on your thoughts. You may not understand it fully, but if it is presented attractively, you might discuss it for a time—until something more entertaining captures your attention. Even that small benefit is short-lived. Soon you forget everything you heard.

We wish we could hope that the Word would remain with you, but your heart is so hardened by constant traffic that there is no place for the seed to take root. Satan continually passes over it with blasphemies, lusts, lies, and empty distractions. Pride rolls across it like heavy wheels. Greed tramples it down until it becomes hard as stone.

The seed finds no resting place. Thoughts rush back and forth constantly. Your soul has become a marketplace where everything is traded. You are busy buying and selling, yet you do not realize that you are selling the truth and buying your own destruction.

You say you have no time to think about spiritual things. The road of your heart is so crowded that there is no room for the seed to grow. If it ever begins to sprout, some new amusement or distraction crushes it before it matures. Just as grain could never grow in the busiest streets of a city, so truth cannot grow in a heart filled with constant noise, pride, worry, and rebellion against God.

We have looked at this hardened roadside; now let us consider what becomes of the good word when it falls on such a heart.

The seed would have grown if it had fallen on proper soil. But it has landed in the wrong place, and it remains as dry as when it first left the sower’s hand. The word of the gospel lies on the surface of that heart but never enters it. It is like snow falling on a busy street: it touches the wet pavement, melts, and disappears at once. The word has no time to awaken life in the soul. It rests there briefly, but it never takes root or produces any lasting effect.

Why do people come to hear if the word never enters their hearts? That question has often puzzled us. Some would not miss a Sunday for anything. They enjoy gathering for worship. Yet no tear falls from their eyes. Their souls never rise to heaven in praise. They do not truly join in confession of sin. They do not think seriously about coming judgment or the future state of their souls. Their hearts are like iron; the minister might as well preach to a heap of stones.

What brings such unfeeling sinners here? At times it seems we would have as much hope of converting wild beasts as these untamed, unresponsive hearts. Has all feeling vanished? Do people attend worship merely because it is respectable? Or does coming help them feel more comfortable in their sins? If they stayed away, conscience might trouble them; but by attending, they persuade themselves that they are religious.

Oh, my hearers, your condition could make an angel weep. The sun of the gospel shines on your face, yet your eyes remain blind. The music of heaven sounds in your ears, yet you do not truly hear it. You can appreciate a turn of phrase. You can admire an illustration. But the spiritual meaning—the living power within the message—you do not grasp. You sit at the wedding feast, but you do not taste the food. Heaven rejoices over redeemed souls, yet you remain unredeemed, without God and without Christ. Though we plead with you, pray for you, and weep over you, you remain as hardened and careless as ever. May God have mercy on you and break up your hard heart so that his word may dwell within you.

The picture is not yet complete. The passage tells us that the birds of the air devoured the seed. Is there a wayside hearer here? Perhaps he did not intend to listen carefully today. When the sermon ends, someone invites him into questionable company. He goes along, and the good seed is quickly devoured.

There are many influences ready to snatch the gospel from a heart. The devil himself—whom Scripture calls the “prince of the power of the air”—is always eager to steal away a good thought.

And he does not work alone. He has countless helpers. A spouse, children, friends, enemies, customers, creditors—any of these may become instruments to consume the seed, and they often succeed. What a tragedy that heavenly seed should become food for the devil—that God’s grain should feed unclean birds.

If you have heard the gospel since childhood, how many wagonloads of sermons have been wasted on you? In your younger days, you may have heard a faithful preacher who prayed for his congregation until his eyes were red with tears. Do you remember the Sundays when you said to yourself, “I will go to my room and pray”? But you did not. The birds devoured the seed, and you continued in sin.

Even now, you are rarely absent from church. Yet the gospel falls on your soul as if it dropped onto iron. The law may be preached with thunder—you do not mock it, but neither are you moved.

Christ may be lifted up before you. His wounds may be described. His blood may be set before your eyes. You may be urged earnestly to look to him and live. But it is like sowing seed along the seashore.

What shall I do for you? Shall I stand here and weep over this hardened path? My tears cannot soften it; it has been trampled too long. Shall I bring the plow of the gospel? The blade cannot penetrate soil so compacted. What then? O God, you alone know how to melt the hardest heart through the precious blood of Jesus. Do it now, we pray. Glorify your grace by causing the good seed to live and produce a heavenly harvest.

Now consider the second kind of hearer. Some seed fell upon rock, and as it grew up, it withered away because it lacked moisture. You can picture that rock in the middle of the field, covered only by a thin layer of soil. The seed falls there as it does everywhere else. It sprouts quickly. It grows rapidly. Then it withers and dies.

Only those who deeply love souls can understand the hopes, joys, and bitter disappointments that these rocky places have caused. There are hearers whose hearts seem soft and responsive. While others feel nothing, these are visibly moved. Whether the message speaks of judgment or of Christ’s love at the cross, they are stirred. Strong impressions are made.

They resolve to change, yet they delay. They are not hardened opponents of God. They appear open and eager. Rejoicing, we direct the message toward them, and it seems to penetrate. But there is hidden armor beneath the surface. No lasting wound is made.

Scripture describes them this way: “And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away” (Mark 4:16–17, ESV).

Have we not seen many who receive the word with joy? They have no deep conviction of sin, yet they quickly profess faith in Christ. Their belief appears genuine. The seed has sprouted. There is a green blade. We thank God, thinking a soul has been saved. But our joy is premature. The same lack of depth that made them respond quickly also causes them to wither when difficulty comes.

We see this often. Someone asks to join the church and tells us how deeply a sermon moved them.

They say they believed at once and have never felt such happiness. We ask about conviction of sin. They believe they were convicted. What they know for certain is that religion brings them great pleasure.

We ask if they will continue, and they are confident that they will. Everything seems new. They claim to hate what they once loved. And all of this has happened suddenly, without deep plowing of the heart. It is as if a field were instantly covered with wheat by magic. Perhaps they are received into fellowship. Within weeks they are less regular. When gently corrected, they explain that opposition has made things difficult. Soon they disappear entirely. A little ridicule or inconvenience has driven them back. The minister feels like a farmer who saw his field green and flourishing, only to wake and find every shoot destroyed by frost.

If it is tragic to be a wayside hearer, it is hardly better to be like the rock. This second group gives more initial hope. They gather eagerly, especially around a new minister. They seem devoted. But time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away.

Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so?

Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid.

May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring honor to Christ.

III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you.

“And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns.

Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing, and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm.

We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear.

They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion.

The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business; their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion keeps on growing in a fashion.

Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no.

They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask, “Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind.

Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow, will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party, that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor, for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics, I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.”

I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich; one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.”

Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls, it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work, for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit a hundredfold to his own glory.

IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice, we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the Word?

The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good root. In some cases it produced fervent love, largeness of heart, and devotedness of purpose of a noble kind, like seed which produces a hundredfold. The man became a mighty servant for God; he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble.

The seed had brought forth in him tenfold, perhaps twentyfold. How many are there of this sort here? Is there one who prays within himself, “God be merciful to me, a sinner”? The seed has fallen in the right place. Soul, your prayer shall be heard. God never sets a person longing for mercy without intending to give it. Does another whisper, “Oh that I might be saved”? Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you, even you, will be saved. Have you been the chief of sinners? Trust Christ, and your great sins shall vanish as a millstone sinks beneath the flood. Is there no one here who will trust the Saviour? Can it be possible that the Spirit is entirely absent? that he is not moving in one soul? not giving life in one spirit? We will pray that he may now descend, that the word may not be in vain.
fields.body_text: The sower scatters seed freely, yet not all soil receives it. Hearts may be hardened, distracted, or entangled, preventing growth. God’s Word calls for receptive ground, patience, and perseverance, reminding us that fruit depends on divine grace, not human effort. “And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: ‘A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.’ As he said these things, he called out, ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’” Luke 8:4–8. In our country, when a farmer goes out to sow, he usually works in an enclosed field, scattering seed from his basket along every ridge and furrow. But in the East, near small towns, farmland was often an open stretch of ground. It was divided into different properties, but there were no visible fences—only ancient boundary markers or perhaps small ridges of stones. Footpaths ran through these open fields. The most traveled paths were called highways, though they were nothing like our paved roads—just well-worn tracks, hardened by constant use. There were also smaller side paths, made by travelers seeking safer routes or shortcuts. Over time, these too became worn and firm. When the sower went out to sow, he worked soil that had been scratched by a simple, primitive plow. He aimed to scatter most of his seed there. But since a path ran through the middle of the field, unless he left a wide strip unused, some seed would fall on the path. In another place, a rock might rise close to the surface, covered only by a thin layer of soil. Seed would fall there as well. In yet another corner, the ground might be tangled with the roots of nettles and thistles. The farmer would scatter seed there too, and both the grain and the weeds would grow together— until the stronger thorns choked the young plants so that they produced no mature fruit. Remembering that the Bible was written in the East, and that its images come from that setting, often helps us understand its meaning more clearly than if we picture only English farming customs. The preacher of the Gospel is like that sower. He does not create the seed; it is given to him by his divine Master. No one can create even the smallest grain that grows in the earth, much less the heavenly seed that gives eternal life. The minister goes to his Master in private prayer and asks to be taught the gospel. In that way, he fills his basket with the good seed of the kingdom. Then he goes out in his Master’s name and scatters the precious truth. If he knew exactly where the best soil was—where hearts had already been prepared by conviction—he might focus only there. But since he cannot see into human hearts, he must preach the gospel to every creature. He must scatter seed on hardened hearts, on distracted minds, and on those entangled in the cares and pleasures of this world. He must leave the results to the Lord who gave him the seed. He is not responsible for the harvest; he is responsible only for faithfully and diligently doing his work. Even if not a single ear of grain should ever make the reaper glad, the sower will still be rewarded by his Master if he has planted the right seed with careful hands. Without this assurance, how could we avoid crying out with the prophet, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1, ESV). Our duty is not determined by the character of our hearers but by the command of our God. We must preach the gospel whether people listen or refuse. We must sow beside all waters. Whatever condition hearts may be in, the minister must preach—to the rock as well as the furrow, to the path as well as the plowed field. Now I will speak about the four kinds of hearers described in our Lord’s parable. First, those like the path—hearers only. Second, those like rocky ground—briefly moved, but without lasting fruit. Third, those among thorns—where the word begins to grow, but is choked by life’s cares, the deceitfulness of riches, and worldly pleasures. And lastly, that small group—may God greatly increase it—the good soil, in whom the Word produces abundant fruit. I. The Path “Some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.” Many of you do not come to worship seeking a blessing. You do not intend to worship God or to be changed by what you hear. You are like the path, never meant to be a field of grain. If even one seed of truth were to grow in you, it would be as surprising as wheat growing in the middle of a busy street. If the seed is skillfully scattered, some may rest briefly on your thoughts. You may not understand it fully, but if it is presented attractively, you might discuss it for a time—until something more entertaining captures your attention. Even that small benefit is short-lived. Soon you forget everything you heard. We wish we could hope that the Word would remain with you, but your heart is so hardened by constant traffic that there is no place for the seed to take root. Satan continually passes over it with blasphemies, lusts, lies, and empty distractions. Pride rolls across it like heavy wheels. Greed tramples it down until it becomes hard as stone. The seed finds no resting place. Thoughts rush back and forth constantly. Your soul has become a marketplace where everything is traded. You are busy buying and selling, yet you do not realize that you are selling the truth and buying your own destruction. You say you have no time to think about spiritual things. The road of your heart is so crowded that there is no room for the seed to grow. If it ever begins to sprout, some new amusement or distraction crushes it before it matures. Just as grain could never grow in the busiest streets of a city, so truth cannot grow in a heart filled with constant noise, pride, worry, and rebellion against God. We have looked at this hardened roadside; now let us consider what becomes of the good word when it falls on such a heart. The seed would have grown if it had fallen on proper soil. But it has landed in the wrong place, and it remains as dry as when it first left the sower’s hand. The word of the gospel lies on the surface of that heart but never enters it. It is like snow falling on a busy street: it touches the wet pavement, melts, and disappears at once. The word has no time to awaken life in the soul. It rests there briefly, but it never takes root or produces any lasting effect. Why do people come to hear if the word never enters their hearts? That question has often puzzled us. Some would not miss a Sunday for anything. They enjoy gathering for worship. Yet no tear falls from their eyes. Their souls never rise to heaven in praise. They do not truly join in confession of sin. They do not think seriously about coming judgment or the future state of their souls. Their hearts are like iron; the minister might as well preach to a heap of stones. What brings such unfeeling sinners here? At times it seems we would have as much hope of converting wild beasts as these untamed, unresponsive hearts. Has all feeling vanished? Do people attend worship merely because it is respectable? Or does coming help them feel more comfortable in their sins? If they stayed away, conscience might trouble them; but by attending, they persuade themselves that they are religious. Oh, my hearers, your condition could make an angel weep. The sun of the gospel shines on your face, yet your eyes remain blind. The music of heaven sounds in your ears, yet you do not truly hear it. You can appreciate a turn of phrase. You can admire an illustration. But the spiritual meaning—the living power within the message—you do not grasp. You sit at the wedding feast, but you do not taste the food. Heaven rejoices over redeemed souls, yet you remain unredeemed, without God and without Christ. Though we plead with you, pray for you, and weep over you, you remain as hardened and careless as ever. May God have mercy on you and break up your hard heart so that his word may dwell within you. The picture is not yet complete. The passage tells us that the birds of the air devoured the seed. Is there a wayside hearer here? Perhaps he did not intend to listen carefully today. When the sermon ends, someone invites him into questionable company. He goes along, and the good seed is quickly devoured. There are many influences ready to snatch the gospel from a heart. The devil himself—whom Scripture calls the “prince of the power of the air”—is always eager to steal away a good thought. And he does not work alone. He has countless helpers. A spouse, children, friends, enemies, customers, creditors—any of these may become instruments to consume the seed, and they often succeed. What a tragedy that heavenly seed should become food for the devil—that God’s grain should feed unclean birds. If you have heard the gospel since childhood, how many wagonloads of sermons have been wasted on you? In your younger days, you may have heard a faithful preacher who prayed for his congregation until his eyes were red with tears. Do you remember the Sundays when you said to yourself, “I will go to my room and pray”? But you did not. The birds devoured the seed, and you continued in sin. Even now, you are rarely absent from church. Yet the gospel falls on your soul as if it dropped onto iron. The law may be preached with thunder—you do not mock it, but neither are you moved. Christ may be lifted up before you. His wounds may be described. His blood may be set before your eyes. You may be urged earnestly to look to him and live. But it is like sowing seed along the seashore. What shall I do for you? Shall I stand here and weep over this hardened path? My tears cannot soften it; it has been trampled too long. Shall I bring the plow of the gospel? The blade cannot penetrate soil so compacted. What then? O God, you alone know how to melt the hardest heart through the precious blood of Jesus. Do it now, we pray. Glorify your grace by causing the good seed to live and produce a heavenly harvest. Now consider the second kind of hearer. Some seed fell upon rock, and as it grew up, it withered away because it lacked moisture. You can picture that rock in the middle of the field, covered only by a thin layer of soil. The seed falls there as it does everywhere else. It sprouts quickly. It grows rapidly. Then it withers and dies. Only those who deeply love souls can understand the hopes, joys, and bitter disappointments that these rocky places have caused. There are hearers whose hearts seem soft and responsive. While others feel nothing, these are visibly moved. Whether the message speaks of judgment or of Christ’s love at the cross, they are stirred. Strong impressions are made. They resolve to change, yet they delay. They are not hardened opponents of God. They appear open and eager. Rejoicing, we direct the message toward them, and it seems to penetrate. But there is hidden armor beneath the surface. No lasting wound is made. Scripture describes them this way: “And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away” (Mark 4:16–17, ESV). Have we not seen many who receive the word with joy? They have no deep conviction of sin, yet they quickly profess faith in Christ. Their belief appears genuine. The seed has sprouted. There is a green blade. We thank God, thinking a soul has been saved. But our joy is premature. The same lack of depth that made them respond quickly also causes them to wither when difficulty comes. We see this often. Someone asks to join the church and tells us how deeply a sermon moved them. They say they believed at once and have never felt such happiness. We ask about conviction of sin. They believe they were convicted. What they know for certain is that religion brings them great pleasure. We ask if they will continue, and they are confident that they will. Everything seems new. They claim to hate what they once loved. And all of this has happened suddenly, without deep plowing of the heart. It is as if a field were instantly covered with wheat by magic. Perhaps they are received into fellowship. Within weeks they are less regular. When gently corrected, they explain that opposition has made things difficult. Soon they disappear entirely. A little ridicule or inconvenience has driven them back. The minister feels like a farmer who saw his field green and flourishing, only to wake and find every shoot destroyed by frost. If it is tragic to be a wayside hearer, it is hardly better to be like the rock. This second group gives more initial hope. They gather eagerly, especially around a new minister. They seem devoted. But time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away. Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so? Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid. May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring honor to Christ. III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you. “And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns. Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing, and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm. We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear. They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion. The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business; their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion keeps on growing in a fashion. Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no. They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask, “Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind. Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow, will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party, that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor, for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics, I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.” I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich; one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.” Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls, it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work, for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit a hundredfold to his own glory. IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice, we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the Word? The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good root. The man became a mighty servant for God; he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble.
