Later he was proclaimed as “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29, ESV), and even in his glory he is described as the Lamb in the midst of the throne. In unfolding this divine picture, I invite you first to consider our Saviour’s patience, shown in the image of a sheep silent before its shearers. Our Lord was brought before the shearers to be stripped of his comfort, stripped of his honour, stripped even of his good name, and at last stripped of his very life; yet under the shearers he was silent like a sheep. Think of how patient he was before Pilate, Herod, and Caiaphas, and upon the cross. There is no record of him crying out in impatience at the pain and shame he suffered at the hands of those wicked men. Not one bitter word escaped him. Pilate said, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you” (Mark 15:4, ESV). Herod was deeply disappointed because he hoped to see some miracle performed by him. The few words our Lord did speak were gentle and submissive, like the quiet sound of a sheep, yet infinitely full of meaning. He said, “For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world—to bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37, ESV), and, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34, ESV). Apart from this, he remained patient and silent. Notice first that our Lord was silent and did not open his mouth against his enemies. He did not accuse a single one of cruelty or injustice. They slandered him, but he did not reply. False witnesses rose up, but he did not answer them. You might think he would have spoken when they spat in his face. Could he not have said, “Friend, why are you doing this? For which of my works do you insult me?” But the time for such questions had passed. When they struck him on the face with their hands, it would not have been surprising if he had asked, “Why do you strike me?” But no— he acted as though he did not hear their insults. He brought no accusation before his Father. He needed only to lift his eyes to heaven, and legions of angels would have driven away the mocking soldiers. One flash of a seraph’s wing, and Herod would have perished; Pilate could have fallen under the judgement he deserved as an unjust judge. The hill of the cross could have become like the mouth of a volcano to swallow up the crowd that stood there mocking and jeering at him. But there was no such display of power. Rather, there was a far greater display of power over himself. He restrained omnipotence itself with a strength beyond measure. Again, as he spoke no word against his enemies, so he spoke no word against any of us. You remember how Zipporah said to Moses, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!” (Exodus 4:25, ESV), as she saw her child bleeding. Surely Jesus could have said to his church, “You are a costly bride to me, bringing me all this shame and bloodshed.” But “God gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5, ESV). He opened the very fountain of his heart and did not rebuke us. He had counted the full cost beforehand. Therefore he endured the cross, despising the shame. “This was compassion like a God, That when the Saviour knew, The price of pardon was his blood, His pity never withdrew.” Without doubt he looked across the ages, for his eyes were not dim, even when filled with blood upon the tree. He must have foreseen your indifference and mine, our cold hearts and our unfaithfulness. He could have left behind words such as these: “I am suffering for those who are unworthy of my love. Their love will be a poor return for mine. Though I give my whole heart to them, how lukewarm their love will be towards me. I am weary of them; it grieves me to lay down my life for such a people.” But there is no trace of such a thought. No. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1, ESV). He did not speak a single word that sounded like regret or complaint for suffering on their behalf, nor any sorrow that he had begun the work. And as there was no word against his enemies, and no word against you or me, so there was no word against his Father, nor a syllable of complaint about the severity of the punishment laid upon him for our sake. You and I have complained under far lighter troubles, feeling that we have been treated unfairly. We have even dared to cry out to God, “My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure” (Job 16:16–17, ESV). But not so the Saviour. No complaint was found in his mouth. We cannot begin to understand how deeply the Father pressed and crushed him, yet there was no rebellion. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, ESV) was a cry of astonished sorrow, not a complaint. It showed true humanity in weakness, but not humanity in revolt. Jeremiah wrote many laments, but Jesus spoke few. Jesus wept, and Jesus sweat great drops of blood, yet he never murmured or rebelled in his heart. Look at your Lord and Saviour lying in quiet surrender beneath the shearers, as they take away everything dear to him, yet he does not open his mouth. Here we see his complete submission. He gave himself fully; there was no holding back. The sacrifice did not need to be tied with ropes to the horns of the altar. How different from you and me. He stood willing to suffer, to be spat upon, to be shamefully treated, and to die, for he was fully surrendered. He was entirely given to do the Father’s will and to accomplish our redemption. There was complete self-control as well. No part of him rose up to demand freedom or to escape the suffering. No part of his body, no thought of his mind, no power of his spirit resisted. All submitted to the will of God. The whole Christ gave his whole being to God so that he might offer himself perfectly, without blemish, for our redemption. There was not only self-control, but complete focus on his mission. The sheep lying there does not think of the pastures; it yields itself to the shearer. The zeal for God’s house consumed our Lord in Pilate’s hall as much as anywhere else, for there he made the good confession. His only concern was to uphold the honour of God and to save his chosen people. Brothers and sisters, I wish we could reach this point: to surrender our whole spirit to God, to learn self-control, and to give our conquered selves entirely to him. The calmness and submission of our Lord are illustrated even more clearly if it is true that sheep in the East are more docile than ours. Those who have seen the noise and rough handling at many of our sheep shearings may struggle to believe the testimony of the ancient writer Philo Judaeus, who said that sheep came willingly to be shorn. He wrote that wool-covered rams, heavy with thick fleeces, place themselves into the shepherd’s hands to have their wool cut, as if paying their yearly tribute to man, their natural ruler. The sheep stands in a quiet, bowed posture, unconstrained under the hand of the shearer. This may sound strange to those unfamiliar with the gentle nature of sheep, but he insists it is true. How wonderful was such submission in our Lord’s case. Let us admire it and seek to follow his example. I have tried, however imperfectly, to describe the patience of our beloved Master. Now, secondly, let us consider our own situation under the same image used of our Lord. Did I not say at the beginning that because we are sheep, he was willing to compare himself to a sheep? Let us look at it from another angle. Our Lord was a sheep before the shearers, and as he is, so are we in this world. Though we will never be offered like lambs in the temple as an atoning sacrifice, yet for ages the saints have been treated as a flock for slaughter. As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36, ESV). Jesus sends us out as sheep in the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16, ESV), and we are to see ourselves as living sacrifices, ready to be offered. But I want to focus especially on this second image: we are brought like sheep under the shearer’s hand. Just as a sheep is taken by the shearer and its wool is cut off, so the Lord sometimes takes his people and shears them, removing their earthly comforts and leaving them stripped. I wish that when our time comes to go through this shearing, it could be said of us as it was of our Lord, “As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” I fear we speak far too much and complain endlessly, often without real cause, or for very small reasons. But now let us consider the image itself. First, remember that a sheep repays its owner for all his care and effort by allowing itself to be shorn. As far as I know, there is nothing else a sheep can do in return. It provides food when it is killed, but while it is alive the one payment it can make to the shepherd is to give its fleece at the proper time. Some of God’s people can offer Christ the tribute of gratitude through active service, and they should do so gladly every day of their lives. But many others cannot do much in active service, and almost the only return they can give to their Lord is to surrender their fleece through suffering when he calls them to suffer, quietly yielding to be stripped of personal comfort when the time comes for patient endurance. Here comes the shearer. He takes the sheep and begins to cut, cut, cut, cutting away the wool in great handfuls. Affliction is often the large pair of shears. A husband, or perhaps a wife, is taken away. Little children are removed. Property is cut off, and health is gone. Sometimes the shears remove a person’s good name; slander arises and comforts disappear. Well, this is your shearing time, and it may be that you cannot glorify God in any great outward way except by going through this process. If that is so, should we not, like good sheep belonging to Christ, surrender ourselves willingly, saying, “I lay myself down with this intention: that you may take from me anything and everything, and do what you will with me; for I am not my own, for I was bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV)? Notice that the sheep itself benefits from the act of shearing. Before the sheep are shorn, the wool is long and old, and every bush and briar tears at it until the sheep looks ragged and miserable. If the wool were left on when the heat of summer came, the sheep would hardly be able to bear it. It would be so overloaded with fleece that it would be as uncomfortable as we are when we keep on our heavy winter clothes far too late in the season. So, brothers and sisters, when the Lord shears us, we do not enjoy the process any more than the sheep do; but first, it is for his glory, and second, it is for our good. Therefore we are bound to submit willingly. There are many things we would have liked to keep which, if we had kept them, would not have been blessings but curses. A blessing that has gone stale becomes a curse. The manna, though it came from heaven, was good only as long as God commanded it to be kept for the proper time. When it was kept beyond that time, it “bred worms and stank” (Exodus 16:20, ESV), and then it was no blessing at all. Many people would keep their mercies until they rot, but God will not allow it. Up to a certain point, your wealth was a blessing; beyond that point it would not have been, and so the Lord took it away. Up to that point, your child was a gift; beyond that, it would not have been so, and therefore sickness came and the child died. You may not be able to see it, but it is true: when God removes a blessing from his people, he takes it away because it would not have remained a blessing. Before sheep are shorn, they are always washed. Have you ever seen the scene when they are driven down to the brook? Men stand in rows leading to the shepherd who waits in the water. The sheep are driven down; the men seize them, throw them into the pool, keep their heads above water, and swirl them round and round to wash the wool before cutting it off. Then you see them come out on the other side trembling, poor creatures, wondering what will happen next. I want to suggest to you, brothers and sisters, that whenever a trial threatens to come upon you, you should ask the Lord to sanctify it to you. If the good Shepherd is about to cut off your wool, ask him to wash it before he removes it. Ask to be cleansed in spirit, soul, and body. Christian people have the good habit of asking a blessing on their meals before eating bread. Is it not even more necessary to ask a blessing on our troubles before we enter them? Your dear child may be near death; will you not, dear parents, come together and ask God to bless even the death of that child, if it must happen? The harvest fails; would it not be right to say, “Lord, sanctify this poverty, this loss, this bad harvest. Make it a means of grace to us”? Why not ask a blessing on the cup of bitterness as well as on the cup of thanksgiving? Ask to be washed before you are shorn, and if the shearing must come, let it be your chief concern to offer clean wool. After the washing, when the sheep has dried, it loses what was its comfort. It is thrown down, and the shearers begin their work. The poor creature loses its warm fleece. You too will have to part with your comforts. Remember this: the next time you receive a fresh blessing, call it a loan. Poor sheep, there is no wool on your back that will not one day be cut off. Child of God, there is no earthly comfort in your possession that will not either leave you, or you will leave it. Nothing truly belongs to us except our God. “Why,” someone says, “not our sin?” Sin was ours, but Jesus took it upon himself, and it is gone. Nothing is truly ours but our God, for all his gifts are held on loan and can be recalled at his sovereign will. We foolishly think our mercies belong to us, and when the Lord takes them away, we begin to complain. A loan, it is said, should go home laughing, and so should we rejoice when the Lord takes back what he lent us. All our possessions are brief favours borrowed for a time. As the sheep yields its wool and loses its comfort, so must we give up all our earthly possessions. Or if they remain with us until death, we shall leave them then. We shall not carry a single one of them across the river of death. The shearers take care not to harm the sheep. They cut as close as possible, but they do not cut the skin. If they can help it, they do not draw blood, not even the smallest amount. When a cut does happen, it is usually because the sheep does not lie still. A careful shearer keeps his shears free from blood. Of this Thomson wrote in his poem The Seasons, and the lines beautifully illustrate the whole subject: “How meek, how patient, the mild creature lies! What softness in its melancholy face, What silent, suffering innocence appears! Fear not, you gentle flocks! It is not the knife Of dreadful slaughter raised above you; No, it is the shepherd’s careful, guided shears, Who, having borrowed your fleece As payment for his yearly care, Will send you back to the hills light and free.” It is the kicking and struggling that make the shearing difficult. If we are silent before the shearers, no harm will come. The Lord may cut very close. I have known him strip some so completely that they seemed to have nothing left, like Job when he said, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return” (Job 1:21, ESV). Yet they have also said with Job, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21, ESV). Notice that shearers always choose the right time. It would be cruel and foolish to begin shearing in winter. There is a saying about God “tempering the wind to the shorn lamb.” Whether or not that is accurate, it would indeed be cruel to shear lambs when bitter winds are blowing. Sheep are shorn in warm, pleasant weather, when they can afford to lose their fleece and are better without it. As summer approaches, shearing time comes. Have you not noticed that when the Lord afflicts us, he chooses the best possible time? He taught his disciples to pray, “Pray that your flight may not be in winter” (Matthew 24:20, ESV). The spirit of that prayer can be seen in the timing of our sorrows. He does not send our heaviest trials at our weakest moments. If your soul is already deeply depressed, the Lord does not add the heaviest burden then. He keeps such loads for times when “the joy of the Lord” is your strength. We often feel that when joy increases, a trial may be near; and when sorrow deepens, deliverance may be approaching. The Lord does not send two burdens at once, or if he does, he gives double strength. His shearing time is chosen with gentle wisdom. There is something else to remember. As with the sheep, new wool grows. Whenever the Lord removes earthly comforts with one hand—one, two, three—he restores with the other hand six, twenty, a hundred. We cry and complain about the small loss, yet that loss is necessary so that we may receive a greater gain. Yes, it will be so. We shall have reason to rejoice, for “weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5, ESV). If we lose one position, another awaits us. If we are driven from one place, a better refuge is prepared. Providence opens a second door when it closes the first. If the Lord took away the manna from Israel, it was because they ate the produce of the land of Canaan. If the water from the rock did not follow them any longer, it was because they drank from the Jordan and from the streams. O sheep of the Lord’s fold, new wool is coming. Therefore do not be anxious about the shearing. I have said these things briefly so that we may come to the final point. Let us try to follow the example of our blessed Lord when our time comes to be shorn. Let us be silent before the shearers, submissive and still, as he was. Everything I have said gives a reason for doing so. Our shearing through affliction glorifies God, honours the Shepherd, and benefits ourselves. The Lord measures and tempers our trials and sends them at the right time. In many ways I have shown that it is wise to submit as the sheep does, and that the more completely we do so, the better. We struggle far too much, and we often excuse ourselves for doing so. Sometimes we say, “This is too painful; I cannot be patient. I could have borne anything but this.” When a father disciplines his child, does he choose something pleasant? No. The pain is part of the discipline. In the same way, the bitterness of sorrow is part of our correction. “By the wounds a heart is healed” (see Proverbs 20:30, ESV). Do not complain because your trial feels sharp and unusual. That would be like saying, “If everything goes my way, I will submit; but if it does not, I will rebel.” That is not the spirit of a child of God. Sometimes we complain about our weakness. “Lord, if I were stronger I would not mind this heavy loss; but I am frail, like a dry leaf blown by the storm.” But who decides what trial suits you—God or you? Since the Lord judges this trial suitable for your weakness, you can be sure it is so. Lie still. Lie still. “But my grief comes from a cruel source,” you say. “This trouble did not come directly from God. It came through my cousin or my brother, who should have treated me better. If it had been an enemy, I could have borne it.” My brother, trial does not truly come from an enemy. God stands behind all your trouble. Look past secondary causes to the great First Cause. It is a serious mistake to focus on the human instrument that strikes us and forget the hand that holds the rod. If I strike a dog, he bites the stick. Poor creature, he knows no better. If he could think more clearly, he would either bite me or quietly accept the blow. You must not start biting the stick. It is your heavenly Father who uses it. Whether the rod is made of ebony or thorn, it is in his hand. It is best to stop trying to choose our trials and to leave everything in the hands of infinite wisdom. The heart of my message is this: believer, yield yourself. Lie quietly in God’s hands. Do not struggle. There is no point in struggling. If the great Shearer intends to shear, he will do so. As I said before, when the sheep struggles, it may be cut by the shears. If we struggle against God, we may receive two blows instead of one. In truth, there is not half as much pain in a trial as there is in fighting against it. The Eastern farmer uses a goad to guide the ox. The gentle prod does little harm, but if the ox kicks, it drives the goad into itself and bleeds. So it is with us. It is hard “to kick against the goads” (Acts 26:14, ESV). We suffer more through rebellion than we would if we submitted to the will of God. What good comes from worrying? We cannot make “one hair white or black” (Matthew 5:36, ESV). You who are troubled cannot change the weather by your sighing. Have you ever earned a penny by fretting, or put bread on the table by complaining? Complaining wastes breath, and worrying wastes time. To lie quietly in God’s hand brings blessing to the soul. I wish I were more calm and self-controlled. I long to say continually, “Lord, do what you will, when you will, as you will, with me your servant. Give me honour or dishonour, wealth or poverty, sickness or health, joy or sorrow, and I will gladly receive it from your hand.” A person is not far from the gates of heaven when he is fully submissive to the Lord’s will. You who have been shorn have, I trust, received comfort through the blessed Spirit of God. May God bless you. And may the sinner also humble himself under the mighty hand of God. “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6, ESV). Submit yourselves to God (James 4:7, ESV). Let every thought be brought captive to him (2 Corinthians 10:5, ESV), and may the Lord send his blessing, for Christ’s sake. Amen.

fields.title: In The Hay - Field
fields.body_html:
Introduction Observe how God “causes the grass to grow for the cattle” (Psalm 104:14, ESV). In every blade of grass, He works, sustains, and provides. Let us open our eyes to His care, and respond by trusting Him fully, knowing He nourishes all who depend on Him.

“He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” — Psalm 104:14 (ESV) At the appointed season all the world is busy with gathering the grass crop, and you can scarcely ride a mile in the country without breathing the delicious fragrance of the new-mown hay and hearing the mower's scythe being sharpened. There is a gospel in the hay-field, and that gospel we intend to bring out as we may be enabled by the Holy Spirit.

Our text brings us immediately to the place, and so we need no preface. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle” — three things we shall notice: first, that grass is in itself instructive; secondly, that grass is far more so when God is seen in it; and thirdly, that by the growth of grass for the cattle, the ways of grace may be illustrated.

First, then, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Here we have something that is in itself instructive. Hardly any symbol, apart from water and light, is used more often in Scripture than the grass of the field.

In the first place, the grass may be looked at instructively as a symbol of our mortality. “All flesh is grass.” The whole history of man can be seen in a meadow. He springs up green and tender, subject to the frosts of infancy that threaten his young life; he grows, he comes to maturity, he puts on beauty just as the grass is adorned with flowers; but after a while his strength goes and his beauty becomes wrinkled, just as the grass withers and is followed by a fresh generation that withers in its turn. Like ourselves, the grass ripens only to decay. The sons of men come to maturity in due time, and then decline and wither like the green herb.

Some grass is not left to come to ripeness at all, but the mower’s scythe removes it, just as swift- footed death overtakes the careless children of Adam. “For all flesh is as grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.” — Isaiah 40:6-7 (ESV) This is very humbling, and we often need to be reminded of it, lest we begin to dream of immortality under the stars. We should never walk on the grass without remembering that while the green sod covers our graves, it also reminds us of them, preaching with every blade a sermon about our mortality, of which the text is, “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.”

Second, grass is often used in Scripture as a picture of the wicked. David tells us from his own experience that the righteous man is prone to grow jealous of the wicked when he sees the prosperity of the ungodly. We have seen them spread themselves out like green trees, seemingly fixed and rooted in their places; and when we have smarted under our own troubles, feeling that all day long we have been beaten and disciplined every morning, we have been inclined to ask, “How can this be consistent with the righteous government of God?” We are reminded by the Psalmist that in a short time we shall pass by the place of the wicked, and see that he is not there; we shall carefully look for his place, and see that it is no longer known; for he is soon cut down like grass, and withers like the green herb.

“But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt.

‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’” — Isaiah 57:20-21 (ESV) The grass withers, the flower fades away, and in the same way the glory of those who place their confidence in temporal things and dig for comfort in the treasures of the earth will pass away forever. As the Eastern farmer gathers up the green herb and, despite its former beauty, throws it into the furnace, such shall be your lot, O boastful sinners! Thus the Judge will command his angels, “Bind them in bundles to burn.”

“So these will I destroy with the people, and they will be included in the nethermost parts of the pit, and your name will be forgotten in the grave…” — Psalm 9:17 (ESV) Where now is your merriment? Where now is your confidence? Where now is your pride and your pomp? Where now are your boastings and your loud-mouthed blasphemies?

They are silent forever; for, just as thorns crackle under a pot but are quickly consumed and leave nothing but a handful of ashes, so it will be with the wicked in this life; the fire of God’s wrath shall devour them.

It is more pleasing to remember that grass in Scripture also pictures the elect of God. The wicked are compared to dragons of the wilderness, but God’s own people shall spring up in their place, for it is written, “In the habitation of jackals, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.”

The elect are compared to grass because of their number in the latter days and because of the rapidity of their growth. You remember the passage, “A handful of this [grain] shall become a large cluster, and the large cluster shall become a young plant in the nation.” O that the long- expected day might soon come, when God's people shall no longer be like a lone tuft of grass, but when they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. Grass and willows are two of the fastest growing things we know; so shall a nation be born in a day, and crowds be converted at once. When the Spirit of God is mightily at work in the church, men shall turn to Christ as doves fly to their dove-cotes, so that the astonished church shall exclaim, “Where did these come from?” O that we might live to see the age of gold, the time prophets have foretold, when the company of God’s people shall be countless as blades of grass in the meadows, and grace and truth shall flourish.

How like grass are God’s people for this reason: they are utterly dependent on the influences of heaven. Our fields become dry if spring showers and gentle dew are withheld; and what are our souls without the gracious visitations of the Spirit? Sometimes through severe trials our wounded hearts are like mown grass, and then we have the promise, “He will come down like rain upon the mown grass, like showers that water the earth.” Our sharp troubles have taken away our beauty, and then the Lord visits us and we revive again. Thank God for the old saying, which teaches a gracious truth as well as a true proverb, “Each blade of grass has its own drop of dew.” God is pleased to give his own special mercies to each one of his servants: “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.”

Once again, grass is like the food with which the Lord supplies the needs of his chosen ones. Take the twenty-third Psalm, and you have the image worked out in the sweetest form of pastoral song: “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.”

Just as the sheep has nourishment suited to its nature, and this nourishment is provided in abundance by its shepherd so that it not only feeds but lies down in the midst of the fodder, satisfied with plenty and perfectly at ease, so are the people of God when Jesus Christ leads them into the pastures of the covenant and reveals to them the precious truths upon which their souls are fed.

Beloved, have we not found that promise true, “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined”? My soul has sometimes fed on Christ until I felt I could receive no more, and then I have lain down in the abundance of my God to take my rest, satisfied with his favour and full of the goodness of the Lord.

Thus you see that the grass itself is not without instruction for those who will incline their ear. In the second place, God is seen in the growing of the grass. He is seen first as a worker — “He causes the grass to grow”. He is seen secondly as a caretaker — “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle”.

First, as a worker, God can be seen in every blade of grass if we have eyes to perceive him. The world is blind when it talks about ‘natural laws’ and ‘natural causes’ and forgets that laws cannot operate by themselves, and that so-called natural causes are not causes at all unless the First Cause sets them in motion. The old Romans used to say, God thundered; God rained. We say, it thunders; it rains. What “it”? All such expressions are attempts to avoid the thought of God. We commonly say, “How wonderful are the works of nature!” But what is “nature”? I remember an unbeliever in the street, speaking about nature, being asked by a Christian whether he could define what nature was. He gave no answer. The production of grass is not the result of natural law apart from the actual work of God; mere law would be powerless unless the great Master himself sent the force through the matter that is governed by the law — much like a steam engine that supplies power to all the wheels of a cotton mill. I find rest on the grass as on a royal couch now that I know my God is there at work for his creatures.

Having asked you to see God as a worker, I want you to make use of this — therefore I urge you to see God in everyday things. He makes the grass grow — grass is common. You see it everywhere, yet God is in it. Study it, break it apart; the attributes of God are shown in every single flower of the field and in every green leaf.

In the same way, see God in your everyday experiences — in your daily troubles, your common joys, your regular mercies. Do not say, “I must see a miracle before I see God.” In truth, everything is full of wonder. See God in the bread on your table and the water in your cup. It will be the happiest way to live if in every event you can say, “My Father has done all this.” See God also in small things. The little things of life are often the greatest troubles. A man will hear that his house has burned down more quietly than he will complain when he sees an ill-cooked joint of meat on his table when he expected it to be perfect. It is the little stone in the shoe that makes the pilgrim limp. To see God in small things as well as in the great — to believe that the guidance of every drop of spray when a wave breaks on the rock is under God’s hand, as much as the movement of the mightiest planet in its orbit — all this is true wisdom.

Think also of God working among solitary things; for grass does not grow only where people tend it, but even on the side of the lonely mountain where no traveller has ever been. Where only the eye of a wild bird has seen the green grass and moss, God’s works show their beauty; for God’s works are fair even to eyes other than those of humans. And you, solitary child of God, living unseen and unknown in a remote village — you are not forgotten by the love of heaven. He makes grass grow all alone; shall he not make you flourish despite loneliness? He can develop your graces and prepare you for heaven in solitude and neglect. Grass lies beneath our feet, and nobody thinks of the fact that it is crushed by the foot, yet God makes it grow. Perhaps you are oppressed and worn down, but do not let that depress you, for God executes righteousness for all those who are oppressed: he causes the grass to grow, and he can make your heart flourish under all the pressures and afflictions of life, so that you will still be joyful and holy even if all the world tramples over you, living in the immortal life that God himself gives you, even if hell itself set its heel upon you.

Poor and needy one, unnoticed, oppressed, and trodden down, God makes the grass grow, and he will care for you.

But I said we should see in the text God also as a great caretaker. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Does God take care of oxen? Or is this only for our sake? “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” That shows that God cares for the beasts of the field; but it shows even more: that he wants those who work for him to be fed as they work. God cares for the cattle and makes grass grow for them. Then, my soul, though sometimes you have said with David, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was like a beast before you,” yet God cares for you.

“He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens when they cry.” There you have an example of God’s care for birds, and here we have his care for cattle; and though you, my listener, may see yourself as black and defiled as a raven and as far from anything spiritually good as beasts are, yet take comfort from this text: he gives grass to cattle, and he will give grace to you, though you think yourself to be like a beast before him.

Notice that he cares for these beasts who are helpless in caring for themselves. The cattle cannot plant the grass or cause it to grow. Though they can do nothing in the matter, yet he does it all for them: he causes the grass to grow. You who are as helpless as cattle to help yourselves, who can only stand and groan in misery yet do not know what to do, God can support you with his loving- kindness and favour you with his tenderness. Let the bleating of your prayers go up to heaven; let the meaning of your desires go up to him, and help will come to you though you cannot help yourselves. Beasts are dumb, speechless creatures, yet God makes the grass grow for them. Will he hear those who cannot speak and not hear those who can? Since our God gives careful attention even to the cattle in the field, he will surely have compassion on his own sons and daughters when they desire to seek his face.

There is this also to be said: God not only cares for cattle, but the food he provides for them is suitable—he causes grass to grow for the cattle, exactly the kind of food ruminants need. In the same way, the Lord God provides appropriate sustenance for his people. Depend on him by faith and wait upon him in prayer, and you will receive food suitable for you. You will find in God’s mercy exactly what your nature requires—provisions matched to your unique needs.

This “suitable” food the Lord ensures for the cattle, for no one else eats the cattle’s food. There is grass for them, and nobody else takes it; it is kept for them. In the same way, God has a special provision for his own people: “The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will show them his covenant” — Psalm 25:14 (ESV). Though the grass is technically free for anyone to eat, no creature cares for it except the cattle for which it was prepared. Similarly, though God’s grace is freely offered to all, only the elect pay attention and are prepared to receive it. There is as much reserve of the grass for the cattle as if walls enclosed it; likewise, though God’s grace is free, it is effectively reserved for those he has chosen.

God is seen in the grass as both worker and caretaker. Let us then observe his hand in providence at all times. See it not only when we enjoy abundance, but even when our supplies are scant; for grass is preparing for the cattle even in the depth of winter. And you, sons of sorrow, in your trials and troubles, are still under God’s care; he will accomplish his gracious purposes in you. Be still and witness the salvation of God. Every winter’s night connects directly to the joyous days of mowing and reaping; every season of grief is linked to future joy.

Our third point is most interesting: God’s work in providing grass for the cattle gives us illustrations of his grace.

I reflect on the text and say to myself, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle. Here I see a full provision for that creature. I am also a creature, but nobler than cattle. Surely God will provide for me as well as for them. Yet naturally I feel uneasy: I cannot find what I want in this world. Even if I obtained all its riches, I would still feel discontented; even if I had all my heart could wish of temporal treasures, my soul would remain empty. There must be something somewhere that can satisfy me as a man with an immortal soul. God fully satisfies the ox; he must have something that will fully satisfy me if I receive it. There is the grass; the cattle eat it and then lie down content; all I have found on earth never satisfied me enough to rest fully. Therefore, there must be something that would satisfy me if I could reach it.” Is not this sound reasoning? I ask both Christians and unbelievers to follow me this far.

Let us proceed another step: the cattle not only have the grass provided, but they actually receive it. Why should I not also obtain what I want? My soul hungers and thirsts after something beyond what I can see or hear; there must be something to satisfy my soul. The cattle feed on what satisfies them; why should I not find satisfaction too? I begin to pray, “O Lord, satisfy my soul with good things, and renew my youth like the eagle’s” — Psalm 103:5 (ESV).

While I pray, I reflect: God has provided for cattle what fits their nature—they are flesh, and flesh eats grass. I too am flesh, but also spirit; to satisfy me I need spiritual nourishment. Where is it?

When I turn to God’s Word, I find, “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” — Isaiah 40:8 (ESV), and the words Jesus speaks are “spirit and life” — John 6:63 (ESV).

“Here is spiritual food for my soul,” I say; “I will rejoice in it.” O may God help me understand what that spiritual food is and enable me to receive it; for though God provides grass for cattle, they must eat it themselves. If they refuse, they are not nourished. I must imitate the cattle and receive what God provides for me. What is provided in Scripture? I am told that the Lord Jesus came to suffer, bleed, and die in my place, and if I trust him I shall be saved. Being saved, the thoughts of his love will give me solace and joy, strengthening me. What else have I to do but feed on these truths? The cattle bring nothing to the pasture except their hunger; they enter it and partake. Likewise, by faith I must live upon Christ. Lord, give me grace to feed on him; make me hungry and thirsty for him; give me the faith to receive him, so that I may be satisfied with favour and full of the goodness of the Lord.

Though the text seems small, it grows under meditation. Let me give further illustrations of divine grace. Preventive grace is symbolised here: grass grew before cattle were created. In Genesis we see that God provided grass before he made the cattle. What a mercy that God’s covenant provisions for his people were prepared before they were born! God gave his Son, Jesus Christ, as Saviour for his chosen before Adam fell; long before sin entered the world, God’s everlasting mercy foresaw it and provided a refuge for every elect soul. What comfort to know that before I hunger, God has prepared the manna; before I thirst, God has caused the rock in the wilderness to produce crystal streams to satisfy my soul’s thirst! See what sovereign grace can do! Before the cattle come to pasture, the grass is ready; before I experience my need for mercy, mercy is already prepared for me.

Here is an illustration of free grace: when the ox enters the field, it brings no money. Similarly, I, a poor, needy sinner, bring nothing but receive Christ without money and without cost. “The Lord makes the grass grow for the cattle, and so he provides grace for my needy soul, though I have no money, no merit, no excellence of my own.”

Why does God give grass to the cattle? Because they belong to him. Scripture affirms, “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts, and the cattle on a thousand hills” — Haggai 2:8 (ESV). God provides grass for his cattle; likewise, grace is provided for God’s people.

Every herd of cattle is God’s: long before the farmer brands a bullock, God has marked it; so, long before the fall of Adam, the stamp of electing love was set on our brow: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when none of them as yet existed” — Psalm 139:16 (ESV).

God also feeds cattle because he has entered a covenant with them. “A covenant with cattle?”

someone asks. Indeed: when God spoke to Noah, after the flood, he said, “I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, of the birds, of the livestock, and of every beast of the earth with you” — Genesis 9:9-10 (ESV). Thus a covenant was made with the cattle: seedtime and harvest would not fail; therefore the earth produces for them, and for them the Lord causes the grass to grow. If God keeps his covenant with cattle, will he not keep it with his beloved? Yes, his chosen are covenanted in Christ, and he provides for all their needs in time and eternity, satisfying them out of the fullness of his everlasting love.

God feeds the cattle, and then the cattle praise him. David writes, “Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and frost, stormy wind fulfilling his command! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!” — Psalm 148:7-10 (ESV). The Lord feeds his people so that their glory may praise him, and not be silent. While other creatures give him glory, let the redeemed of the Lord especially proclaim it, those he has delivered from the hand of the enemy.

Yet even now, our text is not exhausted. Consider the grass itself: “He causes the grass to grow”.

Here is a doctrinal lesson: if grass cannot grow without God, how could grace arise in the human heart apart from divine action? Grace is a far more wonderful product of God’s wisdom than grass.

If grass cannot grow without a divine cause, any growth of grace must be traced to God, and all glory must be given to him.

Furthermore, if God deems it worthwhile to make grass and care for it, much more will he honourably cause his grace to grow in our hearts. If the great invisible Spirit, whose thoughts are high and lofty, condescends to watch over that humble growth by the hedge, surely he will oversee his own seed in us, “the incorruptible seed that lives and endures forever” — 1 Peter 1:23 (ESV).

Mungo Park, exploring the deserts of Africa, took comfort from a small piece of moss, seeing God’s wisdom and power even in that lonely patch of green.

Likewise, when you see fields ripe for mowing, your heart should leap with joy at how God has produced the grass, tending it through the winter cold and spring frost until rain and sunshine bring it to perfection. So, my soul, though you endure many frosts of sorrow and long winters of trial, the Lord will cause you to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
fields.body_text: Introduction Observe how God “causes the grass to grow for the cattle” (Psalm 104:14, ESV). In every blade of grass, He works, sustains, and provides. Let us open our eyes to His care, and respond by trusting Him fully, knowing He nourishes all who depend on Him. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” — Psalm 104:14 (ESV) At the appointed season all the world is busy with gathering the grass crop, and you can scarcely ride a mile in the country without breathing the delicious fragrance of the new-mown hay and hearing the mower's scythe being sharpened. There is a gospel in the hay-field, and that gospel we intend to bring out as we may be enabled by the Holy Spirit. Our text brings us immediately to the place, and so we need no preface. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle” — three things we shall notice: first, that grass is in itself instructive; secondly, that grass is far more so when God is seen in it; and thirdly, that by the growth of grass for the cattle, the ways of grace may be illustrated. First, then, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Here we have something that is in itself instructive. Hardly any symbol, apart from water and light, is used more often in Scripture than the grass of the field. In the first place, the grass may be looked at instructively as a symbol of our mortality. “All flesh is grass.” The whole history of man can be seen in a meadow. He springs up green and tender, subject to the frosts of infancy that threaten his young life; he grows, he comes to maturity, he puts on beauty just as the grass is adorned with flowers; but after a while his strength goes and his beauty becomes wrinkled, just as the grass withers and is followed by a fresh generation that withers in its turn. Like ourselves, the grass ripens only to decay. The sons of men come to maturity in due time, and then decline and wither like the green herb. Some grass is not left to come to ripeness at all, but the mower’s scythe removes it, just as swift- footed death overtakes the careless children of Adam. “For all flesh is as grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.” — Isaiah 40:6-7 (ESV) This is very humbling, and we often need to be reminded of it, lest we begin to dream of immortality under the stars. We should never walk on the grass without remembering that while the green sod covers our graves, it also reminds us of them, preaching with every blade a sermon about our mortality, of which the text is, “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.” Second, grass is often used in Scripture as a picture of the wicked. David tells us from his own experience that the righteous man is prone to grow jealous of the wicked when he sees the prosperity of the ungodly. We have seen them spread themselves out like green trees, seemingly fixed and rooted in their places; and when we have smarted under our own troubles, feeling that all day long we have been beaten and disciplined every morning, we have been inclined to ask, “How can this be consistent with the righteous government of God?” We are reminded by the Psalmist that in a short time we shall pass by the place of the wicked, and see that he is not there; we shall carefully look for his place, and see that it is no longer known; for he is soon cut down like grass, and withers like the green herb. “But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt. ‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’” — Isaiah 57:20-21 (ESV) The grass withers, the flower fades away, and in the same way the glory of those who place their confidence in temporal things and dig for comfort in the treasures of the earth will pass away forever. As the Eastern farmer gathers up the green herb and, despite its former beauty, throws it into the furnace, such shall be your lot, O boastful sinners! Thus the Judge will command his angels, “Bind them in bundles to burn.” “So these will I destroy with the people, and they will be included in the nethermost parts of the pit, and your name will be forgotten in the grave…” — Psalm 9:17 (ESV) Where now is your merriment? Where now is your confidence? Where now is your pride and your pomp? Where now are your boastings and your loud-mouthed blasphemies? They are silent forever; for, just as thorns crackle under a pot but are quickly consumed and leave nothing but a handful of ashes, so it will be with the wicked in this life; the fire of God’s wrath shall devour them. It is more pleasing to remember that grass in Scripture also pictures the elect of God. The wicked are compared to dragons of the wilderness, but God’s own people shall spring up in their place, for it is written, “In the habitation of jackals, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.” The elect are compared to grass because of their number in the latter days and because of the rapidity of their growth. You remember the passage, “A handful of this [grain] shall become a large cluster, and the large cluster shall become a young plant in the nation.” O that the long- expected day might soon come, when God's people shall no longer be like a lone tuft of grass, but when they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. Grass and willows are two of the fastest growing things we know; so shall a nation be born in a day, and crowds be converted at once. When the Spirit of God is mightily at work in the church, men shall turn to Christ as doves fly to their dove-cotes, so that the astonished church shall exclaim, “Where did these come from?” O that we might live to see the age of gold, the time prophets have foretold, when the company of God’s people shall be countless as blades of grass in the meadows, and grace and truth shall flourish. How like grass are God’s people for this reason: they are utterly dependent on the influences of heaven. Our fields become dry if spring showers and gentle dew are withheld; and what are our souls without the gracious visitations of the Spirit? Sometimes through severe trials our wounded hearts are like mown grass, and then we have the promise, “He will come down like rain upon the mown grass, like showers that water the earth.” Our sharp troubles have taken away our beauty, and then the Lord visits us and we revive again. Thank God for the old saying, which teaches a gracious truth as well as a true proverb, “Each blade of grass has its own drop of dew.” God is pleased to give his own special mercies to each one of his servants: “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.” Once again, grass is like the food with which the Lord supplies the needs of his chosen ones. Take the twenty-third Psalm, and you have the image worked out in the sweetest form of pastoral song: “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.” Just as the sheep has nourishment suited to its nature, and this nourishment is provided in abundance by its shepherd so that it not only feeds but lies down in the midst of the fodder, satisfied with plenty and perfectly at ease, so are the people of God when Jesus Christ leads them into the pastures of the covenant and reveals to them the precious truths upon which their souls are fed. Beloved, have we not found that promise true, “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined”? Consider the grass itself: “He causes the grass to grow”. Here is a doctrinal lesson: if grass cannot grow without God, how could grace arise in the human heart apart from divine action? Grace is a far more wonderful product of God’s wisdom than grass. If grass cannot grow without a divine cause, any growth of grace must be traced to God, and all glory must be given to him. Furthermore, if God deems it worthwhile to make grass and care for it, much more will he honourably cause his grace to grow in our hearts. If the great invisible Spirit, whose thoughts are high and lofty, condescends to watch over that humble growth by the hedge, surely he will oversee his own seed in us, “the incorruptible seed that lives and endures forever” — 1 Peter 1:23 (ESV). Mungo Park, exploring the deserts of Africa, took comfort from a small piece of moss, seeing God’s wisdom and power even in that lonely patch of green. Likewise, when you see fields ripe for mowing, your heart should leap with joy at how God has produced the grass, tending it through the winter cold and spring frost until rain and sunshine bring it to perfection. So, my soul, though you endure many frosts of sorrow and long winters of trial, the Lord will cause you to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

fields.title: The Joy Of Harvest
fields.body_html:
Harvest reminds us of God’s faithfulness, provision, and the joy of reaping what He has sown in our lives. Let us open our hearts, rejoice in His blessings, and share the gospel, bearing fruit for His glory.

"They rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest" — Isaiah 9:3 (ESV) The other day I kept the feast with a company who shouted "Harvest Home." I was glad to see the rich and poor rejoicing together; and when the cheerful meal was ended, I was glad to turn one of the tables into a pulpit, and in the large barn to preach the gospel of the ever-blessed God to an earnest audience. My heart was merry in harmony with the occasion, and I shall now keep in the same key, and talk to you a little upon the joy of harvest. Londoners forget that it is harvest time; living in this great desert of dingy bricks we hardly know what a wheat-ear is like, except as we see it dry and white in the window of a corn dealer's shop; yet let us all remember that there is such a season as harvest, when by God's goodness the fruits of the earth are gathered in.

What is the joy of harvest which is here taken as the simile of the joy of the saints before God? I am afraid that to the mere selfish order of spirits the joy of harvest is simply that of personal gratification at the increase of wealth. Sometimes the farmer only rejoices because he sees the reward of his toils, and is so much the richer man. I hope that with many there mingles the second cause of joy; namely, gratitude to God that an abundant harvest will give bread to the poor, and remove complaining from our streets. There is a lawful joy in harvest, no doubt, to the man who is enriched by it; for any man who works hard has a right to rejoice when at last he gains his desire.

It would be well if men would always recollect that their last and greatest harvest will be to them according to their labor. He who sows to his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.

A young man commences life by sowing what he calls his wild oats, which he had better never have sown, for they will bring him a terrible harvest. He expects that from these wild oats he will gather a harvest of true pleasure, but it cannot be; the truest pleasures of life spring from the good seed of righteousness, and not from the hemlock of sin. As a man who sows thistles in his furrows must not expect to reap the golden wheatsheaf, so he who follows the ways of vice must not expect happiness.

On the contrary, they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. When a sinner feels the pangs of conscience he may well say, "This is what I sowed." When he shall at last receive the punishment of his evil deeds he will blame no one but himself; he sowed tares and he must reap tares. On the other hand, the Christian man, though his salvation is not of works, but of grace, will have a gracious reward given to him by his Master. He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him. The joy of harvest in part consists of the reward of labor; may such be our joy in serving the Lord.

The joy of harvest has another element in it, namely, that of gratitude to God for favors bestowed.

We are singularly dependent on God; far more so than most of us imagine. When the children of Israel were in the wilderness they went forth every morning and gathered the manna. Our manna does not come to us every morning, but it comes once a year. It is as much a heavenly supply as if it lay like a hoarfrost round about the camp. If we went out into the field and gathered food which dropped from the clouds we should think it a great miracle; and is it not as great a marvel that our bread should come up from the earth as that it should come down from the sky? The same God who bade the heavens drop with angels' food bids the dull earth in its due season yield corn for mankind. Therefore whenever we find that harvest comes, let us be grateful to God, and let us not suffer the season to pass over without psalms of thanksgiving. I believe I shall be correct if I say that there is never in the world, as a rule, more than sixteen months' supply of food; that is to say, when the harvest is gathered in, there may be sixteen months' supply; but at the time of harvest there is not usually enough wheat in the whole world to last the population more than four or five months; so that if the harvest did not come we should be on the verge of famine. We live still from hand to mouth. Let us pause and bless God, and let the joy of harvest be the joy of gratitude.

To the Christian it should be great joy, by means of the harvest, to receive an assurance of God's faithfulness. The Lord has promised that while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, shall not cease. and when you see the loaded wain carrying in the crop you may say to yourself, "God is true to his promise.

Despite the dreary winter and the damp spring, autumn has come with its golden grain." Depend upon it, that as the Lord keeps this promise he will keep all the rest. All his promises are yea and amen in Christ Jesus; if he keeps his covenant to the earth, much more will he keep his covenant with his own people, whom he hath loved with an everlasting love. Go, Christian, to the mercy- seat with the promise on your lip and plead it. Be assured it is not a dead letter. Let not unbelief cause you to stammer when you mention the promise before the throne, but say it boldly—"Fulfil this word unto thy servant on which thou hast caused me to hope." Shame upon us that we so little believe our God. The world is full of proofs of his goodness. Every rising sun, every falling shower, every revolving season certifies his faithfulness. Wherefore do we doubt him? If we never doubt him till we have cause for it we shall never know distrust again. Encouraged by the return of harvest, let us resolve in the strength of the Spirit of God that we will not waver, but will believe in the divine word and rejoice in it.

Once more. To the Christian, in the joy of harvest there will always be the joy of expectation. As there is a harvest to the husbandman for which he waits patiently, so there is a harvest for all faithful waiters who are looking for the coming and the appearing of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The mature Christian, like the ripe ear of corn, hangs down his head with holy humility.

When he was but green in the things of God he stood erect and was somewhat boastful, but now that he has become full of the blessing of the Lord he is humbled thereby, and bows himself down; he is waiting for the sickle, and he dreads it not, for no common reaper shall come to gather Christ's people—he himself shall reap the harvest of the world.

The Lord leaves the destroying angel to reap the vintage and to cast it into the wine-vat to be trodden with vengeance; but as for the grain which he himself has sown, he will gather it himself with his own golden sickle. We are looking for this. We are growing among the tares, and sometimes we are half afraid lest the tares should be stronger than ourselves and choke the wheat; but we shall be separated by-and-by, and when the corn is well winnowed and stored in the garner, we shall be there. It is this expectation which even now makes our hearts throb with joy. We have gone to the grave with precious sheaves that belonged to our Master, and when we were there we thought we could almost say, "Lord, if they sleep they shall do well. Let us die with them." Our joy of harvest is the hope of being at rest with all the saints, and forever with the Lord.

A view of these shadowy harvests upon earth should make us exceedingly glad, because they are the image and foreshadowing of the eternal harvest above.

So much about the joy of harvest; but I hasten onward. What joys are those which to the believer are as the joy of harvest? It is a common notion that Christians are an unhappy people. It is true that we are tried, but it is false that we are miserable. With all their trials, believers have such a compensation in the love of Christ that they are still a blessed generation, and it may be said of them, "Happy art thou, O Israel."

One of the first seasons in which we knew a joy equal to the joy of harvest—a season which has continued with us ever since it commenced—was when we found the Saviour, and so obtained salvation. You recollect for yourselves, brethren and sisters, the time of the ploughing of your souls. My heart was fallow, and covered with weeds; but on a certain day the great Husbandman came and began to plough my soul. Ten black horses were his team, and it was a sharp ploughshare that he used, and the ploughers made deep furrows. The ten commandments were those black horses, and the justice of God, like a ploughshare, tore my spirit. I was condemned, undone, destroyed, lost, helpless, hopeless—I thought hell was before me. Then there came a cross ploughing, for when I went to hear the gospel it did not comfort me; it made me wish I had a part in it, but I feared that such a boon was out of the question.

The choicest promises of God frowned at me, and his threatenings thundered at me. I prayed, but found no answer of peace. It was long with me thus. After the ploughing came the sowing. God who ploughed the heart made it conscious that it needed the gospel, and the gospel seed was joyfully received. Do you recollect that auspicious day when at last you began to have some little hope? It was very little—like a green blade that peeps up from the soil; you scarce knew whether it was grass or corn, whether it was presumption or true faith. It was a little hope, but it grew very pleasantly. Alas, a frost of doubt came; snow of fear fell; cold winds of despondency blew on you, and you said, "There can be no hope for me." But what a glorious day was that when at last the wheat which God had sown ripened, and you could say, "I have looked to him and have been lightened; I have laid my sins on Jesus, where God laid them of old, and they are taken away, and I am saved." I remember well that day, and so no doubt do many of you. O sirs! no husbandman ever shouted for joy as our heart shouted when a precious Christ was ours, and we could grasp him with full assurance of salvation in him.

Many days have passed since then, but the joy of it is still fresh with us. And, blessed be God, it is not the joy of the first day only that we look back upon; it is the joy of every day since then, more or less; for our joy no man taketh from us; still we are walking in Christ, even as we received him.

Even now all our hope on him is stayed, all our help from him we bring; and our joy and peace continue with us because they are based upon an immovable foundation. We rejoice in the Lord, yea, and we will rejoice.

The joy of harvest generally shows itself by the farmer giving a feast to his friends and neighbors; and, usually, those who find Christ express their joy by telling their friends and their neighbors how great things the Lord hath done for them. The grace of God is communicative. A man cannot be saved, and always hold his tongue about it; as well look for dumb choirs in heaven as for a silent church on earth. If a man has been thirsty, and has come to the living stream, his first impulse will be to cry, "Ho! everyone that thirsts!" Do you feel the joy of harvest, the joy that makes you wish that others should share with you? If so, do not repress the impulse to proclaim your happiness. Speak of Christ to brothers and sisters, to friends and kinsfolk; and, if the language be stammering, the message in itself is so important that the words in which you couch it will be a secondary consideration. Tell it, tell it out far and wide—that there is a Saviour, that you have found him, and that his blood can wash away transgression. Tell it everywhere; and so the joy of harvest shall spread o'er land and sea, and God shall be glorified.

We have another joy which is like the joy of harvest. We frequently have it, too. It is the joy of answered prayer. I hope you know what it is to pray in faith. Some prayer is not worth the words used in presenting it, because there is no faith mixed with it. “With all your sacrifices you shall offer salt”, and the salt of faith is needful if we would have our sacrifices accepted. Those who are familiar with the mercy-seat know that prayer is a reality, and that the doctrine of divine answers to prayer is no fiction. Sometimes God will delay to answer for wise reasons; then his children must cry, and cry, and cry again. They are in the condition of the husbandman who must wait for the precious fruits of the earth; and when at last the answer to prayer comes, they are then in the husbandman's position when he receives the harvest. Remember Hannah's wail and Hannah's word. In the bitterness of her soul she cried to God, and when her child was given to her she called him "Samuel," meaning, "Asked of God;" “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him.” 1 Samuel 1:27.

He was a dear child to her, because he was a child of prayer. Any mercy that comes to you in answer to prayer will be your Samuel mercy, your darling mercy. You will say of it, "For this mercy I prayed," and it will bring the joy of harvest to your spirit.

We have another joy of harvest in ourselves when we conquer a temptation. We know what it is to get under a cloud sometimes; sin within us rises with a darkening force, or an external adversity beclouds us, and we miss the plain path we were accustomed to walk in. A child of God at such times will cry mightily for help; for he is fearful of himself and fearful of his surroundings. Some of God's people have been by the week and month together exposed to the double temptation, from without and from within, and have cried to God in bitter anguish. It is a very hard struggle; the sinful action has been painted in very fascinating colors, and the siren voice of temptation has almost enchanted them. But when at last they have got through the valley of the shadow of death without having slipped with their feet; when, after all, they have not been destroyed by Apollyon, but have come forth again into the daylight, they feel a joy unspeakable, compared with which the joy of harvest is mere childish merriment. Those know deep joy who have felt bitter sorrow. As the man feels that he is the stronger for the conflict, as he feels that he has gathered experience and stronger faith from having passed through the trial, he lifts up his heart, and rejoices, not in himself, but before his God, with the joy of harvest. Brethren beloved, you know what that means.

Again, there is such a thing as the joy of harvest when we have been rendered useful. The master passion of every Christian is to be useful. There should be a burning zeal within us for the glory of God. When the man who desires to be useful has laid his plans and set about his work, he begins to look out for the results; but perhaps it will be weeks, or years, before results will come. The worker is not to be blamed that there are no fruits as yet, but he is to be blamed if he is content to be without fruits.

A preacher may preach without conversions, and who shall blame him? but if he be happy, who shall excuse him? It is ours to break our own hearts if we cannot by God's grace break other men's hearts, if others will not weep for their sins it should be our constant habit to weep for them. When the heart becomes earnest, warm, zealous, God usually gives a measure of success, some fiftyfold, some a hundredfold. When the success comes it is the joy of harvest indeed. I cannot help being egotistical enough to mention the joy I felt when first I heard that a soul had found peace through my youthful ministry.

I had been preaching in a village some few Sabbaths with an increasing congregation, but I had not heard of a conversion, and I thought, "Perhaps I am not called of God. He does not mean me to preach, for if he did he would give me spiritual children." One Sabbath my good deacon said, "Don't be discouraged. A poor woman was savingly impressed last Sabbath." How long do you suppose it was before I saw that woman? It was just as long as it took me to reach her cottage. I was eager to hear from her own lips whether it was a work of God's grace or not. I always looked upon her with interest, though only a poor laborer's wife, till she was taken away to heaven, after having lived a holy life.

Since then have I rejoiced over in the Lord, but that first seal to my ministry was peculiarly dear to me. It gave me a sip of the joy of harvest. If somebody had left me a fortune it would not have caused me one-hundredth part of the delight I had in discovering that a soul had been led to the Saviour. I am sure Christian people who have not this joy have missed one of the choicest delights that a believer can know this side heaven. In fact, when I see souls saved, I do not envy Gabriel his throne nor the angels their harps. It shall be our heaven to be out of heaven for a season if we can but bring others to know the Saviour and so add fresh jewels to the Redeemer's crown.

I will mention another delight which is like the joy of harvest, and that is fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. This is not so much something to talk about as something to experience and enjoy. If we try to describe what communion with Christ is, we fail. Solomon, the wisest of men, when inspired to write about the fellowship of the church with her Lord, had to use allegories and symbolic language, and though to a spiritual mind the Song of Solomon is always delightful, to a worldly mind it seems just like a love poem. The natural person does not accept the things of God, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 Corinthians 2:14 But oh, the happiness of knowing that Christ is yours, and of being close to him. To touch his side and put your finger in the mark of the nails; these are not everyday joys. But when such close and personal communion comes to us on our special days, it lifts our souls like the chariots of Amminadab, or, if you like, it allows us to walk over the world and all that it calls great or valuable.

Our circumstances mean nothing if Christ is with us—he is our God, our comfort, and our everything, and we rejoice before him like we rejoice at harvest.

I do not have time to go into more detail, because I want to end with one practical word. Many of us are eagerly longing for a harvest that would bring us intense joy. Lately, several people have shared with me how deeply they feel compassion for the souls of people. Others of us have felt a mysterious push to pray more than we ever have, and to care more than we ever did that Christ would save those who are perishing. We will not be satisfied until there is a thorough spiritual awakening in this land. We did not create this feeling ourselves, and we do not want to suppress it. We do not believe it can be suppressed; and others will feel the same heavenly concern, and will sigh and cry to God day and night until the blessing comes. This is the sowing, this is the ploughing, this is the harrowing—may it continue until the harvest. I long to hear my brothers and sisters everywhere saying, "We are full of anguish; we are in agony until souls are saved." The cry of Rachel, "Give me children, or I die," is the cry of your minister today, and the longing of thousands more. As that desire grows stronger, a revival approaches. We must have spiritual children for Christ, or our hearts will break because of our longing for their salvation. Oh, for more of these longings, yearnings, cravings, and efforts! If we pray until the harvest of revival comes, we will share in its joy.

Who will have the most joy? Those who have been most concerned about it. Those of you who do not pray in private, and who do not come to prayer meetings, will not have joy when the blessing comes and the church grows. You had no part in the sowing, so you will have little part in the harvest. Those who never speak to others about their souls, who do not participate in Sunday school or mission work, but just enjoy the blessings—they will have none of the joy of harvest, because they do not work for the Lord. And who would want lazy people to be happy? Instead, in our zeal and care, we feel like saying, "Curse Meroz; curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty." — Judges 5:23 (ESV) If you come to help the Lord by his Spirit, you will share the joy of harvest. Perhaps no one will have more joy than those who see their loved ones brought to God. Some of you have children who are a trial to you whenever you think of them; let them be a trial that drives you to constant prayer for them, and if the blessing comes, why should it not come to them? If a revival happens, why should your daughter not be converted, why should your wild son not be saved, or even your grey-headed father, who has been sceptical and unbelieving—why should God’s grace not reach him? And oh, what joy you will have then!

What happiness will fill your spirit when you see those related to you united with Christ your Lord!

Pray earnestly for them, and you will yet experience the joy of harvest in your own home, a shout of harvest home in your own family.

Perhaps, my listener, you have little to do with this joy because you are unsaved. Yet it is a wonderful thing for an unconverted person to be under a ministry blessed by God, and among people who pray for conversions. It is a blessing for you, young man, to have a Christian mother.

It is a great blessing for you, O unconverted woman, to have a godly sister. These give us hope for you. While your relatives are praying, we are hopeful for you. May the Lord Jesus be yours yet.

But, oh, if you remain unbelieving, however rich a blessing comes to others, it will not benefit you. "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land." — Isaiah 1:19 (ESV) But some may cry in sorrow, "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." — Jeremiah 8:20 (ESV) It has been observed that those who pass through a revival and remain unconverted often become more hardened than before. I believe it, and I therefore pray that the Spirit of God comes with such power that none escape his influence.

May you pray: "Pass me not, O mighty Spirit!

You can make the blind to see; Witness of Jesus’ merit, Speak the word of power to me, Even me."

"Have I long been sleeping in sin, Long been ignoring and grieving you?

Has the world kept my heart?

Oh forgive and rescue me, Even me."

Oh, for earnest, persistent prayer from all believers around the world! If our churches were stirred to continuous, intense prayer, giving God no rest until he makes Zion a praise on earth, we might see God’s kingdom come and the power of Satan broken.

As many of you love Christ, I urge you by his name to pray earnestly; as many of you love the Church and desire her growth, I beg you not to hold back in this time of prayer. May the Lord lead you to pray until the joy of harvest is granted. Do you remember me saying one Sabbath, "The Lord will treat you as you treat his work during this next month"? I feel it will be true for many— that the Lord will treat you as you treat his Church. If you sow little, you will reap little; if you pray little, you will receive little favour. But if you act with zeal and faith, and pray and work much for the Lord, good measure, pressed down and overflowing, will be returned to you. If you water others with drops, you will receive drops; but if the Spirit helps you to pour rivers of living water from your soul, floods of heavenly grace will flow into your spirit. May God bring in the unconverted, and lead them to simple trust in Jesus; then they too will know the joy of harvest. We ask it in his name. Amen.

It is true that we are tried, but it is false that we are miserable. With all their trials, believers have such a compensation in the love of Christ that they are still a blessed generation, and it may be said of them, "Happy art thou, O Israel." One of the first seasons in which we knew a joy equal to the joy of harvest—a season which has continued with us ever since it commenced—was when we found the Saviour, and so obtained salvation. You recollect for yourselves, brethren and sisters, the time of the ploughing of your souls. My heart was fallow, and covered with weeds; but on a certain day the great Husbandman came and began to plough my soul. Ten black horses were his team, and it was a sharp ploughshare that he used, and the ploughers made deep furrows. The ten commandments were those black horses, and the justice of God, like a ploughshare, tore my spirit. I was condemned, undone, destroyed, lost, helpless, hopeless—I thought hell was before me. Then there came a cross ploughing, for when I went to hear the gospel it did not comfort me; it made me wish I had a part in it, but I feared that such a boon was out of the question. The choicest promises of God frowned at me, and his threatenings thundered at me. I prayed, but found no answer of peace. It was long with me thus. After the ploughing came the sowing. God who ploughed the heart made it conscious that it needed the gospel, and the gospel seed was joyfully received. Do you recollect that auspicious day when at last you began to have some little hope? It was very little—like a green blade that peeps up from the soil; you scarce knew whether it was grass or corn, whether it was presumption or true faith.
